That pairing of prohibition and forbearance reflects the sūrah's broader pattern of setting limits — *ḥudūd* — and then showing the path back for those who crossed them before the limit was drawn. The sūrah has already linked limits to Gardens and Fire (4:13–14) and defined soon repentance versus delayed words at death (4:17–18); here it applies that pattern to family formation: the limit is now clear, the past is pardoned where it was done without that clarity, and persistence after clarity changes the moral status entirely.

**Honouring the Father Without Inheriting the Woman**

The prohibition complements the earlier verse that forbade inheriting women against their will (4:19): there the practice was to inherit widows as part of the estate; here the specific form is the son taking the father's widow. Both practices share the same error — treating a woman as transferable property rather than as a rights-bearing person who has her own obligatory share (4:7, 4:12), her own dowry (4:4), and her own choice. The sūrah's opening — *be mindful of your Lord who created you from a single soul, and from it its mate* (4:1) — already frames women as the mate from the single soul, not an item to be passed. The prohibition therefore does more than regulate marriage; it rehumanises the widow at the moment when custom had depersonalised her: she is not to be claimed by a son, not to be blocked from remarriage, and not to be priced. Her future is to be decided by her own consent within the lawful degrees that follow, where her choice is respected and her dowry is again secured.

**A Shameless Path That Leaves No Good Behind**

The final phrase *sāʾa sabīlā* — evil way — warns that allowing this path harms more than the two persons involved: a way — *sabīl* — is a beaten track; once opened, others follow. If sons could marry fathers' widows, households would become sites of expectation and rivalry while the father lived, and of dispute and coercion after he died. The sūrah's later command to appoint mediators from both families when a split is feared (4:35) assumes families can mediate because roles are clear; a practice that confuses father and son destroys that clarity. By naming the practice *fāḥishah*, *maqt*, and evil way, the verse makes its rejection a matter of taste as well as law: the believer is asked not only to obey a rule but to feel dislike for what God calls hateful. That dislike, once learned, steadies the longer list of prohibitions that follows — if the son's claim to his father's wife is hateful, then the other forms of overreaching with women — seizing dowries, harassing wives to ransom themselves, the list of forbidden marriages — will be recognised as part of the same wrong and left behind as well.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:23

> ˹Also˺ forbidden to you for marriage are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal and maternal aunts, your brother's daughters, your sister's daughters, your foster-mothers, your foster-sisters, your mothers-in-law, your stepdaughters under your guardianship if you have consummated marriage with their mothers—but if you have not, then you can marry them—nor the wives of your own sons, nor two sisters together at the same time—except what was done previously. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**A List That Defines the Family**

This verse gathers the core of the prohibited degrees — *al-muḥarramāt* — into one place: mothers, daughters, sisters, paternal and maternal aunts, brother's and sister's daughters, foster-mothers and foster-sisters, mothers-in-law, stepdaughters under guardianship where the mother's marriage was consummated, sons' wives, and two sisters together. The previous verse singled out the father's former wife as a distinct prohibition with three condemnations (4:22); this verse completes the circle. The list is not random: it moves outward from the closest ties — parents and children — to the extended family, then to ties created by nursing and marriage, then to the temporal bar of combining sisters. By naming each degree, the Qur'an removes ambiguity in a context where lineage and inheritance had been blurred, giving the new community a clear map of who is permanently outside the choice for marriage.

**Blood, Nursing, and Marriage as Three Kinds of Tie**

The prohibitions rest on three distinct bonds, each treated as creating a sanctity. Blood ties — mothers, daughters, sisters, aunts, nieces — are inviolable because they share a common lineage that marriage would confuse; the sūrah has already rooted humanity in a single soul and its mate (4:1) and built inheritance on that lineage (4:7, 4:11–12). Nursing ties — foster-mothers and foster-sisters — are treated like blood ties, as Prophetic teaching clarified that nursing creates the same prohibitions as birth, so that a foster relationship is not a metaphor but a legal kinship. Marriage ties — mothers-in-law, stepdaughters, sons' wives — become prohibitions through the covenant itself. The verse adds a condition for stepdaughters: *allātī fī ḥujūrikum min nisāʾikum allātī dakhaltum bihinna* — those under your guardianship if you have consummated marriage with their mothers; if consummation has not occurred, the bar does not apply. That condition was noted as precise mercy: the prohibition attaches where intimacy has already joined households, not where a contract was made but not completed. The same precision applies to the bar on combining two sisters — it forbids having both as wives at the same time, while after death or divorce the other sister becomes permissible, protecting the bond between sisters from rivalry in one home.

**Why Each Mention Matters**

Each name in the list answers a real temptation or custom. Marrying a daughter or a sister was already seen as foul, but the explicit naming removes any claim that near kin could be chosen for advantage. Aunts and nieces were sometimes married for alliance; the verse closes that path to keep the extended family as a space of protection rather than competition. Foster ties mattered in a society where nursing by another woman created lasting family-like bonds; treating those bonds as marriage bars honours the nurture that was given. Mothers-in-law, stepdaughters, and sons' wives protect the household that has already been joined: a man who marries a woman does not then marry her mother; a son's wife is not to be claimed by his father, just as a father's former wife is not to be claimed by his son (4:22). Two sisters together are barred because sisterhood would be turned into co-wife rivalry, which the verse spares. The sūrah has repeatedly told the community to live with women fairly (4:19) and to speak kindly at wealth division (4:8); these bars are the structure that makes that fairness possible, by keeping roles distinct.

**Except What Was Done Previously — and All-Forgiving, Most Merciful**

The exception *illā mā qad salaf* — except what was done previously — appears here for the bar on combining two sisters, as it did for the father's former wife (4:22). It functions as clemency for marriages contracted before revelation, requiring separation where the bar now applies but not imposing retroactive worldly punishment for what was done without the light of the new limit. The closing *inna Allāha kāna ghafūran raḥīmā* — surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — gives the reason that correction is met with forgiveness when it is accepted. The sūrah uses the same pairing after defining repentance that must be soon (4:17) and after the command to lighten burdens (4:28); here it tells families that have to untangle prior marriages that the path back is mercy, not humiliation. That mercy does not reopen the prohibited degree; it forgives the past while holding the limit firm for the future. The pattern matches the sūrah's treatment of limits elsewhere (4:13–14): the limit is clear, crossing it deliberately has consequence, but turning back when the limit becomes clear is met with pardon.

**Marriage Within Limits, Not Without**

The verse does not only forbid; it implies what remains lawful. The next verse will note that beyond the named degrees marriage remains open when sought through proper dowry and chaste intent (4:24), confirming that outside the barred list the field is lawful when approached in the right way. That framing matters because the list could be read as restriction alone, while the Qur'an presents it as clarification that makes the lawful field safe to enter: a community that knows who is permanently outside choice can choose inside the lawful field without confusion about lineage — which the inheritance laws depend on — and without rivalry between mothers and daughters, sisters, or foster kin. The sūrah's earlier training in handling wealth as a trust (4:2, 4:5–6) finds a parallel here in handling persons as trusts: just as wealth has fixed shares and guarded handovers, family has fixed bars and guarded entrances. Both guards come from the same source — the One described as All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:11, 4:26), who knows which ties, if crossed by marriage, would injure the household, and who is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful when the community realigns its marriages to the map He has drawn.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:24

> Also ˹forbidden are˺ married women—except ˹female˺ captives in your possession. This is Allah's commandment to you. Lawful to you are all beyond these—as long as you seek them with your wealth in a legal marriage, not in fornication. Give those you have consummated marriage with their due dowries. It is permissible to be mutually gracious regarding the set dowry. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**The Married Woman Is Not Available**

The verse begins by completing the list of forbidden degrees: *wa al-muḥṣanātu min al-nisāʾ illā mā malakat aymānukum* — also forbidden are married women, except female captives in your possession. *Muḥṣanāt* here was read as women protected by marriage, whose bond is not to be breached: the general rule is that a woman under a valid marriage is outside the field of choice until that marriage ends by death, divorce, or annulment. The exception for female captives — *mā malakat aymānukum* — addressed a specific seventh-century circumstance where captives whose previous marriages were regarded as dissolved by captivity entered the household under distinct rules; early authorities detailed conditions, waiting periods, and consent considerations that tightly regulated that category, and the Qur'an elsewhere encourages freeing slaves and marrying them as free believers (4:25), showing the direction of the law toward liberty. The phrase *kitāba Allāhi ʿalaykum* — this is Allah's commandment to you, literally Allah's writing upon you — marks the entire roster from the father's former wife (4:22) through this verse as inscribed law, not advice: to treat a married woman as available is not a private indiscretion but a breach of an inscribed bar.

**Lawful Beyond These, Sought in the Right Way**

The verse then opens the lawful field: *wa uḥilla lakum mā warāʾa dhālikum an tabtaghū bi amwālikum muḥṣinīna ghayra musāfiḥīn* — lawful to you are all beyond these, as long as you seek them with your wealth in a legal marriage, not in fornication. Two conditions define the lawful path. First, it is sought *with your wealth* — *bi amwālikum* — meaning through dowry and maintenance, the same wealth the sūrah has taught to guard as a standing support (4:5) and to give graciously as *ṣaduqah* with *niḥlah* (4:4): marriage is a commitment of provision, not a seizure. Second, it is as *muḥṣinīna* — seeking chastity, protection — not as *musāfiḥīn* — fornicators who pour out desire without bond. The contrast *muḥṣin / musāfiḥ* frames marriage as the shelter for desire rather than its mere outlet; the sūrah repeats that shelter language for those who marry believing bondwomen, requiring chastity and avoidance of secret affairs (4:25). Here the same standard applies to all: the wealth is spent to build a lawful, protective tie, and the act is chaste. That pairing of wealth and chastity keeps the law from becoming a list of names alone; it makes the method of seeking part of lawfulness.

**Give Those You Have Consummated Marriage With Their Due Dowries**

The command *fa mā istamtaʿtum bihi minhunna fa ātūhunna ujūrahunna farīḍah* — give those you have consummated marriage with their due dowries — restates the dowry as an obligation, *farīḍah*. The word *istimtāʿ* — enjoyment, consummation — refers to the completion of marriage's intimacy, the same *ifḍāʾ* that the sūrah called the context of a firm commitment (4:21). Once that stage is reached, the dowry is not a promise to be debated but a portion due. The Qur'an already secured the dowry as the woman's gracious gift (4:4) and forbade reclaiming even a heap when wishing to replace a wife (4:20–21); here it secures the dowry again at the point where the lawful field is opened, so that opening is not mistaken for licence to seek without commitment. The dowry is not a fee for access; it is the sign of seriousness — *ṣaduqah* — that makes the shelter real. The sūrah has guarded that sign at entry, during marriage, and at replacement; this verse guards it at consummation, marking the moment when the obligation hardens. The insistence on *farīḍah* also explains why the verse repeats what was said before: the rule needs to be present wherever marriage is sought, including where new lawful matches are being considered.

**Mutual Graciousness Regarding the Set Dowry**

The allowance *wa lā junāḥa ʿalaykum fīmā tarāḍaytum bihi min baʿdi al-farīḍah* — it is permissible to be mutually gracious regarding the set dowry — adds flexibility after the obligation is fixed. Spouses may, by mutual content, adjust what was set — increase, decrease, remit a portion, or defer — so long as the adjustment is with genuine willingness. The same standard of *ṭīb al-nafs* — a contented soul — that governed the wife's remission earlier (4:4) governs here as mutual consent — *tarāḍī*. Jurists noted that this permission does not allow coercion to reduce the dowry, nor does it allow a guardian to waive what belongs to the woman without her leave; it allows what a free, unpressured agreement allows. That balance reflects the sūrah's broader ethic where wealth moves by right and by kindness together: strictly by obligation where the right is fixed, gently by consent where discretion remains. The dowry therefore has two aspects — the fixed portion due upon consummation, and the human space around it where generosity can flow either way without harm.

**All-Knowing, All-Wise at the Gate of the Lawful**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna ʿAlīman Ḥakīmā* — surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise — appears where the entire list of prohibitions ends and the lawful field is opened; the pairing matches its use after the inheritance shares (4:11) and after the promise to make things clear (4:26). Knowledge covers every degree that, if crossed, would injure lineage and affection; wisdom explains why marriage is tied to wealth spent in chastity rather than to wealth spent for display. The Name *ʿAlīm* also watches the private adjustments to the set dowry, where mutual graciousness could be genuine or pressured, while *Ḥakīm* places that watch inside wisdom that seeks to protect the shelter marriage is meant to be. The sūrah will immediately follow with guidance for those who cannot afford a free believing wife and may marry a believing bondwoman with permission and fair dowry (4:25), showing that the same Two Names govern the easier path as well. The command written upon the community — *kitāba Allāhi ʿalaykum* — is therefore not a hard wall alone; it is a gate whose bars are known and whose opening beyond the bars is lawful when sought with wealth, with chastity, and with the woman's due given as an obligation that may then be softened only by true mutual grace.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:25

> But if any of you cannot afford to marry a free believing woman, then ˹let him marry˺ a believing bondwoman possessed by one of you. Allah knows best ˹the state of˺ your faith ˹and theirs˺. You are from one another. So marry them with the permission of their owners, giving them their dowry in fairness, if they are chaste, neither promiscuous nor having secret affairs. If they commit indecency after marriage, they receive half the punishment of free women. This is for those of you who fear falling into sin. But if you are patient, it is better for you. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**A Lawful Path When Means Are Limited**

This verse opens a second door for those who cannot reach the first: *wa man lam yastaṭiʿ minkum ṭawlan an yankiḥa al-muḥṣanāt al-muʾmināt fa mimmā malakat aymānukum min fatayātikumu al-muʾmināt* — but if any of you cannot afford to marry a free believing woman, then let him marry a believing bondwoman possessed by one of you. *Ṭawl* — means, capacity — was read as wealth to pay the dowry and provide maintenance for a free wife. The verse does not command such a marriage; it permits it, as a mercy for those who lack means and fear falling into unlawful intercourse. The sūrah has already limited polygamy to four and tied it to justice (4:3), listed the prohibited degrees (4:22–23), and described lawful seeking as spending wealth in chastity (4:24); here it acknowledges that lawful spending may be beyond some, and provides a path that still meets the sūrah's core requirements: faith, permission, dowry, and chastity. The Qur'an elsewhere encourages freeing slaves as an act of piety and as expiation, and this permission sits inside that larger movement toward liberty, where the bondwoman is not a casual liaison but a wife entered through covenant, with a named owner's permission and a known gift.

**You Are From One Another**

The phrase *wa Allāhu aʿlamu bi īmānikum baʿḍukum min baʿḍ* — Allah knows best the state of your faith, and yours; you are from one another — addresses the social barrier that might have kept such marriages from happening. In a society where free and enslaved carried different rank, the Qur'an equalises by faith and by origin: *baʿḍukum min baʿḍ* — you are from one another — recalls the single soul from which all were spread (4:1) and tells the suitor that the bondwoman who believes shares his humanity and his covenant. Faith is the measure God knows best — not the outward rank that people see. That line also explains why the verse specifies *believing* bondwomen as the permitted choice when means fail for a free believing woman: the common faith is the tie that makes marriage meaningful as a shelter — *muḥṣin* — rather than a mere arrangement. Elsewhere the Qur'an says *a believing bondwoman is better than a polytheist woman even if she pleases you* (2:221), and the same ranking operates here: where a free polytheist might be sought for status, the believing bondwoman is offered as the lawful, faithful alternative for the man of limited means.

**With Permission and Fair Dowry, in Chastity**

The conditions *fa ankiḥūhunna bi idhni ahlihinna wa ātūhunna ujūrahunna bi al-maʿrūf* — so marry them with the permission of their owners, giving them their dowry in fairness — restore full marriage procedure to a relationship that could otherwise have been casual. Permission from the owner protects the existing tie and prevents secret union, while *maʿrūf* — fairness, what is recognized as good — for dowry ensures the woman receives a gift that is hers, as every free woman receives hers graciously (4:4). The character required — *muḥṣanāt ghayra musāfiḥāt wa lā muttakhidhāti akhdān* — chaste, neither promiscuous nor having secret affairs — repeats the sūrah's definition of lawful seeking as chaste, not fornicating (4:24), and applies equally to the bondwoman as bride. That equality was emphasized because a bondwoman might have been assumed to have less claim to chastity protections; the verse denies that: she is to be sought as a chaste wife, not as a hidden liaison, and her dowry is to be given fairly, not as a token. The owner's permission does not make her property to be passed; it makes the marriage open and witnessed, as every marriage under the sūrah's law should be.

**Half the Punishment, and the Meaning of That Halving**

The clause *fa idhā uḥṣinna fa in atayna bi fāḥishatin fa ʿalayhinna niṣfu mā ʿalā al-muḥṣanāti min al-ʿadhāb* — if they commit indecency after marriage, they receive half the punishment of free women — was understood as half the fixed penalty for unlawful intercourse where the offender is unmarried, since the married free person's penalty was clarified through Prophetic practice beyond lashing. The halving reflects both the bondwoman's prior vulnerability and the law's calibration of responsibility to situation: it does not mean the act is trivial; it means the recompense accounts for the difference in protection and agency she had before marriage. Jurists detailed how halving applies to lashing rather than to penalties whose nature cannot be halved, showing again that the Qur'an measures even punishment with precision, as it measured inheritance with halves, thirds, sixths, and eighths. The same precision that gave the wife a quarter or eighth (4:12) now gives proportion in penalty, keeping justice from becoming severity. The sūrah elsewhere promises to multiply a good deed many times over and to give a great reward out of grace (4:40); here it shows the other side of that mercy — where penalty must fall, it is measured and halved.

**For Those Who Fear Falling Into Sin**

The restriction *dhālika li man khashiya al-ʿanata minkum* — this is for those of you who fear falling into sin — frames the permission as tied to need and to fear of transgression, not as an ideal to be preferred over marrying a free woman where means exist. *ʿAnat* — hardship, falling into sin — was read as the distress and risk that comes from unmet desire that may push toward *fāḥishah*. The sūrah therefore keeps its earlier advice — if you fear you cannot be just, then one (4:3) — and adds here that if you cannot afford a free wife and you fear sin, the believing bondwoman is lawful, but patience may still be better. That restraint — *wa an taṣbirū khayrun lakum* — but if you are patient, it is better for you — acknowledges that marriage to a bondwoman brings complexities: the owner's ongoing role, the child's status, and the limits on full cohabitation that free marriage does not face. The sūrah does not decide for the individual whether patience is possible; it offers both — permission where fear is real, and the counsel that forbearance, if it can be borne without falling, is the more excellent path. That counsel fits the sūrah's repeated wish to lighten burdens (4:28) while keeping moral shelter intact.

**All-Forgiving, Most Merciful Over Means and Restraint**

The closing *wa Allāhu ghafūrun raḥīm* — and Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — gathers this detailed law into divine forbearance: the forgiveness covers both the difficulty that led to limited means and the imperfections in choosing the lesser path; the mercy covers the provision of a lawful way where otherwise only hardship or sin would remain. The sūrah began by spreading humanity from a single soul (4:1), guarded the orphan's wealth with witnessing and reckoning (4:6), fixed shares for heirs (4:11–12), and guarded marriage with lists and dowries (4:22–24). Here it shows that guarding marriage also means guarding those who cannot afford its usual form — by giving them a form they can afford that still requires permission, dowry, chastity, and accountability, and by reminding the free community *you are from one another*. A household entered through that door, with half penalty where sin occurs and with patience still named as better, is not a second-class contract in faith, even if it is a second choice in means. The One who knows best the state of faith is also the One who forgives what is lacking in provision and who shows mercy by keeping the lawful way open.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:26

> It is Allah's Will to make things clear to you, guide you to the ˹noble˺ ways of those before you, and turn to you in mercy. For Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**A Will to Make Things Clear**

The verse opens with *yurīdu Allāhu li yubayyina lakum* — it is Allah's Will to make things clear to you. After twenty-five verses of intricate law — orphan wealth, marriage limits, dowry, prohibited degrees, the lawful field beyond them — the sūrah pauses to name the intention behind the detail. Clarity is not incidental to the legislation; it is the aim. The verb *yubayyin* conveys explaining until a matter becomes distinct, until what is lawful and what is barred can be seen without blur. The sūrah has just distinguished the father's former wife from other prohibitions (4:22), blood from nursing from marriage ties (4:23), the married woman as forbidden from the lawful field beyond (4:24), and the free woman from the believing bondwoman for those of limited means (4:25) — each distinction removing an ambiguity that custom had left cloudy. To say that Allah wills to make this clear is to say that the burden of confusion is not placed on the believer; the map is being drawn plainly. The same concern for clarity appears elsewhere where the Qur'an says it was sent to explain, so that people may reflect — here that explanation takes the form of precise family law.

**To Guide You to the Ways of Those Before You**

The second purpose *wa yahdiyakum sunana alladhīna min qablikum* — and guide you to the noble ways of those before you — places the new community inside a longer history of guidance. *Sunan* — ways, paths, established practices — were explained as the upright practices of prophets and righteous communities who lived by limits around property and family, honoured covenants, and guarded chastity. By guiding to those ways, the sūrah tells the Medinan believers that they are not inventing a new ethic from nothing; they are being returned to a pattern that earlier communities knew when they were faithful. That framing matters after a list of prohibitions that might feel restrictive: the limits are not a novel hardship for this generation alone; they are the restored noble way that earlier peoples walked when they were closest to revelation. Al-Rāzī notes that the verse therefore links law to precedent: what is commanded here aligns with what was commanded to those before, so that obedience feels like joining a lineage rather than breaking from one.

**And to Turn to You in Mercy**

The third purpose *wa yatūba ʿalaykum* — and turn to you in mercy — shows that clarity and guidance are directed toward pardon. *Yatūba* here is God's turning, His acceptance, as when the sūrah earlier promised *Allah will pardon them* for those who repent soon after acting ignorantly (4:17). The sequence matters: first He makes clear, then He guides to the path, then He turns to those who take it. Clarity without mercy would be exposure; guidance without acceptance would be demand without help. The sūrah therefore presents law as a means to mercy, not its opposite. The same verse that promises to make things clear also promises to accept the return of those who had previously blurred the lines — whether by consuming orphan wealth hastily (4:6), reclaiming dowries (4:20–21), or marrying where it was hateful (4:22). The sūrah repeats that desire to turn in grace in the next verse (4:27), and adds that He wishes to lighten burdens because humankind was created weak (4:28). Here the turn is offered as the outcome of understanding: once you see the distinction, walk its way — and you will find Him turning toward you.

**All-Knowing, All-Wise Over Detail and Time**

The closing *wa Allāhu ʿAlīmun Ḥakīm* — for Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise — matches the two purposes that came before. *ʿAlīm* knows every family configuration, every temptation to treat a widow as inheritable property (4:19), every pressure to reclaim a heap of gold (4:20), every case where means fail and a believing bondwoman becomes the lawful choice (4:25): that knowledge is what makes the distinctions precise — the law is not guesswork about what might harm lineage but knowledge of what will. *Ḥakīm* places that knowledge inside wisdom: the distinctions are not only accurate but beneficial, producing households where trust can be kept and wealth divided without rancour. The same pair closed the inheritance shares (4:11) and the dowry flexibility (4:24), showing that both arithmetic and mercy belong to the same wisdom. The sūrah's detailed legislation could have been heard as burdensome without that closing; with it, the detail itself becomes assurance: the One who knows each tie's sensitivity is the One who draws its limit — and He draws it so that the path of those before you becomes walkable for you, and His turning toward you becomes near.

**A Verse That Holds the First Third Together**

Read after twenty-five verses, this verse gathers the opening third of al-Nisāʾ into a sentence about divine intent. It tells the reader that the laws about a single soul and womb-ties (4:1), about testing orphans and witnessing handovers (4:6), about obligatory shares after debts and bequests (4:11–12), about disgust for marrying a father's widow (4:22), and about lawful seeking with wealth in chastity (4:24–25) are not a collection of disconnected rulings but a single clarifying, guiding, and pardoning will. The sūrah has moved from creation to trust to property to family formation, and this verse names the thread: Allah wills to make all of it clear, to place you on the noble way others walked, and to turn to you when you do. That naming prepares the next two verses, which contrast that will with the wish of those who follow desires to see you deviate entirely (4:27), and which add that weakness is the reason burdens are lightened (4:28). Clarity, precedent, and mercy together form the ground on which the lighter burden can be borne: without the will to make things clear, the law would remain opaque; without guidance to the ways before, it would feel rootless; without the turn in mercy, it would feel unattainable. With all three, the community is given both the map and the help to walk it.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:27

> And it is Allah's Will to turn to you in grace, but those who follow their desires wish to see you deviate entirely ˹from Allah's Way˺

**Two Wills Facing One Another**

This verse places two intentions side by side in one sentence. *Wa Allāhu yurīdu an yatūba ʿalaykum* — and it is Allah's Will to turn to you in grace — repeats the promise of the previous verse that He wishes to make things clear, guide to the noble ways, and turn to you in mercy (4:26); the repetition is not redundancy but the isolation of the turning as the focus. Immediately beside it stands a contrary wish: *wa yurīdu alladhīna yattabiʿūna al-shahawāt an tamīlū maylan ʿaẓīmā* — but those who follow their desires wish to see you deviate entirely. The verb *yurīdu* — to will, to want — is used for both, making the contrast a contest of wills: on one side the will that clarifies limits and then pardons those who keep them; on the other the will that blurs limits and draws people into gross deviation. The Qur'an elsewhere says that Satan wants to lead astray and that human whims invite to the same, and the sūrah has shown what that deviation looks like in practice: consuming orphan wealth (4:10), exceeding inheritance limits (4:14), treating women as inheritable (4:19), reclaiming dowries by slander (4:20), marrying where God said do not. Those who follow desires benefit from each blur, because in each the strong gain at the weak's expense. The verse tells the believer that the line he keeps is not a private preference but a front between two larger intentions.

**Who Are Those Who Follow Desires**

The phrase *alladhīna yattabiʿūna al-shahawāt* was read broadly by early authorities. Some identified them as those who pursue unlawful sexual relations and want others to join them so that their own choice feels less isolated. Others read it as those who follow cravings in general — for wealth, dominance, and display — and therefore want the community's law to bend so that their cravings can be satisfied without censure. The sūrah's immediate context supports both, because the preceding laws covered both *fāḥishah* and property: those who committed indecency and needed four witnesses to prove it (4:15–16) would wish the barrier of proof lowered or the act normalised; those who ate orphan wealth or seized dowries would wish the limits on property lifted. In each case the wish is not only to do wrong but to see the community deviate — *an tamīlū* — to incline away, to swerve off the path that was just made clear (4:26). The addition *maylan ʿaẓīmā* — a great, profound deviation — was explained as not a small slip but a wholesale turn, where the exception becomes the norm and what was once called *maqt* — despicable (4:22) — is renamed as freedom. The verse warns that the pressure to deviate will be presented as tolerance or as alignment with desire, but its size is great and its direction is away.

**Turning in Grace Against the Pull of Deviation**

The contrast between *yatūba* — to turn in grace — and *tamīlū* — to tilt, to deviate — is spatial: one turn brings the community upright; the other tilts it off balance. The Qur'an uses *mayl* elsewhere for tilting toward one wife at the expense of another where justice is required, cautioning *do not incline completely toward one, leaving another suspended* (4:129) — showing how *mayl* operates in family life as well. Here the tilt is entire — *ʿaẓīm*, a comprehensive swerve from the noble ways just mentioned. The sūrah's answer to that pull is not to deny desire but to place it inside limits where it can be chaste and sheltered: the lawful field beyond the prohibited degrees, sought with wealth, in protection, not in fornication (4:24), and the permission for a believing bondwoman where means fail (4:25), already showed that desire has a lawful home. The wish of those who follow desires is to remove the walls of that home and call the open field liberation; the divine will to turn in grace offers the opposite — walls that protect, clarity that distinguishes, and pardon that follows when the walls are kept. That is why the sūrah pairs the two wills in one breath: the believer must choose which will he aligns with, knowing both are inviting.

**Why the Verse Repeats Allah's Will to Turn**

Repeating *Allah wishes to turn to you* immediately after saying He wishes to make things clear and guide to the ways before (4:26) isolates grace as the purpose of law. Law without the promise of turning would be heard as burden alone, and the next verse says explicitly that Allah wishes to lighten your burdens because you were created weak (4:28); here the lightening is already implied — to be turned toward in grace after clarification is to be given a way back when the law has been broken. That way back was already detailed: repent soon after acting ignorantly (4:17); repent and mend and be relieved (4:16); give back what was taken and speak equitably (4:9). The wish of the followers of desire is to keep people from that return by normalising deviation until the return no longer seems needed. The sūrah has already defined the failed repentance that comes only when death is present (4:18); the deviators' wish is to keep people persisting until that failure becomes inevitable. By naming both wishes together, the verse makes the choice urgent: one will has prepared a painful punishment for persistence (4:18) but has also prepared Gardens for keeping limits (4:13) and forgiveness for soon return; the other will has no garden to offer, only the satisfaction of seeing others swerve greatly with them.

**A Community Invited to Stay on the Clear Path**

The verse's practical effect is to steady a community that has just received many boundaries. New boundaries attract critique — that they are too strict, too traditional, or too lenient — and that critique often comes from desire dressed as advice. The sūrah answers by personifying the critique: it comes from those who follow desires, and it wants not a small adjustment but a great inclination. To stay on the path that was made clear is therefore not rigidity; it is loyalty to the will that wills to turn toward you. The Qur'an elsewhere says *Allah does not wish to place hardship upon you* (5:6), and here it says He wishes to turn toward you — both statements showing that the limits are meant to shelter, not burden. A community that keeps the orphan's wealth with witnesses (4:6), honours fixed shares after debts (4:11–12), and seeks marriage with wealth in chastity (4:24–25) will appear distinct from those around it; that distinctness may feel like deviation to outsiders, but the verse reframes it: the great deviation would be to tilt away from those limits at the invitation of desire. Remaining upright, with the help of the One who wills to turn toward you when you do, is the sūrah's definition of staying on the way.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:28

> And it is Allah's Will to lighten your burdens, for humankind was created weak

**A Will to Lighten**

After saying that Allah wills to make things clear and guide to the noble ways and turn to you in mercy (4:26), and that those who follow desires wish you to swerve greatly (4:27), the sūrah adds a third divine will: *yurīdu Allāhu an yukhaffifa ʿankum* — and it is Allah's Will to lighten your burdens. The verb *yukhaffif* — to lighten, to make less heavy — was understood as easing the legal and moral load to what people can bear, without removing the limits that protect them. The context shows where that easing appears: the prohibition on marrying former wives of fathers was softened with *except what was done previously* (4:22); combining two sisters carries the same exception (4:23); the field lawful beyond the prohibited degrees is opened widely when sought with wealth in chastity (4:24); the bar of inability to afford a free believing wife is eased by permission to marry a believing bondwoman with permission and fair dowry (4:25); and the set dowry itself is made adjustable by mutual graciousness (4:24). Each of those details is a lightening inside a limit. The verse gathers them and says the pattern is intentional: the limits are fixed, but the way of keeping them is made lighter.

**For Humankind Was Created Weak**

The reason given — *wa khuliqa al-insānu ḍaʿīfan* — was read as comprehensive, covering several domains the sūrah has touched. Physically, people need shelter and maintenance, which marriage provides when it is *muḥṣin* — protective. Sexually, desire is strong and persistent, which is why unlawful intercourse is called *fāḥishah* and why chastity is protected by requiring four witnesses and by disciplining the pair and then relieving them when they mend (4:15–16). Intellectually, people know the right but act ignorantly under impulse, which is why repentance is accepted for those who act in ignorance and turn soon (4:17) and not for those who persist until death is present (4:18). Socially, kin groups press individuals to favour custom over revelation, as with inheriting women against their will (4:19) and reclaiming dowries (4:20–21). To be created weak in all these directions is not an insult; it is an explanation that makes easing a mercy rather than an indulgence. The Qur'an elsewhere says *Allah does not charge a soul beyond what it can bear* (2:286), and this verse is the social law counterpart: the soul that is weak is not charged with what would crush it.

**How Lightening Works in This Sūrah**

Lightening does not mean erasing. The orphan's wealth must still be returned with witnesses and reckoning (4:6), but the guardian who is well-off is asked to abstain while the poor guardian may take what is fair, and the test for *rushd* — sound judgment — allows return when readiness appears rather than at a single arbitrary age (4:6). The inheritance shares remain fixed — half, quarter, eighth, sixth, third, two-thirds — after debts and bequests (4:11–12), but bequests themselves remain permitted up to one-third, and mutual graciousness about dowries is allowed (4:24). Prohibited degrees are fixed, but the past is pardoned and the lawful field beyond is broad. Fornication is not permitted, but marriage is made reachable even where means fail, with the concession for the believing bondwoman where fear of sin is real and patience still named as better (4:25). In each case the law keeps its bar and widens its door — exactly what lightening inside limits looks like. The sūrah therefore answers the deviators' claim that limits are harsh (4:27) not by removing limits but by showing how many lawful paths exist to live well inside them.

**Weakness and the Need for Turn and Clarity**

The three divine wills of verses 26 through 28 belong together: to make clear, to guide to the ways before and turn toward you, and to lighten because you are weak. Without clarity, weakness would be left to guess; without turning, weakness would be left to despair; without lightening, weakness would be left to break. The sūrah has already supplied all three — clarity in the detailed lists of who may and may not be married, guidance in the precedent of noble ways, and turning in the acceptance of soon repentance (4:17) and in the command to relieve those who amend (4:16). Lightening completes the set by shaping the law so that the weak can actually walk it. Al-Rāzī notes that the verse's placement after the concession for bondwomen is deliberate, because that concession is the clearest instance of lessening a burden without surrendering the value — chastity — the burden protects. The same logic extends to the coming warnings about devouring wealth illegally (4:29) and about major sins (4:31): the sūrah will threaten Fire for deliberate overstep, but it will also promise absolution of lesser faults for those who avoid the great ones — another lightening for the weak who will inevitably stumble in small ways.

**A Word That Invites Reliance**

The statement that humankind was created weak was heard by early commentators as both realism and invitation: realism, because it tells the believer not to rely on his own strength to keep limits he cannot keep alone; invitation, because it points him to the One who wills to lighten and to turn toward him. The verse draws the same response as the sūrah's opening — *be mindful of your Lord who created you from a single soul* (4:1) — where creation grounds duty; here creation grounds dependence: the same Creator who spread countless men and women from one soul knows the weakness of each and eases the path He asks them to walk. That easing does not remove accountability; it makes accountability bearable. A guardian can keep an orphan's wealth faithfully when the rule allows fair provision and requires witnesses (4:6); an heir can divide a large estate justly when the fractions are fixed and the bequest is limited; a man of small means can marry lawfully when a believing bondwoman is permitted with conditions, or can choose patience if he can bear it (4:25). Each is a burden lightened, not lifted, so that weakness is neither ignored nor indulged but supported. In that support the sūrah's purpose becomes visible: a law that is clear, a way that is noble, a turn that is gracious, and a load that the weak can carry.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:29

> O believers! Do not devour one another's wealth illegally, but rather trade by mutual consent. And do not kill ˹each other or˺ yourselves. Surely Allah is ever Merciful to you

**Do Not Devour One Another's Wealth Illegally**

The address *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū* — O believers — reappears to mark a new, general principle after the detailed family laws. *Lā taʾkulū amwālakum baynakum bi al-bāṭil* — do not devour one another's wealth illegally — uses the same verb *akala* — to eat — that earlier described consuming orphans' wealth as eating fire (4:10), warned against mixing orphan wealth with one's own (4:2), and against hasty consumption before the orphan grows up (4:6). Here the scope widens from guardianship to all transactions among believers. *Bi al-bāṭil* — illegally, by falsehood — covers every means where consent or right is absent: theft, fraud, usury where increase is taken without trade, gambling where property changes hands without productive exchange, bribery, and taking by coercion. The sūrah has spent its first thirty verses guarding wealth at its most sensitive points — orphan property, dowries, inheritance shares, and the estate around which relatives, orphans, and the needy gather (4:8). This verse lifts that guard to the level of the market and the household economy as a whole: what was forbidden with the orphan because he cannot defend himself is forbidden with everyone, because no one's wealth is lawful to another without right.

**But Trade by Mutual Consent**

The exception *illā an takūna tijāratan ʿan tarāḍin minkum* — but rather trade by mutual consent — defines the lawful path that replaces *bāṭil*. *Tijārah* was read as exchange where both parties knowingly consent to the object, the price, and the terms, without deception or compulsion. *Tarāḍ* — mutual pleasure, contentment — matches the standard the sūrah already set for dowries, where only what is waived with a contented soul is wholesome (4:4), and for adjustments to the set dowry where only what is mutually agreed is permitted (4:24). The same standard appears here for every sale: consent must be real, not assumed; knowledge must be shared, not hidden. The Qur'an elsewhere requires witnessing for debts and discourages concealing defects, both of which protect *tarāḍ* from being a formality. Trade that hides a flaw, invents a price under pressure, or exploits information asymmetry fails that test, even if the paperwork is correct, because the consent was not true.

**Do Not Kill Each Other or Yourselves**

The second prohibition *wa lā taqtulū anfusakum* — and do not kill each other or yourselves — was read in two linked senses, both supported by the wording *anfusakum* — yourselves, your own selves, one another. One sense is literal: do not kill one another, which the Qur'an elsewhere forbids except by right of justice, and do not kill yourselves, which Prophetic teaching counts among grave sins. The other sense is social: in a community described as being from a single soul (4:1) and as *you are from one another* (4:25), killing another is killing the collective self, and devouring another's wealth illegally is a slow killing of the community's life as well. The placement is deliberate: after forbidding fraudulent enrichment, the verse forbids the violent taking of life, showing that both are forms of taking what is not yours — property and blood. The next verse adds the direct threat: *whoever does this sinfully and unjustly, We will burn them in the Fire* (4:30). The sequence keeps property and life under the same guard.

**Surely Allah Is Ever Merciful to You**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna bikum raḥīmā* — surely Allah is ever Merciful to you — gives the reason that both prohibitions are mercy themselves. The mercy is not only in forgiving those who have done wrong and then turn soon (4:17); it is also in forbidding the wrong that would destroy them and others. A market where *bāṭil* is allowed quickly becomes a place where the weak — the very orphans, women, and needy the sūrah has been protecting — are devoured; a community where killing is tolerated cannot keep any of the family limits the sūrah has drawn. By prohibiting both, God spares the community the fire that illicit gain already is (4:10) and the Fire that deliberate injustice leads to (4:30). The Name *Raḥīm* here matches its use after the concession for bondwomen where patience is better (4:25) and after the promise to make things clear and lighten burdens (4:26–28): in each place mercy appears as the character of the lawgiver who both draws the line and eases the path inside it.

**Trade as the Lawful Alternative to Devouring**

The juxtaposition of *bāṭil* and *tijārah ʿan tarāḍ* teaches that economic life has only two modes in this sūrah's vision: devouring or trading. Devouring is taking without right — substitution of bad for good (4:2), seizure of dowries (4:20–21), excess bequests that harm heirs (4:12). Trading is giving and receiving with knowledge and willingness. The sūrah's repeated insistence on witnesses, documentation, and measured shares is the infrastructure for trade: it makes consent verifiable. Even the provision for relatives, orphans, and the needy present at distribution, offered with kind speech (4:8), is a form of lawful transfer where consent is not between buyer and seller but between heir and bystander, yet it still requires the heir's genuine willingness, not compulsion. The verse therefore does more than condemn fraud; it commends a market ethic where the other's contentment is a condition of lawfulness. A profit taken with someone's hidden ignorance or pressured silence may look like trade, but the sūrah calls it devouring, because the soul inside the transaction did not truly consent. That redefinition trains the reader to audit not only contracts but conversations.

**A Guard That Holds Property and Life Together**

Placed after the verses on lightening burdens, this double prohibition holds the community's two most basic trusts together. The sūrah began with creation from a single soul and watchfulness over womb-ties (4:1), moved through guardianship of orphans with witnessing and reckoning (4:6), fixed inheritance after debts and bequests (4:11–12), and governed marriage with dowries and chastity (4:24–25). Now it says, in the market and in the street, keep the same guard: do not take wealth by falsehood, and do not take life without right. Both takings are framed as eating and killing that rebound on the taker — here as burning in the next verse, earlier as eating fire (4:10), always under a Reckoner who suffices (4:6). The closing mercy — ever Merciful to you — assures the believer that the command is not a burden added to weakness but a protection given to weakness, so that trade can be pursued with confidence and life lived without fear of the neighbour's hand. Where that protection is kept, wealth circulates by consent and lives are spared; where it is crossed, the sūrah's next sentence names the end.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:30

> And whoever does this sinfully and unjustly, We will burn them in the Fire. That is easy for Allah

**Whoever Does This**

The pronoun *hādhā* — this — refers to the two prohibitions just named: devouring one another's wealth illegally and killing one another or yourselves (4:29). The verse does not repeat those acts in detail; it gathers them as a single *this* and adds the condition that determines its recompense. The sūrah has spent its opening passages defining what counts as *bāṭil* — mixing orphan wealth with one's own (4:2), substituting bad for good, hastily consuming before the orphan grows up (4:6), reclaiming dowries by slander (4:20), exceeding inheritance limits (4:14) — and what counts as lawful trade by mutual consent (4:29). Now it says that doing *this* — the devouring or the killing — with two additional qualities leads to a named end. The brevity matters: after a long sequence of family and market laws, the warning is condensed to a single sentence so that it can be remembered in the market and at the estate table. A person who handles a sale or a legacy can recall *whoever does this* and know immediately which acts are meant, because the sūrah has already shown their many forms.

**Sinfully and Unjustly — the Inner State and the Outer Wrong**

The condition *ʿudwānan wa ẓulman* — sinfully and unjustly — was explained as covering both the motive and the measure. *ʿUdwān* — aggression, overstepping, hostility — describes the inner drive to transgress a limit knowingly, to push beyond what is allowed because desire or anger urges. *Ẓulm* — injustice, misplacement — describes the outer act of putting a thing where it does not belong, taking a share that was not assigned, spending another's property as one's own. Early authorities noted that the pair excludes the person who errs out of ignorance and then returns soon (4:17), or who acts under mistake, coercion, or genuine doubt. The sūrah has repeatedly distinguished ignorance with soon repentance, which is pardoned, from persistence until death is present, which is not (4:17–18); here the same distinction operates at the level of commerce and homicide. The one who devours wealth or sheds blood while knowing it is forbidden and intending to overstep is the one the threat addresses. That qualification keeps the law from becoming a trap for the weak — whom the sūrah has already called created weak (4:28) — while keeping it firm against the strong who calculate overstep as policy.

**We Will Burn Them in the Fire**

The recompense *fa sawfa nuṣlīhi nāran* — We will burn them in the Fire — uses the emphatic future *sawfa* to stress certainty. *Nuṣlīhi* — to roast, to cause to burn — conveys direct contact with fire, as the same verb described those who unjustly consume orphans' wealth eating fire in their bellies and then being burned in a blazing Hell (4:10), and those who exceed limits abiding in Fire with humiliation (4:14). The sūrah keeps the image of burning for wealth wrongs for a reason: wealth taken as food becomes fire as food, and wealth taken as gain becomes fire as dwelling. The Fire is not an arbitrary penalty attached to a civil infraction; it is the true form of the act when its cover is removed. The Qur'an elsewhere says that wrongfully taken wealth will be hung around necks on the Day of Resurrection, showing that the property itself becomes the punishment. The subject is *whoever* — any person, regardless of status — which matches the sūrah's consistent equalisation from a single soul (4:1) to equal witnessing for the orphan (4:6) to obligatory shares for men and women (4:7).

**That Is Easy for Allah**

The closing *wa kāna dhālika ʿalā Allāhi yasīrā* — and that is easy for Allah — was read as both warning and reassurance. As warning, it says the punishment is not difficult for God to execute; the barrier is not capability but forbearance, which is why the sūrah elsewhere calls Him All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:25–26) and Most Forbearing (4:12) yet still names the burning as sure for the deliberate overstep. As reassurance, it tells the wronged that justice does not depend on their own power to enforce it: the orphan whose wealth was eaten, the heir whose share was withheld, the victim of a killing — none needs to produce the Fire; the One who is Reckoner (4:6) and Witness over all things (4:33) will see that what is easy for Him is done. The phrase also deters the calculation that power protects from consequence. A person who devours a small amount may think the amount is too small to matter, or that his status will shield him; the verse answers that the act's ease for God makes status irrelevant.

**When Ease Should Deter**

The practical force of *that is easy for Allah* is deterrence through proportion. A person weighing whether to falsify a measure or pressure a widow to surrender a dowry may weigh the immediate gain against the likelihood of being caught by people. The verse shifts the scale to being caught by God, for whom it is easy — a shift already prepared by *Allah is ever Watchful over you* (4:1), *sufficient is Allah as Reckoner* (4:6), and *Allah is a Witness over all things* (4:33). Each of those Names makes detection certain; this clause makes recompense certain as well. At the same time, the qualifier *ʿudwānan wa ẓulman* keeps the deterrence from becoming despair: a person who slipped, who devoured out of ignorance and then turned soon (4:17), is not the one the burning addresses; it addresses deliberation and injustice persisted in. That distinction lets the weak who err take the next verse's promise as their own — avoid the major sins and lesser faults will be absolved, with entry into a place of honour (4:31) — while those who calculate overstep read this verse as addressed directly to them. The Fire that is easy for Allah to fuel is therefore also easy for the deliberate wrongdoer to avoid: do not do this sinfully and unjustly, and the path to honour remains open.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:31

> If you avoid the major sins forbidden to you, We will absolve you of your ˹lesser˺ misdeeds and admit you into a place of honour

**Avoiding the Major to Be Forgiven the Lesser**

The verse offers a precise undertaking: *in tajtanibū kabāʾira mā tunhawna ʿanhu nukaffir ʿankum sayyiʾātikum wa nudkhilkum mudkhalan karīmā* — if you avoid the major sins forbidden to you, We will absolve you of your lesser misdeeds and admit you into a place of honour. The language was explained as God's promise to handle the small faults of those who guard against the great ones. *Kabāʾir* — major sins — were listed by early authorities with variations, but a core was consistent: associating partners with God, killing a soul, consuming orphan wealth (4:10), devouring wealth illegally and killing deliberately (4:29–30), disobedience to parents, false testimony, and the *ḥudūd* violations the sūrah has detailed such as illicit intercourse (4:15–16), exceeding inheritance limits (4:13–14), and reclaiming dowries by slander (4:20). *Sayyiʾāt* — lesser misdeeds, evil deeds that stain even if smaller — are the slips that weakness (4:28) makes inevitable. The sūrah has already said humankind was created weak and that God wills to lighten and turn toward you (4:26–28); here it gives the mechanism of that lightening: guard the great, and the small is effaced. The promise does not trivialise the small; it says the small is covered when the great dam holds.

**We Will Absolve You of Your Lesser Misdeeds**

The phrase *nukaffir ʿankum sayyiʾātikum* uses *kaffara* — to cover, to efface — as though the small faults are stains that can be wiped. The covering is God's act, not a self-erasure through ritual alone, though prayer, charity, and seeking forgiveness were mentioned as means that invite that covering. The Qur'an elsewhere says that good deeds remove evil ones and that seeking forgiveness immediately after a lapse is the mark of the mindful (3:135); this verse adds a structural covering: avoidance of the great itself becomes a cause for wiping the small. That structure keeps the believer from two extremes. One extreme counts small faults as nothing and therefore drifts into the great; the other counts small faults as unforgivable and despairs. The promise addresses both: take the great seriously enough to avoid it, and know that the small, while still needing to be turned from, will be handled with mercy. The sūrah has already promised that for those who repent soon after acting ignorantly, God will pardon (4:17); this verse extends that pardoning logic to the many lesser missteps that never reached the level of the major but still weigh on the heart.

**And Admit You Into a Place of Honour**

The reward *wa nudkhilkum mudkhalan karīmā* — and admit you into a place of honour — was read as entry into the Garden described earlier as *Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there forever, that is the ultimate triumph* (4:13), now named by its quality. *Karīm* — noble, generous, honourable — suggests not only a pleasant location but a reception that honours the entrant: the one who avoided eating orphan wealth, refused to devour by falsehood, and kept inheritance and marriage within limits is welcomed as an honoured guest, not a tolerated entrant. The word *mudkhal* — place of entry, way in — implies that the path itself is honourable, not only the destination, matching the sūrah's earlier promise to make things clear and guide to noble ways (4:26). The honourable entry is the counterpart to the humiliating punishment named for exceeding limits (4:14) and to the burning that is easy for God for deliberate devouring and killing (4:30). The sūrah keeps the two ends visible so that the middle path — avoidance of the major — feels both urgent and inviting.

**A Verse That Lightens Without Loosening**

Read with the verses on weakness and lightening, this verse shows how burden is lifted without law being loosened. *Humankind was created weak* (4:28) explains why lesser faults will occur; *We will absolve you of lesser misdeeds* explains how they are handled when the great is avoided. The law remains firm where it must — the orphan's wealth with witnesses (4:6), the fixed shares after debts (4:11–12), the bar on reclaiming a heap of gold (4:20), the bar on killing and devouring (4:29) — but the moral economy around the law is merciful. The believer is not asked to be flawless; he is asked to be serious about the great and quick to return from the small. Prophetic tradition listed seven destructive sins and taught that avoiding them, maintaining prayer, paying alms, and seeking forgiveness secures that covering, which shows that the verse was heard as both comfort and discipline: comfort, because perfection is not demanded; discipline, because the major is not negotiable. Between those poles the weak person can walk without despair and without complacency, knowing that the One who is All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:26) knows which faults are major, and that the One who is ever Merciful (4:29) has promised to cover the rest when the great is avoided, and to admit to honour those He covers.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:32

> And do not crave what Allah has given some of you over others. Men will be rewarded according to their deeds and women ˹equally˺ according to theirs. Rather, ask Allah for His bounties. Surely Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things

**Do Not Crave What Was Given to Another**

The prohibition *wa lā tatamannaw mā faḍḍala Allāhu bihi baʿḍakum ʿalā baʿḍ* — and do not crave what Allah has given some of you over others — addresses the envy that the sūrah's distribution laws could stir. After fixing shares for men and women whether little or much (4:7), detailing sons and daughters, parents and siblings after debts and bequests (4:11–12), and describing trade by mutual consent (4:29), a listener might look at another's portion — larger inheritance, larger dowry, larger earning — and wish it were his. The Qur'an names that wish as *tamannī* — craving, wishing — not planning to earn, but longing to possess what another was given. The verse was revealed in a context where some men wished they had the double share and some women wished they had the same share as men, and where people coveted the rewards of others. The answer gathers both sexes and says the division of favour — *faḍl* — belongs to God's apportioning, not to envy. The sūrah elsewhere says *We have allocated among them their livelihood in this world* (43:32), and here it asks that allocation to be met with asking, not craving.

**Men According to Their Deeds, Women According to Theirs**

The corrective *lil-rijāli naṣībun mimmā iktasabū wa lil-nisāʾi naṣībun mimmā iktasabna* — men will be rewarded according to their deeds and women equally according to theirs — provides the alternative accounting. *Iktasaba* — to earn, to acquire through striving — places the measure on what each does, not on what each wishes another had not been given. The echo of *naṣīb* — share — from the inheritance verses (4:7) is deliberate: just as men and women have obligatory shares in estates, they have shares in earnings before God. A man's deeds are his share, and a woman's deeds are hers; neither is credited to the other by gender. The identical structure — *mimmā iktasabna* for women as *mimmā iktasabū* for men — shows parallel agency. The Qur'an elsewhere promises that *whoever does good, whether male or female, while faithful, We will give a good life* (16:97), and that God never wrongs even an atom's weight but multiplies good many times over (4:40). This verse's pairing makes that promise concrete at the point where comparison is most tempting. The antidote to craving another's favour is to turn to one's own field and work it, knowing the harvest is kept without diminishment.

**Rather Ask Allah for His Bounties**

The positive command *wa asʾalū Allāha min faḍlihi* — rather, ask Allah for His bounties — redirects the energy of envy into supplication. *Faḍl* — bounty, surplus, favour — is the same word used for the apportioning among people; to ask Him for His bounty is to ask the Source rather than to resent the recipient. The Qur'an elsewhere says *If you are grateful, I will give you more* (14:7) and encourages asking from the same bounty that sustains trade and family. The sūrah has already taught that God is ever Watchful (4:1), sufficient as Reckoner (4:6), a Witness over all things (4:33), and ever Merciful to you (4:29); asking Him is therefore not a vague hope but a request to the One who sees, counts, and shows mercy. Asking for bounty can mean asking for lawful earnings, for knowledge, for patience to avoid major sins (4:31), and for the ability to trade by mutual consent (4:29) — each a form of *faḍl* that can be requested without craving what another was given.

**Perfect Knowledge Over Every Deed and Apportioning**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna bi kulli shayʾin ʿalīmā* — surely Allah has perfect knowledge of all things — is the guarantee behind both sides of the verse. He knows what favour was given to each — wealth, strength, lineage, opportunity — and why it was given in that measure. He also knows what each earned — *mā iktasabū* and *mā iktasabna* — with nuance that people miss, including the hidden effort, intention, and constraint behind an outward deed. That twofold knowledge removes the ground for envy: if the apportioning was done with perfect knowledge, it was not arbitrary; if earnings are recorded with perfect knowledge, no deed done faithfully is lost, even if its worldly return seems smaller than another's. The sūrah has closed similar verses with All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:11, 4:26) and All-Knowing, Most Forbearing (4:12); here the knowledge is said to cover *all things* — *bi kulli shayʾ* — because the temptation to compare covers all things as well. The one who remembers that God knows both gifts and earnings can leave craving aside and turn to asking.

**A Cure for Comparison After Law**

Placed between the promise that avoiding major sins brings an honourable entry (4:31) and the reminder that heirs are appointed and pledges must be honoured (4:33), this verse cures the comparison that law can breed. Law that divides — obligatory shares, dowries, trade — invites the eye to compare; the sūrah answers that invite with a different economy: shares in the next life are by deeds, equally open to men and women, and bounty in this life is to be asked from God, not extracted by envying people. The counsel is practical. A woman who sees a brother's larger inheritance is told her deeds are counted as hers; a man who sees another's profitable trade is told to ask God for his own bounty rather than to devour by falsehood (4:29). The sūrah has already said humankind was created weak (4:28) and that God wills to lighten and turn toward you (4:26–28); here it lightens the specific weight of envy by giving the weak a prayer that is always available. To ask rather than crave is itself a deed that earns a share, and the One who knows all things will not forget it. In that exchange — asking instead of craving, earning instead of envying — the earlier promise holds: the lesser faults are covered, and the major sin of devouring another's portion, whether in thought or in act, is avoided.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:33

> And We have appointed heirs to what has been left by parents and next of kin. As for those you have made a pledge to, give them their share. Surely Allah is a Witness over all things

**Heirs Appointed for What Is Left**

The verse states *wa li kullin jaʿalnā mawāliya mimmā taraka al-wālidāni wa al-aqrabūn* — and We have appointed heirs to what has been left by parents and next of kin. The pronoun *We* — divine appointment — matches the earlier framing of shares as an obligation from Allah (4:11) and as limits set by Allah (4:13): inheritance is not a tribal negotiation left to custom; it is an appointment. The word *mawālī* — heirs, close kin, protectors — was read as those who inherit by fixed portions and those who inherit as residuary kin where fractions leave a remainder. The phrase *mimmā taraka al-wālidāni wa al-aqrabūn* gathers every estate, whether little or much (4:7), under the same appointment: no heir is an afterthought. The Qur'an elsewhere says *to Allah belongs the heritage of the heavens and the earth* (3:180), so the appointment is also a redistribution of what already belongs to Him — which explains why the portions are obligatory rather than suggested.

**Give Those You Have Pledged Their Share**

The second clause *wa alladhīna ʿaqadat aymānukum fa ātūhum naṣībahum* — as for those you have made a pledge to, give them their share — addresses a specific practice of the early community. In the pre-Islamic and early Islamic period, men might make a pact of brotherhood or alliance — *ʿaqd* — promising mutual support, protection, and sometimes inheritance between those not related by blood. Commentators relate that such pledges were made between the migrants and the hosts, and between individuals who sought to secure support in a city new to many. The Qur'an does not erase the pledge; it commands fulfilment of its share where it was made, while the fixed inheritance shares now govern kinship. Some understood the pledge as referring to marriage covenants where a wife's share must be honoured, or to emancipation ties where a freed person has a claim; the common point is fidelity to a contract voluntarily entered. The sūrah elsewhere commands fulfilling oaths and covenants and describes the marital bond as a firm commitment — *mīthāq ghalīẓ* (4:21) — so giving the pledged share is of a piece with keeping the firm word. The community that was just told not to crave what another was given (4:32) is now told to give what it pledged, which breaks envy at its root by turning promise into payment.

**Between Fixed Law and Voluntary Pledge**

The pairing of appointed heirs and pledged associates displays the sūrah's balance between what God fixes and what people undertake. Fixed heirs — *mawālī* — are not chosen by the deceased; they are appointed by the verse and quantified in the fractions already given (4:11–12). Pledged associates are chosen — the result of *ʿaqadat aymānukum*, what your right hands have tied. Both generate a *naṣīb* — a share — that must be given: the first obligatory by divine appointment, the second obligatory by personal commitment kept before God. Together they show that property moves by two just means — law and promise — both of which exclude seizing by desire or by *bāṭil*, falsehood, condemned just before (4:29). Trade by mutual consent (4:29) and the dowry given graciously (4:4) already taught that willingness makes transfer lawful; this verse adds that a pledge made willingly also makes transfer obligatory. The sūrah therefore trains the reader to see wealth as moving along clear tracks: appointed shares where kinship is the track, and pledged shares where contract is the track, with neither track to be diverted by envy (4:32) or by devouring (4:29–30).

**Surely Allah Is a Witness Over All Things**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna ʿalā kulli shayʾin shahīdā* — surely Allah is a Witness over all things — supplies the watcher for both tracks. *Shahīd* — witness, present observer — matches *Raqīb* — ever Watchful (4:1) — and *Ḥasīb* — sufficient as Reckoner (4:6) — and *ʿAlīm* — All-Knowing (4:11, 4:26, 4:32); the difference is that *Shahīd* stresses presence at the act of transfer. The apportioning of an estate often happens in a family home without a judge; the fulfilment of a pledge often happens between two persons without an audience. The verse says the division and the fulfilment are already witnessed. That matters for the heirs appointed — parents, children, spouses, siblings — whose shares could be trimmed if no one sees, and for the pledged person whose share could be denied if the pledge is forgotten after death. Elsewhere the Qur'an says *Allah is Witness over what you do* and requires witnesses at the orphan's handover (4:6); this verse is the general principle behind that requirement. What is witnessed by God need not be witnessed by many people to be binding, but human witnesses remain the community's way of aligning its practice with the divine watch.

**Law and Loyalty Together**

Read with verses 7 through 12, this verse finishes the sūrah's inheritance architecture by adding loyalty to law. Verses 7 and 11–12 gave the law — men and women have obligatory shares, with precise fractions after debts and bequests. Verses 8–10 gave the ethic around the law — provision for bystanders with kind speech, fear for one's own weak children as a motive, fire for eating orphan wealth. Verses 13–14 gave the sanction — Gardens for keeping limits, humiliation for crossing them. Verse 32 warned against craving another's portion and invited asking God for bounty instead. This verse adds the pledge: where you have tied your word, give the share. The placement is deliberate — a person who has learned to ask rather than crave is ready to give what he promised without resenting the gift. The Witness over all things sees both the appointed share handed to a parent or spouse and the pledged share handed to an ally or a freed person, and counts both as fulfilment. The sūrah therefore does not separate civil law from personal honour; it joins them under the same watch. To keep the fixed shares is obedience; to keep the pledge is fidelity; to know both are witnessed is to handle wealth as one who knows he is seen, and who wishes his handling to be worthy of that sight.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:34

> Men are the caretakers of women, as men have been provisioned by Allah over women and tasked with supporting them financially. And righteous women are devoutly obedient and, when alone, protective of what Allah has entrusted them with. And if you sense ill-conduct from your women, advise them ˹first˺, ˹if they persist,˺ do not share their beds, ˹but if they still persist,˺ then discipline them ˹gently˺. But if they change their ways, do not be unjust to them. Surely Allah is Most High, All-Great

**Caretakers, Not Controllers**

The verse opens with *al-rijālu qawwāmūna ʿalā al-nisāʾ bi mā faḍḍala Allāhu baʿḍahum ʿalā baʿḍ wa bi mā anfaqū min amwālihim* — men are the caretakers of women, as men have been provisioned by Allah over women and tasked with supporting them financially. The word *qawwām* — caretaker, maintainer, one who stands and keeps upright — is stronger than a claim to superiority; it describes a role of standing guard, providing, and managing affairs so that the household remains upright. That role is grounded in two facts, not in a claim of greater worth. First, *bi mā faḍḍala Allāhu baʿḍahum ʿalā baʿḍ* — as God has provisioned some over others — which the sūrah earlier framed as bounty to be asked for rather than envied (4:32), and which elsewhere appears as differences in strength and in means. Second, *wa bi mā anfaqū min amwālihim* — and as they spend from their wealth — the financial maintenance the sūrah has already secured through the dowry as a gracious gift (4:4), the prohibition on reclaiming it (4:20–21), and the inheritance fractions that assign the larger share to the party bearing maintenance. The verse therefore ties authority to responsibility: the caretaking is not licence to dominate but an assignment to provide.

**Devoutly Obedient and Protective When Alone**

The description *fa al-ṣāliḥātu qānitātun ḥāfiẓātun lil-ghaybi bi mā ḥafiẓa Allāh* — righteous women are devoutly obedient and, when alone, protective of what Allah has entrusted them with — pairs obedience to God with guardianship in absence. *Qānitāt* — devoutly obedient, humbly constant — was read as obedience to God that includes fidelity to the marital trust, while *ḥāfiẓāt lil-ghayb* — protective in the unseen, when alone — was read as guarding chastity, property, and household secrets when the husband is not present, because God has guarded them. The phrase *bi mā ḥafiẓa Allāh* links her guarding to God's guarding: she protects what He has enabled her to protect. The sūrah has already described wealth as a standing support to be kept upright (4:5) and the orphan's property as requiring witnesses and reckoning (4:6); here that ethic of guarding appears inside marriage. What is entrusted — wealth from dowry and maintenance, the home, the children, and honour — is to be kept faithfully in absence as in presence. The Qur'an elsewhere praises *those who guard their chastity except with their spouses*, and the same guard is implied here, so that the home remains a shelter — *muḥṣin* — as lawful marriage was defined (4:24–25).

**Three Steps When Ill-Conduct Is Sensed**

The counsel *wa allātī takhāfūna nushūzahunna fa ʿiẓūhunna wa ahjurūhunna fī al-maḍājiʿ wa aḍribūhunna* — if you sense ill-conduct from your women, advise them first, if they persist, do not share their beds, but if they still persist, then discipline them gently — sets a graded response to *nushūz* — rising up, ill-conduct, breach of marital harmony. The first step *ʿiẓūhunna* — advise, admonish — is speech that reminds of God, of limits, and of the covenant as a firm commitment (4:21). The second step *ahjurūhunna fī al-maḍājiʿ* — do not share their beds, forsake them in the sleeping place — was read as withholding intimate closeness within the home, not as expelling or humiliating in public: a pause that signals seriousness without severing. The third step *aḍribūhunna* was read by early authorities and by Prophetic clarification as a light, non-injurious gesture that does not wound, break, or humiliate; many commentators and jurists emphasized that the Prophet ﷺ never struck a woman or servant, and described the best men as those who are best to their wives, with some holding that abandoning the third step is more excellent. The grading matters: each step is only reached if the prior did not amend, and each is bounded. The sūrah elsewhere commands *live with them in kindness* (4:19) and says to appoint mediators when a split is feared (4:35), showing that the aim is amendment and reconciliation, not punishment for its own sake.

**But If They Change Their Ways, Do Not Be Unjust to Them**

The limit *fa in aṭaʿnakum fa lā tabghū ʿalayhinna sabīlā* — but if they change their ways, do not be unjust to them, do not seek a way against them — closes the sequence. *Fa lā tabghū* — do not seek, do not pursue — forbids continuing the discipline after amendment, harassing with reminders, or reopening the matter to assert dominance. The verse requires that when harmony returns, the path against them ends. The sūrah has applied the same principle to the pair disciplined for *fāḥishah* — relieve them when they repent and mend (4:16) — and to trade where consent ends devouring (4:29); here it applies to the home: once the breach is mended, the household returns to kindness. The Qur'an elsewhere says that God loves not the aggressor, and this clause ensures the caretaking role does not become aggression.
