The caretaker who was tasked to spend from his wealth and to guard the family is now told that his very success in amending requires him to stop: the guard does not become a warden, and the home does not become a place of tallying past faults.

**Surely Allah Is Most High, All-Great**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna ʿaliyyan kabīrā* — surely Allah is Most High, All-Great — places the household under a higher authority than either spouse. *ʿAliyy* — Most High — and *Kabīr* — All-Great — remind the caretaker that his standing over maintenance is itself under a greater standing. The sūrah has used similar closings to temper power: All-Knowing, All-Wise over shares (4:11, 4:26), Most Forbearing over division (4:12), Witness over pledges (4:33), and here High and Great over domestic authority. Al-Rāzī notes that the verse therefore warns the husband who might misuse *qiwāmah* — caretaking — that there is a higher Maintainer who sees. That reminder is not abstract: the Prophetic teaching that the best of men are best to their wives makes the standard concrete, and the sūrah's next verse — appoint a mediator from his family and one from hers when a split is feared (4:35) — shows that the home is not a private realm where power is unchecked but a community matter where families are called in. To be caretaker is therefore to be accountable to the Most High, and to know that the authority given to keep the household upright will itself be weighed.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:35

> If you anticipate a split between them, appoint a mediator from his family and another from hers. If they desire reconciliation, Allah will restore harmony between them. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware

**When a Split Is Feared, Bring the Families In**

The verse begins with *wa in khiftum shiqāqa baynihimā* — if you anticipate a split between them. *Shiqāq* — a split, a rift, a pulling apart where each side goes to its own *shiqq* — edge, side — describes a marriage where harmony has cracked and the two are veering apart. The subject *khiftum* — you fear, you anticipate — was read as addressed to the community, the rulers, or the families who become aware, not only to the couple themselves, because the couple inside the rift may not see or want mediation. The command *fa abʿathū ḥakaman min ahlihi wa ḥakaman min ahlihā* — appoint a mediator from his family and another from hers — brings kin into the room for a reason the sūrah has been building: the family knows the history, the temperaments, the pressures, and the wealth that has been handled as a trust (4:2–6, 4:29). Two mediators — *ḥakaman* — one from each side — balance concern, so that neither spouse fears the other's family will dominate. The sūrah has already shown that family is both a tie of mercy — *arḥām* sharing the root of *raḥmah* (4:1) — and a structure for justice — heirs, witnesses, and shares. Here that structure becomes a shelter for the marriage itself, before the split becomes final.

**Two Mediators, One Purpose**

The choice of one from his family and one from hers was explained as wisdom about knowledge and trust: a mediator from his family can speak to him plainly without the defensiveness a stranger would trigger, and a mediator from her family can do the same for her. Both can hear what outsiders would not be told and can verify what each claims about dowry, maintenance, and conduct. The pair are called *ḥakam* — arbiters, judges — but their role in this verse was read as reconciliatory first: to listen, to advise, to remind of the firm commitment — *mīthāq ghalīẓ* (4:21) — and of the command to live with women fairly (4:19) and speak equitably (4:9). The sūrah's prior gradation for ill-conduct — advise, forsake in bed, discipline gently, and then cease when amendment appears (4:34) — already assumed that correction is attempted inside the home; this verse assumes that where the rift persists, help from outside the home is better than hardening inside it. The two mediators therefore embody the sūrah's larger method: bring the womb-tie back into the household that is at risk, because the same tie that was to be honoured at creation (4:1) can now be the tie that repairs.

**If They Desire Reconciliation, Allah Will Restore Harmony**

The promise *in yurīdā iṣlāḥan yuwaffiqi Allāhu baynahumā* — if they desire reconciliation, Allah will restore harmony between them — places success on two conditions and one divine act. The pronoun *in yurīdā* was read as the two spouses desiring, or as the two mediators desiring, or as all four desiring together, but the core is the same: where the will for *iṣlāḥ* — mending, reconciliation — is sincere, *tawfīq* — the bringing together, the enabling — comes from God. *Yuwaffiq* carries the sense of making two things meet at the right point, like a seam that holds. The sūrah has already promised that for those who repent and mend, relief follows (4:16), and that God wills to turn toward you and lighten your burdens (4:26–28); this verse is that lightening in the domain of marriage — where people want mending, God brings the fit. That does not guarantee that every mediation ends in staying together; the law allows separation with fairness where staying would be harm. But it guarantees that where the desire for repair is real, the help to repair will be given. The community that appoints the two mediators is therefore not only managing a dispute; it is creating a space where divine help can arrive, because God helps the hearts that have turned toward mending.

**All-Knowing, All-Aware Over What Is Hidden**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna ʿalīman khabīrā* — surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware — fits a verse about private conflict. *ʿAlīm* knows the history each spouse brings — the words said in the home, the wealth spent or withheld, the dowry given or pressured (4:19–21). *Khabīr* — All-Aware, intimately informed — knows the subtle motives the mediators cannot fully see: whether the desire for reconciliation is sincere or a tactic, whether the claim of ill-conduct masks a wish to reclaim a gift, whether fear of God or fear of family opinion is speaking. That pairing deters two abuses at once: the couple cannot deceive the mediators without God seeing, and the mediators cannot favour one side without God knowing. The sūrah has used similar closings to temper power — Most High, All-Great over caretaking (4:34), Witness over pledges (4:33), All-Knowing, All-Wise over shares (4:11, 4:26); here awareness tempers both spouses and families, reminding all that the arbitration table is also watched, and that the success of its work — *yuwaffiqi Allāhu* — depends on a sincerity that only God can fully weigh. Honesty before that watch is the first step of any settlement.

**Mediation Before Dissolution**

Placed after the caretaking and discipline gradation (4:34) and before the comprehensive ethic of kindness that will follow (4:36), this verse positions mediation as the sūrah's preferred way to handle a feared split. It does not rush to dissolution, nor does it urge the couple to endure harm without help; it brings the families in early, when *khiftum* — fear — first appears, so that the rift does not harden into enmity. That early entry reflects the Medinan community's new kinship, where migrants and hosts were already bound by pledge — give them their share when you have pledged (4:33) — and where inheritance and maintenance had been made precise to reduce quarrels. The mediators from each side extend that kinship into the home. By appointing both, the verse also protects the woman's voice where custom had once inherited her against her will (4:19): she is given an arbiter from her own family who knows her right to dowry and to kind companionship. A split that might have become a contest of power becomes a conversation between two families whose interests are aligned toward *iṣlāḥ* if that remains possible; where it is not, the same families will ensure that separation, if it comes, is done with witnesses and with *sufficient is Allah as Reckoner* (4:6) still true.

**The Path That Desires Mending**

The verse's conditional promise — if they desire reconciliation, Allah will bring harmony — teaches that the outcome rests on desire as much as on procedure. Two mediators can meet, but if both spouses desire dominance rather than mending, no *tawfīq* will hold. Conversely, a couple that desires mending will find that desire itself becomes the invitation for divine help, even where means are small. That pattern matches the sūrah's opening will to make things clear and turn toward you (4:26) and to lighten because you are weak (4:28): the law provides the mediators, but God provides the joining. The sūrah will soon broaden that ethic outward — worship God, be kind to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, neighbours near and distant, companions, travellers, and those in your possession (4:36) — showing that mending between two spouses is a single case of a larger repair the community is asked to undertake. A community that learns to appoint fairly, to desire sincerely, and to trust the All-Knowing, All-Aware to bring the seam together will have learned more than how to save a marriage; it will have learned how to hold itself together.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:36

> Worship Allah ˹alone˺ and associate none with Him. And be kind to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, near and distant neighbours, close friends, ˹needy˺ travellers, and those ˹bondspeople˺ in your possession. Surely Allah does not like whoever is arrogant, boastful—

**Worship Alone, Then Kindness Outward in Circles**

The verse begins with the foundation of all duty: *wa ʿbudū Allāha wa lā tushrikū bihi shayʾā* — worship Allah alone and associate none with Him. After thirty-five verses of law about orphans, dowries, shares, and marriage, the sūrah returns to the root that makes those laws worship rather than mere administration. Association — *shirk* — is not only bowing to an idol; it is placing any partner beside God in devotion, trust, or obedience, including the wealth, lineage, or desire that the sūrah has shown can rival revelation. The command is followed immediately by kindness in expanding circles: *wa bi al-wālidayni iḥsānan wa bi dhī al-qurbā wa al-yatāmā wa al-masākīn wa al-jāri dhī al-qurbā wa al-jāri al-junub wa al-ṣāḥibi bi al-janb wa ibni al-sabīl wa mā malakat aymānukum* — be kind to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, near and distant neighbours, close friends, needy travellers, and those in your possession. The list moves from the closest tie — parents — to the widest — the traveller far from home — and to the most dependent — those in your possession. The sūrah has already guarded each of those groups separately: parents with a fixed third or sixth (4:11), orphans with return and witnesses (4:6), the poor and needy present at distribution (4:8), and bondspeople with permission, dowry, and half penalty (4:25). Here they are gathered into one ethic of *iḥsān* — kind, beautiful doing — that flows from worship without association: the One worshipped alone is the One whose mercy is to be mirrored in layers outward.

**Why Parents Follow Worship Without Gap**

The pairing *wa bi al-wālidayni iḥsānan* directly after worship was explained as showing that gratitude to the Creator is followed by gratitude to the means of creation. The Qur'an elsewhere says *Be grateful to Me and to your parents* (31:14), and the same adjacency appears here. Parents are named first among people because the sūrah opened with *He created you from a single soul, and from it its mate, and spread countless men and women* (4:1), rooting family in creation; to be kind to parents is therefore to honour the channel of that spreading. The sūrah has already secured parents' shares equally when offspring exist (4:11) and told the child not to crave what another was given but to ask God for bounty (4:32); kindness to parents completes that picture with conduct, not only fractions. *Iḥsān* here was read as good companionship, gentle speech, provision without reminder, and obedience in what is lawful. Kindness here is the moral counterpart to the fixed share there: one gives the portion, the other gives the manner.

**Relatives, Orphans, and the Poor Near the Heart of the Law**

The triad *dhī al-qurbā wa al-yatāmā wa al-masākīn* — relatives, orphans, the poor — repeats the core of the sūrah's first laws. Relatives were to be honoured as womb-ties sharing the root of mercy (4:1); orphans were to have wealth returned without substitution (4:2), tested and witnessed (4:6), and not consumed as fire (4:10); the poor and needy present at distribution were to receive provision with kind words (4:8). To list them together here as objects of *iḥsān* shows that the sūrah's ethic is not episodic but sustained: the same persons who receive legal protection also deserve habitual kindness beyond the moment of settlement. The Qur'an elsewhere says *righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the east or west, but that you believe and give wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveller* (2:177), and that verse helps read this one: the donation at distribution (4:8) is a single instance of a larger generosity that does not wait for an estate to divide. A community that learns to give to relatives, orphans, and the poor when it has little will give justly when it has much, because the habit precedes the occasion. The sūrah therefore lifts the specific rulings into a character.

**Neighbours Near and Far, and the Companion at Your Side**

The list widens to *al-jāri dhī al-qurbā wa al-jāri al-junub wa al-ṣāḥibi bi al-janb* — near and distant neighbours, and the close companion. Near neighbour was read as the neighbour who is also kin or whose home is close; the distant neighbour is the one farther in kin or distance; the companion at the side includes the spouse, the travel companion, and the colleague in work or study. The inclusion matters because the sūrah has focused on household law — dowries, shares, caretaking — and could be heard as concerned only with kin; by naming neighbours and companions, it extends *iḥsān* to the streets around the house and the road beside the traveller. The Prophet ﷺ emphasized neighbourhood rights so strongly that companions thought the neighbour might be made an heir — a report that shows how seriously the community heard this verse. The sūrah has already said *you are from one another* (4:25) and *you know not which of them are nearer to you in benefit* (4:11); those principles apply to neighbours as well, whose benefit may come in need at night, in security, or in daily peace. To honour the neighbour near and distant is to honour the single soul from which all spread (4:1) at the scale of daily life.

**The Traveller and Those in Your Possession**

The closing pair *ibni al-sabīl wa mā malakat aymānukum* — needy travellers and those in your possession — reaches the most transient and the most dependent. The traveller — *ibn al-sabīl*, literally child of the road — is far from his own support; the sūrah elsewhere lists him among those entitled to provision, and the Medinan community of migrants knew that state personally. Those in your possession — bondspeople — were under the household's direct authority; the sūrah has already regulated their marriage with permission, fair dowry, and chastity (4:25), and has encouraged freeing as a path. *Iḥsān* to them was read as kind treatment, sufficient provision, not overburdening, and mercy in command. The sūrah began by spreading humanity from one soul and then protected the weakest holders of property; here it protects the weakest persons under a household's hand. The verse closes with *inna Allāha lā yuḥibbu man kāna mukhtālan fakhūrā* — surely Allah does not like whoever is arrogant, boastful — whose full description spills into the next verse (4:37) as stingy, promoting stinginess, and concealing bounty. Arrogance and boastfulness were seen as the inner block to the entire list: the one who worships alone does not see himself as source, and the one who is kind in circles does not see himself as higher. That block will be detailed next, but this verse already names its antidote — worship without partner, and kindness that moves outward until it reaches the traveller passing by and the servant inside the home.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:37

> those who are stingy, promote stinginess among people, and withhold Allah's bounties. We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment

**Arrogant and Boastful Made Visible Through Stinginess**

This verse completes the portrait begun at the end of the previous one: *surely Allah does not like whoever is arrogant, boastful* (4:36) — *alladhīna yabkhalūna wa yaʾmurūna al-nāsa bi al-bukhl wa yaktumūna mā ātāhumu Allāhu min faḍlihi* — those who are stingy, promote stinginess among people, and withhold Allah's bounties. The connection was read as cause and effect. *Ikhtiyāl* — arrogance, strutting — and *fakhr* — boasting — inflate the self, and the inflated self holds wealth tightly because wealth is the prop of its image. *Bukhl* — stinginess — is therefore not only a habit with coin; it is the financial form of arrogance. The sūrah has just commanded *iḥsān* — kind, beautiful doing — to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, neighbours near and distant, companions, travellers, and those in possession (4:36). Stinginess is the refusal of that entire movement outward: it keeps what was given as standing support — *qiyāman* (4:5) — for the household and the community locked in the hand, rather than letting it circulate as provision, dowry, inheritance shares, and trade by mutual consent (4:29). The verse therefore draws a straight line from worship without association (4:36) to openness of hand; to associate oneself with God in pride is to close the hand that worship should open.

**Promoting Stinginess Among People**

The addition *wa yaʾmurūna al-nāsa bi al-bukhl* — and promote stinginess among people — deepens the fault from private tightness to social teaching. The stingy person does not only withhold; he counsels others to withhold, normalising restraint as prudence and caricaturing generosity as waste. Early commentators noted that this promotion could be open — telling others not to give — or quiet — modelling hesitation, praising hoarding, or shaming those who give to orphans, relatives, or neighbours. The sūrah has seen both forms already: guardians who consumed orphan wealth hastily before the child grew to demand it (4:6) and those who devoured wealth by falsehood in trade (4:29) each needed a justification that made taking look careful and giving look naive; to command stinginess is to provide that justification for others. The Qur'an elsewhere condemns those who *enjoin miserliness* and links it to disbelief in God's bounty, because the call to withhold is also a call to distrust the One who replenishes. In a community learning to distribute estates with provision for bystanders (4:8), to give dowries graciously (4:4), and to return pledges (4:33), a voice that says keep, do not give, pulls directly against the sūrah's ethic of circulation.

**Withholding What Allah Gave of His Bounty**

The third trait *wa yaktumūna mā ātāhumu Allāhu min faḍlihi* — and withhold Allah's bounties — uses *katama* — to conceal, to hide — the same verb the sūrah uses for those who conceal what God gave of the Scripture (4:44). Here the concealment is of bounty — *faḍl* — the surplus God gave to be spent, shared, and acknowledged. *Faḍl* in this sūrah has appeared as the apportioning among people not to be craved but to be asked for (4:32), and as the bounty of Gardens for those who keep limits (4:13). To hide bounty is both to hide wealth itself — not spending it where *iḥsān* would — and to hide gratitude — not admitting it came from God. The Qur'an elsewhere says *if you are grateful, I will give you more* (14:7), making gratitude the condition for increase; concealment is the opposite, a denial that the gift needs acknowledgment. The sūrah has already said God is ever Merciful to you (4:29); the stingy person acts as though mercy will not return if he gives.

**Prepared Humiliating Punishment**

The recompense *wa aʿtadnā lil-kāfirīna ʿadhāban muhīnā* — We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment — gathers the three traits into the category of *kufr* — covering, ingratitude, disbelief — where the gift is covered rather than shared. *Muhīn* — humiliating — appears again for those who exceed God's limits (4:14), showing that humiliation is the proper reversal for the arrogant and boastful: what was concealed as bounty becomes exposed as lack when the punishment arrives, and what was boasted as status becomes humbled. The verb *aʿtadnā* — We have prepared — stresses that the recompense is not improvised; like the Gardens prepared for those who keep limits (4:13) and the painful punishment prepared for those who defer repentance until death (4:18), it is readied. The sūrah elsewhere promises that *Allah never wrongs even by an atom's weight, and if it is good He multiplies it many times over* (4:40), and that multiplication is the alternative economy the stingy refuse to trust. The verse therefore contrasts two economies: one where giving is loss, and one where giving is multiplication; one where withholding looks safe, and one where it is prepared humiliation. The sūrah invites the first to be exchanged for the second before the preparation becomes arrival.

**A Community Trained to Circulate**

Placed between the comprehensive ethic of kindness (4:36) and the warning against spending to show off (4:38), this verse identifies the inner disease that blocks that ethic. The sūrah has taught the community to circulate wealth at every sensitive point — return the orphan's wealth with witnesses (4:6), give women dowries graciously (4:4), divide estates after debts and bequests (4:11–12), offer provision to bystanders with kind speech (4:8), trade by mutual consent (4:29), and ask God for bounty rather than crave another's (4:32). Each act requires a hand that opens. Stinginess closes that hand, and promoting stinginess closes others' hands as well. The verse does not only threaten; it diagnoses: the one who does not like to give is the one who loves to be seen as high — *mukhtāl fakhūr* — and who believes bounty is his own achievement to be hidden rather than God's gift to be shared. To heal that, the sūrah offers the opposite practice: worship without partner, which humbles the self before God, and *iḥsān* that moves outward in circles until it reaches the traveller and the servant. A community that learns those two moves will find stinginess unnatural, because the hand that has been opened in worship does not easily close when a relative, orphan, or neighbour is in need.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:38

> Likewise for those who spend their wealth to show off and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. And whoever takes Satan as an associate—what an evil associate they have

**Spending to Be Seen**

The verse adds a second example of disliked giving to complement stinginess: *wa alladhīna yunfiqūna amwālahum riʾāʾa al-nāsi wa lā yuʾminūna bi Allāhi wa lā bi al-yawmi al-ākhiri* — likewise for those who spend their wealth to show off and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. The previous portrait was the hand that never opens — the stingy who promote stinginess and conceal bounty (4:37); this portrait is the hand that opens only for eyes. *Riʾāʾ* — show, display — was read as doing a deed so that people see and praise, rather than so that God accepts. The act itself — spending — may look generous; orphans might be fed, neighbours might receive, trade might flow, yet the motive empties it. The sūrah has just commended *iḥsān* to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, neighbours, companions, travellers, and those in possession (4:36), and has warned against devouring wealth by falsehood (4:29). Showing off corrupts *iḥsān* at its source, because the recipient becomes a prop for reputation rather than a person honoured for God's sake. The Qur'an elsewhere says *do not nullify your charities with reminders and hurt, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people* (2:264) — an image of nullification that matches the prepared humiliating punishment for the concealer (4:37): both spenders find their spending erased, one by withholding, the other by misdirection.

**Spending Without Belief in God or the Last Day**

The clause *wa lā yuʾminūna bi Allāhi wa lā bi al-yawmi al-ākhiri* ties the motive to the creed. Not believing in God or the Last Day does not only mean formal denial; it includes acting as though no watch is kept and no return is coming. The sūrah has insisted that God is ever Watchful (4:1), sufficient as Reckoner (4:6), Witness over all things (4:33), All-Knowing, Most Forbearing (4:12), and ever Merciful to you (4:29); to spend for show is to act as though that watch is absent and as though the only accounting is people's praise today. The Last Day is the other half of the same belief, because it promises that even an atom's weight will be counted and that good will be multiplied many times over (4:40). The ostentatious spender does not trust that multiplication; he seeks immediate multiplication in reputation. That is why the verse pairs spending to be seen with disbelief in the Last Day, not only with love of praise. The sūrah has already contrasted the Gardens that flow for keeping limits (4:13) and the Fire prepared for exceeding them (4:14) and for persisting until death (4:18); the spender to be seen has chosen the audience of the market over the audience of that Day, and his deed follows the audience he chose.

**Whoever Takes Satan as an Associate**

The warning *wa man yakun al-shayṭānu lahu qarīnan fa sāʾa qarīnā* — and whoever takes Satan as an associate, what an evil associate they have — names the companion behind both portraits. *Qarīn* — close associate, companion at the side — echoes *al-ṣāḥibi bi al-janb* — the companion at your side — commended for kindness in 4:36, but here the companion is the adversary who whispers that withholding is prudence and that showing off is prudence's twin. The sūrah elsewhere says that Satan commands indecency and love of hoarded wealth, and that the deviators prefer his fellowship when they wish others to swerve greatly (4:27). To take him as *qarīn* is to keep his counsel, to follow the inclination that tightens the hand or opens it for eyes. *Fa sāʾa qarīnā* — what an evil companion — is both description and discouragement: a companion shapes the walk, and a companion at the side is present at the moment of spending, trading, and dividing estates. The Qur'an elsewhere says that when witnesses are brought on the Day of Judgment, the person will wish that between himself and his *qarīn* there were the distance of east and west. The verse anticipates that wish by naming it now, when the choice of companion can still be changed.

**Two Failures With One Root**

Read with the previous verse, the pair forms a complete diagnosis of corrupted generosity. Stinginess withholds God's bounty and teaches others to withhold (4:37); ostentation spends bounty but diverts its aim from God and the Last Day to people's eyes. Both refuse the same centre: spending for God who gave the bounty and who will multiply it on a Day that is coming. The sūrah has shown the correct centre repeatedly — give women dowries graciously as a free gift (4:4), return the orphan's wealth with witnesses under God as Reckoner (4:6), divide after debts and bequests within limits watched by the Witness (4:33), trade by mutual consent under the ever Merciful (4:29), and ask God for bounty rather than crave another's (4:32). Each act is done with God and the Last Day in view, even when the transaction is small. Ostentatious spending may mimic those acts in form — a gift to a relative, a provision to a bystander, a trade that looks consensual — but the sūrah distinguishes by audience: if the audience is people, the act is with Satan as *qarīn*; if the audience is God, the act is with Him as Guardian and Helper (4:45). The sūrah leaves no middle where spending counts without an audience; it asks only which audience is chosen.

**The Humiliating and the Evil as Two Ends**

The recompense for the stingy was a prepared humiliating punishment (4:37); the companion for the ostentatious is an evil associate (4:38). The two names match the two sins' pretensions: stinginess pretended to be status, so it is humiliated; ostentation pretended to be honour, so it is left with an evil companion. Both are social in nature, because both sins are social — one teaches others to withhold, the other performs for others to see. The sūrah's next verse will ask *what harm could have come to them if they had believed in Allah and the Last Day and donated from what Allah provided for them?* (4:39), making the alternative explicit: belief and donation from what was provided, audience God, Day believed, companion God as Guardian and Helper. Between the two verses, the reader is given a simple audit for his own spending: is this bounty being concealed, spent for show, or donated from what was provided with the Last Day in view? The answer determines not only whether others benefit but who walks at his side as he gives, and whose prepared recompense awaits him.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:39

> What harm could have come to them if they had believed in Allah and the Last Day and donated from what Allah has provided for them? And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of them

**What Harm Would Belief and Donation Have Done**

The question *wa mādhā ʿalayhim law āmanū bi Allāhi wa al-yawmi al-ākhiri wa anfaqū mimmā razaqahumu Allāh* — what harm could have come to them if they had believed in Allah and the Last Day and donated from what Allah has provided for them — follows the double portrait of the stingy who conceal bounty (4:37) and the ostentatious who spend for eyes without belief (4:38). Both portraits showed wealth held or spent without God as audience; this verse asks what would have been lost if the same wealth had been donated with belief. The answer implied is nothing — the harm is imagined, not real. Belief in God does not subtract from wealth; belief in the Last Day does not impoverish; donating *mimmā razaqahumu Allāh* — from what Allah provided — returns to the Giver a portion of what He gave. The Qur'an elsewhere says that donation does not decrease wealth but multiplies it, and the sūrah will immediately confirm that God never wrongs even by an atom's weight and multiplies good many times over (4:40). The question therefore reframes generosity as costless in the true accounting and stinginess as the only costly choice: the harm feared — less to keep, less to show — is shown to be no harm at all.

**Belief in God, Belief in the Last Day**

The pairing *āmanū bi Allāhi wa al-yawmi al-ākhiri* gathers the two beliefs that correct the two corruptions. Belief in God corrects spending without Him as audience: to believe He gave the provision is to want to spend it where He sees. Belief in the Last Day corrects concealment and show, because both assume that the only return is immediate — either saved in the chest or praised in the market. The sūrah has prepared both beliefs: God is ever Watchful (4:1), sufficient as Reckoner (4:6), Witness over all things (4:33), All-Knowing and Most Forbearing (4:12), ever Merciful to you (4:29); the Last Day is the time when a witness is brought from every community and the Messenger is brought as witness against his own (4:41), when deniers will wish to be dust and will not be able to hide anything from God (4:42). To believe those two is to spend differently today — not because wealth is less loved but because it is more understood. The one who believes that provision came from God sees donation as returning, not losing; the one who believes that an atom's weight of good will be multiplied (4:40) sees withholding as the only loss.

**Donated From What Allah Provided**

The phrase *mimmā razaqahumu Allāh* was stressed as both the source and the limit of donation. The wealth proposed for spending is not an alien exaction but a portion of what was already given as *faḍl* — bounty — the same bounty the stingy concealed (4:37) and that others were told to ask for rather than crave (4:32). The Qur'an elsewhere says *spend from what We have provided you before a Day comes where there is no trade* (2:254), and the same urgency underlies this question: to donate from what was provided is to acknowledge receipt, and that acknowledgment is itself worship, as the sūrah opened the ethic of kindness with *worship Allah and associate none with Him, and be kind* (4:36). Donation without belief, as in ostentation, is activity without worship; withholding with concealment is worship of wealth; donation from what was provided, with belief, is worship that includes wealth. The amount is not specified — *mimmā*, some of what — leaving room for the small provision for bystanders at distribution (4:8), the fair provision for a poor guardian (4:6), the gracious dowry (4:4), and trade by mutual consent (4:29): each is a form of spending from what was provided.

**And Allah Has Perfect Knowledge of Them**

The closing *wa kāna Allāhu bihim ʿalīmā* — and Allah has perfect knowledge of them — answers the hidden calculation behind stinginess and ostentation. The stingy hide bounty as though God will not note the concealment; the ostentatious spend for people as though God will not see the motive. The sūrah has repeated that He is Watchful (4:1), Reckoner (4:6), Witness (4:33); here knowledge is said to cover *them* — *bihim* — the very persons who made the choice. That knowledge does two things. For the one who feared harm from believing and donating, it reassures: the donation done with belief is known, and what is known is not lost — it will be multiplied (4:40) and brought with witnesses (4:41). For the one who thought hiding or showing would pass, it warns: the concealment and the show are also known, and on the Day when nothing can be hidden from God (4:42), the audience that was sought — people's eyes — will not avail. Perfect knowledge is therefore the quiet audit behind the question what harm would belief and donation have done; the answer, no harm, is guaranteed because the One who knows is also the One who multiplies and rewards out of grace.

**The Easy Alternative**

Read with the verses before and after, this question is the sūrah's gentlest invitation to change. Between the diagnosis of stinginess and ostentation with Satan as evil companion (4:37–38) and the promise that not an atom's weight is wronged and that good is multiplied many times (4:40), it places a simple reflection. No new law is added; no new penalty is named. The reader is asked to imagine the alternative path — belief and donation from what was provided — and to weigh its cost. The cost is none; the gain is knowledge, multiplication, and a great reward from grace. The alternative path's companions are the opposite of the evil associate: Allah as Guardian and Helper (4:45), and the witnesses who will be brought to confirm. In that light, the sūrah's earlier ethic of *iḥsān* to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, neighbours, companions, travellers, and those in possession (4:36) becomes not a burden but the very donation the question proposes. To have believed and to have given from what was provided is to have walked the clear, guided, and lightened way (4:26–28) while the chance remained — and to have left nothing for perfect knowledge to record as harm.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:40

> Indeed, Allah never wrongs ˹anyone˺—even by an atom's weight. And if it is a good deed, He will multiply it many times over and will give a great reward out of His grace

**Not Even by an Atom's Weight**

The assurance *inna Allāha lā yaẓlimu mithqāla dharratin* — indeed, Allah never wrongs even by an atom's weight — follows the question what harm would belief and donation have done (4:39) and answers it with a measure smaller than sight. *Dharrah* — atom, speck, the smallest mote seen in a sunbeam — was read as the least conceivable quantum of weight; to say God does not wrong by that weight is to say justice at the smallest scale is exact. The sūrah has been precise about small amounts before — whether inheritance is little or much (4:7), a small provision for bystanders (4:8), provision from orphan wealth without waste (4:5–6), trade by mutual consent where consent must be genuine (4:29). Here precision becomes a divine attribute: the One who appointed fractions — half, quarter, eighth, sixth, third, two-thirds — after debts and bequests (4:11–12), who required four witnesses before sanction (4:15), and who halved penalty where appropriate (4:25) is now said to weigh at a resolution finer than any human scale. The Qur'an elsewhere says *whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it* (99:7–8), and this verse is the premise that makes that seeing just. Nothing is rounded away — neither a hidden donation nor a concealed bounty.

**If It Is a Good Deed, He Will Multiply It**

The second clause *wa in taku ḥasanatan yuḍāʿifhā* — and if it is a good deed, He will multiply it many times over — reverses the economy of withholding. Stinginess and ostentation (4:37–38) were both calculations that giving loses; this verse says giving gains, not one-to-one but multiplied. *Yuḍāʿif* — to double, to make many — was read as at least tenfold, as elsewhere *whoever brings a good deed will have ten like it* (6:160), and in other passages as seven hundredfold or without count where God wills, showing that multiplication is not a fixed rate but a generosity. The sūrah has already promised that avoiding major sins leads to covering lesser ones and an honourable entry (4:31), and that belief and donation from what was provided would have harmed no one (4:39); multiplication explains why. A small provision offered with kind speech (4:8), a fair dowry given graciously (4:4), a just division witnessed (4:6), or a quiet trade done with genuine mutual content (4:29) — each may seem modest, but the One who weighs atoms multiplies them. That multiplication is not a metaphor for market profit; it is the market of the next life, where the currency is grace and the auditor is the One who never wrongs by even an atom.

**And Will Give a Great Reward Out of His Grace**

The addition *wa yuʾti min ladunhu ajran ʿaẓīmā* — and will give a great reward out of His grace — separates multiplication from grace. Multiplication is recompense for the deed; the great reward — *ajr ʿaẓīm* — is from *ladunhu* — from His presence, out of His grace. The sūrah elsewhere calls that great reward Gardens under which rivers flow for those who keep limits (4:13) and an honourable entry for those who avoid major sins (4:31); here it is promised for the atom's weight of good that He multiplies, showing that even the smallest good, once multiplied, is then further crowned with a gift beyond calculation. The pairing matters because it answers two fears at once: the fear that a small good will be ignored, and the fear that the great reward is unreachable for the weak. The first is answered by *not even an atom's weight is wronged*; the second is answered by grace that gives beyond multiplication. The weak for whom the sūrah wills to lighten burdens (4:28) and to turn in mercy (4:26–27) are precisely those who can offer only an atom's weight, and the verse tells them that weight is enough to set multiplication and grace in motion.

**A Verse That Secures Trust in Division and Donation**

Placed where it is, this verse secures trust at the two points where trust is most tested: division and donation. Division of estates and trade requires confidence that a sixth or eighth will be counted exactly and that mutual consent will be honoured; the atom's weight that is never wronged is that confidence. Donation to relatives, orphans, neighbours, and travellers (4:36) requires confidence that what is given from what was provided (4:39) will not be lost; multiplication and a great reward out of grace is that confidence. The sūrah has warned that deliberate devouring and killing will be met with Fire that is easy for God (4:30), and that stinginess concealing bounty and spending for show with Satan as associate (4:37–38) lead to humiliation and evil company; this verse is the other side of that economy, where the One who finds punishment easy also finds it easy to multiply. The same ease that burns the deliberate overstep multiplies the atom's weight of good, because both proceed from perfect knowledge. The Name that closed the previous verse — *Allah has perfect knowledge of them* (4:39) — becomes here the guarantee that knowledge is not idle: what is known at the smallest scale is weighed justly and then exceeded in generosity.

**Justice That Is Exact and Grace That Exceeds**

The sūrah's balance between justice and grace is stated here in a single sentence. Justice is exact — not even an atom's weight of wrong — so that the wronged — orphan, widow, heir, neighbour — can trust that no portion is rounded away. Grace exceeds — multiplication and a great reward from His presence — so that the doer of good, even with a single sincere good deed, can hope for more than its flat value. That pairing reflects the divine Names that have closed this section: All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:26), All-Knowing, Most Forbearing (4:12), Witness over all things (4:33), and ever Merciful to you (4:29) — knowledge ensures the atom is not missed; wisdom determines its multiplication; witness secures it; mercy adds the great reward. For the weak created weak (4:28), that pairing is the lightest of burdens: keep the major limits (4:31), believe and donate from what was provided (4:39), and know that even the smallest good is never wronged but multiplied and crowned. The next verses will bring witnesses from every community and the Messenger as witness (4:41); what those witnesses will confirm is exactly this — that not an atom's weight was lost, and that what was done for God was multiplied many times over and met with a great reward from His grace.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:41

> So how will it be when We bring a witness from every faith-community and bring you ˹O Prophet˺ as a witness against yours

**A Question That Opens the Day of Witnesses**

The verse asks *fa kayfa idhā jiʾnā min kulli ummatin bi shahīdin wa jiʾnā bika ʿalā hāʾulāʾi shahīdā* — so how will it be when We bring a witness from every faith-community and bring you as a witness against yours? The question *kayfa* — how — invites the listener to imagine a scene whose gravity cannot be answered with words. After promises that not an atom's weight is wronged and that good is multiplied (4:40), and after the offer to cover lesser faults for those who avoid major sins (4:31), the sūrah turns to the Day when those promises are seen. The witnesses — *shahīd* — from every *ummah* were explained as the prophets sent to each community, who will testify whether they conveyed, whether they were believed, and how people responded to limits about property, marriage, and worship. The Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ is then brought as witness over his own community — the one addressed throughout al-Nisāʾ with *yā ayyuhā al-nās* (4:1) and *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū* (4:29). The Qur'an elsewhere says *We have made you a middle community that you may be witnesses over people and the Messenger may be witness over you* (2:143), showing that witness is both a burden and an honour. The question *how will it be* does not seek information; it seeks awe before a court where every *ummah* stands with its prophet, and this *ummah* stands with its own.

**Every Community With Its Witness**

The phrase *min kulli ummatin bi shahīdin* was read as each community brought with its messenger, who will confirm the message delivered. The sūrah has detailed what that message contained in this context: creation from a single soul and guarding womb-ties (4:1), returning orphan wealth with witnesses (4:6), honouring obligatory shares after debts (4:11–12), guarding marriage through dowries and chastity (4:4, 4:24), and forbidding devouring by falsehood (4:29). On the Day, the question will be whether those limits were kept. The witness from each community will speak not from hearsay but from presence, as one who lived among his people and warned them. The scene therefore mirrors the sūrah's insistence that human witnesses secure handovers (4:6) and that God is Witness over all things (4:33): what was done with witnesses on earth — the estate divided, the dowry given, the trade made by mutual consent — will be confirmed by the greater witnesses who saw the community as a whole.

**And You as Witness Against Yours**

The addition *wa jiʾnā bika ʿalā hāʾulāʾi shahīdā* — and bring you as witness over these — singles out the Prophet ﷺ for this audience. His witness was understood as twofold: that he conveyed the limits about inheritance and marriage that the sūrah has spelled out, and that he saw how his community received them — who kept limits and entered Gardens (4:13) and who exceeded them and faced humiliation (4:14). The Prophet ﷺ is elsewhere described as witness, bearer of good tidings, and warner, and this verse places that witness at the climax of history. The community that was told *obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you, and refer disputes to Allah and His Messenger* (4:59) will find the one to whom disputes were to be referred now testifying about how they were resolved. The question *how will it be* therefore carries a personal weight for believers: the one who knows their names will be the one who speaks. The sūrah has said that the Messenger's clarification makes obedience to him part of keeping limits (4:13–14); here that clarification becomes testimony.

**A Scene That Holds Atom's Weight and Great Reward Together**

The verse follows the assurance that not an atom's weight is wronged and that good is multiplied with a great reward from grace (4:40), and it shows where that assurance is displayed. The witnesses are brought because accounting must be seen to be exact. The atom's weight that was never wronged in the estate division, the dowry left where it was given despite a heap of gold (4:20), the small provision offered with kind speech (4:8) — all will appear not as hidden details but as recorded deeds with witnesses. The promise of multiplication and grace and the warning of Fire that is easy for God (4:30) are both made credible by the court that this verse opens: without witnesses, the promises could feel distant; with prophets and with the Prophet ﷺ as witnesses, the promises become a scene the reader can picture and therefore prepare for. The sūrah has already said that God is ever Watchful (4:1) and sufficient as Reckoner (4:6) and Helper (4:45); this verse is that watch and reckoning made visible, with human witnesses who lived the law brought to confirm.

**How Will It Be — the Question That Changes How One Counts**

The unanswered *how* is the verse's teaching. It does not describe the outcome for the disobedient in this sentence; the next verse will say they will wish to be dust and will not be able to hide anything from God (4:42). Here the question is left hanging so that the listener supplies the answer with his own conduct. A person who handles an orphan's property, a dowry, or a sale while remembering that a witness from his own community — the Prophet ﷺ — will be brought about those very transactions will count differently. The sūrah's earlier question — *how could you take it after intimacy and firm commitment?* (4:21) — worked the same way, inviting conscience to answer; this greater *how* does the same on the scale of history. The sūrah began with creation from a single soul and will soon remind that every soul will be judged with a witness; between those two moments, the believer is given the map — make things clear, guide to noble ways, turn in mercy (4:26), lighten because you are weak (4:28), avoid major sins (4:31), ask God for bounty rather than crave another's (4:32). The witness scene gathers that map and asks, when all of that is brought with its witnesses, *how will it be?* The one who keeps limits while remembering the witness will hope that the answer for him is Gardens and honour; the one who exceeds them will already feel why the next verse says wishing to be dust will be the only wish left.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:42

> On that Day, those who denied ˹Allah˺ and disobeyed the Messenger will wish they were reduced to dust. And they will never be able to hide anything from Allah

**Wishing to Be Dust**

The verse answers the hanging *how* of the previous scene. *Yawmaʾidhin yawaddu alladhīna kafarū wa ʿaṣaw al-rasūla law tusawwā bihimu al-arḍ* — on that Day, those who denied and disobeyed the Messenger will wish they were reduced to dust, that the earth were levelled over them. The wish *law tusawwā bihimu al-arḍ* — that the earth were made even with them — was explained as the desire to be nothing rather than to face the witness brought from every community and the Prophet ﷺ as witness over his own (4:41). The sūrah has shown what was denied and disobeyed: limits about orphans' wealth (4:10), inheritance after debts (4:11–12), guarding marriage and dowry (4:19–21), and trade by mutual consent (4:29). To have denied that those limits came from God, and to have disobeyed the Messenger who clarified them, was to choose custom over revelation. On the Day when witnesses confirm that the message was made clear (4:26) and that burdens were lightened because humankind was created weak (4:28), that choice stands exposed. The wish to be dust is not repentance; it is the final awareness that disobedience was not hidden, as the next clause says — and that being nothing would be easier than being seen as one who was shown clarity and turned away.

**Those Who Denied and Disobeyed the Messenger**

The pairing *kafarū wa ʿaṣaw al-rasūla* gathers two groups and two modes. *Kafarū* — denied — covers those who covered the bounty and the sign, as the stingy concealed what God gave and the ostentatious spent for eyes without belief (4:37–38). *ʿAṣaw al-rasūla* — disobeyed the Messenger — covers those who heard the shares, the bar on reclaiming dowries, and the command to appoint mediators yet followed desires to deviate greatly (4:27). The sūrah has linked disbelief and disobedience throughout: *whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and exceeds His limits will be cast into Fire* (4:14), and *whoever takes Satan as associate, what an evil associate* (4:38), where the associate's counsel is disobedience. The Day groups them because their outcome converges: to deny is to refuse the source; to disobey the Messenger is to refuse the route that makes the source practicable. Both leave the person without a limit to keep and without a turn to take, because turning depends on believing and on following the one sent to make things clear. The wish to be levelled with earth therefore follows both paths, because both end at the same court without an answer.

**And They Will Never Be Able to Hide Anything from Allah**

The clause *wa lā yaktumūna Allāha ḥadīthā* — and they will never be able to hide anything from Allah — closes the scene with knowledge. *Ḥadīth* — speech, statement, narration — was read as any statement they might wish to hide: the hidden mixing of orphan wealth (4:2), the pressured dowry return (4:19–20), the fraudulent trade (4:29), the words of distortion such as *we hear and we disobey* (4:46). On the Day when witnesses are brought (4:41), hiding fails because the One who is ever Watchful (4:1), sufficient as Reckoner (4:6), Witness over all things (4:33), and All-Knowing, All-Aware (4:35) is the One to whom no speech is concealed. The Qur'an elsewhere says that hands, feet, and skin will testify, and that records will not leave small or great except counted. Here the same certainty is stated simply: no hiding. The sūrah has warned that God has perfect knowledge of them (4:39) and that He never wrongs even by an atom's weight but multiplies good (4:40); that atom-level accounting now becomes the reason no speech can be hidden. What was concealed as bounty (4:37) will be known as concealed; what was spent for show (4:38) will be known as shown. The Day does not need new evidence; it reveals what perfect knowledge already contained.

**Dust as the Desired Alternative to Exposure**

To wish to be dust is the final form of the sūrah's earlier wish to deviate. Those who follow desires wished you to deviate greatly (4:27), to tilt away from the clear path; here the deviators wish the tilt had never happened and that the earth would cover them. The image of dust recalls the creation from a single soul and the spreading as countless men and women (4:1), and the reminder that humankind was created weak (4:28) — dust is the beginning of that creation, *from dust He created you*, and the end to which the defiant would rather return than face the witness of the Messenger. The Qur'an elsewhere has the disbeliever cry *O would that I were dust* (78:40), and this verse places that cry at the specific court of witnesses the previous verse opened. The cry does not avail, because the One who spread humanity from one soul is also the One who brings each soul with its witness. To be reduced to dust would be to escape accounting, but the sūrah has already said that account is prepared — Fire prepared for disbelievers as humiliating punishment (4:37) and Gardens prepared for those who keep limits (4:13) — and that preparation assumes presence, not absence. The wish remains a wish.

**A Scene That Holds the Sūrah's Warnings Together**

Read with 4:41, this verse completes the witness tableau that the sūrah will use for its pivot to purification and to the People of the Book. The court is assembled with a witness from every community and the Prophet ﷺ over his own; those who denied and disobeyed are present and wish to be levelled; no speech can be hidden from God. The tableau gathers the three threads that have run together: God's will to make clear and turn toward you (4:26–27), the limits whose keeping is obedience and whose exceeding is Fire (4:13–14, 4:30), and the mercy that covers lesser faults for those who avoid major sins (4:31). Those who kept the major limits and turned soon after ignorance (4:17) will stand differently under that sky than those who persisted until death was present (4:18). The verse does not name the believers' recompense here; it leaves their standing implied by the sūrah's larger pattern of honourable entry (4:31) and the Gardens with pure spouses that follow (4:57). For the deniers and disobedient, the recompense is named as a wish that cannot be granted and a concealment that cannot be kept — which is itself a form of exposure. The Day that begins with *how will it be* ends here with *they will wish they were dust*, showing that the community's choice between clarity and desire, made in matters as small as a sixth and as serious as *shirk*, will have a weight that even the earth cannot cover.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:43

> O believers! Do not approach prayer while intoxicated until you are aware of what you say, nor in a state of ˹full˺ impurity—unless you merely pass through ˹the mosque˺—until you have bathed. But if you are ill, on a journey, or have relieved yourselves, or been intimate with your wives and cannot find water, then purify yourselves with clean earth, wiping your faces and hands. And Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving

**Prayer Guarded by Awareness**

The verse opens with a direct address — *lā taqrabū al-ṣalāta wa antum sukārā ḥattā taʿlamū mā taqūlūn* — O believers, do not approach prayer while intoxicated until you are aware of what you say. The condition *ḥattā taʿlamū mā taqūlūn* — until you know what you are saying — makes awareness the threshold for standing in prayer: prayer in the Qur'an is remembrance, recitation, and supplication where heart and tongue must align, and intoxication removes that alignment. Early reports place this verse in the Medinan period before the full prohibition of wine, when drinking remained common and a person might come to prayer with speech blurred. The sūrah therefore holds the line at the meeting point of worship and heedlessness: do not bring the state that empties words to the act that depends on words. The Qur'an elsewhere says that wine has benefit and great sin and that sin outweighs benefit (2:219), and later it says *wine, gambling, idols, and fortune arrows are defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid them entirely* (5:90). This verse is the middle step in that gradual legislation, keeping prayer clear while the community is being prepared for the final bar.

**Impurity and the House of Prayer**

The second bar *wa lā junuban illā ʿābirī sabīl ḥattā taghtasilū* — nor in a state of full impurity unless you merely pass through, until you have bathed — guards the same awareness in the body. *Junub* — one in major impurity after intimacy or discharge — is not impure in essence; the instruction is about readiness for prayer, which the Qur'an elsewhere describes as standing before God purified. *ʿĀbirī sabīl* — passing through, crossing a way — was read as walking through the mosque to reach another place without lingering to pray, which is permitted, while stopping to pray without bathing is not. The distinction shows that the law aims at the act of approaching prayer, not at banishing the person from the community's space entirely. The sūrah has already linked intimacy and covenant — *how could you take it after you have enjoyed each other and a firm commitment was taken?* (4:21) — and here it links intimacy to purification, so that the same closeness that is honoured in marriage is followed by a washing that prepares for the next standing before God. The body's state and the tongue's clarity together frame prayer as an act that gathers the whole person.

**When Water Is Not Found**

The concession *wa in kuntum marḍā aw ʿalā safarin aw jāʾa aḥadun minkum min al-ghāʾiṭ aw lāmastumu al-nisāʾ fa lam tajidū māʾan fa tayammamū ṣaʿīdan ṭayyiban fa amsaḥū bi wujūhikum wa aydīkum* — but if you are ill, on a journey, or have relieved yourselves, or been intimate with your wives and cannot find water, then purify yourselves with clean earth, wiping your faces and hands — is the sūrah's lightening because humankind was created weak (4:28) made concrete. Four cases are named: illness where water would harm, travel where water is scarce, relieving oneself, and intimacy after which bathing is normally required. If water cannot be found, the alternative is *tayammum* — seeking clean earth — *ṣaʿīdan ṭayyiban*, clean, wholesome ground — and wiping faces and hands. That wiping was detailed in practice as striking the earth with palms, dusting, then passing over face and hands, a gesture that replaces washing where washing would be harm or is impossible. The concession keeps prayer daily without forcing the ill to worsen or the traveller to chase water beyond reach. It shows that the bar on approaching prayer while intoxicated or impure is not a bar on prayer itself; it is a bar on approaching without the awareness and purity that prayer requires — and where those cannot be achieved through water, they are achieved through earth.

**Earth as Purifier Where Water Is Absent**

The choice of *ṣaʿīd ṭayyib* — clean earth, high ground, dust — as purifier was noted for its availability: earth is where people stand, whether healthy or ill, at home or on a journey; to make it a means of purification is to make purification available in the very place where water fails. The Qur'an elsewhere says *Allah does not wish to place hardship upon you, but to purify you and complete His favour upon you* (5:6), and this verse is the classic instance. The sūrah has already said God wills to make things clear and to lighten burdens (4:26–28); here clarity and lightening meet in a single rite — clear instruction about when not to approach, and a lightened way to be ready when water is absent. The wiping of face and hands also carries meaning beyond convenience: the face is the site of prostration, the hands the instruments of trade and giving that the sūrah has guarded from devouring by falsehood (4:29). To wipe both with clean earth is to mark the whole person — seeing and doing — as ready, even where full bathing is not possible.

**Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving Over Slip and Need**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna ʿafuwwan ghafūrā* — and Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving — matches the two bars and the one concession. *ʿAfuww* — pardoning, effacing — was read as wiping out the trace, as earth wipes the requirement of water; *Ghafūr* — forgiving, covering — as covering the shortfall where the believer tried to prepare but was hindered by illness, travel, or lack. The sūrah has closed similar lightenings with All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:25) and with All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:26); here the pardon covers both the person who once approached without full awareness in the stage before the final prohibition, and the one in major impurity who feared prayer would be lost where water was absent. The gradual bar on wine shows pardon in legislation itself: the community was not condemned as though it had always known the final rule, but was taught until *until you know what you are saying* became the standard for standing. The earth that purifies where water fails is the image of that pardon: where the means are lacking, the way remains — and the One who commands awareness is also the One who pardons its absence when the excuse is real, and who forgives what still falls short.

**A Verse That Holds Worship and Weakness Together**

Placed between the scene of witnesses and dust (4:41–42) and the exposure of those who trade guidance for misguidance (4:44), this verse holds worship and weakness together without loosening either. It keeps prayer guarded by knowledge of what is said and by bodily readiness, and it keeps weakness honoured by providing clean earth where water cannot be found. A community that learns not to approach prayer without awareness will learn not to approach any act requiring awareness — division of estates, giving of dowries, trade by consent — without knowledge either; a community that learns that illness and travel do not cancel prayer but change its purification will learn that limits remain but their burden is lightened. In that double training, the sūrah's larger purpose becomes visible again: to make things clear, to guide to noble ways, to turn in mercy, and to lighten because humankind was created weak (4:26–28). Prayer guarded by awareness and eased by earth is the daily rehearsal of that purpose — where the tongue knows what it says and the body is made ready, or where earth stands in for water and pardon covers what remains.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:44

> Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who were given a portion of the Scriptures yet trade it for misguidance and wish to see you deviate from the ˹Right˺ Path

**Have You Not Seen**

The question *a lam tara ilā alladhīna ūtū naṣīban min al-kitāb yashtarūna al-ḍalālata wa yurīdūna an taḍillū al-sabīl* — have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scriptures yet trade it for misguidance and wish to see you deviate from the Right Path — is not a request for information. *A lam tara* — have you not seen, do you not consider — was read as an alert that calls the Prophet ﷺ and the listeners to look at a pattern they know and recognise its present instance. Those who were given a portion of the Book — *naṣīban min al-kitāb* — were given a share of guidance: the Torah and what came with it, with its own limits, family laws, and rites, many of which the sūrah has just restated as clarity made anew (4:26). To trade that portion — *yashtarūna al-ḍalālah* — is to give up guidance and take misguidance in exchange, as though the Book were goods to be sold. The same verb *ishtarā* appears elsewhere for selling the verses for a small price and for selling faith for worldly gain. The sūrah has warned against devouring wealth by falsehood and against spending for show (4:29, 4:37–38); here the trade is of the most valuable wealth — revelation — for the territory of wandering.

**Trading a Portion for Misguidance**

The phrase *yashtarūna al-ḍalālata* was explained as actively seeking misguidance though they already possessed a share of the Book that could have guided them. *Ḍalāl* — wandering, straying — is the opposite of the *hudā* — guidance — the sūrah says God wills to give and to make clear. To buy wandering while holding a portion of guidance is to reverse the transaction the sūrah invites when it asks *what harm would it have been if they had believed and donated from what Allah provided?* (4:39) and promises multiplication for an atom's weight of good (4:40). The purchase also recalls the stingy who conceal bounty and promote stinginess (4:37) and the ostentatious who spend for show without belief (4:38); each conceals or diverts a trust — wealth or revelation — for a nearer gain. Here the gain is described as desire for the community to deviate. The verse was revealed concerning Jewish scholars in Madinah who knew descriptions of the Prophet ﷺ in their Scriptures yet hid them, altered wording, or priced access to interpretation, and who counselled Muslims to doubt. The type, however, was read more broadly: any person given a share of the Book who prefers to keep influence by keeping others astray — who trades the share he was given for the profit of leading others off the path.

**And Wish to See You Deviate from the Path**

The second trait *wa yurīdūna an taḍillū al-sabīl* — and they wish you to deviate from the Right Path — matches the diagnosis given earlier: *those who follow their desires wish to see you deviate entirely from Allah's Way* (4:27). The same verb *yurīdūna* appears in both, showing that the wish to misguide is not incidental to trading revelation; it is its aim. Those who have sold guidance need others to wander so that their own wandering looks like leadership. The path — *al-sabīl* — in this sūrah is the clear, guided, lightened way the sūrah has been drawing: limits kept, orphan wealth guarded, marriage sought with wealth in chastity (4:24), trade by mutual consent (4:29), and prayer approached with awareness (4:43). To wish that believers deviate from that path is to wish that the Medinan community lose the clarity God wills to give (4:26). The verse therefore places the Prophet ﷺ as addressed — *have you not seen* — to assure believers that the One who knows best who enemies are (4:45) sees the wish and is sufficient as Guardian and Helper: the wish of the misguiders to make others wander is already noted by the One who guides.

**Given a Portion, Not the Whole, Yet Accountable**

The phrase *ūtū naṣīban min al-kitāb* — given a portion of the Scriptures — was noted as precise: they were given a share, not the final Book in its completion, yet that share was enough to recognise truth when it came. The sūrah elsewhere says *O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have revealed confirming your own* (4:47), making the portion they hold a trust to be confirmed, not contradicted. To be given a portion and then to sell it is graver than never having been given, because the light was already in hand. The Qur'an elsewhere says that those given the Book know the Prophet ﷺ as they know their own sons, yet a party conceals. That knowledge is the background to the transaction here: the sellers are not ignorant wanderers but possessors who exchange. The sūrah has already said that God never wrongs even by an atom's weight but multiplies good (4:40); to trade an atom's weight of guidance for its opposite is therefore not a small miscount but a reversal of the economy the sūrah has been teaching, where bounty asked from God (4:32) is multiplied and bounty concealed is humiliation prepared (4:37). The portion given was bounty; to sell it is to conceal bounty in its most serious form.

**A Warning Inside a Question**

The question form does more than expose; it cautions the believers not to imitate the sellers. A community given the final portion — the Qur'an — could also trade it for desire, as the deviators wish them to do, by using verses for status, selling interpretation, or bending limits about wealth and marriage to suit appetite. The sūrah's repeated calls to refer disputes to Allah and His Messenger (4:59) are the guard against that trade: to keep the Book is to keep the limits the sūrah has made clear; to trade it is to lose the limits and then wish others to lose them as well. The next verses will detail how some distort wording — *we hear and we disobey*, *rāʿinā* twisted — and how a different phrasing would have been better and more proper (4:46), showing in language what trading the Book sounds like. This verse is the headline for that detail: a portion was given, it was sold for misguidance, and the sellers wish you to wander. The answer is not to meet trade with trade but to hold the portion, to believe and donate from what was provided, and to trust the One who is sufficient as Guardian and Helper to keep the path straight.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:45

> Allah knows best who your enemies are! And Allah is sufficient as a Guardian, and He is sufficient as a Helper

**Allah Knows Best Who Your Enemies Are**

The statement *wa Allāhu aʿlamu bi aʿdāʾikum* — and Allah knows best who your enemies are — follows the exposure of those who were given a portion of the Book yet trade it for misguidance and wish you to deviate (4:44). The community in Madinah lived among groups whose enmity was not always declared as open battle; some concealed it behind counsel, distorted phrasing, and the wish to mislead. The sūrah has just said those sellers wish you to deviate from the path (4:44) and earlier that those who follow desires wish you to swerve greatly (4:27). To know the enemy in that setting is not to know only the battlefield opponent but to know the whisperer who trades guidance for influence. *Aʿlamu* — knows best — was read as both comfort and warning: comfort, because the believer need not uncover every hidden motive — the One who is ever Watchful (4:1), Witness over all things (4:33), and All-Knowing, All-Aware (4:35) already knows; warning, because the believer should not mistake a wish to misguide for friendship. The Qur'an elsewhere says *He knows the treachery of the eyes and what breasts conceal*, and that knowledge is the background to naming enemies here without needing to list each name.

**Sufficient as Guardian**

The reassurance *wa kafā bi Allāhi waliyyā* — and Allah is sufficient as a Guardian — addresses the fear that follows knowledge of enmity. *Walī* — guardian, protector, near ally — was explained as the one who takes charge of affairs, who stands over the ward as a guardian stands over the orphan's wealth with witnessing and reckoning (4:6). The sūrah has built the image of guardianship from the first verse — *Allah is ever Watchful* (4:1) — through debt and bequest order, marriage law, and the promise that not an atom's weight is wronged but good is multiplied (4:40). To say He is sufficient as *Walī* is to say that those trusts need no other guarantor where enmity is present. Those who trade the Book for misguidance may wish you to deviate, but the Guardian who willed to make things clear and to guide to noble ways (4:26) is sufficient to keep the path clear. The phrase *kafā bi* — sufficient is — appears after detailed legislation to steady those who must apply it under pressure: a judge who must refuse a bequest that harms heirs (4:12), a guardian who must return an orphan's wealth with witnesses, a family that must appoint mediators (4:35) — each faces pressure from those who benefit from blur; sufficiency as Guardian tells them the law has a Keeper beyond people.

**Sufficient as Helper**

The second sufficiency *wa kafā bi Allāhi naṣīrā* — and He is sufficient as a Helper — addresses the need for support, not only protection. *Naṣīr* — helper, giver of victory — was read as the One who aids against both open opposition and hidden misguidance. The sūrah has shown help as turning toward you when you turn (4:27–28) and as lightening because you were created weak (4:28); help here is the active side of guardianship — not only guarding the limits but giving the community strength to keep them. The context was one where scholars in Madinah sought to draw believers away from the Messenger's clarification, and the believers were still few and recently tasked with inheritance and marriage reforms that met resistance. To say God is sufficient as Helper is to say that the success of those reforms does not depend on the approval of those who wish deviation. The Qur'an elsewhere says *if Allah helps you, none can overcome you*, and the same help underlies the promise that if mediators desire reconciliation, God will bring harmony (4:35). Help is promised where desire is for repair, and guard is promised where knowledge of enmity is needed; together they cover the community's public and private need.

**Knowledge, Guardianship, and Help Together**

The three clauses belong together: He knows enemies, He suffices as Guardian, He suffices as Helper. Knowledge without guardianship would leave the believer exposed; guardianship without help would leave him watched but not aided. The sūrah's earlier Names joined knowledge with wisdom (4:11, 4:26), knowledge with forbearance (4:12), and knowledge with awareness (4:35); here knowledge is joined with sufficiency. That sufficiency was already implied when the sūrah said *you are from one another* (4:25) and *you know not which are nearer to you in benefit* (4:11) — both statements that ask the believer to trust the apportioning of the One who knows. In a city where portions of Scripture were traded and wording was twisted — *we hear and disobey*, *rāʿinā* with a twist (4:46) — the believer might doubt whether clarity can survive distortion. The verse answers that clarity survives because its Guardian is sufficient; the believers' task is not to outwit every distortion but to hold the Book, refer disputes to Allah and the Messenger (4:59), and trust the Helper who multiplies an atom's weight of good (4:40).

**A Verse for a Community Under Pressure**

Placed between the exposure of sellers of misguidance (4:44) and the detailed examples of word distortion (4:46), this verse steadies the community before the examples are given. It tells them that the pattern they are about to hear — words taken out of context, greetings twisted, terms played with — is known better by God than by those who utter them, and that the response is not fear but reliance. The sūrah has moved from the Day when witnesses are brought and no speech can be hidden (4:41–42) to the daily guard of prayer with earth where water fails (4:43); this verse bridges the two by saying the same watch that secures the Day secures the street. The enemies who wish deviation (4:44) cannot remove the Guardian who suffices, and the deviation they wish cannot succeed where the Helper who suffices aids the weak whom He created weak. For the Medinan believers learning to divide estates, protect dowries, and pray with awareness, that double sufficiency was not a slogan; it was the condition that let them keep limits while surrounded by those who traded limits — and to do so without harshness, because the One who knows enemies is also the One who turns toward those who keep His path.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:46

> Some Jews take words out of context and say, "We listen and we disobey," "Hear! May you never hear," and "Râ'ina!" [Herd us!]—playing with words and discrediting the faith. Had they said ˹courteously˺, "We hear and obey," "Listen to us," and "Unẓurna," [Tend to us!] it would have been better for them and more proper. Allah has condemned them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except for a few

**Distorting Words After Their Places**

The verse describes *mina alladhīna hādū yuḥarrifūna al-kalima ʿan mawāḍiʿihi* — some Jews take words out of context, distorting wording after its proper place. *Taḥrīf* — to tilt, to turn aside — was explained as altering pronouncement or meaning: changing a word's sound slightly, shifting its context, or reinterpreting it to mean what it does not. The sūrah has just said that God knows best who enemies are and is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45), and that a portion of the Book was traded for misguidance with the wish to make believers deviate (4:44); here the trade becomes audible. Three phrases are quoted as examples: *samīʿnā wa ʿaṣaynā* — we listen and we disobey — said where *we hear and obey* was due; *ismaʿ ghayra musmaʿ* — hear, may you never hear — a curse disguised as greeting; and *rāʿinā* — twisted from *unẓurnā* — look upon us, tend to us — by playing on a similar-sounding root that could be stretched to mean *foolish* or *shepherd us*, used with a drawl and wink to insult while seeming to ask for attention. The verse names the devices — *layyan bi alsinatihim wa ṭaʿnan fī al-dīn* — playing with tongues, twisting with words, and stabbing at the faith — showing that distortion is both diction and intent.

**Three Sayings That Twist Courtesy Into Contempt**

*We listen and we disobey* was heard as a public declaration that replaces obedience with defiance while claiming to have listened — preserving the form of reception and emptying it. *Hear, may you never hear* was read as a curse to the Prophet ﷺ delivered as though it were a greeting, a double tongue that could be denied as mishearing. *Rāʿinā* was the most subtle, because the call sounds like *unẓurnā* but can be twisted into insult while seeming to ask for attention. The Qur'an elsewhere tells believers *do not say rāʿinā but say unẓurnā and listen* (2:104), replacing the ambiguous with the clear to close the opening for mockery. The sūrah's concern for clarity — *Allah wills to make things clear* (4:26) — is therefore protected at the level of vocabulary: a single word's tilt can tilt the community's hearing, which is why the verse details the tilt rather than summarising it.

**What They Could Have Said**

The verse offers the straight alternative: *wa law annahum qālū samīʿnā wa aṭaʿnā wa asmaʿ wa unẓurnā la kāna khayran lahum wa aqwam* — had they said we hear and obey, listen to us, and tend to us, it would have been better for them and more proper. *Samīʿnā wa aṭaʿnā* — we hear and obey — is the phrase the believers use elsewhere, gathering hearing and action together. *Ismaʿ* — listen — without the curse, and *unẓurnā* — tend to us — with the unambiguous root, would have secured the request without the twist. The pair *khayran lahum wa aqwam* — better for them and more proper, more upright — shows that straight speech is both more beneficial and more correctly aimed, like an arrow that flies true. The sūrah has praised *qawlan maʿrūfā* — kind speech at distribution (4:5, 4:8) — and *qawlan sadīdā* — straight, true speech (4:9); here it shows what crooked speech sounds like and what straight speech would have been.
