The difference is not eloquence but sincerity: a community that learns to say *we hear and obey* will also learn to handle deposits, shares, and dowries as heard and obeyed limits, while a community that says *we hear and disobey* will treat limits as sounds to be played with.

**Condemned for Disbelief — Faith Except for a Few**

The closing *wa lākin laʿanahumu Allāhu bi kufrihim fa lā yuʾminūna illā qalīlā* — Allah has condemned them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except for a few — ties distortion to its root. *Laʿn* — to expel from mercy, to condemn — was read as the consequence of covering the bounty and trading it (4:37, 4:44): because they distorted, they were condemned, and because they were condemned for persistent disbelief, the habit of faith left them, except for a few who turned — such as those who accepted the Prophet ﷺ and whose belief the Qur'an elsewhere acknowledges. The clause *illā qalīlan* — except a few — keeps the door ajar for the individual: the condemnation is not ethnic fate but response to a chosen practice of turning words after their places, and the few who said *we hear and obey* were not condemned. The sūrah has already said that God forgives anything less than association with Him for whomever He wills (4:48) and that a painful punishment is prepared for those who persist until death (4:18); here the same structure applies in the domain of speech. Persistent twisting hardens into disbelief that makes belief rare, while a straight word at the start — *unẓurnā* instead of *rāʿinā* — would have been better and more proper, and would have kept the way open.

**Words, Faith, and the Guarded Path**

Placed after the verse that entrusts enemies to God as Guardian and Helper (4:45), this verse shows how enmity actually sounded in the streets of Madinah and how believers are to answer it. The answer is not to mimic the twist but to replace it with clarity: do not use the ambiguous *rāʿinā*; say *unẓurnā*. The sūrah's larger purpose — to make things clear, guide to noble ways, turn in mercy, and lighten because humankind was created weak (4:26–28) — is undone by those who play with tongues to discredit faith; it is restored when the community chooses words that are better and more upright. The three twisted phrases and the three straight ones taught the believers to listen for tilt and to correct it — not with harshness alone but with a better phrasing they themselves would use. A community that guards its words in that way will also guard the other trusts the sūrah has named — the orphan's wealth with witnesses, the wife's dowry as *niḥlah*, the estate's shares after debts — because each of those trusts is also kept or broken first by what people say.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:47

> O you who were given the Book! Believe in what We have revealed—confirming your own Scriptures—before We wipe out ˹your˺ faces, turning them backwards, or We condemn the defiant as We did to the Sabbath-breakers. And Allah's command is always executed

**Believe in What Confirms Your Own**

The call *yā ayyuhā alladhīna ūtū al-kitāba āminū bi mā nazzalnā muṣaddiqan li mā maʿakum* — O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have revealed, confirming your own — addresses those who already hold a portion of revelation (4:44) and who were seen distorting words (4:46). *Muṣaddiqan li mā maʿakum* — confirming what is with you — was stressed as proof that the new revelation is not alien to theirs: the Torah that warned against devouring wealth, that set limits for family, and that commanded worship without association finds its confirmation in the Qur'an that has just guarded orphans, fixed shares, and chastity. To believe in the confirming Book is therefore not to abandon the earlier Book but to be faithful to it. The sūrah has said God wills to make things clear and guide to the noble ways of those before you (4:26); here that guidance takes the form of confirming what those before you were given. The believers who were told not to crave another's portion (4:32) and to ask God for bounty are here shown the greatest bounty — a Book that confirms theirs; to refuse it is to refuse the part they already hold, because confirmation strengthens rather than cancels.

**Before We Wipe Out Faces**

The warning *min qabli an naṭmisa wujūhan fa naruddahā ʿalā adbārihā aw nalʿanahum kamā laʿannā aṣḥāba al-sabt* — before We wipe out faces, turning them backwards, or We condemn the defiant as We did to the Sabbath-breakers — uses an image of erasure. *Ṭams* — to efface, to wipe out features so that eyes, nose, and mouth are levelled — was read either as a literal transformation for a people who distorted words with tongues and faces, or as a metaphor for being turned away from guidance, so that faces meant to face God are turned to the back. The pairing with *naruddahā ʿalā adbārihā* — turning them backwards — shows reversal as the recompense for reversal: those who took words out of context (4:46), traded the Book for misguidance, and wished believers to deviate (4:44) turned guidance backward; to have faces turned backward mirrors that turning. The second option — *or We condemn them as We condemned the Sabbath-breakers* — recalls the people who broke the Sabbath limit by stratagem, were warned in their own law, persisted, and were cursed and transformed — a story the Qur'an elsewhere says was made an example for those present and those to come. The sūrah places that example beside distorted speech for a reason: both broke a limit set by God, and both used a trick to seem not to.

**The Sabbath-Breakers as Precedent**

The reference to the Sabbath-breakers was read as more than a scare; it was a legal analogy. The Sabbath limit was a *ḥadd* — a divine boundary — like the inheritance limits called *ḥudūd* (4:13–14) and the marriage bars (4:22–23). Those who broke it by setting nets before the Sabbath and collecting after, claiming they had not fished on the day, were condemned because the stratagem kept the form while breaking the substance — much as *rāʿinā* kept the sound of *unẓurnā* while meaning insult. The sūrah has guarded against similar stratagems with wealth: hasty consumption before the orphan grows (4:6), bequests that harm heirs (4:12), devouring by falsehood in trade (4:29) — each uses a form that looks lawful while its substance is taking. To warn with the Sabbath-breakers is to say that God's limits are not defeated by wordplay. The condemnation — *laʿn* — that expels from mercy is the same word used for those condemned for distortion and disbelief (4:46), tying the two groups together: what was done to those who broke a temporal limit would be done to those who break the confirming Book's limit, because the limit's Owner is the same.

**And Allah's Command Is Always Executed**

The closing *wa kāna amru Allāhi mafʿūlā* — and Allah's command is always executed — seals the warning with inevitability. *Amr* — command, affair — was read as both decree and order: what He commands to be, is, and what He warns will happen if belief is refused will not be delayed by anyone's plan. The sūrah has said that God never wrongs even by an atom's weight but multiplies good (4:40) and that He has perfect knowledge of them (4:39); that knowledge now becomes capability, as the command that is executed shows. The phrase follows the double threat — wiping faces or condemning as the Sabbath-breakers — to make clear that neither is bluster. The community that heard *have you not seen those who trade a portion for misguidance?* (4:44) might have thought the traders would simply persist without consequence; this verse says persistence ends in an executed command. Yet the call before the threat remains belief — *āminū* — which is still possible while the warning is given. The sūrah's pattern of clarity before sanction — limits named, then Gardens and Fire named (4:13–14) — is kept: the confirming Book is named, the confirmation explained, the threat described, and the command's execution guaranteed, so that choice is made with open eyes.

**A Call That Confirms Rather Than Cancels**

Read after the diagnosis of twisted phrases, this verse is the sūrah's invitation to the very group diagnosed: believe in what confirms your own. It does not ask those given the Book to erase their history; it asks them to see its fulfilment. The limits they were given — about property, family, and worship — are made clear again and lightened because humankind was created weak (4:28); the Book that makes them clear is the same that confirms. To refuse that confirmation while trading the portion they have (4:44) is to turn faces away from the direction they were meant to face, and the executed command will then do what their own turning refused — turn them backward. The sūrah leaves the path open before that execution — believe now — because the One who warns is also the One who said *Allah wishes to turn to you in grace* (4:27) and *Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving* (4:43). The faces that could be wiped can instead be turned forward in belief, where the confirming Book is recognised and the warning is no longer needed.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:48

> Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating others with Him ˹in worship˺, but forgives anything else of whoever He wills. And whoever associates others with Allah has indeed committed a grave sin

**A Boundary That Does Not Move**

The statement *inna Allāha lā yaghfiru an yushraka bihi wa yaghfiru mā dūna dhālika li man yashāʾ* — indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but forgives anything less than that for whomever He wills — places one sin outside the general amnesty the sūrah has been offering for lesser faults. The previous promise *if you avoid major sins, We will cover your lesser misdeeds and admit you to honour* (4:31) and the assurance that repentance soon after ignorance is accepted (4:17) could be heard as though every fault, if deferred, would eventually be covered; this verse corrects that hearing by naming the limit. *Shirk* — associating others with God in worship, devotion, or ultimate trust — is not a lesser fault to be covered by avoiding other majors; it is the breach of the first command the sūrah gave in its ethic: *worship Allah and associate none with Him* (4:36). The verse therefore draws a line that the ethic of *iḥsān* to parents, relatives, orphans, neighbours, and travellers circles around but does not cross. All else — *mā dūna dhālika*, anything below that — remains under divine will to forgive, which the sūrah has described as perfect knowledge of them (4:39), never wronging by an atom's weight but multiplying good (4:40), and Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving (4:43).

**Forgives Anything Else of Whoever He Wills**

The phrase *wa yaghfiru mā dūna dhālika li man yashāʾ* was read as vast in scope. *Mā dūna* — what is below, less than — covers every sin that is not *shirk*, from consuming orphan wealth (4:10) to devouring by falsehood (4:29) to illicit intercourse (4:15–16), provided the conditions for forgiveness elsewhere are met — repentance soon after ignorance (4:17) rather than deferral until death is present (4:18), and avoidance of persistence as habit. *Li man yashāʾ* — for whomever He wills — was stressed as showing that forgiveness is not automatic; it is will, knowledge, and wisdom together, as the sūrah closes similar verses with All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:11, 4:26) and All-Knowing, Most Forbearing (4:12). The will to forgive those who turn is real — *Allah wishes to turn to you in grace* (4:27) and to lighten because you are weak (4:28) — but it remains His will, not a claim any sinner can demand. That balance keeps the community from two errors: despair that assumes no forgiveness, and presumption that assumes forgiveness on demand. A person who has committed a major sin that is not *shirk* is not told forgiveness is impossible; he is told it is possible for whomever God wills — and that will is known to be merciful to those who avoid the major and turn soon.

**A Grave Sin in Itself**

The closing *wa man yushrik bi Allāhi fa qad iftarā ithman ʿaẓīmā* — and whoever associates others with Allah has indeed fabricated a grave sin — uses *iftarā* — to fabricate, to invent a lie — and *ithm ʿaẓīm* — grave, immense sin — to describe *shirk* as both lie and weight. It is a lie because it attributes to another what belongs to God — creation from a single soul, watching over womb-ties (4:1), appointing heirs (4:11), multiplying an atom's weight (4:40); and a weight because it displaces the foundation on which all other limits stand. The sūrah has shown that limits about property and family hold only if the One who set them is worshipped alone; to associate another is to put a second source of limits beside Him. The same fabrication appears in the next verse's portrait of those who elevate themselves and claim God told them they are pure (4:49), and in those who fabricate lies against God (4:50) — *shirk* is the root fabrication of which those are branches. The Qur'an elsewhere calls *shirk* *ẓulm ʿaẓīm* — great injustice — because it misplaces worship itself, the act that should be given only to the One who never wrongs by an atom.

**Why This Verse Comes Here**

Placed after the warning that faces could be wiped or the defiant condemned like Sabbath-breakers (4:47), this verse explains the theology behind that severity. Wiping faces and *laʿn* were not arbitrary penalties for wordplay; they were responses to disbelief that includes association — taking scholars, desires, or idols as arbiters beside God. The sūrah will go on to describe those who believe in idols and false gods and claim they guide better than believers (4:51), showing the live form of association the verse addresses. By naming the unforgiven sin here, the sūrah clarifies the path back: believe in what was revealed confirming your own (4:47), worship without association and be kind to parents and others (4:36), and ask God for bounty rather than crave another's (4:32). Those who do so remain under *li man yashāʾ* — the will that forgives what is below *shirk* — where soon repentance (4:17) and avoidance of major sins (4:31) bring covering. Those who persist in association have fabricated the one lie that covers over the source of forgiveness itself, which is why it is not forgiven when held to death.

**A Verse That Holds Mercy Without Negating Justice**

Read with the sūrah's larger movement, this verse holds mercy and justice together without blurring either. Mercy is vast — anything below association may be forgiven for whomever God wills; justice is exact — association itself, if held to death without turning, is not forgiven, and the one who does it has fabricated a grave sin. The sūrah has already said that failure to repent until death is present is not accepted (4:18) and that exceeding God's limits brings abiding humiliation (4:14); this verse adds the theological ground: the limit that cannot be exceeded with pardon is to place another beside God, because that act denies the very One who pardons. Yet even this strict word is surrounded by mercy: before it came the invitation to believe before faces are wiped (4:47), and after it comes the exposure of self-purification and fabrication (4:49–50) as correctable before death. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28) and for whom earth was made purifier where water failed (4:43), the verse is not crushing; it is clarifying. Keep the foundation — worship without partner — and every other fault, while serious, remains under a will that is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving, and that multiplies an atom's weight of good many times over.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:49

> Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who ˹falsely˺ elevate themselves? It is Allah who elevates whoever He wills. And none will be wronged ˹even by the width of˺ the thread of a date stone

**Have You Not Seen Those Who Declare Themselves Pure**

The question *a lam tara ilā alladhīna yuzakkūna anfusahum* — have you not seen those who falsely elevate themselves, who declare themselves pure — follows the sūrah's exposure of distorted words (4:46) and the warning against association (4:48). *Yuzakkūna* — to declare pure, to praise as purified — was read as claiming righteousness for oneself: telling others that God has approved them, or that lineage, worship, or status makes them clean without need for turning. In the Madinan setting the phrase was linked to claims that they were God's children and beloved, or that none would enter the Garden except their own, and to similar claims by others who elevate themselves. The sūrah has just said that God does not forgive *shirk* but forgives what is below it for whomever He wills (4:48); to declare oneself pure is to pre-empt that will, to assign to oneself the judgment that belongs to Him. The Qur'an elsewhere says *do not claim purity for yourselves; He knows best who is mindful* (53:32), and this verse is the sūrah's instance, placed where self-elevation was being used to excuse word distortion and the trade of the Book.

**It Is Allah Who Elevates Whoever He Wills**

The correction *bali Allāhu yuzakkī man yashāʾ* — rather, it is Allah who elevates whoever He wills — returns the act of purification to its Owner. *Yuzakkī* — to purify, to elevate, to cause to grow — is God's act, not a status claimed by speech. The sūrah has shown that purification comes through His ways: making things clear (4:26), guiding to noble ways, turning toward you and lightening because you are weak (4:26–28), covering lesser faults when major sins are avoided (4:31), and accepting soon repentance for ignorance (4:17). To claim purity without that path is to claim the fruit without the root. *Man yashāʾ* — whoever He wills — was stressed as will joined to knowledge and wisdom, as the sūrah closes similar verses with All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:26) and Most Forbearing (4:12). The will to purify is not arbitrary; it follows the pattern the sūrah has taught: the one who worships without association and is kind to parents, orphans, neighbours, and travellers (4:36), who gives dowries graciously (4:4), who trades by mutual consent (4:29), and who asks God for bounty rather than craves another's (4:32) is the one God elevates. The self-praiser who conceals bounty and promotes stinginess (4:37) is not elevated by his own claim, because the elevation he seeks is in people's eyes, not before the One who sees.

**Not Even by the Width of a Date Thread**

The assurance *wa lā yuẓlamūna fatīlā* — and none will be wronged even by the width of the thread of a date stone — follows the correction to calm both hope and fear. *Fatīl* — the thin thread in the groove of a date pit — was read alongside *naqīr* — speck on a date stone (4:53) — and *qiṭmīr* — the membrane on a date pit elsewhere — as images of the smallest amount. The sūrah has used such measures to stress precision: inheritance must be shared *whether it is little or much* (4:7), a small provision for bystanders with kind speech (4:8), an atom's weight never wronged but multiplied (4:40). To say no one will be wronged by a *fatīl* is to say that God's purification does not overlook the smallest good that deserves elevation, nor ignore the smallest wrong that claims it. The Qur'an elsewhere says that on the Day when a witness is brought and no speech can be hidden (4:41–42), the record will not leave small or great except counted. Here the same exactness is promised before that Day, so that the self-praiser cannot think his claim will be rounded up and the quiet doer cannot fear his atom will be rounded down.

**Why Self-Elevation Blocks Purification**

To declare oneself pure blocks the very return the sūrah invites. Purification — *tazkiyah* — in the Qur'an is linked to turning — *tawbah* — and to being made clear; the sūrah says God wills to make clear and turn toward you (4:26–27) and to lighten because you are weak (4:28). The one who says he is already pure sees no need to be made clear, no need to be turned toward, and no weakness to be lightened. Early commentators noted that self-elevation also feeds the other faults diagnosed: it feeds the arrogance and boastfulness God does not like (4:36), the stinginess that conceals bounty (4:37), and the taking of words out of context to discredit faith (4:46), because the self-pure can justify distortion as insight. The correction *Allah elevates whomever He wills* therefore humbles without crushing; it moves the standard from claimed status to divine will joined to deed. The one who is elevated is not the one who says he is, but the one whom God — who knows best who enemies are and is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45) — knows to be mindful and whom He therefore purifies. That knowledge is the same that never wrongs by a *fatīl*.

**A Community Invited to Be Purified, Not to Claim Purity**

Placed between the grave sin of association (4:48) and the blatant fabrication of lies against God (4:50), this verse steadies the community between two traps: despair that no one can be pure, and presumption that some already are by birth. The sūrah's answer is that purity is given, not taken, and that it is given without wrong by even a thread. The poor guardian who took only what is fair (4:6), the heir who kept limits and was promised Gardens (4:13), the couple who sought mediators desiring reconciliation and found God bringing harmony (4:35), the spender who believed and donated from what was provided (4:39) — each may be elevated, not because they claimed it but because God wills it and does not wrong by a *fatīl*. The question *have you not seen* is therefore both exposure and invitation: have you not seen the self-praisers? Do not be them. And have you not seen that the only true elevation is God's act? Ask Him for it, as the earlier verse invited — *ask Allah for His bounty* (4:32) — and let Him purify you on the Day when not a thread's width is missed. The self-declared pure will find their claim weighs less than a *fatīl*; the quietly purified will find their atom multiplied many times over.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:50

> See how they fabricate lies against Allah—this alone is a blatant sin

**See How They Fabricate**

The command *unẓur kayfa yaftarūna ʿalā Allāhi al-kadhib* — see how they fabricate lies against Allah — directs the gaze to a practice just described: declaring themselves pure (4:49) while Allah alone purifies whomever He wills without wronging by a thread. *Iftarā* — to fabricate, to cut out a lie and present it as truth — was read as inventing a claim and attaching God's Name to it, saying God has approved what He has not. In the Madinan context that fabrication took forms the sūrah has traced: that only one group will enter the Garden, that God loves them because of lineage, that distorted words — *we hear and disobey* veiled as obedience (4:46) — represent His intent, or that trading a portion of the Book for misguidance (4:44) is guidance. The verb *yaftarūna* suggests ongoing work; the lie is not a slip but a craft, repeated until it feels like doctrine. The sūrah elsewhere says *whoever associates with Allah has fabricated a grave sin* (4:48), showing that *shirk* is the root fabrication; this verse shows the branch that grows from self-purification — the claim that God has already endorsed the claimant, which is a lie against Him.

**This Alone Is a Blatant Sin**

The clause *wa kafā bihi ithman mubīnā* — this alone is a blatant sin, sufficient as a clear sin — measures the fabrication without needing to add other faults. *Kafā bihi* — sufficient is it — was read as this single lie sufficing to be counted as manifest sin, even if no other deed were considered. *Ithm mubīn* — clear, open, evident sin — was used earlier for reclaiming a heap of gold by slander — *buhtānan wa ithman mubīnan* (4:20) — showing that fabrication against God and fabrication against a wife share the same structure: a lie told to justify taking or keeping what is not one's own. The sūrah has shown both forms — the husband who invents fault to reclaim a dowry, and the scholar who invents approval to keep influence. Both are called *buhtān* and *iftirā*, both *mubīn* — clear — because the lie is open once the Book confirms what was hidden. The verse therefore does not say this is one sin among many; it says this alone is enough to be called blatant — which is why the previous verse corrected self-elevation with *Allah purifies whomever He wills* (4:49), and the verse before that placed association outside pardon (4:48). To fabricate against Him is to misplace His will and His knowledge.

**Fabrication After Self-Elevation**

The link to the previous verse is direct. Those who elevate themselves — *yuzakkūna anfusahum* (4:49) — must supply a story for why they are elevated; the story becomes a lie against God: *He told us we are pure, He will not punish us, He favours our lineage*. The Qur'an elsewhere records such claims — *we are God's children and beloved* and *none will enter the Garden except us* — each attributing to God a promise He did not make. The verse says look at how the fabrication is done: by taking a thread's width of status and spinning it into a garment of purity, then presenting it as revelation. The earlier warning that no one will be wronged by even a thread — *fatīl* (4:49) — and by even a speck on a date stone — *naqīr* (4:53) — is the measure that exposes the fabrication: a community where an atom's weight is not wronged (4:40) cannot also have purity assigned by birth without deed, because the second claim would wrong every doer whose atom was counted. The fabrication therefore contradicts the sūrah's ethic of deed-based shares — *men according to what they earned and women according to what they earned* (4:32) — and the ethic of asking God for bounty (4:32) rather than claiming it.

**A Sin That Is Clear Without Further Evidence**

To call the fabrication *ithman mubīnan* — a blatant sin — is to say it is evident without needing a hidden motive to be uncovered. The lie is blatant because the Book that confirms (4:47) is present to compare, because the Witness over all things (4:33) is invoked, and because the atom's weight that is never wronged is the standard that shows the lie's excess. Early authorities noted that the sūrah makes this sin visible by its own method: it quotes the distorted phrases — *we hear and disobey, rāʿinā* (4:46) — and then the straight ones — *we hear and obey, unẓurnā* — so the fabrication can be heard. Here it quotes the act of self-elevation and then the correction — *Allah purifies whomever He wills* — so the sin's clarity is audible as well. The verse does not detail the punishment here, as it did for devouring orphan wealth (4:10) or exceeding limits (4:14), because *kafā bihi* — sufficient is it — already tells the reader that this fabrication alone suffices to be counted as grave. The next verses will add the broader idolatry where those given a portion of the Book reassure disbelievers they are better guided than believers (4:51), showing how one fabrication leads to another — but this verse holds the focus on the lie against God as enough on its own.

**Looking So That You Do Not Imitate**

The opening *unẓur kayfa* — see how — was read as both observation and caution: see how they fabricate, so that you recognise the pattern; see how, so that you do not reproduce it. The sūrah has taught a community that was learning to divide estates, guard dowries, and trade by consent to look at how others handle trusts; here it teaches them to look at how others handle the greatest trust — speaking about God. The community that has been told to be kind to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, neighbours, companions, travellers, and those in possession (4:36) might still be tempted to claim purity because it has done some of that; the verse warns that to turn that deed into a claim — *God has made us pure* — is to fabricate. The purer way is the one the sūrah has shown: do the deed, ask for bounty, avoid major sins so lesser faults are covered (4:31), and trust the One who elevates whomever He wills without wronging by a thread. That way leaves no room for a lie against Him, because it does not need one. The blatant sin is sufficient warning that the path of self-elevation ends not in purity but in a fabrication whose clarity no tongue can hide.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:51

> Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who were given a portion of the Scriptures yet believe in idols and false gods and reassure the disbelievers that they are better guided than the believers

**Have You Not Seen Again**

The question *a lam tara ilā alladhīna ūtū naṣīban min al-kitāb yuʾminūna bi al-jibti wa al-ṭāghūt* — have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scriptures yet believe in idols and false gods — repeats the alert of 4:44 but deepens the diagnosis. There the trade was a portion for misguidance and the wish to make you deviate; here the trade has become belief in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* — terms that early authorities explained as idols, sorcery, divination, and any false authority elevated to be followed beside God, including the chiefs of misguidance who command worship. To be given *naṣīban min al-kitāb* — a portion of the Book — and then to believe in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* is to reverse the very purpose of the portion, which was to teach *worship Allah and associate none with Him* (4:36). The verse was linked to Jewish leaders in Madinah who, when asked by the Quraysh whether the polytheists or the Muslims were better guided, answered that the polytheists were — out of envy and desire for alliance, despite knowing from their own Scriptures that the Prophet ﷺ confirmed what was with them (4:47). The question *have you not seen* is therefore not only exposure but amazement: how does one given a share of the Book come to credit idols and to reassure idolaters that they are on the better way?

**Reassuring the Disbelievers They Are Better Guided**

The second trait *wa yaqūlūna lilladhīna kafarū hāʾulāʾi ahdā min alladhīna āmanū sabīlā* — and they reassure the disbelievers that they are better guided than the believers — makes the reversal public. The same scholars given a portion of the Book become referees who declare the polytheists — whose worship the sūrah has called *shirk*, unforgiven if held to death (4:48) — to be *ahdā sabīlā*, better guided than the believers who worship without association and keep limits about wealth and marriage. The claim was explained as flattery toward the Quraysh and hostility toward the Prophet ﷺ, but its effect is theological: it tells the disbeliever that his path is straighter. The sūrah has already said that God wills to make things clear and guide to noble ways (4:26), and that He knows best who enemies are and is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45). To tell the disbeliever he is better guided is to trade that clarity for favour, to sell a portion for an alliance, as though the Book were goods to be priced by politics. The Qur'an elsewhere says those who sell the verses for a small price trade guidance for error, and this reassurance is that trade spoken aloud.

**Belief in Jibt and Ṭāghūt After a Portion of the Book**

The phrase *yuʾminūna bi al-jibti wa al-ṭāghūt* was read as more than consulting an idol for a day; it is belief — *īmān* — misdirected. The portion of the Book taught *tawḥīd* — worship without partner — and taught that good is multiplied and that even an atom's weight is not wronged (4:40); to give belief to *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* is to give that trust to what cannot weigh or multiply — to a false judge the believers are commanded to reject, as the later verse says: *have you not seen those who claim belief yet seek judgment of false judges, which they were commanded to reject, and Satan desires to lead them farther away* (4:60). Early commentators listed *jibt* as sorcery, idols, and whoever is followed in disobedience, and *ṭāghūt* as the head of falsehood who is obeyed beyond his limit. Here the same pattern appears at the level of doctrine: those given the Book, whose portion should have taught rejection of *ṭāghūt*, become its believers, and in that belief they validate the disbelievers' path. The reversal is complete: the teachers of *tawḥīd* become teachers that *shirk* is better guided.

**Why the Question Exposes the Seller**

The question *a lam tara* does not ask the Prophet ﷺ for news he lacks; it asks the community to see what the sellers have become. By naming the sellers as those given a portion, the verse reminds them that knowledge came first; unbelief in idols was not too high for them, because they had the Book that forbade it. To believe in *jibt* after that is chosen, not inherited — which is why the next verse says *they are the ones condemned by Allah* (4:52). The sūrah has already placed the unforgiven sin as *shirk* (4:48) and the blatant sin as fabricating lies against God (4:50); belief in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* and the reassurance to polytheists gather both. The reassurance fabricates that disbelief is guidance, and the belief brings *shirk* where *tawḥīd* was taught. The community that was told *do not crave what Allah gave some over others but ask Him for bounty* (4:32) and *what harm if they had believed and donated from what was provided?* (4:39) is here shown the opposite trade: those who had a portion did not ask for more bounty from God; they gave belief to idols and told others that the better path is the one God said He will not forgive if held to death.

**A Warning Not to Sell Guidance for Alliance**

Placed between the blatant fabrication (4:50) and the condemnation with no helper (4:52), this verse warns the believers not to imitate the sellers. A portion of the Book — now the Qur'an — has also been given to them; to use it to reassure those who deny God and disobey the Messenger that they are better guided would be to repeat the same sale. The sūrah will soon command *return trusts to rightful owners and judge with fairness* (4:58) and *obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you, and refer disputes to them* (4:59), showing where guidance is to be sought — not from *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* but from the Book and the Messenger. To have been given a portion and then to believe in false gods and to call the disbeliever better guided is to fail that referral at its first step. The verse therefore asks *have you not seen* so that the believers see and do not become like those who, having been given a share of guidance, believed in the very thing the guidance came to remove — and then told others that the removed thing guides better.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:52

> It is they who have been condemned by Allah. And whoever is condemned by Allah will have no helper

**Condemned by Allah**

The verse states *ulāʾika alladhīna laʿanahumu Allāh* — it is they who have been condemned by Allah — referring to those described just before as given a portion of the Scriptures yet believing in idols and false gods and reassuring disbelievers they are better guided than believers (4:51). *Laʿn* — to condemn, to expel from mercy — was read as God's declaration that the offender is removed from His special mercy, the mercy that elsewhere is promised as turning toward you and lightening burdens because you were created weak (4:26–28). The sūrah has used *laʿn* for those who distort words and say *we hear and disobey* (4:46), and in the threat before faces are wiped or the defiant condemned like Sabbath-breakers (4:47). Here condemnation is not a prediction but a status: they have been condemned. The reason gathers the sequence: they were given a portion of the Book; they traded it for misguidance and wished believers to deviate (4:44); they played with words to discredit faith (4:46); they were invited to believe in what confirms their own before a severe transformation (4:47); they were warned that *shirk* is not forgiven when held to death while what is below it may be forgiven for whomever God wills (4:48) — yet they chose belief in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* and told polytheists they were better guided. To be condemned after that series is not arbitrary; it is the name for persisting in the trade after the price and the alternative were made clear.

**Whoever Is Condemned Will Have No Helper**

The sentence *wa man yalʿani Allāhu fa lan tajida lahu naṣīrā* — and whoever is condemned by Allah will have no helper — universalises the status. *Naṣīr* — helper, giver of victory — echoes *Allah is sufficient as a Guardian and sufficient as a Helper* (4:45), where the same root *n-ṣ-r* promised that God's help suffices against enemies who trade the Book. Here the reversal is stated: when God condemns, no helper suffices. The *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* in whom they believed (4:51) will not help, the polytheists they reassured will not help, and the alliances they sought by saying the disbelievers are better guided will not help. The Qur'an elsewhere says that on the Day when a witness is brought from every community (4:41), those who denied and disobeyed will wish to be dust and will not be able to hide any statement from God (4:42); help on that Day is the help that matters, and the condemned will have none. The sūrah has already said that whoever takes Satan as associate has an evil associate (4:38); to have the evil associate as the only companion is to have no helper where help is needed.

**Condemnation After a Portion Given**

The placement emphasises that condemnation follows knowledge, not ignorance. They were given a portion of the Book — *naṣīban min al-kitāb* — and therefore the path of *worship Allah and associate none with Him; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, neighbours, companions, travellers, and those in your possession* (4:36) was known to them, as was the ethic of trade by mutual consent (4:29) and the promise that not an atom's weight is wronged (4:40). To believe in idols after that is not a mistake about small detail; it is a choice to give *īmān* to *ṭāghūt* after *īmān* was offered its proper object. That is why the sūrah treats the condemnation as God's act — *laʿanahumu Allāh* — not merely as people's dislike. The sūrah elsewhere says *Allah has condemned them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except for a few* (4:46), showing that condemnation hardens the heart that persists; here the focus is on the general rule: once condemnation as *laʿn* is declared, the condemned will find no helper to reverse it. The invitation to believe in what confirms their own before faces are wiped (4:47) was the open door before that declaration; after it, the door is the one God declares closed.

**No Helper Where Help Is Most Needed**

The phrase *lan tajida lahu naṣīrā* — you will never find for him a helper — was read as addressed to the Prophet ﷺ and to any listener, as though to say: look for a helper for them and you will not find one. That search was imagined on the Day when witnesses are brought (4:41), when wealth that was concealed (4:37), speech that was distorted (4:46), and idols that were believed (4:51) each fail to intercede. The sūrah has repeatedly contrasted two companionships: the evil associate — Satan as *qarīn* — and the sufficient Guardian and Helper — God Himself (4:45). To be condemned is to be left with the first and to lose the second. The sūrah will soon ask *do they have shares of the kingdom? If so, they would not give a speck* (4:53) and *do they envy people for God's bounties?* (4:54), showing that those with no share of kingdom and with envy as motive cannot help even themselves, let alone another. The verse therefore answers the alliance the sellers sought when they reassured polytheists: they sought helpers among the powerful disbelievers; the verse says the condemned will have no helper at all, because the only Helper who suffices has condemned them.

**A Verse That Steadies the Believers' Trust**

Between the exposure of belief in false gods (4:51) and the question about kingdom shares (4:53), this short verse steadies the believers' trust. The community that was told to refer disputes to Allah and the Messenger (4:59) and to return trusts and judge with fairness (4:58) might fear that alliances of sellers of misguidance and polytheists will overwhelm them. The verse says the calculus is simpler: whoever God condemns will have no helper — and God knows best who enemies are and suffices as Guardian and Helper (4:45). The sūrah has already shown that God never wrongs even by an atom's weight but multiplies good many times over (4:40), and that He will cover lesser faults for those who avoid major sins (4:31); those promises remain for the believers who keep limits. For the condemned, the opposite promise holds: no helper will appear to cover the *shirk* that is not forgiven when held to death (4:48) or the fabricated lie against God that is sufficient as blatant sin (4:50). The verse's brevity matches its function: after the detailed trade of a portion for *jibt* and the reassurance to disbelievers, a single sentence about condemnation and no helper tells the community where that trade ends — and whom to trust instead.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:53

> Do they have control over shares of the kingdom? If so, they would not have given anyone so much as the speck on a date stone

**Do They Have Shares of the Kingdom**

The question *a lahum naṣībun min al-mulk fa idhan lā yuʾtūna al-nāsa naqīrā* — do they have control over shares of the kingdom? If so, they would not have given anyone so much as the speck on a date stone — follows the condemnation of those who believe in idols and declare polytheists better guided (4:51) and who have no helper once condemned (4:52). The sūrah now asks whether such people possess any share of dominion — *naṣīb min al-mulk* — that would justify their judgment about who is better guided, or their claim to distribute favour. *Mulk* — kingdom, authority, dominion — in this sūrah has appeared as God's appointment of heirs (4:33) and as the heritage to which He multiplies reward (4:40); to have a share of it would be to have a stake in apportioning guidance, provision, and intercession. The verse denies they have any. Their portion was a share of the Book — *naṣīban min al-kitāb* (4:44, 4:51) — which they traded for misguidance; they have no share of kingdom. The Qur'an elsewhere says that if people possessed the treasuries of mercy, they would withhold from fear of spending, because humanity is ever stingy; this verse is that truth applied to those who claim better guidance for disbelievers. If the keys were theirs, they would not open them even a *naqīr* — the speck in the groove of a date stone.

**A Speck on a Date Stone**

The image *naqīr* — speck, the tiny dot on a date stone — joins *fatīl* — thread (4:49) — and *qiṭmīr* — membrane elsewhere — as measures of the smallest amount. The sūrah has used such measures to stress that God never wrongs even by an atom's weight but multiplies good (4:40), and that none will be wronged by a thread (4:49). To say the condemned would not give even a *naqīr* is to say they are the opposite of the divine economy they claim to judge: God withholds no *naqīr* of justice; He gives bounty where He wills and multiplies an atom's weight many times over. The sellers of misguidance, by contrast, would withhold even a speck if they controlled shares — which is why they reassured disbelievers they were better guided: not from magnanimity but from stinginess toward believers, a form of *bukhl* already condemned as concealing bounty and promoting stinginess (4:37). The sūrah has described the stingy as those who withhold what God gave of His bounty and teach others to withhold; this verse shows that stinginess would govern even dominion if they had it, so that their judgment about guidance is also a judgment about withholding. They declare the polytheist better guided because they begrudge the believer the bounty of being called better.

**Why the Question About Kingdom Follows Belief in Idols**

The sequence is deliberate. Belief in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* (4:51) is a claim to an alternative kingdom — a false authority whose judgment is obeyed. To ask *do they have a share of the kingdom?* is to ask whether that false authority owns any real dominion. The answer is none. Those who take Satan as associate have an evil associate (4:38), but they have no share of *mulk* to distribute; the associate they took cannot give. The sūrah has shown true kingdom in its own domain: He appoints heirs; He sets limits — *ḥudūd* — whose keeping brings Gardens and whose crossing brings humiliating Fire (4:13–14); He brings witnesses from every community (4:41); He turns toward those who turn soon (4:17). That kingdom is not shared with those who believe in idols; it judges them. The verse therefore exposes the sellers' boast as empty: they acted as though they could grant guidance by declaring disbelievers better guided, but the verse says if guidance and kingdom were theirs to apportion, they would keep even a *naqīr* to themselves — which proves they do not possess it. The only kingdom that matters — God's — is generous to an atom and beyond, which is why belief in Him and donation from what He provided would have harmed no one (4:39).

**Stinginess With Guidance as With Wealth**

The stinginess with *naqīr* mirrors the stinginess with wealth diagnosed earlier. There, those who were arrogant and boastful withheld bounty, promoted stinginess, and hid what God gave (4:37); here, those given a portion of the Book withhold the better description of guidance from those who follow the Prophet ﷺ and give it to the polytheists instead. Both are forms of covering — *kufr* — where what should be acknowledged is hidden. The sūrah elsewhere says that those given the Book who envy believers for God's bounties do so after descendants of Abraham were given Book, wisdom, and great authority (4:54), showing that envy, not lack, drives the withholding. If the envious had shares of kingdom, envy would make them even tighter, not looser. The speck on a date stone is therefore not only a measure of smallness but a measure of character: a hand that will not give a *naqīr* is not a hand that was denied kingdom; it is a hand that, if given kingdom, would still not give. The verse tells the believers that the one who tells the disbeliever he is better guided is not generous toward the disbeliever; he is stingy toward the believer — and that stinginess reveals he controls nothing.

**A Verse That Frees the Believers From Envy of Power**

Placed before the question about envying people for God's bounties (4:54), this verse frees the believers from envying the sellers' apparent influence. Influence that cannot give a *naqīr* if it had kingdom is not influence to be envied. The sūrah has taught not to crave what God gave some over others but to ask Him for bounty (4:32), and has asked what harm belief and donation from what was provided would have done (4:39); here the same lesson is applied to power. Those who seem to decide who is better guided have no share to decide with, and their decision, if it had power, would be withholding. The community that was told God knows best who enemies are and is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45) needs no share from such hands: the One who never wrongs by a *naqīr* and who multiplies good many times (4:40) is the only distributor whose share matters — and His distribution, Book and wisdom and great authority to the family of Abraham, will be named next as the true bounty the envious eye resents.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:54

> Or do they envy the people for Allah's bounties? Indeed, We have given the descendants of Abraham the Book and wisdom, along with great authority

**Envy for Bounty Given**

The question *am yaḥsudūna al-nāsa ʿalā mā ātāhumu Allāhu min faḍlihi* — or do they envy the people for Allah's bounties — diagnoses the motive behind belief in idols and the reassurance that polytheists are better guided (4:51), and behind withholding even a speck if they had kingdom (4:53). *Ḥasad* — envy — was read as wishing the bounty removed from its recipient, not merely wishing for similar bounty. The sūrah has tracked *faḍl* — bounty — as the surplus God apportions: not to be craved in another's hand but to be asked from Him (4:32); concealed by the stingy (4:37); spent for show without belief (4:38); and donated from what He provided without harm (4:39). Here the bounty envied is the Book, prophethood, and the following that the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ and his community received — a bounty the sūrah has called being made clear and guided to noble ways (4:26) and being turned toward in grace (4:27). The question *do they envy* does not seek information; it exposes that the sellers' trade of a portion for misguidance and their wish to make believers deviate were not from lack of knowledge but from resentment that bounty came to another. The Qur'an elsewhere says envy drove many of those given the Book to wish believers back to disbelief after the truth became clear, and this verse places that wish at its root.

**Indeed We Have Given the Descendants of Abraham**

The answer *fa qad ātaynā āla Ibrāhīma al-kitāba wa al-ḥikmata wa ātaynāhum mulkan ʿaẓīmā* — indeed, We have given the descendants of Abraham the Book and wisdom, along with great authority — was read as both history and present proof. *Āl Ibrāhīm* — family of Abraham — gathers prophets and kings from his line, to whom God gave *kitāb* — Book, revelation — *ḥikmah* — wisdom, understanding of the Book and sound judgment — and *mulk ʿaẓīm* — great authority, kingdom. Early authorities noted that among his descendants were Yūsuf with governance, Dāwūd with kingdom, Sulaymān with kingdom and wisdom, and many prophets whose Books formed the portions — *naṣīb* — those in Madinah had been given. The point is that bounty to a family of Abraham is not new; it is the established way God deals with that lineage. To envy the Prophet ﷺ — himself a descendant of Abraham through Ismāʿīl — for receiving Book and wisdom and a growing authority is to envy the same pattern that had already favoured their own ancestors. The verse was linked to Jewish envy that prophethood came to an Arab of Ismāʿīl's line rather than remaining within Isḥāq's line, but the type reaches any who envy a bounty because it came to another branch of the same human family that began from a single soul (4:1).

**Book and Wisdom and Great Authority Together**

The triad *kitāb wa ḥikmah wa mulk ʿaẓīm* was explained as the complete bounty that makes guidance effective. *Kitāb* is the inscribed limit — *ḥudūd* — the inheritance shares after debts (4:11–12), the marriage bars (4:22–23), the lawful field beyond them sought with wealth in chastity (4:24). *Ḥikmah* is the understanding that makes the Book live — the prophetic clarification that debts precede bequests, that four witnesses are required for *fāḥishah*, that earth purifies where water fails (4:43). *Mulk ʿaẓīm* is the authority that lets Book and wisdom be applied — the community, the judgment between people with fairness (4:58), and obedience to those in authority within obedience to God and Messenger (4:59). The sūrah has shown all three in this community's early life: the Book that makes things clear (4:26), the wisdom that guides to noble ways (4:26), and the authority that returns trusts and judges with fairness. To have been given those three in the family of Abraham before is to know that the same three given now to this branch is not usurpation but continuity. The enviers' claim that polytheists are better guided (4:51) is therefore not only false; it is ungrateful to the bounty their own family received in all three forms.

**Why Envy Follows the Speck**

The verse follows the rhetorical question about shares of kingdom where even a *naqīr* would be withheld (4:53) because envy explains that withholding. If those given a portion of the Book had shares of dominion, they would not give a speck — and the reason is *ḥasad*: they begrudge the *faḍl* given to others. The sūrah has diagnosed envy as a social force before — *do not crave what Allah gave some over others; ask Him for bounty* (4:32) — and here it names its historical root. The cure the sūrah offered there is the cure here as well: instead of envying the people for what God gave, ask Him for what He gives, because the distributor is not the family that envies; it is the One who never wrongs by a *fatīl* (4:49) and who multiplies good many times over (4:40). The sūrah has also said God knows best who enemies are and is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45), so the envious wish to see believers deviate (4:44) cannot remove the bounty it envies; it can only expose the envier.

**A Verse That Returns Bounty to Its Giver**

Read with the verses that frame it, this question and answer return bounty to its Giver. The bounty envied — Book, wisdom, kingdom — was given by *We* — divine giving — to the family of Abraham, as it is given now to this community. That giving is *faḍl* — surplus, bounty — the same word used for the bounty the stingy conceal (4:37) and the bounty to be asked for (4:32). To envy the people for it is to dispute the distribution of the One who never wrongs even by an atom and who will give a great reward out of grace (4:40). The sūrah leaves the enviers with the reminder that great authority was already in their own lineage, so the present authority is not a theft from them but a continuation among *you are from one another* (4:25). The next verse will say that some believed in him while others turned away, and that Hell is sufficient as torment (4:55), showing where envy leads when it is followed; this verse shows where it comes from. Between the two, the community is invited to see that the proper response to another's bounty is not to believe in idols and call disbelief better guided, nor to withhold a speck, but to recognise that Book, wisdom, and authority have always been God's to give to descendants of Abraham — and to ask Him for their share of that bounty with belief, rather than to begrudge those who received it.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:55

> Yet some believed in him while others turned away from him. Hell is sufficient as a torment

**Some Believed, Others Turned Away**

The verse states *fa minhum man āmana bihi wa minhum man ṣadda ʿanhu* — yet some believed in him while others turned away from him. The pronoun *bihi* — in him — was read as belief in the Prophet ﷺ who is the descendant through whom Book, wisdom, and great authority have newly come, or in the Book itself that confirms what was with them (4:47), and some linked it to Abraham himself; the breadth of the antecedent is the point. Whoever is given Book, wisdom, and authority from the family of Abraham will be met with two responses: belief and turning away. The sūrah has just said that God gave that triad to the family of Abraham (4:54) and that envy for bounty drove those given a portion of the Book to believe in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* and to reassure disbelievers they were better guided (4:51). This verse's division — some believed, some turned away — is the human outcome of that bounty and that envy. It is the same division the sūrah opened with witnesses from every community and the Prophet ﷺ as witness (4:41–42): some will stand with their witness, others will wish to be dust. The sūrah does not treat turning away as a passing hesitation; *ṣadda ʿanhu* — to turn away, to bar, to hinder — was read as active turning that also turns others, as the promoters of stinginess teach stinginess (4:37) and the traders of misguidance wish you to deviate (4:44).

**Hell Is Sufficient as Torment**

The closing *wa kafā bi jahannama saʿīrā* — and Hell is sufficient as a torment — uses *kafā bi* — sufficient is — the same phrase that declared God sufficient as Guardian and sufficient as Helper (4:45). There sufficiency was reassurance for believers surrounded by those who trade the Book; here sufficiency is warning for those who turn away. *Saʿīr* — blaze, fierce flame — was read as the Fire already kindled, the blaze that consumes, as *We will burn them in the Fire* was said for deliberate devouring and killing where *that is easy for Allah* (4:30), and as will be described next: for those who reject signs, whenever their skin is burnt it will be replaced (4:56). *Kafā* — sufficient — was stressed as saying no additional torment is needed to prove the seriousness of envy that becomes barring; Hell suffices, and that suffices as deterrence. The sūrah has already described humiliating punishment prepared for concealing bounty (4:37) and association not forgiven (4:48); this blaze is the same recompense named at the scale of the bounty refused. Great authority rejected meets great torment as its counterpart: the sufficiency on one side — God as Guardian and Helper — meets sufficiency on the other — Hell as blaze — showing that the community's help and the deviator's penalty are both assured without need for another witness.

**Why the Division Is Mentioned Here**

The verse follows the triad of Book, wisdom, and great authority (4:54) because that triad always divides. The sūrah has been dividing since it set limits — *ḥudūd* — whose keeping brings Gardens and whose crossing brings Fire (4:13–14), and since it said *if you avoid major sins We will cover lesser ones and admit you to honour* (4:31). To be given bounty is to be tested by it. Some among those given a portion will be among the few who are elevated — *Allah elevates whomever He wills and none is wronged even by a thread* (4:49) — while others fabricate lies against God as blatant sin (4:50). The same test now operates around the Prophet ﷺ: his presence makes the bounty visible as a person to be believed or turned from, which is why the verse names belief *in him* and turning *from him* as the two branches. The sūrah does not treat the turn as neutral; those who turn also wish others to deviate greatly (4:27), promote stinginess (4:37), and reassure disbelievers (4:51). Turning is therefore not only rejection but mission against belief, which is why Hell as blaze suffices as its name. The believers who believed in him, though few among those given a portion, join the larger *you are from one another* (4:25) — migrants and hosts who believed — and for them the sūrah has said God suffices as Guardian.

**A Sufficiency That Holds Both Sides**

Placed between the bounty to Abraham's family (4:54) and the detailed recompense of Fire with skin replaced (4:56), this short verse holds both sides of the sūrah's equation. Book, wisdom, and authority given become a cause for envy in some, for belief in others; Hell as blaze suffices for the enviers who bar, while multiplication of an atom's weight and a great reward out of grace (4:40) suffice for the believers who give. The sufficiency of Hell as torment therefore does not stand alone; it stands opposite the sufficiency of God as Guardian and Helper, and opposite the sufficiency of atom-exact justice. *Kafā* in 4:45 tells the believer not to fear the traders of misguidance; *kafā* here tells the trader that the consequence is sufficient without addition. Between the two, the sūrah leaves the reader with the same choice it has posed since *how will it be when We bring a witness?* (4:41): to believe in him through whom Book and wisdom came and find Guardianship that suffices — or to turn away and find a blaze that also suffices, with no helper once condemned (4:52) and not even a speck given where kingdom is imagined (4:53).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:56

> Surely those who reject Our signs, We will cast them into the Fire. Whenever their skin is burnt completely, We will replace it so they will ˹constantly˺ taste the punishment. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise

**Those Who Reject Our Signs Will Be Cast Into Fire**

The verse states *inna alladhīna kafarū bi āyātinā sawfa nuṣlīhim nārā* — surely those who reject Our signs, We will cast them into the Fire. After the division where some believed in him and others turned away and Hell sufficed as blaze (4:55), this verse names the content of rejection: *āyātinā* — Our signs. The sūrah has shown what those signs include in this context: verses about creation from a single soul (4:1), about orphan wealth and witnesses (4:6), about fixed inheritance after debts (4:11–12), about lawful marriage with dowry and chastity (4:24), and about belief in Allah and the Last Day with donation from what was provided (4:39). To reject those signs after they were made clear (4:26) is not a casual dismissal; it is to cover what was shown. The verb *kafara* — to cover, to deny — matches the fabrication of lies against God called blatant sin (4:50) and the belief in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* (4:51). The recompense is *nuṣlīhim* — the same roasting verb used for deliberate devouring where *We will burn them in the Fire, and that is easy* (4:30). The Fire is not a new threat added for this group alone; it is the prepared recompense the sūrah has named for humiliating withholding (4:37), for association not forgiven (4:48), and for envy that bars (4:55) — here attached directly to rejection of signs.

**Whenever Their Skin Is Burnt We Will Replace It**

The detail *kullamā naḍijat julūduhum baddalnāhum julūdan ghayrahā li yadhūqū al-ʿadhāb* — whenever their skin is burnt completely, We will replace it so they will constantly taste the punishment — was read as both literal and moral. Literally, the skin that is the locus of sensation is restored so that sensation does not numb; the punishment is tasted anew — *li yadhūqū* — each time, without the relief that comes when a burn deadens nerves. The Qur'an elsewhere describes the Fire as surrounding and the drink as boiling, and this verse adds the renewal of the sensing surface itself, making the tasting continuous — *constantly*, as the translation renders. Morally, the detail mirrors the persistence of rejection: those who persistently covered signs — envying bounty (4:54), believing in false gods (4:51), distorting words (4:46) — persisted in a choice that, had it been reversed by soon repentance (4:17), would have been covered. Instead, the covering was on their side, and the recompense is a surface that is renewed only to be burned again. The phrase *kullamā* — whenever — makes the renewal regular, matching the regularity of the choice that led to it.

**So They Will Constantly Taste the Punishment**

The purpose *li yadhūqū al-ʿadhāb* — so they will taste the punishment — was stressed as tasting, not only enduring. *Dhawq* — taste — implies direct experience, not hearsay. The sūrah has used tasting for fire before — eating fire into bellies (4:10) — where what was eaten as wealth became fire as food. Here tasting is of punishment itself, renewed with skin, so that knowledge of the Fire is not abstract. The verse generalises what earlier verses specified for consuming orphan wealth hastily (4:6) and devouring by falsehood deliberately (4:30): all share the same end where the act is tasted as fire. The continuity — skin after skin — also mirrors the continuity of the sūrah's ethic of deed: not an atom's weight is wronged but multiplied where good is concerned (4:40), and persistence in rejection is met with persistence in recompense. The one who tasted illicit gain as if it were nourishment will now taste punishment as it is, with the vessel of taste restored each time so that the lesson is not dulled.

**Indeed Allah Is Almighty, All-Wise**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna ʿazīzan ḥakīmā* — indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise — gives the ground for both casting and replacing. *ʿAzīz* — Almighty, Mighty, invincible — was read as the power to cast into Fire and to renew skin without diminishment; nothing restrains the execution of *Allah's command is always executed* (4:47). *Ḥakīm* — All-Wise — was read as the wisdom that places that power where rejection of signs persisted after clarity, guidance, and lightening (4:26–28). The pair appears here as it does after similar severe recompense, because the sūrah wants the reader to see that the severity is not vengeance but wise placement of might: the One who is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45) is mighty to help those who believed and did good (4:57) and mighty to cast those who rejected signs; the One who wills to make things clear and turn toward you (4:26–27) is wise to renew tasting for those who covered what was made clear. The Names therefore hold the verse between power and reason, so that the promise to believers that follows can be heard as equally assured.

**A Verse That Follows Envy and Precedes Gardens**

Placed between the sufficiency of Hell as blaze where some turned away (4:55) and the Gardens with pure spouses and vast shade where believers do good (4:57), this verse details the Fire that suffices. It tells the community that the signs rejected are not minor regulations but the very limits and mercies that protect orphans, widows, heirs, and neighbours; to reject them is to reject the *āyāt* that make the community humane. The detail of skin replaced shows that the recompense fits the persistence: a persistent covering of signs meets a persistent tasting of fire. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28) and for whom avoidance of major sins covers lesser faults (4:31), the verse is not meant to crush but to define what major to avoid — rejection of signs after they were made clear. For those who believed and did good, the same Mighty and Wise who renews skin for tasting will renew shade and spouses for honour. The sūrah therefore leaves the reader with two renewals side by side — one of skin for tasting, one of Gardens for abiding — and asks, while the signs are still with you and the choice is still to believe in him or turn away (4:55), which renewal do you seek?
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:57

> As for those who believe and do good, We will admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there for ever and ever. There they will have pure spouses, and We will place them under a vast shade

**Those Who Believe and Do Good**

The verse opens with *wa alladhīna āmanū wa ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt* — as for those who believe and do good — the counterpart to those who rejected signs and will be cast into Fire with skin renewed for tasting (4:56). The sūrah has defined belief in this context as trust in God and the Last Day with donation from what was provided (4:39), as belief in what was revealed confirming what was with them (4:47), and as not elevating oneself but letting God elevate whomever He wills without wrong even by a thread (4:49). Doing good — *ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt* — was read as acting in the ways the sūrah has detailed: returning trusts, giving dowries graciously, honouring obligatory shares, provision to bystanders with kind speech, trade by mutual consent, and seeking reconciliation with two mediators. The pairing of belief and doing good gathers the two parts of the sūrah's ethic: the inner turn toward God who wills to make clear and turn toward you (4:26–27), and the outer deed that keeps limits inside weakness (4:28, 4:31). To believe and do good here is to have lived the sūrah's first fifty verses as worship.

**Gardens Under Which Rivers Flow, Forever and Ever**

The reward *sa nudkhiluhum jannātin tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhār khālidīna fīhā abadā* — We will admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there for ever and ever — repeats the sūrah's earlier promise for keeping limits (4:13) with the intensified *abadā* — for ever and ever. The doubled phrase was stressed as permanence without end, answering the impermanence of estates divided — whether little or much (4:7) — of dowries given, and of trade that passes. The sūrah has already said that whoever keeps God's limits is admitted to Gardens with ultimate triumph (4:13) and that whoever avoids major sins is admitted to a place of honour (4:31); this verse gathers those promises into the final form where the honour is named as everlasting. The image of rivers flowing under Gardens was read as abundance without labouring for allotment — the opposite of the anxious division of shares, half, quarter, eighth, sixth, third, that required witnesses and calculation (4:11–12). There, water must be measured; here, rivers flow without measuring. The permanence answers the Fire's renewal of skin for tasting (4:56): where one side renews for pain, the other abides for delight without renewal needed, because the abode itself is vast shade.

**Pure Spouses and Vast Shade**

The two gifts *lahum fīhā azwājun muṭahharatun wa nudkhiluhum ẓillan ẓalīlā* — there they will have pure spouses, and We will place them under a vast shade — were read as the personal and the environmental. *Azwāj muṭahharah* — pure spouses — were explained as spouses purified of physical and moral impurity; in the sūrah's context they complete the marriage ethic that began with limits on marrying former wives of fathers (4:22), the list of prohibited degrees (4:23), the lawful field sought with wealth in chastity (4:24), and the concession for believing bondwomen with chastity and permission (4:25). The pure spouse is the counterpart to the shelter — *muḥṣin* — that lawful marriage was meant to be: where chastity was kept and dowries given graciously (4:4), the recompense is companionship that is pure without effort. *Ẓill ẓalīl* — vast, deep, dense shade — was read as shade that is both cool and lasting, the opposite of the blazing Hell — *saʿīr* — that sufficed as torment (4:55) and the Fire that burns skin anew (4:56). The Qur'an elsewhere describes shade as a Garden's comfort where the sun does not blaze; here the shade is called vast, suggesting a canopy that does not thin. Together the pure spouse and the vast shade gather intimacy and rest — the two things marriage and household were meant to provide on earth, now given without flaw.

**A Promise That Balances the Preceding Threat**

The verse follows the severest description of Fire with a parallel description of Gardens, so that the two renewals stand side by side. Rejected signs lead to skin renewed for tasting (4:56); belief and good deeds lead to Gardens that need no renewal, with *khālidīna abadā* stressing that the abiding itself is the gift. The sūrah has balanced promise and threat since it said *these are the limits; whoever obeys... Gardens; whoever disobeys and exceeds... Fire, humiliating, abiding* (4:13–14), and it keeps that balance here at the wider scale. The pairing also mirrors the sūrah's ethic of *iḥsān* (4:36) and its warning that God does not like the arrogant boaster who is stingy and promotes stinginess (4:37). To believe and do good is to have spent for God, not for show (4:38), from what He provided, believing in Him and the Last Day (4:39); the recompense for that spending is Gardens and shade and pure companionship, where spending is no longer needed. The symmetry teaches that the choice between Fire and Garden was never only about after; it was about how one handled trusts, limits, and words while *Allah is ever Watchful* (4:1) and *Witness over all* (4:33).

**The Human Weakness That Can Still Enter Gardens**

The promise is placed after the sūrah's lightening — *humankind was created weak* (4:28) — and its covering of lesser faults when major sins are avoided (4:31), so that the Gardens do not seem unreachable for the weak. To believe and do good does not require the self-purification that fabricates (4:49–50) but the purification God gives — *Allah elevates whomever He wills* (4:49) — without wrong even by a thread. The small good that is never wronged but multiplied (4:40) is enough to set the multiplication and the great reward from grace in motion, and that great reward is named here as vast shade. The sūrah therefore invites the weak to see themselves in this verse: the one who returned orphan wealth with witnesses, who gave a small provision with kind speech (4:8), who traded by mutual consent (4:29), who asked God for bounty rather than craved another's (4:32), is among those who believe and do good. For them, the rivers that flow without allotment and the shade that never thins are the counterpart to the charity they kept flowing on earth, and the pure spouses are the counterpart to the chastity they guarded when they could have sought those beyond the limits *in fornication* but chose the shelter instead.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:58

> Indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners; and when you judge between people, judge with fairness. What a noble commandment from Allah to you! Surely Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing

**Return Trusts to Their Rightful Owners**

The command *inna Allāha yaʾmurukum an tuʾaddū al-amānāt ilā ahlihā* — indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners — gathers the sūrah's long training about entrusted wealth into a single principle. *Amānāt* — trusts — was read as every trust: the property of orphans to be returned without substitution (4:2) and after testing with witnesses (4:6); dowries given graciously as a free gift (4:4) and not reclaimed even where a heap was given (4:20–21); obligatory shares after debts and bequests (4:11–12); deposits and pledges to be fulfilled (4:33). The sūrah has shown what happens when trusts are eaten as fire (4:10), devoured by falsehood (4:29), or exceeded beyond limits with humiliating abiding (4:14). To return trusts *ilā ahlihā* — to their rightful owners — was stressed as returning to those who are entitled, not to those who claim loudly: the phrase *ahl* — people of, those worthy and entitled — echoes the sūrah's *mawālī* — heirs appointed — and *dhī al-qurbā* — relatives present at distribution. Trusts are not returned to the strongest claimant but to the rightful one, as God appoints. The verse was linked to many occasions — from the keys of the Kaʿba to deposits generally — showing that the rule spans the sacred and the civil: what is entrusted — keys, property, testimony, office — must be returned to its proper holder.

**When You Judge Between People, Judge With Fairness**

The second command *wa idhā ḥakamtum bayna al-nāsi an taḥkumū bi al-ʿadl* — and when you judge between people, judge with fairness — pairs return of trusts with justice in judgment. *Ḥakama* — to judge, to decide — was read as any arbitration: a judge between litigants, a family mediator between spouses (4:35), an executor dividing an estate, a ruler distributing provision. *ʿAdl* — fairness, equity — was explained as putting each thing in its place, giving each his *naṣīb* — share — without favour. The pairing matters because returning trusts correctly often requires a judgment: who is the rightful owner, whose share is a half or sixth, whose dowry is due, whose trade was by mutual consent. The sūrah has prepared judgment with procedure: witnesses at handover (4:6), four witnesses before sanction for *fāḥishah* (4:15), two mediators from the families (4:35), and the promise that God is Witness over all things (4:33). To judge with *ʿadl* in that setting is to align human judgment with the divine appointment of shares and with the prophetic clarification of how to apply them. The Qur'an elsewhere says *when you judge, judge with justice; Allah loves the just*, and this verse is the sūrah's instance at the point where trusts meet disputes.

**What a Noble Commandment From Allah to You**

The exclamation *niʿimmā yaʿiẓukum bihi* — what a noble commandment, what an excellent exhortation Allah gives you — was read as praise for the two commands together. *Niʿimmā* — how good, how excellent — is commendation that marks the instruction as beneficial in itself, not only as duty: to be told to return trusts and judge with fairness is itself a favour, because a community that does so lives without the rancour that comes from withheld shares and crooked judgments. The sūrah has just contrasted the blaze prepared for those who reject signs, with skin renewed for tasting (4:56), and Gardens with vast shade for those who believe and do good (4:57); this noble exhortation is the path between them made practical. Returning trusts and judging fairly are *ʿamal ṣāliḥ* — good deeds — that faith performs, and they lead to the Gardens' shade. The phrase also echoes the sūrah's repeated *Allah wishes to make things clear and guide you to noble ways and turn to you* (4:26); the exhortation is good because it clarifies, guides, and opens the turn. The community that hears *niʿimmā yaʿiẓukum* is being told that the instruction is not a burden added to weakness but a lightening, since humankind was created weak (4:28).

**Surely Allah Is All-Hearing, All-Seeing**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna samīʿan baṣīrā* — surely Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing — gives the watcher for trusts and judgments. *Samīʿ* — All-Hearing — was read as hearing the claim and the counterclaim, the kind word and the harsh, the just pronouncement and the distorted *rāʿinā* played with tongues (4:46). *Baṣīr* — All-Seeing — was read as seeing the handover, the mixing of wealth (4:2), the hasty consumption before the orphan grows (4:6), the trade by mutual consent or falsehood (4:29), and the mediation where harmony is desired and God brings it about (4:35). The sūrah has used similar closings — All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:11, 4:26); Most Forbearing (4:12); All-Aware (4:35); Witness over all (4:33); never wronging by an atom but multiplying good (4:40). Here hearing and seeing are chosen because trusts and judgments are acts of speech and sight: the judge hears testimony and sees records. To know that God hears and sees steadies both parties — the holder of the trust who might be tempted to withhold, and the judge who might be tempted to favour. What is heard and seen by Him need not be perfectly proved before people to be recorded; yet human hearing and seeing in courts and family meetings are the way the community aligns its practice with His.

**A Verse That Holds the Sūrah's Ethics in One Line**

Placed between the promise of Gardens and the call to obey Allah and the Messenger and those in authority (4:59), this verse summarises the sūrah's public ethic in two imperatives. Return the trust; judge with fairness — the first governs what is held, the second governs how disputes about what is held are decided. Between them they cover the estate with orphans and heirs, the dowry with the bride, the market with mutual consent, and the home with mediators. The noble exhortation is that a community which does both will have little need for the punishments named — humiliating (4:37), blaze sufficient (4:55), Fire with skin renewed (4:56) — because the occasions for them will shrink. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the two commands are also achievable: returning a trust is a discrete act, and judging with fairness is a single stance taken again and again. The All-Hearing who hears the return and the All-Seeing who sees the judgment are the same who multiply an atom's weight of good many times over (4:40) — so that the noble commandment to return and to judge fairly is itself the path to the vast shade where trust is no longer at risk.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:59

> O believers! Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. Should you disagree on anything, then refer it to Allah and His Messenger, if you ˹truly˺ believe in Allah and the Last Day. This is the best and fairest resolution

**Three Obediences, One Root**
