The address *aṭīʿū Allāha wa aṭīʿū al-rasūla wa ulī al-amri minkum* — O believers, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you — orders obedience in layers. *Aṭīʿū Allāha* — obey God — is the root that appeared as *ḥudūd Allāh*, limits set by God, for inheritance (4:13–14) and as *worship Allah and associate none* (4:36). *Aṭīʿū al-rasūla* — obey the Messenger — repeats the verb *aṭīʿū* rather than subsuming the Messenger under God, stressing that his clarification is obedience itself, as in *whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah*, and as in the witness scene where he is brought as witness over his community (4:41). *Ulī al-amri minkum* — those in authority among you — was explained as rulers, judges, scholars, and commanders who execute the law, including the judges who return trusts and judge with fairness (4:58) and the mediators appointed from families (4:35). Their obedience is commanded without a third *aṭīʿū*, signalling that it holds within obedience to God and His Messenger. The sūrah has shown that authority can be misused — belief in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* and seeking false judges (4:51, 4:60) — so authority is to be obeyed when it stands inside that alignment, not when it commands deviation. The community that learned to say *we hear and obey* rather than *we hear and disobey* (4:46) is here told whom to hear.

**Should You Disagree, Refer It to Allah and His Messenger**

The condition *fa in tanāzaʿtum fī shayʾin fa ruddūhu ilā Allāhi wa al-rasūli in kuntum tuʾminūna bi Allāhi wa al-yawmi al-ākhiri* — should you disagree on anything, refer it to Allah and His Messenger, if you truly believe in God and the Last Day — was read as the sūrah's method for disputes. *Tanāzaʿ* — to dispute, to pull against — covers disagreements about shares, dowries, trade, and judgment where trusts and fairness are at issue (4:58). *Ruddūhu* — refer it, return it — was explained as returning the question to the Book — *to Allah* — and to the prophetic clarification — *to the Messenger* — the two that make things clear (4:26). The clause *in kuntum tuʾminūna* ties referral to faith and to the Last Day where witnesses are brought and no statement can be hidden (4:41–42): to believe in that Day is to want the dispute judged by the standards of that Day. The Qur'an says that those who claim belief yet seek judgment of false judges, though commanded to reject them, are led by Satan farther away (4:60); referral to *ṭāghūt* is the opposite of the referral here. The sūrah's promise that God is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45) underwrites it: the dispute returned to the Book and the Messenger finds guardianship and help.

**The Best and Fairest Resolution**

The closing *dhālika khayrun wa aḥsanu taʾwīlā* — this is the best and fairest resolution — was read as comparing referral to any other arbitrament. *Khayr* — best — was explained as best in this world, because it keeps limits from being exceeded and trusts from being eaten; *aḥsanu taʾwīlā* — fairest in final interpretation, best in outcome — as best in the next, where the judgment will stand before the All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:58). The sūrah has shown two resolutions: keeping limits brings Gardens and ultimate triumph (4:13) while exceeding them brings humiliating abiding (4:14); avoiding major sins leads to an honourable entry (4:31) while persisting until death is present is not accepted (4:18). Referral to God and the Messenger is the mechanism that secures the better outcome at the level of dispute. A family that disagrees about a mother's third or sixth after siblings (4:11), a wife's quarter or eighth (4:12), or a bondwoman's fair dowry (4:25) — each finds the *khayr* and *aḥsan* by returning the question to the Book and the Messenger rather than to custom, desire, or a false judge. The phrase also answers the enviers who called disbelievers better guided (4:51): the fairest interpretation is not theirs, but the one that returns to the confirming revelation.

**Obedience That Protects Trusts and Judgments**

Read after *return trusts to rightful owners and judge with fairness* (4:58), this verse supplies the authority that makes those commands possible. Trusts are returned and judgments are fair only if the judge has a standard higher than the parties' desires and the community accepts it. Obedience to God and His Messenger provides that standard; obedience to those in authority among you executes it; referral resolves the remainder. The sūrah's earlier training — the witness scene (4:41), the guard of prayer by awareness (4:43), the sufficiency of God as Helper (4:45) — all converge here. To obey and to refer is not a burden added to weakness but a lightening, because *humankind was created weak* (4:28), and the surest way for the weak to avoid devouring wealth by falsehood (4:29) or killing and being burned where *that is easy for God* (4:30) is to have a clear place to bring the disagreement. The verse therefore draws the community's public life into the same shape as its private worship: as prayer is guarded by knowing what is said, disputes are guarded by knowing where they are referred.

**A Community Whose Disputes Return Upward**

Placed between the noble exhortation to return trusts (4:58) and the exposure of those who claim belief yet seek false judges (4:60), this verse defines the community that earns the Gardens of 4:57. It is a community that obeys, that honours authority within that obedience, and that, when it disputes — *in tanāzaʿtum fī shayʾin*, any thing — refers it upward. That upward referral is the opposite of the downward deviation that those who follow desires wish for you (4:27) and of the wordplay that takes words from their places (4:46). The sūrah has shown that God never wrongs by an atom but multiplies good and gives a great reward from grace (4:40); to refer disputes to Him and His Messenger is to place those multiplied goods where they will be counted exactly, and to find that the best and fairest outcome is not the one the strongest party could force but the one the All-Hearing, All-Seeing will endorse. The weak for whom the law was lightened can trust that referral, because the One to whom disputes are returned is the One who wills to make things clear, guide to noble ways, and turn toward those who return.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:60

> Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who claim they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you? They seek the judgment of false judges, which they were commanded to reject. And Satan ˹only˺ desires to lead them farther away

**Have You Not Seen Those Who Claim Belief**

The question *a lam tara ilā alladhīna yazʿumūna annahum āmanū bi mā unzila ilayka wa mā unzila min qablika yurīdūna an yataḥākamū ilā al-ṭāghūt* — have you not seen those who claim they believe in what was revealed to you and what was revealed before you, yet seek judgment of false judges — exposes a contradiction between claim and referral. *Yazʿumūna* — they claim, they assert — was stressed as mere profession: the sūrah has just said that true belief refers disputes to Allah and His Messenger (4:59), and that true belief worships without association and is kind in circles (4:36). To claim belief in what was revealed to you — the Qur'an that confirmed what is with those given a portion of the Book (4:47) — and in what was revealed before — the Torah and Gospel in their true light — and then to desire judgment from *ṭāghūt* — the false judge, the overstepping authority followed beyond its limit — is to belie the claim at its first test. Early reports placed the verse among hypocrites in Madinah who, when a dispute arose between a believer and a Jew, saw the Jew accept the Prophet ﷺ as arbiter while the hypocrite sought a soothsayer or a chief who judged by custom and bribe. The type was read broadly: any person who says he believes yet takes his case to a forum that judges by desire rather than by Book and Messenger.

**Which They Were Commanded to Reject**

The clause *wa qad umirū an yakfurū bihi* — though they were commanded to reject it — makes the referral doubly blameworthy. *Kufr bi al-ṭāghūt* — to deny, to reject the false authority — was commanded as the counterpart to belief in God, as in *whoever rejects ṭāghūt and believes in Allah has grasped the firm handhold*. The sūrah has already described belief in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* by those given a portion of the Book as trading guidance for misguidance (4:51), and has linked *ṭāghūt* to idols and false gods whose judgment lacks the *ʿadl* — fairness — commanded for judges (4:58). To seek judgment from what you were commanded to reject is to reverse the sūrah's ethic of referral — *refer it to Allah and His Messenger*, the best and fairest outcome (4:59) — and to choose the forum that follows desire and leads away. The sūrah's warnings *do not devour wealth by falsehood* and *do not kill* where *that is easy for God* (4:29–30) stand behind this: seeking *ṭāghūt* was read as the institutional form of that devouring, where property and life are taken by a judgment that is neither mutual consent nor fairness but overstep.

**Satan Desires to Lead Them Farther Away**

The closing *wa yurīdu al-shayṭānu an yuḍillahum ḍalālan baʿīdā* — and Satan only desires to lead them farther away — names the companion behind the forum. *Ḍalālan baʿīdā* — far, distant straying — was explained as the opposite of the noble ways God wills to guide to (4:26) and of the clear path He wills to make plain. The sūrah paired two wills before — *Allah wishes to turn to you, but those who follow desires wish you to deviate greatly* (4:27) — and here Satan's will is the deeper source of that wish. The false judge is not neutral; he is the instrument of a straying that grows with each step, as the sūrah showed where trading a portion for misguidance and reassuring disbelievers they are better guided (4:51) ends with no helper once condemned (4:52). The distance — *baʿīd* — was heard as both moral and spatial: far from the limits set as *ḥudūd* (4:13–14), far from the trust returned to rightful owners (4:58), and far from the Garden whose rivers flow and whose shade is vast (4:57). The hypocrites who seek *ṭāghūt* while claiming belief think they are choosing a convenient forum; the verse says they are being led farther from the path that was made clear and lightened because they are weak (4:28).

**Claim, Referral, and Far Straying as a Sequence**

The verse traces a sequence the sūrah has exposed in stages. First, the claim — *yazʿumūna annahum āmanū* — where belief is professed but not practised as referral; that claim was already diagnosed in *we hear and we disobey* said as though it were *we hear and obey* (4:46). Second, the referral — *yurīdūna an yataḥākamū ilā al-ṭāghūt* — where the dispute is taken to the wrong authority, the opposite of *fa ruddūhu ilā Allāhi wa al-rasūl* (4:59). Third, the straying — *yuḍillahum ḍalālan baʿīdā* — where Satan's desire moves the first detour into far wandering. The sūrah has shown that far wandering ends in wishes to be dust and no speech hidden from God (4:42), in Fire with skin renewed for tasting (4:56), and in condemnation with no helper (4:52). The distance is therefore not an abstraction; it is the measured gap between Gardens and Fire that the sūrah keeps open. To seek *ṭāghūt* is to step deliberately onto the side where *rāʿinā* is played with tongues and faith is discredited, rather than the side where *unẓurnā* is said and *it would have been better and more proper* (4:46).

**A Test of Belief That Is Practical**

Placed after the command to return trusts and judge with fairness, the noble exhortation of the All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:58), and the command to obey and refer disputes (4:59), this verse tests belief at the point where it costs. It is easy to claim belief in what was revealed to you and before you while there is no dispute; the test comes when a dispute arises over property, marriage, or honour — the very matters this sūrah has regulated — and the claimant must choose the judge. To choose the Book and the Messenger is to accept that inheritance shares after debts (4:11–12), dowry not reclaimed (4:20–21), and trade by mutual consent (4:29) will be the standard; to choose *ṭāghūt* is to seek a standard that follows desire, as those who follow desires wish you to deviate greatly (4:27). The sūrah therefore makes referral the measure of sincerity: the one who claims belief and then seeks the false judge has claimed one thing and willed another — *yazʿum* and *yurīd* — and the will exposes the claim. Satan's desire to lead farther away is already at work in that will, which is why the sūrah follows this exposure with the hypocrites' stubborn turning when called to the revelations and the Messenger (4:61), and with the disaster that later brings them back swearing they intended only good (4:62).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:61

> When it is said to them, "Come to Allah's revelations and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turn away from you stubbornly

**Come to the Revelations and the Messenger**

The verse pictures a call and a response: *wa idhā qīla lahum taʿālaw ilā mā anzala Allāhu wa ilā al-rasūl* — when it is said to them, come to Allah's revelations and to the Messenger — referring to those who claim belief yet seek judgment of false judges (4:60). The invitation *taʿālaw* — come, come up — carries elevation, as though the Book and the Messenger are higher ground. The revelations — *mā anzala Allāhu* — include the shares after debts, the dowry protection, trade by mutual consent, and the command to return trusts and judge with fairness (4:58), while the Messenger is the one who makes those matters clear and guides to noble ways. To come to both is to refer disputes where the sūrah said referral secures the best and fairest outcome (4:59). The call is passive — *qīla lahum*, it is said to them — showing that the community itself calls, not only the Prophet ﷺ alone: the believers who were told to obey and refer are the ones who say *come*, because the sūrah's ethic is communal — return trusts, appoint mediators, speak kindly. The invitation therefore tests whether the claim of belief is willing to be judged by what it claims to believe.

**You See the Hypocrites Turn Away Stubbornly**

The response is *raʾayta al-munāfiqīna yaṣuddūna ʿanka ṣudūdā* — you see the hypocrites turn away from you stubbornly, barring, holding back. The doubled form — verb plus verbal noun, *yaṣuddūna ṣudūdā* — stresses stubborn barring, not a polite excuse. The hypocrites were explained as those who display belief with the tongue while preferring another judge with the heart, as in the report of a Jew and a hypocrite who disputed and the Jew accepted the Prophet ﷺ while the hypocrite sought a soothsayer. The turning is *ʿanka* — from you — personal to the Messenger ﷺ, showing that referral to the Book is inseparable from referral to him. The sūrah has said that God is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45) and that whoever takes Satan as associate has an evil associate (4:38); to turn from the Messenger to *ṭāghūt* is to choose the second companionship. The doubling *ṣudūdā* suggests both that they turn themselves away and that they bar others, as earlier they wished you to deviate greatly (4:27) and promoted stinginess (4:37). To see them turn in that way is to see the earlier diagnosis made visible: those given a portion who trade it for misguidance (4:44) and who believe in *jibt* (4:51) do not merely hold an opinion; they move.

**Why the Call Exposes the Hypocrite**

The call to *come to what Allah revealed and to the Messenger* exposes what seeking *ṭāghūt* had concealed. A person can claim *we believe in what was revealed to you and before you* (4:60) while no dispute is present; the claim is cheap where it costs nothing. When a real dispute over property, marriage, or alliance requires a judgment that will give a wife her quarter or an orphan his share, the claim is tested. The hypocrite turns because the Book's judgment will not favour the desire that sent him to the false judge. The sūrah has prepared this test since it defined trade by mutual consent (4:29) and said deliberate devouring leads to Fire that is easy for God (4:30); the hypocrite prefers the judge whose consent is to power, not to truth. The verse therefore links to 4:59's condition for true believers: *if you disagree, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you truly believe in God and the Last Day*. The hypocrite's turning shows the condition was not met — belief in the Last Day, where a witness is brought and nothing hidden (4:41–42), would have made him come; he turns because he trusts the nearer gain of *ṭāghūt* more than the distant witness.

**Turning as Barring**

The emphatic *yaṣuddūna ʿanka ṣudūdā* was read as both intransitive and transitive: they turn away and they bar. The same root *ṣadda* described those who turned away from him (4:55) — *man ṣadda ʿanhu* — where Hell sufficed as blaze. Here the hypocrites are *yaṣuddūna* — barring — implying they not only refuse to come but keep others from coming, by example, excuse, or alliance with those who distort words — *we hear and disobey* (4:46). The sūrah has shown that barring is the method of those who follow desires and wish you to deviate (4:27) and of those who reassure disbelievers they are better guided (4:51). The hypocrite's stubborn turning is therefore not a private withdrawal; it is a public barricade. The Prophet ﷺ is told *you see them* — *raʾayta* — you see it plainly, implying the turning is not hidden behind courtesy. That seeing prepares the counsel of the next verses: God knows what is in their hearts, so turn away from them, caution them, and speak a penetrating word (4:63) — advice that reaches the soul rather than only the tribunal.

**A Picture That Precedes the Next Disaster**

Placed after the exposure of seeking false judges (4:60) and before the scene where disaster strikes because of what hands have done and the same people come swearing they intended only goodwill (4:62), this verse sets the picture of stubborn turning before its consequence. The sūrah has said that God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing over trusts and judgments (4:58) and All-Knowing, All-Aware over mediations where harmony is desired (4:35); here seeing — *raʾayta* — is given to the Prophet ﷺ as human witness to the same. The believers who were taught to appoint mediators from both families where a split is feared (4:35) will now apply the same realism to the community's split: when the call to the Book and the Messenger is met with barring, they know whom they see. The verse does not yet command what to do with the hypocrites; it says *look*. That looking prepares the next steps — disaster that brings them back swearing, and the counsel to turn away, caution, and speak to their souls — without rushing to force. The stubborn turning is first named, then its fruit will be tasted, and then the way of dealing with those who turn will be shown as both firm and inward.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:62

> How ˹horrible˺ will it be if a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have done, then they come to you swearing by Allah, "We intended nothing but goodwill and reconciliation."

**How Will It Be When a Disaster Strikes Them**

The question *fa kayfa idhā aṣābathum muṣībatun bi mā qaddamat aydīhim* — how will it be if a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have done — mirrors the sūrah's earlier *how will it be when We bring a witness from every community* (4:41). *Muṣībah* — disaster, affliction that hits the mark — was read as any calamity that exposes the hypocrite's referral to false judges (4:60) and his stubborn turning from the revelations and Messenger (4:61): defeat, exposure, punishment, or the failure of the alliance with *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* that did not help (4:52). *Bi mā qaddamat aydīhim* — because of what their hands have done — ties the disaster to their own prior acts, as the sūrah tied Fire to deliberate devouring where *that is easy for Allah* (4:30) and humiliating punishment to concealing bounty (4:37). The question *kayfa* — how — is left hanging, as it was with the witness scene, so the listener feels the shame before it is described. Those who sought the false judge for advantage will find advantage become affliction, because the false judge's path is Satan's desire to lead farther away (4:60), and farther away ends in no helper.

**Then They Come to You Swearing Goodwill**

The scene that follows — *thumma jāʾūka yaḥlifūna bi Allāhi in aradnā illā iḥsānan wa tawfīqā* — then they come to you swearing by Allah, we intended nothing but goodwill and reconciliation — was read as the hypocrites returning after the disaster with oaths that they meant only good. *Iḥsān* — kindness, doing good — and *tawfīq* — reconciliation, bringing together — sound like the sūrah's own aims where it said appoint mediators from families, and if they desire reconciliation God will bring harmony (4:35). The hypocrites borrow that language after the fact, claiming their request to *ṭāghūt* was an attempt to reconcile rather than to deviate. Early reports placed this among hypocrites who, after being exposed, excused their resort to a soothsayer as seeking amicability between factions. The sūrah presents the excuse as oath — *yaḥlifūna bi Allāhi*, swearing — the same form the Qur'an elsewhere says the hypocrites use as a shield. To swear by God that only goodwill was intended while the Book and Messenger were turned from (4:61) is to use the Name of the One who is ever Watchful (4:1) and All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:58) as cover for what the hands already did. The sūrah has said that on the Day when witnesses are brought, no statement can be hidden from God (4:42); this oath anticipates that Day on a smaller stage, where the speaker thinks words can hide hands.

**Because of What Their Hands Have Done**

The phrase *bi mā qaddamat aydīhim* was stressed as tying the disaster to prior choice, not to fate alone. The hands that sought *ṭāghūt* — the hands that signed, paid, or promised alliance — are the same hands to which the disaster is traced. The sūrah has tracked hands throughout: the hand that mixes orphan wealth (4:2), that reclaims a heap of gold by slander (4:20), that trades a portion of the Book (4:44), that distorts words with tongues (4:46), that fabricates lies against God as blatant sin (4:50) — each act done by hands that later claim goodwill. To say disaster strikes because of what hands put forward is to say recompense is continuous, as skin renewed for tasting is continuous (4:56) and as an atom's weight of good is multiplied continuously (4:40). The hypocrites' oath tries to separate intention from act, claiming a good will behind a bad referral; the verse keeps intention and act together by attributing the *muṣībah* to what hands did. A will that chose *ṭāghūt* over the Book and Messenger is already known — *Allah knows what is in their hearts*, as the next verse says (4:63) — so the hands' work is the evidence of it.

**Goodwill and Reconciliation as Borrowed Language**

The words *iḥsān* and *tawfīq* in the oath are not condemned in themselves; the sūrah commends both where they are real — *iḥsān* to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, neighbours, companions, travellers, and those in possession (4:36), and *tawfīq* between spouses where mediators desire harmony and God brings it (4:35). What the verse exposes is borrowed goodness after disaster, not goodwill before. To seek *ṭāghūt* for judgment is not *iḥsān* toward the community, because *iḥsān* in judgment is to return trusts and judge with fairness as a noble exhortation (4:58) and to refer disputes to God and Messenger as best outcome (4:59); to seek *ṭāghūt* is the opposite of *tawfīq* — it leads farther away, as Satan desires (4:60). When disaster follows — exposure, loss of trust, or defeat — to come swearing goodwill is to ask that the borrowed words cover the referral. The sūrah has already said that failure to repent until death is present is not accepted (4:18) while turning soon is accepted (4:17); the oath after disaster is closer to the first than the second, because it comes after the hands' work and only when the cover is needed.

**How Will It Be — the Unanswered Question as Warning**

As with 4:41's *how will it be when witnesses are brought*, the question *how will it be if a disaster strikes* is left open, inviting the listener to imagine the hypocrites' standing before the Prophet ﷺ with oaths, and more broadly before God with perfect knowledge of them (4:39) and before the Day when no speech can be hidden (4:42). The horror lies in the combination: a disaster earned by hands, and oaths that try to rename the hands' work as goodwill. The sūrah prepares the answer with the counsel that God knows their hearts and directs turning away, cautioning, and penetrating inner advice (4:63) — counsel that treats the oaths as known and insufficient. What is needed is not more oaths but an admonition that reaches the soul. For the believers the question is also a mirror: to avoid being those who must come swearing after disaster, refer disputes while they are small to the Book and Messenger, keep trusts, judge fairly, and desire reconciliation sincerely — so that when hardship comes it finds hands that had put forward belief, good, and a great reward from grace, rather than hands that had already put forward a referral to false judges.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:63

> ˹Only˺ Allah knows what is in their hearts. So turn away from them, caution them, and give them advice that will shake their very souls

**Allah Knows What Is in Their Hearts**

The clause *ulāʾika alladhīna yaʿlamu Allāhu mā fī qulūbihim* — only Allah knows what is in their hearts — follows the oath of the hypocrites that they intended nothing but goodwill and reconciliation after disaster struck because of what their hands put forward (4:62). The oaths were *yaḥlifūna bi Allāhi* — swearing by God — yet the verse says the hearts behind the oaths are known to Him. The sūrah has prepared that knowledge: He is ever Watchful over you (4:1), sufficient as Reckoner (4:6), Witness over all things (4:33), All-Knowing, All-Aware where mediators desire harmony (4:35), All-Hearing, All-Seeing over trusts and judgments (4:58), with perfect knowledge of them (4:39). To say He knows what is in hearts is to say oaths do not change the record; the hands' referral to false judges (4:60) and the stubborn turning from the Book and Messenger (4:61) are already entered. The Qur'an elsewhere says that God knows the treachery of the eyes and what breasts conceal, and that He knows the hypocrites' excuse before it is spoken. Here that knowledge is placed at the head of the counsel, so that what follows is done with clarity: the Prophet ﷺ and the community are not told to uncover hearts by force; they are told that hearts are already known to the One who will reckon.

**Turn Away From Them**

The first instruction *fa aʿriḍ ʿanhum* — so turn away from them — was read as turning away from their oaths, their company where it seeks *ṭāghūt*, and their attempt to draw the Prophet ﷺ into endorsing their excuse. *Iʿrāḍ* — to turn aside, to withdraw face — matches the earlier scene where they turned away stubbornly — *yaṣuddūna ʿanka ṣudūdā* (4:61) — and answers it with a measured withdrawal rather than harsh exposure. The sūrah has used *aʿriḍ* for the community's relief of those who repent and mend after discipline (4:16), showing that turning away can be mercy where amendment appears; here it is discipline for those whose oaths are known to be hollow. It denies the social reward of being taken at their word while disaster is still fresh, without yet removing the chance to hear. The community that was told to refer disputes to God and Messenger as best outcome (4:59) is here told not to refer to the hypocrites' oaths as evidence: the referral goes upward, not outward to their sworn excuses. Turning away therefore protects the community from being softened by oaths that the All-Knowing has already weighed.

**Caution Them**

The second instruction *wa ʿiẓhum* — and caution them, exhort them — adds the voice of warning. *Waʿẓ* — admonition that reaches the heart — was explained as private caution that names what was done — seeking false judges though commanded to reject them, turning from the revelations and the Messenger — and what follows if it persists: condemnation with no helper (4:52), blaze sufficient (4:55), Fire with skin renewed (4:56). The sūrah has shown caution as part of handling ill-conduct in the home — advise them first (4:34) — and as part of the noble exhortation to return trusts and judge with fairness (4:58); here caution is directed at the community's internal ill-conduct, where hypocrisy seeks to make the Book one judge among others. To caution is to bring the hypocrite back to the referral that defines belief: come to what God revealed and to the Messenger (4:61). The caution is not public shaming but moral alert, because the One who knows hearts also wills to turn toward those who turn (4:26–27) and to lighten because weakness is real (4:28) — caution keeps that turn possible.

**Advice That Will Shake Their Souls**

The third instruction *wa qul lahum fī anfusihim qawlan balīghā* — and give them advice that will shake their very souls — was read as speech that reaches inside — *fī anfusihim*, in their selves — and is *balīgh*: reaching, penetrating, eloquent in the sense of arriving. It is not a slogan for crowds; it is the word that finds the hypocrite alone and tells him what God knows is in his heart. Early authorities described *qawlan balīghā* as speech that makes the hearer fear the standing before witnesses where no statement can be hidden (4:41–42), that recalls the atom's weight that is never wronged but multiplied (4:40), and that reminds that soon repentance for ignorance is accepted while deferral until death is present is not (4:17–18). The sūrah has praised *qawlan maʿrūfā* — kind speech at distribution (4:8) — and *qawlan sadīdā* — straight speech (4:9); here it adds penetrating speech that moves the private self. The progression of three — turn away, caution, penetrate — was stressed as a graduated response: withdraw social endorsement, warn of limits and recompense, then speak to the soul that alone can choose belief before the disaster becomes the greater one. *Qawlan balīghā* is not harsh for harshness; it is precise, as a physician's word that reaches the illness, because the illness is in the heart.

**A Method for Hearts That Swear**

Placed between the oath of goodwill after disaster (4:62) and the promise that those who wronged themselves and came seeking forgiveness would find God ever Accepting, Most Merciful if the Messenger prayed for them (4:64), this verse gives the method for hearts that swear. It tells the Prophet ﷺ not to be taken by the oath, not to expose vindictively, but to combine distance, warning, and inward speech. The sūrah has shown that God is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45) and that He knows best who enemies are; here that sufficiency becomes practice: the community leans on the One who knows hearts while it turns, cautions, and speaks penetratingly. The three steps keep the door open where the hypocrites' own turning had closed it stubbornly (4:61), but they keep it open only as a path back to the Book and Messenger, not as a path back to *ṭāghūt*. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the verse is also a mercy: the advice that shakes the soul is the same that invites the soul to be among those who believe and do good and are admitted to Gardens with pure spouses and vast shade (4:57) — after being told that avoidance of major sins covers lesser ones and opens honour (4:31).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:64

> We only sent messengers to be obeyed by Allah's Will. If only those ˹hypocrites˺ came to you ˹O Prophet˺—after wronging themselves—seeking Allah's forgiveness and the Messenger prayed for their forgiveness, they would have certainly found Allah ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful

**Messengers Sent to Be Obeyed by Allah's Leave**

The statement *wa mā arsalnā min rasūlin illā li yuṭāʿa bi idhni Allāh* — We only sent messengers to be obeyed by Allah's Will — follows the counsel to turn away from hypocrites, caution them, and speak penetratingly to their souls (4:63). The verse gives the reason referral to the Messenger is not optional. A messenger is not sent to be one judge among false judges — *ṭāghūt* — whom they were commanded to reject (4:60), nor to be heard and disobeyed with distorted *rāʿinā* (4:46); he is sent *li yuṭāʿa* — to be obeyed — and that obedience is *bi idhni Allāh* — by Allah's leave, permission, and enabling. Obedience to the Messenger is therefore not a separate loyalty but the form obedience to God takes where He has sent a clarifier. The sūrah has said to obey God and obey the Messenger and those in authority within that obedience, and to refer disputes to them as best outcome (4:59); here it explains why — the sending itself was for obedience. The hypocrites' stubborn turning from the revelations and the Messenger (4:61) contradicts the very purpose of sending. The sūrah has shown that God wills to make things clear and guide to noble ways and turn toward you (4:26); the messenger is that clarity and guide made a person, and to be sent to be obeyed is how the will to turn becomes practicable.

**Had They Come After Wronging Themselves**

The counterfactual *wa law annahum idh ẓalamū anfusahum jāʾūka fa astaghfarū Allāha wa astaghfara lahumu al-rasūl* — if only, after wronging themselves, they had come to you seeking Allah's forgiveness and the Messenger prayed for their forgiveness — pictures the alternative to seeking *ṭāghūt* and swearing goodwill after disaster (4:62). *Ẓalamū anfusahum* — wronging themselves — was read as the referral to false judges and the barring from the Book and Messenger, the same *ẓulm* that elsewhere describes devouring orphan wealth and exceeding limits. To come — *jāʾūka* — is to reverse the turn; to seek forgiveness — *istaghfarū Allāha* — is to name the wrong as sin needing pardon, not as goodwill; to have the Messenger seek forgiveness for them is to join the community's intercession to their turn. The sūrah has said that repentance is accepted for those who act ignorantly and turn soon (4:17); the Messenger's prayer for forgiveness is part of that path, since sincere return from hands that put forward the referral to false judges requires both recognition and supplication. The verse is therefore not a ritual of coming to a man; it is coming to the one sent to be obeyed so that obedience can be restored where it was refused.

**They Would Have Found Allah Ever Accepting, Most Merciful**

The promise *la wajadū Allāha tawwāban raḥīmā* — they would have certainly found Allah ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful — gives the outcome of that coming. *Tawwāb* — ever Accepting, repeatedly turning — was explained as God turning toward the servant who turns toward Him, again and again, as He turns toward those who repent soon after ignorance (4:17). *Raḥīm* — Most Merciful — is the sūrah's refrain for the weak for whom burdens are lightened (4:28) and for whom earth purifies where water fails (4:43). The pair tells the hypocrites that the door they closed by seeking *ṭāghūt* is still the door of mercy if they come through the Messenger. The sūrah has stressed that God forgives what is below *shirk* for whomever He wills (4:48), while *shirk* held to death without turning is not forgiven — yet the turn remains possible while breath remains and before death is present (4:18). To find Him *tawwāb* is to find that coming after wronging oneself, with *istighfār* and the Messenger's *istighfār*, is the soon return that is accepted. The verse does not guarantee acceptance without coming; it guarantees acceptance with it.

**Why the Messenger's Prayer Matters**

The addition of the Messenger's seeking forgiveness — *astaghfara lahumu al-rasūl* — was read as more than courtesy. The Messenger is the witness brought over his community (4:41) and the one whose acceptance as judge proves the claim to believe (4:65), so his prayer for them signifies that their return is not isolated but rejoined to the community. Early authorities noted that the hypocrites who had sought *ṭāghūt* had broken the communal trust that disputes are referred to Book and Messenger as best outcome (4:59); to return and seek forgiveness with his prayer repairs that breach. The Qur'an elsewhere says that if they had come seeking forgiveness, it would have been better and more proper — as straight speech would have been better than *rāʿinā* (4:46). Here the same better and more proper is enacted as movement — come, seek, have him seek — rather than as wording alone. The sūrah's ethic of *iḥsān* (4:36) and of appointing mediators where harmony is desired and God brings it (4:35) finds an echo: where the soul desires reconciliation, God brings it, and where the hypocrite desires forgiveness, the Messenger's prayer joins — and God is found ever Accepting.

**A Verse That Keeps Obedience and Mercy Together**

Placed between the counsel to speak penetratingly to souls (4:63) and the oath that true belief requires accepting the Prophet ﷺ as judge without resistance (4:65), this verse holds obedience and mercy together. Obedience — messengers sent to be obeyed by God's leave — is the structure; mercy — *ever Accepting, Most Merciful* for those who come after wronging themselves — is the purpose of the structure. The structure without mercy would be harsh, and mercy without structure would leave hypocrites seeking false judges and swearing goodwill as sufficient. The verse joins them: the structure is to obey the sent one, and the mercy is found by coming to him after wronging, seeking God's forgiveness with his supplication. The sūrah has shown that avoidance of major sins covers lesser faults and opens honour (4:31) and that not an atom's weight is wronged but good is multiplied (4:40); this verse is the social form of that covering, where the major of referring to *ṭāghūt* is undone by coming, seeking, and being prayed for. For the weak for whom *He wishes to lighten your burdens* (4:28), the way back from a grave referral is not distant: it is to walk to the one sent to be obeyed, to seek pardon, and to find the One who is ever ready to turn.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:65

> But no! By your Lord, they will never be ˹true˺ believers until they accept you ˹O Prophet˺ as the judge in their disputes, and find no resistance within themselves against your decision and submit wholeheartedly

**By Your Lord, They Will Never Be Believers Until**

The oath *fa lā wa rabbika lā yuʾminūna ḥattā yuḥakkimūka fī mā shajara baynahum* — but no, by your Lord, they will never be true believers until they accept you as judge in their disputes — follows the promise that those who wronged themselves and came seeking forgiveness with the Messenger's prayer would find God ever Accepting (4:64). The oath *wa rabbika* — by your Lord — personalises the guarantee to the Prophet ﷺ; the Lord who sent messengers to be obeyed by His leave is invoked as witness that faith remains incomplete until judgment is accepted from the sent one. *Yuḥakkimūka* — to make you judge, to seek your arbitration — was read as referral in any dispute — *mā shajara baynahum*, what sprouts, what tangles between them — whether about property, marriage, or alliance. The sūrah has just said to refer disputes to Allah and His Messenger as best and fairest outcome (4:59) and to reject false judges though commanded (4:60); this verse makes that referral the measure of faith itself. Claim — *yazʿumūna*, that they believe (4:60) — is not enough; the test is whether the claimant, when entangled, makes the Prophet ﷺ the judge.

**Disputes That Sprout Between People**

The phrase *fī mā shajara baynahum* — with *shajara* evoking what branches and entangles — was explained as any quarrel that grows between people where rights are tangled: the same quarrels the sūrah has regulated — a mother's third or sixth (4:11), a wife's quarter or eighth (4:12), a dowry left or reclaimed (4:20–21), a trade by mutual consent or falsehood (4:29), a split where mediators are appointed (4:35). The sūrah has shown that those quarrels are resolved by returning trusts to rightful owners and judging with fairness as a noble exhortation from the All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:58); here the exemplar of that fairness is the Prophet ﷺ himself. Early reports placed the verse after a dispute where a Jew accepted the Prophet's judgment while a hypocrite sought another arbiter, and after an incident where a Companion expected favour and did not receive it; the general rule was read as covering every *shajara* where faith and desire pull against each other. To accept him as judge in that tangle is to accept that the limits — *ḥudūd* — he clarified are the standard, and that the clarity God wills (4:26) is the clarity he brings.

**No Resistance Within Themselves**

The second condition *thumma lā yajidū fī anfusihim ḥarajan mimmā qaḍayta* — and find no resistance within themselves against your decision — moves from outer referral to inner acceptance. *Ḥaraj* — tightness, constriction, resistance — was read as the reluctance that remains after the mouth says *I accept* but the chest tightens against the share given. The sūrah has diagnosed that tightness elsewhere: craving what God gave some over others (4:32), begrudging the people for bounty (4:54), promoting stinginess (4:37). To find no *ḥaraj* is to be free of that constriction — to assent where the judgment gives a wife her quarter or gives a daughter her half, as God appointed. The verse requires not only outward compliance but inward ease. The hypocrites who turn away stubbornly (4:61) and then come swearing goodwill after disaster (4:62) show outward movement without inner openness; this verse demands the opposite — referral with an open chest. The Qur'an elsewhere says that God expands the chest for guidance, and that expansion is the counterpart to the constriction removed here. The sūrah has said that God suffices as Guardian and Helper (4:45) and that He multiplies an atom's weight (4:40); to find no resistance is to trust that the judgment that seems to reduce one's share will be multiplied elsewhere.

**Submit Wholeheartedly**

The third condition *wa yusallimū taslīmā* — and submit wholeheartedly — was read as full surrender, the doubled verbal noun stressing total submission without reservation. *Taslīm* was explained as peace in submission, the opposite of the *ṣudūd* — barring — that marks the hypocrite (4:61). The sūrah has shown submission in action: avoiding major sins to be admitted to honour (4:31), asking God for bounty rather than craving another's (4:32), returning trusts and judging with fairness (4:58); here submission is the inner counterpart to those outer acts, where the dispute is not about a small provision but about a right the self resists yielding. The doubling was heard as requiring submission that is not partial or conditional — not *I submit if the judgment favours me* — but submission that remains even when it fails to favour. That wholeness is why the verse is an oath: faith is not complete until the judgment of the sent one is accepted, felt as ease, and lived as surrender — which is also why the sūrah will say that had they done what they were advised, it would have been better and more reassuring and would have brought great reward and guidance to the straight path (4:66–68).

**A Measure of True Belief**

Placed between the open door of coming after wronging oneself to find God ever Accepting (4:64) and the reminder that doing what was advised would have been better (4:66), this oath defines the threshold of true belief. It is not a demand for perfection from the weak — the sūrah has said He wills to lighten because humans were created weak (4:28) and to cover lesser faults where major sins are avoided (4:31) — but a demand for sincerity where judgment is given. The community that was taught to appoint mediators where a split is feared (4:35) and to refer disputes upward (4:59) is here told that the referral must be without inward *ḥaraj* and with whole *taslīm*. The Prophet ﷺ as judge in tangled disputes is the living form of the sūrah's ethic of limits. To accept his judgment without resistance is to live as one who believes that not an atom's weight is wronged, that good is multiplied many times, and that the One who is All-Hearing, All-Seeing will see the surrender. The oath *by your Lord* makes that acceptance not a recommendation but the line between claim and faith — between professing belief in what was revealed and actually coming to it when the dispute sprouts.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:66

> If We had commanded them to sacrifice themselves or abandon their homes, none would have obeyed except for a few. Had they done what they were advised to do, it would have certainly been far better for them and more reassuring

**A Hard Command They Would Not Have Borne**

The verse states *wa law annā katabnā ʿalayhim an iqtulū anfusakum aw ikhrujū min diyārikum mā faʿalūhu illā qalīlun minhum* — if We had commanded them to sacrifice themselves or abandon their homes, none would have obeyed except for a few. The sūrah has just set an oath that true belief requires accepting the Prophet ﷺ as judge without inward resistance and with whole submission (4:65). That oath is demanding, yet this verse says a still harder command — to kill themselves or to leave their homes — would have been obeyed by even fewer. *Anfusakum* — yourselves — was read as sacrificing their own lives, and *min diyārikum* — from your homes — as exodus, as the migrants endured when they left Makkah. The sūrah therefore measures the community against a harsher test and finds only a few would have passed — which is not condemnation of all but realism about weakness. The same weakness explained as *humankind was created weak* (4:28) and met with lightening is shown here as historical fact: given a command that cut at life and home, most would have held back. The verse was linked to hypocrites who claimed belief yet turned from the Book and Messenger (4:60–61); the harder command exposes that softer claims of obedience already falter, so harder claims would have failed almost entirely.

**Had They Done What They Were Advised**

The alternative *wa law annahum faʿalū mā yūʿaẓūna bihi la kāna khayran lahum wa ashadda tathbītā* — had they done what they were advised to do, it would have been far better for them and more reassuring — names the better path that was actually asked. *Mā yūʿaẓūna bihi* — what they were advised, what they were exhorted to do — gathers the noble exhortations the sūrah has given: return trusts to rightful owners and judge with fairness (4:58); obey God and the Messenger and refer disputes (4:59); accept the Prophet ﷺ as judge without *ḥaraj* and with *taslīm* (4:65); avoid major sins (4:31); trade by mutual consent (4:29). None of those require leaving homes or self-sacrifice; they require keeping limits about wealth and marriage, referral to the Book, and obedience where obedience is the purpose of sending (4:64). To have done that *would have been khayr* — better — in both worlds, and *ashadda tathbītā* — more reassuring, firmer in grounding. *Tathbīt* — to make firm, to reassure — was read as inner firmness, steadiness after the wavering that marks the hypocrite. The sūrah elsewhere says *if you avoid major sins We will cover lesser ones and admit you to honour* (4:31); doing what was advised is that avoidance made active, and firmness is its inner reward.

**Better and More Firm Than a Harder Test**

The verse contrasts two goods: doing the harder hypothetical command and doing the actual advice. The hypothetical — sacrifice or exodus — would have been a great test, but the verse says few would have done it, so its good would have been rare. The actual advice — the Book's limits and the Messenger's judgment — was within reach, and doing it would have been *khayran lahum*, better for them, than failing the harder one, and *ashadda tathbītā*, more reassuring, than the anxiety that comes from claiming belief while seeking false judges (4:60). Early authorities noted that the sūrah's actual commands are lightened because the human was created weak (4:28), and lightened law obeyed is better than heavy law ignored. The hypocrites sought honour through alliance with *ṭāghūt* and rejoiced when absent from hardship; to have done what was advised — return trusts, judge fairly, come to the Messenger after wronging themselves to find Him ever Accepting (4:64) — would have replaced that shallow relief with deep reassurance. The reassurance is not only moral but practical: a community that keeps shares and trusts has less to fear from disaster, and a heart that submits without resistance has less inner constriction.

**A Few Who Would Have Obeyed Even the Hard**

The phrase *illā qalīlun minhum* — except for a few — was read as the sincere among them, the same few acknowledged after condemnation for distorting words (4:46) and after the division where some believed in him (4:55). Those few would have obeyed even a command to sacrifice or emigrate, as the true migrants did and as the few who accept the Prophet ﷺ as judge without *ḥaraj* do now. The verse does not name them to praise them as exclusive; it names them to show that obedience at the hard level exists, which makes obedience at the lighter level more shameful to refuse. If a few would have given life and home for God, then all can give a sixth to a mother or a dowry to a wife or a referral to the Book. The sūrah's ethic is therefore scaled: the same willingness that would have left a home is asked to leave a claim that exceeds a limit. The one who would not leave a home when commanded would also not leave a false judge when commanded to reject him; the one who would have left would also return a trust. The verse therefore measures sincerity by readiness — and tells the majority that the better and more firm path remains open without requiring the hardest test.

**Advice That Firms the Heart**

Placed after the oath of faith as submission (4:65) and before the promise of great reward and guidance to the straight path for doing what was advised (4:67–68), this verse is the sūrah's pastoral diagnosis for wavering hearts. It acknowledges that a community learning to divide estates with *whether little or much* (4:7), to guard the orphan's property with witnesses (4:6), and to defend the oppressed (4:75) will find the commands heavy if measured against a still heavier command that only a few would bear. To have done what was advised — come to the Messenger, seek forgiveness, accept judgment, avoid major sins, trade by mutual consent — would have been better and more reassuring, not because the advised acts are small, but because they are the deeds that make the heart firm. The next verses say that doing them brings great reward by grace and guidance to the straight path (4:67–68); this verse says they also bring *tathbīt* — firmness — now, where the hypocrite feels only the tug between claiming belief and seeking *ṭāghūt*. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the better and firmer path is not the imagined heroic sacrifice alone, but the daily exhortation lived — which steadies the step before the harder road is ever required.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:67

> and We would have granted them a great reward by Our grace

**A Great Reward by Our Grace**

The promise *wa idhan la ātaynāhum min ladunnā ajran ʿaẓīmā* — and We would have granted them a great reward by Our grace — continues the counterfactual: had they done what they were advised to do, it would have been better and more reassuring (4:66), *and then* We would have granted a great reward — *ajran ʿaẓīmā* — from *ladunnā* — from Our presence, out of grace. The sūrah has used *ajr ʿaẓīm* before for the atom's weight multiplied — *We will multiply it many times over and give a great reward out of grace* (4:40) — and for those who strive in God's cause, whether they meet martyrdom or victory (4:74). Here it is the reward for doing what was advised — the ordinary exhorted acts of returning trusts, judging with fairness (4:58), referring disputes (4:59), and accepting the Prophet ﷺ as judge without resistance (4:65). *Min ladunnā* was stressed as grace beyond exact recompense — the same grace that makes the great reward more than multiplication. The counterfactual shows that the reward is not distant: it would have followed the advised deeds directly — *idhan*, then — without a long delay. The sūrah therefore invites the wavering to see that the great reward is not only for the hard command to sacrifice or emigrate that few would have done (4:66), but for the advised path that was within reach and was better.

**Grace That Makes the Reward Great**

The phrase *min ladunnā* was read as marking the source that makes the reward *ʿaẓīm* — great: a gift from a great giver is great because of the giver. The sūrah has already said that God never wrongs even by an atom's weight but multiplies good and gives a great reward out of grace (4:40), and that He is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45); that sufficiency is the background to this promise — the One who is sufficient to help against traders of misguidance is sufficient to grant. Early authorities linked *ajr ʿaẓīm* here to the Gardens promised for keeping limits (4:13), for believing and doing good with vast shade (4:57), and for obeying God and the Messenger so as to be in the company of the blessed (4:69). The reward is therefore not a single coin but a company and a place. The verse generalises what earlier verses specified: the honourable entry for avoiding major sins (4:31), the Gardens with rivers for keeping limits, the multiplication for an atom's weight. Had they done what was advised, that entire economy of grace would have been theirs — without needing to face the harder test.

**Had They Done — the Unlived Alternative**

The *law* — had they done — frames the great reward as an unlived alternative for the hypocrites who instead sought false judges and turned away stubbornly (4:60–61). The alternative was close: come to the revelations and the Messenger (4:61); refer disputes to them (4:59); accept judgment without *ḥaraj* (4:65). The Qur'an elsewhere says *whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger will be in the company of the blessed* (4:69), and this counterfactual shows the company missed. The phrasing *la ātaynāhum* — We would have given them — with the emphatic *lām* and *idhan*, was read as certainty, not hesitation: there was no doubt about the giver; the doubt was about the doers — few would have obeyed the hard command, and fewer still did the advised one. The great reward therefore hangs not on divine reluctance but on human doing. The sūrah has already said *Allah does not wrong even by an atom* (4:40) and *what harm if they had believed and donated from what was provided?* (4:39); the same logic operates: no harm would have come, and great reward would have, had the advised been done.

**Better, More Reassuring, Then Great Reward**

The three results form a progression: *khayr* — better — for the doer in outcome; *ashadda tathbītā* — more reassuring, firmer — for the heart in steadiness (4:66); *ajr ʿaẓīm* — great reward — from grace for the recompense beyond. The first is comparative benefit; the second is inner firmness; the third is outer honour. The sūrah elsewhere pairs *khayr* and *aḥsanu taʾwīlā* — best and fairest in outcome — for referral (4:59); here it pairs better and firmer with great reward. Doing what was advised therefore yields a better life where trusts are returned, a firmer heart where *ḥaraj* is removed, and a great reward where grace adds to multiplication. The progression mirrors the sūrah's movement from creation to trust to judgment to defending the oppressed (4:75): each step, when done, yields immediate betterment and firmness before any final reward. The hypocrites who claimed goodwill after disaster (4:62) sought reassurance through oaths; the verse says true reassurance — *tathbīt* — comes from doing what was advised, not from swearing after.

**A Verse That Holds the Door Open**

Placed between the better and more reassuring and the guidance to the straight path (4:68), this short promise holds the door open where the previous diagnosis could have closed it. The sūrah has said only a few would have obeyed the hard command (4:66), which could be heard as despair for the many; this verse says the many were not asked to do the hard but the advised, and that advised path, had it been taken, would have brought a great reward from grace. The invitation remains for the living, who were told *if only they had come after wronging themselves seeking forgiveness and the Messenger prayed for them, they would have found God ever Accepting* (4:64): to come now is to do what was advised now, and the reward then is still great and still from *ladunnā* — the presence that suffices. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the verse is the lightest of burdens: do what you were exhorted to do — return, judge fairly, refer, accept — and the great reward that elsewhere required sacrifice and emigration will be granted by grace. The sūrah therefore leaves the counterfactual not as regret but as map: the better, the firmer, and the great are still ahead for those who now do what they were advised.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:68

> and guided them to the Straight Path

**Guided to the Straight Path**

The promise *wa la hadaynāhum ṣirāṭan mustaqīmā* — and We would have guided them to the Straight Path — completes the counterfactual: had they done what they were advised, it would have been better and more reassuring (4:66); We would have granted a great reward by grace (4:67); and guided them to the straight path. The sūrah has used *ṣirāṭ mustaqīm* as the way God wills to make clear and to guide to — the noble ways of those before you (4:26) — the opposite of the far straying Satan desires when they seek false judges (4:60). To be guided to the straight path was explained as being shown the road and being made to walk it with firmness — *tathbīt* — the same firmness named as more reassuring in 4:66. The three results therefore form one movement: better outcome, firmer heart, great reward, straight guidance. The path is called straight — *mustaqīm* — because it does not tilt toward one at another's expense (4:129), nor deviate greatly as those who follow desires wish (4:27), nor turn away stubbornly as hypocrites do from the revelations and Messenger (4:61). The straight path was read as the Book and the prophetic way taken together, the same pair that disputes are referred to as best outcome (4:59); guidance to it is therefore not only information but enablement.

**Guidance as the Fruit of Doing**

The verse makes guidance a fruit of doing what was advised, not only of hearing it. The sūrah has warned against those who were given a portion of the Book yet trade it for misguidance and wish you to deviate (4:44), and who believe in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* and call disbelievers better guided (4:51). To do what was advised — return trusts to rightful owners and judge with fairness (4:58), obey and refer (4:59), accept the Prophet ﷺ as judge without inward resistance (4:65) — is the practice that keeps the path straight. Early authorities noted that *hadaynāhum* — We would have guided them — implies God's act of guidance follows the servant's act of obedience, as elsewhere *those who are guided, He increases them in guidance* and *whoever believes in God, He guides his heart*. The sūrah has also said that avoidance of major sins leads to an honourable entry (4:31) and that an atom's weight of good is multiplied with a great reward (4:40); guidance to the straight path is the form that entry takes when viewed as a road. The path is straight because it was made clear — *yubayyina* (4:26) — and because it is the way of those before who kept limits; to be guided to it is to be placed among them.

**The Path That Desires Made Deviate**

The contrast with 4:27 sharpens the promise. There, those who follow desires wish you to deviate greatly from God's Way; here, doing what was advised leads to being guided to the straight path, the opposite of deviation. The straight path is also the opposite of the false judge's way, to which Satan desires to lead farther away (4:60). The sūrah therefore presents two possible guidances: to the straight path by doing what was advised, or to far straying by seeking *ṭāghūt*. The choice is enacted in the same matters the sūrah has regulated: a guardian who returns orphan wealth with witnesses (4:6) walks straight; one who consumes it hastily before the orphan grows strays; a husband who gives the dowry graciously (4:4) walks straight; one who reclaims it by slander strays (4:20). Guidance to the straight path is therefore not a separate religious act added to those decisions; it is those decisions made consistently. The sūrah will soon say that whoever obeys God and the Messenger will be with the blessed — prophets, people of truth, martyrs, the righteous — what honourable company (4:69), and that company is the fellowship of the straight path.

**Why Great Reward and Straight Path Pair**

The verse pairs *ajr ʿaẓīm* — great reward by grace (4:67) — with *ṣirāṭ mustaqīm* — straight path — to show that recompense and direction belong together. Reward without guidance would be a gift without a road; guidance without reward would be a road without arrival. The sūrah joins them because the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28) need both: a path they can walk and a reward that makes walking worthwhile. The sūrah has already said that God wishes to lighten burdens because humankind was created weak, and that He wishes to turn toward you (4:26–27); to guide to the straight path is the form that turning takes when the servant does what was advised. The counterfactual — *had they done* — is therefore not a lament for a lost opportunity but a map for the living: do what you were advised now, and the two that were promised then — great reward and straight guidance — are still the sequence. The one who does not crave another's bounty but asks God for His (4:32), who does not devour by falsehood but trades by mutual consent (4:29), is already on the straight path, even if he has not yet seen its end.

**A Path That Holds After Witnesses and Before Battle**

Placed between the great reward and the company of the blessed (4:69), this verse holds the moral road between the witness scene (4:41–42) and the coming call to fight for the oppressed (4:75). The straight path that would have been granted had they done what was advised is the same path the believers are now called to walk when they take precautions and go forth in groups or together (4:71). It is straight because it does not seek false judges (4:60), does not distort words (4:46), does not believe in *jibt* (4:51), and does not envy for bounty (4:54) — each of those is a bend that the sūrah has straightened with a limit, a trust, or a referral. To be guided to that path is to have the heart made firm — *ashadda tathbītā* — so that when the order to fight comes, the group that fears people as God should be feared (4:77) will not turn, and when the order to give comes, the hand that was stingy will open. The verse generalises the promise beyond the hypocrites who failed the test: any who do what they were advised will find the same guidance. For the weak who were told that avoidance of major sins covers lesser ones (4:31), that promise is the straight road ahead, leading to the company the next verses name as the honourable fellowship of the guided.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:69

> And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger will be in the company of those blessed by Allah: the prophets, the people of truth, the martyrs, and the righteous—what honourable company

**Obedience That Places Among the Blessed**

The verse states *wa man yuṭiʿi Allāha wa al-rasūla fa ulāʾika maʿa alladhīna anʿama Allāhu ʿalayhim min al-nabiyyīna wa al-ṣiddīqīna wa al-shuhadāʾi wa al-ṣāliḥīn* — and whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger will be in the company of those blessed by Allah: the prophets, the people of truth, the martyrs, and the righteous. After the counterfactual — had they done what was advised it would have been better, more reassuring, with great reward and guidance to the straight path (4:66–68) — this verse names the positive fulfilment: obedience to God and the Messenger brings companionship with the most honoured. *Anʿama ʿalayhim* — those blessed, favoured — was read as those upon whom God bestowed bounty — *niʿmah* — the same bounty the sūrah said to ask for rather than crave in another's hand (4:32). The list moves in rank: prophets who receive revelation; people of truth — *ṣiddīqīn* — who embody truth without gap; martyrs — *shuhadāʾ* — who bear witness with blood; and the righteous — *ṣāliḥīn* — who do good. The sūrah has shown what that doing looks like: returning trusts, judging fairly (4:58), referring disputes (4:59), accepting the Prophet ﷺ as judge without inward resistance (4:65). To obey in those matters is to join the fellowship that walked them most fully.

**Prophets, People of Truth, Martyrs, and the Righteous**

Each group was explained with familiar names. Prophets — *nabiyyīn* — include Abraham, whose family was given Book, wisdom, and great authority (4:54), and among whom this Prophet ﷺ stands as the confirming heir. People of truth — *ṣiddīqīn* — were exemplified as Abū Bakr, who was called *al-Ṣiddīq* for immediate belief, and generally as those who never wavered when the order to fight came (4:77) or when trusts were to be returned. Martyrs — *shuhadāʾ* — were explained as those who fight in God's cause and achieve martyrdom or victory and are honoured with a great reward (4:74), and as witnesses who stand with the witness of every community (4:41). The righteous — *ṣāliḥīn* — were read as those who believe and do good, who enter Gardens with vast shade (4:57) and who avoid major sins and are admitted to honour (4:31). The verse was linked to a report that a Companion feared being separated from the Prophet ﷺ in the next life because of rank, and the verse came to assure that obedience joins, not rank alone. The sūrah has said that God elevates whomever He wills without wrong by a thread (4:49); here elevation joins obedience, not claim.

**What Honourable Company**

The exclamation *wa ḥasuna ulāʾika rafīqā* — what honourable company, how good are they as companions — was read as both description and longing. *Rafīq* — companion, fellow traveller — was explained as one who softens the path, whose nearness eases the journey. The Qur'an elsewhere says that on the Day when witnesses are brought and no statement can be hidden (4:41–42), people will be with those they followed; this verse names the company the obedient will have when that Day comes. To be *maʿa* — with — the prophets and the truthful is not to be a prophet but to share their blessed nearness, as the migrants and hosts who believed and fought for the oppressed (4:75) share the same cause though not the same rank. The sūrah has shown companionship as *al-ṣāḥibi bi al-janb* — the companion at your side deserving *iḥsān* (4:36); here companionship becomes eternal, where the *qarīn* is not Satan as evil associate (4:38) but the best of humans as *rafīq*. The exclamation invites the reader to desire that company, which is itself a form of obedience, because desire for that fellowship leads to the deeds that earn it.

**Obedience as the Sūrah Has Defined It**

The verse generalises obedience after a sūrah that has detailed what obedience looks like in many domains. To obey Allah and the Messenger here includes keeping limits about inheritance after debts (4:11–12), guarding the orphan's wealth with witnesses (4:6), giving dowries graciously (4:4), living with wives fairly even when dislike occurs (4:19), seeking marriage with wealth in chastity (4:24), trading by mutual consent (4:29), and fighting for the oppressed who cry for a helper (4:75). Each was commanded with the sūrah's refrain that God is All-Knowing, Witness, All-Hearing, All-Seeing — so obedience is not abstract. The verse was linked to the oath that faith is incomplete until the Prophet ﷺ is made judge in entanglements without resistance and with whole submission (4:65): to obey is to accept that judgment. The sūrah will soon command taking precautions and going forth in groups or together (4:71) and will describe believers who fight for God and disbelievers who fight for the Devil whose schemes are weak (4:76); obedience in that call is the same that places among martyrs and righteous. The verse therefore gathers the sūrah's public and private commands into a single companionship, showing that where obedience is, the blessed are.

**A Promise After Better, Reassuring, Reward, and Path**

Placed after better and more reassuring (4:66), great reward by grace (4:67), and guidance to the straight path (4:68), this verse adds the fellowship that makes those three sweet. A better outcome, a firmer heart, a great reward, and a straight path are crowned with company. The sūrah has just said that doing what was advised would have brought all three; this verse says obedience as lived brings the fourth — *with the blessed*. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28) and for whom not an atom's weight is wronged but multiplied (4:40), the promise means that the weak who obey in their measure are not separated by rank from the prophets who obeyed in theirs; they are with them as *rafīq*. The question *have you not seen* that exposed hypocrites (4:60–61) and traders of misguidance (4:44) is answered here with a better seeing: see the company that obedience yields. The honourable company is not only a future fellowship; it is already anticipated where believers stand together, refer disputes upward, and desire reconciliation — and God brings harmony between them (4:35).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:70

> This is Allah's favour, and Allah fully knows ˹who deserves it˺

**This Is Allah's Favour**

The verse states *dhālika al-faḍlu min Allāh* — this is Allah's favour — referring to the promise that whoever obeys God and the Messenger will be with the blessed: prophets, people of truth, martyrs, righteous, what honourable company (4:69). *Faḍl* — bounty, surplus, favour beyond exact recompense — was read as the surplus by which a servant's obedience places him among ranks he could not claim by deed alone: the same surplus the sūrah told the envious to stop craving in others' hands and to ask from God (4:32), and the same bounty the stingy conceal (4:37) — yet God multiplies an atom's weight many times over and adds a great reward from grace (4:40). To call that companionship *faḍl* is to say it is not a wage for hours; it is favour that crowns obedience. The sūrah has shown favour as *We have given the descendants of Abraham Book and wisdom and great authority* (4:54) — not earned by the recipient's claim but given — and as *great reward by Our grace* (4:67) for doing what was advised. Here favour is the fellowship that guidance to the straight path (4:68) yields. Obedience walks the path; favour admits to the company. The pronoun *dhālika* — this — points back to the entire promise, making the whole companionship, not only a part, the favour.

**And Allah Fully Knows Who Deserves It**

The clause *wa kafā bi Allāhi ʿalīmā* — and Allah fully knows who deserves it — was read as both reassurance and warning. *ʿAlīm* — All-Knowing — was explained as knowing the deed, the intention, and the capacity behind obedience — the same knowledge that never wrongs even by an atom's weight (4:40) and that is perfect knowledge of them (4:39). To say He knows who deserves the favour is to say the distribution is neither arbitrary nor based on claim. The sūrah has exposed those who falsely elevate themselves — *it is Allah who elevates whomever He wills, and none will be wronged even by a thread* (4:49) — those who fabricate lies against Him as blatant sin (4:50), and those who believe in *jibt* and declare disbelievers better guided (4:51). Each claims a status the verse denies; the true elevation to the honourable company is by *faḍl* distributed with perfect knowledge. Early authorities linked *kafā bi Allāhi ʿalīmā* — sufficient is Allah as Knower — to the sūrah's refrain of sufficiency: sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45), sufficient as Witness (4:79), sufficient as Trustee (4:81). Here sufficiency is of knowledge: no other auditor is needed to sort who walks the straight path with firmness (4:66) and who turns away stubbornly (4:61).

**Favour That Rests on Knowledge, Not on Claim**

The pairing of *faḍl* and *ʿalīm* corrects two errors at once. If favour were without knowledge, it would be random; if knowledge were without favour, the weak would despair. The sūrah has held both since it said humankind was created weak and therefore burdens were lightened (4:28), and that God wills to make clear and turn toward you (4:26–27): favour is given where knowledge sees obedience — not self-elevation — and weakness met with doing what was advised. The sūrah has also said *We would have granted a great reward by Our grace and guided to the straight path* (4:67–68) had they obeyed; to call that reward and guidance *faḍl* from God is to remind that the straight path itself is a gift, not only the company at its end. The hypocrites who sought false judges while claiming belief (4:60) claimed a favour — alliance and ease — that knowledge would not ratify; the believers who accept the Prophet ﷺ as judge without resistance and submit wholeheartedly (4:65) receive favour that knowledge does ratify. The verse therefore draws a line between favour claimed and favour given — between *yuzakkūna anfusahum*, they declare themselves pure, and *yuzakkī man yashāʾ*, God purifies whomever He wills (4:49).

**A Short Verse That Holds the Sūrah's Economy**

Placed where it is, this short verse holds the sūrah's economy of favour together. The economy was stated as: do not crave what God gave some over others; ask Him for bounty (4:32) — because the distributor is not the envied person but the All-Knowing. It was shown as: those who spend to be seen without belief take Satan as associate — an evil companion (4:38) — while those who believe and donate from what was provided would have harmed no one and would have found perfect knowledge remembering it (4:39). It was measured as: not an atom wronged, but multiplied many times, with a great reward from grace (4:40). To call the companionship of the blessed *faḍl min Allāh* and to add *Allah fully knows who deserves it* is to say that entire economy ends here: obedience places with the blessed by favour, and the favour is distributed by perfect knowledge that misses no thread and no atom. The sūrah has warned that the evildoers who fight for the Devil have weak schemes (4:76) and that the hypocrites' disaster comes because of what their hands put forward (4:62); the favour of honourable company is the opposite destiny for hands that put forward referral, fairness, and submission. Sufficiency as Knower guarantees both.

**The Invitation Inside the Statement**

The statement *this is God's favour* is also invitation. The sūrah does not list the deeds that earn the company as unattainable acts reserved for prophets; it lists them as the advised acts that would have been better and more reassuring — return trusts, judge fairly, refer disputes, accept judgment (4:66) — and as obedience to God and the Messenger as the sūrah has detailed them. To call the result favour is to tell the weak that the distance between his obedience and the prophet's company is bridged not by his own rank but by God's giving. That giving is known, witnessed, and measured with the same precision that guards the orphan's sixth and the wife's eighth — so that the weak who fears his atom is too small hears *Allah fully knows* as reassurance: his atom is known and will be favoured. The verse therefore follows the exclamation *what honourable company* (4:69) with the quiet reason company is honourable: it is from God, and it is known. The community that was told to take precautions and go forth (4:71) can thus go forth not with the boast that it has taken favour, but with the trust that favour will be given by the One who knows who deserves it — and that the knowledge that suffices is also the knowledge that elevates without wrong by even a thread.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:71

> O believers! Take your precautions and go forth either in groups or together

**Take Your Precautions**

The command *khudhū ḥidhrakum* — O believers, take your precautions — follows the promise that obedience places with the blessed and that God knows who deserves favour (4:69–70), and calls to action. *Ḥidhr* — precaution, guard, readiness — was explained as preparation that befits the threat: arms, knowledge of terrain, counsel, and caution in movement. The sūrah has shown that precaution accompanies all trusts — witnesses at the orphan's handover (4:6), four witnesses before sanction for *fāḥishah* (4:15), two mediators from families where a split is feared (4:35), fairness in judgment (4:58); to take *ḥidhr* in the field is that same ethic applied to fighting. The verse generalises what earlier verses specified for the market and the home: do not approach the weighty act without awareness. Prayer is not approached without knowing what is said or without purification, with earth where water fails (4:43); battle is not approached without guard. The sūrah has called humankind weak and promised lightening (4:28); precaution is part of that lightening, because the weak are not told to fight unwatched but to fight guarded.

**Go Forth Either in Groups or Together**

The detail *fa anfirū thubātin aw infirū jamīʿā* — go forth either in groups or together — was read as tactical flexibility. *Thubāt* — groups, bands — and *jamīʿā* — together, as a whole — give the community two forms of mobilisation: small expeditions that can scout and skirmish, and the full muster that meets a large threat. The choice was seen as entrusted to those in authority among you (4:59), whose obedience within obedience to God and Messenger makes the question of *how* to go forth a matter of counsel, not of private impulse. The sūrah has shown that authority is to be obeyed and disputes referred to the Book and Messenger as best outcome (4:59); going forth is the field where that obedience is tested. The verse was revealed concerning expeditions from Madinah where hypocrites lagged, as the next verses describe — saying *blessed we were not there* when disaster strikes (4:72) and *would that we had been there for great gain* when bounty comes (4:73). To say go forth in groups or together before that diagnosis is to tell believers to move as the community decides, not as the lagger decides — so that the bond between you is not treated as if it were none.

**A Community That Knows Its Weakness and Its Guard**
