Placed between the honourable company for obeying (4:69–70) and the portrait of laggers (4:72–73), this verse steadies the community that was learning to fight for the oppressed who cry *deliver us, appoint for us a helper* (4:75). The oppressed — men, women, and children — call for a *walī* and *naṣīr* — guardian and helper — the same two sufficiencies the sūrah said God alone provides (4:45); to answer that call the believers must go forth, but they must go forth with *ḥidhr*. The sūrah has paired *Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving* (4:43) with purification through earth, and *guided them to the straight path* (4:68) with doing what was advised; here it pairs *take precautions* with *go forth* to show that courage is not carelessness. The believers who fight for God and the disbelievers who fight for the Devil with weak schemes (4:76) are distinguished not only by cause but by preparation. Those who take *ḥidhr* and go forth as commanded fight for God with the means that make fighting responsible; those who lag behind or rush without order fight for other causes or not at all. The verse therefore trains readiness as worship.

**Readiness That Honours the Trust of Life**

The call to take guard honours the trust of life that the sūrah has guarded from its opening. *Be mindful of your Lord who created you from a single soul* (4:1), *do not kill yourselves, surely Allah is ever Merciful to you* (4:29), and *Allah is Watchful over you* (4:1) together teach that life is not to be thrown away in zeal nor hoarded in cowardice. Precaution stands between those two, as *tathbīt* — firmness — stands between hasty consumption before the orphan grows (4:6) and neglecting his need. Early reports show the Prophet ﷺ ordering scouts and rear guards even where victory was promised, showing that trust in God's sufficiency as Guardian (4:45) did not cancel taking means; it gave means their meaning. A community that learns that readiness to go forth — in groups for a skirmish or together for a muster — is part of obedience will also learn the earlier readinesses — witnesses at handover, dowry given, shares divided after debts — as the same obedience in different fields.

**Precaution as Obedience**

The command to take precautions was read as obedience itself, not as worldly prudence added to obedience. The Prophet ﷺ took *ḥidhr* in every expedition — scouts, guards, night watch — while trusting in God as sufficient Trustee (4:81) and Witness (4:79). The sūrah's promise that *whoever fights, whether martyred or victorious, We will give a great reward* (4:74) does not remove the need for guard; it secures the meaning of guard, so that precaution is not fear but preparation that trusts. A community that learns to take precautions as commanded will not be hurried by news of security or fear that the coming verses say should be referred to the Messenger and authorities (4:83). To go forth in groups or together after taking precautions is to act where the order to fight comes (4:77) with the awareness that death overtakes wherever you are, even in fortified towers (4:78) — yet *what is with God is better and more lasting*. The sūrah therefore makes precaution the middle between the fear that says *delay fighting* (4:77) and the recklessness that ignores *do not kill yourselves* (4:29). Take guard, then go forth — in the form the lawful authority decides — and the weak who were promised lightening will find that the guarded going is the straight path walked.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:72

> There will be some among you who will lag behind so that if you face a disaster, they will say, "Allah has blessed us for not being there among them."

**Among You Who Will Lag Behind**

The verse says *wa inna minkum la man layabṭaʾanna* — and there will be some among you who will lag behind — addressing the community that was just told to take precautions and go forth in groups or together (4:71). *Layabṭaʾanna* — to lag, to hold back — was read as deliberate slowness, both staying behind and causing others to stay behind by talk. The phrase *minkum* — among you — was stressed as showing that the lagger is inside the community, not clearly outside among open disbelievers — the same position as the hypocrites who claim belief yet seek false judges (4:60) and turn away stubbornly (4:61). The sūrah has shown that God knows best who enemies are and that He suffices as Guardian and Helper (4:45), and that among those given a portion some believed and some turned away (4:55); here the divider is not doctrine alone but readiness to go forth. The one who lags does not say he disbelieves; he simply does not take *ḥidhr* and go forth as commanded — and his absence is explained as blessing when disaster strikes. The sūrah therefore diagnoses hypocrisy not only by distorted words — *we hear and disobey* (4:46) — but by the foot that does not move.

**If You Face a Disaster — Allah Has Blessed Us**

The portrait continues *fa in aṣābatkum muṣībatun qāla qad anʿama Allāhu ʿalayya idh lam akun maʿahum shahīdā* — so that if you face a disaster, they will say, Allah has blessed me for not being there among them as witness. *Muṣībah* — disaster, calamity that hits — recalls *how will it be if a disaster strikes them because of what their hands did?* (4:62), where hypocrites swore goodwill after hands had sought *ṭāghūt*. Here the *muṣībah* is in battle — setback, loss, injury — the kind the sūrah warns will come to those who do not fight for the oppressed (4:75). The lagger's comment calls absence a blessing — *anʿama Allāhu ʿalayya* — a phrase the Qur'an uses for real divine favour, here applied to staying away. The word *shahīd* — witness, present — was read as being present at the event, sharing the trial. To thank God for not being present where believers fought for Him is to thank Him for missing the honour that obedience would have given — the honourable company with prophets, the truthful, martyrs, and righteous (4:69). The lagger mistakes safety from a *muṣībah* as *niʿmah* — favour — while the sūrah has defined favour as being with the blessed by obedience (4:69–70) and as an atom's weight not wronged but multiplied (4:40): his definition is inverted.

**Blessing Misnamed**

The lagger's *Allah has blessed me* was read as a misuse of *niʿmah* that mirrors the earlier misuse *we intended nothing but goodwill and reconciliation* (4:62). Both borrow the sūrah's language — *niʿmah*, *iḥsān*, *tawfīq* — and apply it to avoidance. The sūrah corrects that language throughout: true *niʿmah* is favour from God known to Him (4:70); true *iḥsān* is kindness to parents, relatives, orphans, neighbours, and travellers (4:36); true *tawfīq* is harmony God brings when mediators desire it (4:35). To call sitting out a disaster a blessing is to call the opposite of those goods a good — which is why the next verse shows the same lagger, when bounty comes, saying *would that I had been there to share the great gain* (4:73), revealing that his measure is gain and safety, not obedience. The sūrah has already asked *what harm if they had believed and donated from what was provided?* (4:39) to expose that withholding harms none but the withholder; here it shows the withholder of presence believing absence helped him, while the sūrah will soon say that those who sell this life for the next will fight and be honoured whether martyred or victorious (4:74).

**Among You — a Test of the Bond**

The phrase *minkum* — among you — was stressed as a test of the bond that the next verse says will be treated *as if there had been no bond between you* (4:73). The community described as being from a single soul (4:1), as *you are from one another* (4:25), and as appointed heirs after debts (4:11–12) is a community of ties. The lagger is among those ties yet not with them — *lam akun maʿahum*, I was not with them. His absence severs the bond in practice while keeping the name *among*. The sūrah has shown that hypocrisy after disaster swears goodwill; here hypocrisy before disaster declares its own blessing for absence — the same self-interest before and after. For the believers told to go forth in groups or together, the verse is a warning to recognise the lagger within — the foot that hesitates, the tongue that discourages — and not to be made to lag by him. Just as *rāʿinā* required replacing an ambiguous word with a clear one, *unẓurnā* (4:46), lagging requires replacing the blessing named for absence with the favour named for obedience — the favour the sūrah defines as being with the blessed.

**A Preview of the Next Reversal**

Placed where it is, this verse previews the reversal the next verse will complete. Here the lagger is grateful for not being present at disaster; there he will be envious for not being present at bounty, saying *would that I had been there* as if no bond had been. The two statements together show that his measure never was the bond — *you are from one another* — but the outcome: safety or gain. The sūrah therefore holds up the lagger as the opposite of the one who accepts the Prophet ﷺ as judge without resistance and submits wholeheartedly (4:65) and of the one who does what was advised and is more reassured and guided (4:66–68). The lagger's *would that* when gain comes will be shown as hollow, because the gain he craves is called *fawz ʿaẓīm* — great triumph — elsewhere for obedience (4:13), not for absence. The verse's short portrait — among you, lagging, calling absence blessing at disaster — thus does more than describe a type; it asks every listener among whom the lagger is: where will his own foot be when the call to take precautions and go forth is given, and will he call that going a blessing or call staying back one?
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:73

> But if you return with Allah's bounties, they will say—as if there had been no bond between you—"We wish we had been there with them to share the great gain!"

**If You Return With Bounty, They Wish They Had Been There**

The verse continues *wa laʾin aṣābakum faḍlun min Allāhi la yaqūlanna ka an lam takun baynakum wa baynahu mawaddatun yā laytanī kuntu maʿahum fa afūza fawzan ʿaẓīmā* — but if you return with Allah's bounties, they will say, as if there had been no bond between you, we wish we had been there with them to share the great gain. The contrast with the previous portrait is deliberate: at disaster — *muṣībah* — the lagger said *Allah has blessed us for not being there* (4:72); at bounty — *faḍl min Allāh* — the same person says *would that I had been there to share*. The sūrah has defined *faḍl* as bounty to be asked from God rather than craved from another (4:32), as what the stingy conceal (4:37), and as what would have caused no harm if believed and donated from (4:39). Here the bounty is gain after going forth — victory, safety, spoils — the *fawz ʿaẓīm* that the lagger now claims to want. The wish *yā laytanī kuntu maʿahum* — would that I had been with them — was read as regret not for missing obedience but for missing share: the sūrah has called the ultimate triumph *fawz ʿaẓīm* for keeping limits (4:13), and the lagger's use of the same phrase for worldly gain shows that his measure of *fawz* is gain, not Gardens.

**As If There Had Been No Bond Between You**

The clause *ka an lam takun baynakum wa baynahu mawaddah* — as if there had been no bond between you — was explained as the lagger speaking as though he were a stranger who happened to miss a caravan, not as one *among you* (4:72) whose absence at disaster was already a statement. *Mawaddah* — affection, bond, love — was read as the tie that should have made him go forth with them as one body: the tie the sūrah rooted in *created from a single soul* (4:1) and *you are from one another* (4:25), and appointed in heirs and pledges (4:33). To speak as if no *mawaddah* existed reveals that the bond was never acted as bond; it was kept as name while the foot stayed back. The Qur'an elsewhere says the hypocrites' hearts are divided though you think them together; this speaking — wishing to be there only when gain is sure — proves it. The believers were told to take precautions and go forth in groups or together (4:71); the lagger who stays, then at gain says *would that I had been there*, treats going forth as a market to join when profitable, not as a duty to share. *Ka an lam takun* — as if there had never been — shows that for him the community's *mawaddah* was conditional on outcome, which is the opposite of the reconciliation the sūrah asks mediators to seek where God brings harmony when desire is for repair (4:35).

**Great Gain as Worldly Measure**

The phrase *fa afūza fawzan ʿaẓīmā* — to share the great gain — was stressed as the lagger's definition of greatness. The sūrah has called the Gardens with rivers, staying forever, the ultimate triumph — *fawz ʿaẓīm* (4:13) — and martyrdom or victory in God's cause followed by a great reward as honour (4:74); the lagger's *fawz ʿaẓīm* is spoils, not that. To call spoils *ʿaẓīm* — great — while calling absence at disaster a blessing (4:72) shows that his great and his blessing are both measured without God as Helper whose help suffices (4:45). The sūrah will soon say *let those who would sacrifice this life for the Hereafter fight in God's cause; whoever fights, whether martyred or victorious, We will give a great reward* (4:74), where *ʿaẓīm* returns as divine reward for fighting, not for wishing to have fought. The lagger's *yā laytanī* is therefore not repentance; it is envy that the bounty came without him — as those who envy the people for God's bounties (4:54) envied Book and wisdom given to Abraham's family. The gain he now wants is the *faḍl* whose distribution he earlier begrudged.

**Would That I Had Been There — the Wish That Costs Nothing**

The wish *yā laytanī* was read as the cheapest substitute for action, the same substitute the hypocrites offered after disaster with *we intended nothing but goodwill* (4:62). Both utterances come after the moment where doing mattered — disaster or bounty — and both reframe absence as if it were presence. The sūrah has shown that God fully knows who deserves favour (4:70) and never wrongs even by a thread (4:49), so the wish cannot create share where presence was withheld. The believers who fought, whether achieving martyrdom or victory, will be honoured with a great reward (4:74) because they went forth; the wisher who stayed will not be honoured as though he went, because *whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger will be with the blessed* (4:69) — and obeying included going forth. The wish after bounty is therefore the counterpart to thanking God for not being there at disaster: both reveal a heart that measures blessedness by outcome — safety or spoils — while the sūrah measures blessedness by obedience and favour from God (4:70). The two measures do not meet, which is why the wisher must speak *as if there had been no bond*; to acknowledge the bond would be to acknowledge that wishing after is not being with.

**A Portrait That Asks the Reader His Own Wish**

Placed between the lagger at disaster and the cry of the oppressed who call for a helper (4:75), this portrait asks the reader to examine his own *yā laytanī*. The sūrah has shown that the straight path is not wishing after gain but doing what was advised — returning trusts, judging fairly, referring disputes, accepting judgment without resistance (4:66–68) — which would have been better and more reassuring and would have brought great reward and guidance. The lagger's wish after gain is the opposite: he did not do, he was not with, he was not present as witness — *shahīd* — and now he wishes he had been. The sūrah leaves the wish hanging, as it left *how will it be* hanging (4:41, 4:62), so that the listener supplies the answer: had you wished to be with them before, you would have been. The next verses address that wish directly — *what is it with you that you do not fight for the oppressed?* (4:75) and *believers fight for God while disbelievers fight for the Devil whose schemes are weak* (4:76). The one who now says *fawzan ʿaẓīmā* for spoils is invited to seek the greater *fawz* — Gardens with vast shade — by fighting for the cause that makes spoils *faḍl* from God rather than the measure of all, and by being there when the call to take precautions and go forth is given, not only when the gain is counted.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:74

> Let those who would sacrifice this life for the Hereafter fight in the cause of Allah. And whoever fights in Allah's cause—whether they achieve martyrdom or victory—We will honour them with a great reward

**Let Those Who Sell This Life for the Next Fight**

The verse commands *fa al-yuqātil fī sabīli Allāhi alladhīna yashrūna al-ḥayāta al-dunyā bi al-ākhirati* — let those who would sacrifice this life for the Hereafter fight in the cause of Allah. The phrase *yashrūna al-ḥayāta al-dunyā bi al-ākhirati* — to sell this life for the next — reverses the trade condemned earlier: those given a portion of the Book who trade it for misguidance (4:44) and who trade guidance to reassure disbelievers they are better guided (4:51). To sell the *dunyā* for the *ākhirah* is the straight trade — the same logic as *what harm if they had believed and donated from what was provided?* (4:39), where belief and donation cost nothing in the true accounting and gain multiplication. Here the cost is greater — the present life offered — but the logic is the same: the *dunyā* is little enjoyment and the *ākhirah* is better for the mindful (4:77). The call to fight is therefore addressed not to all indiscriminately as compulsion beyond capacity, but to those who have already chosen that sale in their hearts. The sūrah has said humankind was created weak and burdens lightened (4:28), and that burdens for fighting include taking precautions and going forth in groups or together (4:71); the seller described here is the one whose weakness has been steadied by desire for the next, so that fighting becomes bounty rather than burden.

**In the Cause of Allah**

The qualification *fī sabīli Allāh* — in the cause of Allah — was stressed to distinguish the believer's fighting from fighting for the Devil: the next verse says *believers fight for God while disbelievers fight for the Devil; so fight the Devil's forces, his schemes are weak* (4:76). *Sabīl Allāh* in this sūrah was shown as the clear path God wills to make plain (4:26), the noble ways of those before, the limits about wealth and marriage whose keeping is obedience, and the help for the oppressed who cry *appoint for us a saviour, a helper — all by Your grace* (4:75). To fight in that path is to answer that cry, as the next verse asks *what is it with you that you do not fight for the oppressed men, women, and children?* (4:75). The sūrah's prohibitions — *do not devour wealth by falsehood* and *do not kill* (4:29), with Fire for the deliberate (4:30) — stand behind this: fighting in God's cause is the opposite taking — not devouring wealth or killing without right, but risking wealth and life for those whose wealth was devoured and whose lives are oppressed. The cause therefore gathers the sūrah's ethic of *iḥsān* (4:36) into a field; kindness to the traveller and to those in possession becomes, at scale, deliverance for those under oppressors.

**Whether Martyred or Victorious — a Great Reward**

The promise *wa man yuqātil fī sabīli Allāhi fa yuqtal aw yaghlib fa sawfa nuʾtīhi ajran ʿaẓīmā* — whoever fights in God's cause, whether they achieve martyrdom or victory, We will honour them with a great reward — was read as securing both outcomes. *Yuqtal* — is killed — was explained as martyrdom — *shahādah* — the witness that joins the company of the blessed: prophets, the truthful, martyrs, righteous — what honourable company (4:69). *Yaghlib* — prevails, is victorious — is the gain the lagger envied when he said *would that I had been there to share the great gain* (4:73), but here the gain follows fighting, not wishing. *Ajr ʿaẓīm* — great reward — appeared for doing what was advised (4:67), for the atom multiplied (4:40), and here for fighting whether martyred or victorious — showing that the reward is not tied to worldly outcome but to cause and resolve. The sūrah has already said *had they done what they were advised, We would have granted great reward and guided to the straight path* (4:67–68); fighting in God's cause is the advised act for those whose trade is the next life, and the guidance and reward follow either way. The lagger at disaster who called absence a blessing (4:72) and at bounty who wished he had been there misses both, because he neither sold the *dunyā* nor fought.

**The Trade That Makes Fighting Gain**

To sell this life for the next was explained as seeing this life as capital to invest rather than hoard. The sūrah has warned that the enjoyment of this world is little and the next is better for the mindful, and that none is wronged even by a thread (4:77); that little, when held, is the lagger's *Allah blessed me for not being there*; when sold, it becomes the martyr's *shahādah* and the victor's *ghalabah*, both called great reward. Early authorities linked the trade to the migrants who left homes — the hard command few would have obeyed (4:66) — and who found that leaving became the price of the honourable company. Here the price is fighting after taking precautions and going forth as commanded (4:71). The sūrah does not command all to sell in the same way at the same time; it says *let those who would sell fight*, leaving room for the ill, the traveller, and those whose news should be referred (4:83), while still asking *what is it with you that you do not fight for the oppressed?* (4:75) to move those who can. The trade therefore respects weakness while inviting strength: the weak are not condemned for not selling all at once, but the one who would sell is told where the sale is — in God's cause — and what its price brings — a great reward either way.

**A Verse Between Lagging and the Oppressed's Cry**

Placed between the portrait of wishing after gain and the cry of the oppressed, this verse turns wishing into doing. The lagger wishes *fawzan ʿaẓīmā* after (4:73); the fighter is promised *ajran ʿaẓīmā* whether martyred or victorious before the outcome is known. The oppressed men, women, and children who cry for a saviour (4:75) are the reason the sale matters beyond self-gain: to sell this life is to buy deliverance for them with the help of the sufficient Guardian and Helper (4:45). The sūrah has shown that God never wrongs even by an atom but multiplies good (4:40) and that He fully knows who deserves favour (4:70); the fighter who sells this life knows that no sacrifice is unrecorded and that the great reward is from *ladunnā* — from His presence — as *ajr ʿaẓīm* by grace (4:67). For the community told to return trusts and judge with fairness as a noble exhortation from the All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:58), fighting in that cause is the public form of returning the trust of protection to its rightful owners — the oppressed — and the recompense is the same great reward that crowns the private trusts kept.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:75

> And what is it with you? You do not fight in the cause of Allah and for oppressed men, women, and children who cry out, "Our Lord! Deliver us from this land of oppressors! Appoint for us a saviour; appoint for us a helper—all by Your grace."

**What Is It With You That You Do Not Fight**

The question *wa mā lakum lā tuqātilūna fī sabīli Allāhi* — and what is it with you, you do not fight in the cause of Allah — is not a request for information; it is a rebuke that awakens. The sūrah has just called *let those who would sell this life for the next fight in God's cause* and promised a great reward whether martyred or victorious (4:74); now it asks why the broader community hesitates when the cause is not only the path of God but the distress of people. The lagger who called absence at disaster a blessing (4:72) and wished to have been there at bounty (4:73) is the type for whom the question is asked; the fighter who sells this life for the next is the answer. The sūrah elsewhere says *take your precautions and go forth in groups or together* (4:71) and *believers fight for God while disbelievers fight for the Devil whose schemes are weak* (4:76); this question is the moral pressure between those two, aimed at the gap between knowing the cause and moving for it. The cause — *sabīl Allāh* — was shown as the clear path God wills to make plain (4:26), the limits about wealth and marriage whose keeping is obedience, and the help for the weak; fighting in that path here means fighting where the weak cannot fight for themselves.

**For Oppressed Men, Women, and Children**

The addition *wa al-mustadʿafīna min al-rijāli wa al-nisāʾi wa al-wildāni* — and for the oppressed among men, women, and children — specifies whose cause is God's cause at this moment. *Mustadʿafīn* — those made weak, deemed weak, oppressed — were explained as believers held under the power of oppressors, unable to emigrate or to defend themselves. Among them were men, women, and children — the very groups the sūrah has been guarding: men and women with obligatory shares (4:7, 4:11–12), women with dowries and a firm commitment (4:19–21), children with tested competence and witnesses at handover (4:6). To fight for the oppressed of each is to bring the sūrah's ethic of *iḥsān* — kind doing — to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, neighbours, companions, travellers, and those in possession (4:36) into the field. The sūrah's own logic of trusts — *return trusts to rightful owners and judge with fairness* (4:58) — becomes, at scale, deliverance for those whose trusts — freedom, property, worship — are denied. Fighting for the oppressed is therefore not a separate cause beside God's; it is the form God's cause takes where oppression exists.

**Deliver Us From This Land of Oppressors**

The quoted cry *rabbanā akhrijnā min hādhihi al-qaryati al-ẓālimi ahluhā* — Our Lord, deliver us from this land whose people are oppressors — was heard as a daily prayer of the detained, a *duʿāʾ* that names the place by its people's character rather than by a tribe name: what makes the town oppressive is that its people are oppressors. The sūrah has named *ẓulm* throughout — consuming orphan wealth unjustly (4:10), devouring by falsehood deliberately (4:30), fabricating against God (4:50), envy that withholds (4:54); to be oppressed is to live where those forms are the rule. The cry asks not only for removal — *akhrijnā*, deliver us out — but for governance after removal, which is why it continues *appoint for us a guardian and appoint for us a helper — all by Your grace*. The phrase *min ladunka* — from Your presence — matches *ajr ʿaẓīm min ladunnā* — great reward from Our presence (4:67, 4:74) — showing that the deliverance and the reward share the same source. The oppressed do not ask first for wealth or revenge; they ask for a *walī* and *naṣīr*, the two sufficiencies the sūrah said God Himself provides (4:45) — and now provides through those who fight.

**Appoint for Us a Saviour, Appoint for Us a Helper**

The double request *wa ajʿal lanā min ladunka waliyyan wa ajʿal lanā min ladunka naṣīrā* — appoint for us, from Yourself, a guardian and a helper — was read as asking for leadership that is itself a mercy, not only rescue. *Walī* — guardian, protector who takes charge — and *naṣīr* — helper who brings victory — gather the sūrah's two sufficiencies — *sufficient is Allah as Guardian and Helper* (4:45) — into a human form that God appoints. The oppressed recognise that the guardian who returns trusts and the helper who curbs the disbelievers' might must come *min ladunka* — from His presence — as grace. Early authorities linked this population to believers left in Makkah after the migration — including the weak, women, and children — whose prayer was answered through the believers who fought. The prayer model matters: it is made by the weak, not by the strong describing the weak. The sūrah therefore teaches the community to hear the prayer as addressed to them through God: when the weak cry for a *walī* and *naṣīr*, the answer is the fighter who sells this life for the next (4:74), going forth with precautions (4:71) in God's cause. The cause and the cry meet in the same act.

**A Question That Holds the Community to Its Name**

Placed after the promise to the fighter and before the distinction that believers fight for God and disbelievers for the Devil with weak schemes (4:76), this rebuke holds the community to its name as *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū* — O believers. To be among those who were told to obey and refer disputes, to return trusts, and to be kind in circles is to be among those the oppressed now call upon. The question *what is it with you* assumes that such people would fight, so the fact that some do not is surprising and needs reason. The coming verses will give reasons some hesitate — fearing people as God should be feared, saying *why have You ordered us to fight? Delay us* (4:77) — and will answer that the *dunyā* is little and the next better, and that death overtakes even in fortified towers (4:78). Here the question is left as spur: the oppressed are men, women, and children — the same groups whose shares and dowries were guarded — crying for a guardian and helper from God's grace. To hear that cry and remain as the lagger — among you yet not with you — is to be the one the question addresses. To hear it and fight — whether martyred or victorious — is to be the one the great reward awaits, and to become, by fighting, the *walī* and *naṣīr* from His presence for whom the oppressed prayed.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:76

> Believers fight for the cause of Allah, whereas disbelievers fight for the cause of the Devil. So fight against Satan's ˹evil˺ forces. Indeed, Satan's schemes are ever weak

**Two Causes, Two Fightings**

The verse states *alladhīna āmanū yuqātilūna fī sabīli Allāh wa alladhīna kafarū yuqātilūna fī sabīli al-ṭāghūt* — believers fight for the cause of Allah, whereas disbelievers fight for the cause of the Devil, the false authority. The pairing gathers the sūrah's long contrast between the path God wills to make clear (4:26) and the far straying Satan desires when people seek false judges (4:60). To fight *fī sabīli Allāh* was explained as fighting to remove oppression, to deliver the weak who cry for a guardian and helper (4:75), to return trusts and judge with fairness (4:58), and to secure the limits about wealth and marriage the sūrah has set. To fight *fī sabīli al-ṭāghūt* — in the way of the overstepping — was explained as fighting to keep the land of oppressors as it is: to keep idols and false gods believed (4:51), to keep women inherited against their will (4:19), and to keep wealth devoured by falsehood (4:29). The sūrah has shown that those who follow desires wish you to deviate greatly (4:27) and that those given a portion who trade it for misguidance wish you to deviate from the path (4:44); their fighting is that wish armed. Believers and disbelievers are therefore not distinguished here by tribe but by cause — and cause determines whose fighting has a future.

**So Fight Against Satan's Forces**

The command *fa qātilū awliyāʾ al-shayṭān* — so fight against Satan's evil forces — follows as corollary. *Awliyāʾ al-shayṭān* — allies, close friends of Satan — was read as those who take him as associate — *qarīn*, what an evil associate (4:38) — and who take him as guardian instead of God who suffices as Guardian and Helper (4:45). The verse tells believers not to fear the name that accompanies opposing forces; those who fight for *ṭāghūt* may appear numerous — the polytheists, their allies among those given a portion who reassure them they are better guided (4:51), and the laggers who wish for gain (4:73) — but they are called *awliyāʾ al-shayṭān*, a party whose patron is already the defeated. The command is given to believers who were told to take precautions and go forth in groups or together (4:71); to fight the forces is to fight prepared, not heedless. The sūrah says *take your precautions* before *go forth*, showing that the community that fights for God does not fight with the Devil's method — deceit, wordplay, and coercion — but with guard, referral to Book and Messenger (4:59), and acceptance of judgment without resistance (4:65). To fight Satan's allies is therefore not to mimic them but to oppose them where they make oppression.

**Indeed Satan's Schemes Are Ever Weak**

The reassurance *inna kayda al-shayṭāni kāna ḍaʿīfā* — indeed, Satan's schemes are ever weak — was explained as the reason not to fear. *Kayd* — scheme, plot, stratagem — was read as the whisper that makes stinginess look like prudence (4:37), ostentation look like honour (4:38), word distortion — *rāʿinā* for *unẓurnā* — look like cleverness (4:46), and belief in *jibt* look like guidance (4:51): each was a scheme to keep a limit blurred. The sūrah has said that God is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45), that He never wrongs even by an atom but multiplies good (4:40), and that He gives a great reward for fighting whether martyred or victorious (4:74). Against that sufficiency and multiplication, the Devil's schemes are *ḍaʿīf* — weak, frail — not because they are few but because they have no weight where God's cause is fought. Early authorities noted that the weakness is intrinsic: Satan promises and his promise is delusion; he commands stinginess and his command impoverishes. The believers who fight for God fight for the oppressed who ask for a guardian and helper from God's grace (4:75); the disbelievers who fight for the Devil fight to keep that helper from arriving. The first fight is supported by the sufficient Helper; the second is supported by a weak plot. That is why the verse ends where it does: the weakness is not a prediction but a standing truth — *kāna ḍaʿīfā* — it was ever weak, and is weak.

**A Verse Between the Oppressed's Cry and the Fearful's Delay**

Placed between the cry of the oppressed (4:75) and the exposure of those told *do not fight; establish prayer and give alms* who then feared people as God should be feared when fighting was ordered (4:77), this verse is the sūrah's pivot from motive to courage. The oppressed need a fight in God's cause; the fearful delay because they see the enemy as strong. The verse says the enemy's camp fights for a weak cause whose patron's schemes are ever weak, while you fight for the cause whose Guardian suffices. The lagger who lagged at disaster and wished after bounty (4:72–73) measured strength by outcome — safety or spoils — and therefore saw the Devil's forces as strong when they were many. The sūrah measures strength by cause and patron, and therefore sees them as weak even when they are many, because their patron could not give even a speck if he controlled kingdom (4:53). For the believers told that humankind was created weak and burdens lightened (4:28), the reassurance is not that they are strong in themselves but that the opponent's scheming is weak before the Helper who suffices. To fight the forces of the weak schemer is therefore not a gamble but the straight path walked — the path He promised to make clear while lightening burdens (4:27–28).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:77

> Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who had been told, "Do not fight! Rather, establish prayer and pay alms-tax."? Then once the order came to fight, a group of them feared those ˹hostile˺ people as Allah should be feared—or even more. They said, "Our Lord! Why have You ordered us to fight? If only You had delayed ˹the order for˺ us for a little while!" Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ "The enjoyment of this world is so little, whereas the Hereafter is far better for those mindful ˹of Allah˺. And none of you will be wronged ˹even by the width of˺ the thread of a date stone

**From Restraint to Command**

The verse recalls *a lam tara ilā alladhīna qīla lahum kuffū aydiyakum wa aqīmū al-ṣalāta wa ātū al-zakāta* — have you not seen those who had been told, do not fight, rather establish prayer and pay alms? — a reference to the early Makkan period when fighting was withheld and the community was commanded to worship and give. Early reports place this among believers in Makkah who asked permission to fight when oppressed, were told to restrain their hands and to establish prayer and zakāh instead, and then, after migration when the order to fight came, a group among them faltered. The sūrah has shown a similar pattern of gradual legislation — lightening because humans were created weak (4:28) and making things clear before imposing; the progression from *restrain your hands* to *fighting* is that method applied. To pray and to give are themselves preparation for fighting: prayer teaches awareness before standing (4:43), and giving teaches that wealth is a trust to be circulated (4:37–38). Those who learned those two when fighting was barred would later fight for the oppressed who cry for a helper (4:75) with the right cause — for God, not for *ṭāghūt* (4:76). The verse therefore recalls a stage where restraint was obedience, so that later fighting would also be obedience, not desire for gain such as the laggers show (4:73).

**A Group Feared People as Allah Should Be Feared**

The portrait continues *fa lammā kutiba ʿalayhimu al-qitālu idhā farīqun minhum yakhshawna al-nāsa ka khashyati Allāhi aw ashadda khashyah* — then once fighting was prescribed, a group of them feared people as Allah should be feared, or even more. *Khashyah* — fear that humbles and restrains — belongs to God; the sūrah elsewhere says to be mindful of God, that He is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45), and that Satan's schemes are ever weak (4:76). To fear people with that fear is to place the creature where the Creator belongs; to fear them more is the precise reversal of the trust the sūrah builds. The fear was explained as fear of the hostile forces' numbers, of death even in fortified towers (4:78), and of losing the little enjoyment of this world. The Qur'an elsewhere shows that true fear of God leads to keeping limits about wealth and marriage, while fear of people leads to seeking false judges (4:60) and distorting words (4:46); here fear of people leads to asking why fighting was ordered and wishing it delayed.

**Why Have You Ordered Us to Fight? Delay Us**

The quoted plea *rabbanā li ma katabta ʿalaynā al-qitāla law lā akhkhartanā ilā ajalin qarīb* — our Lord, why have You ordered us to fight? If only You had delayed us for a little while — was read as the hesitant asking for postponement. *Law lā akhkhartanā* — if only You had delayed — matches the lagger's *Allah blessed me for not being there* at disaster (4:72): both wish the time of action were later, when safety is surer. Early authorities noted that the delay sought was not for preparation — *take precautions and go forth* had already been commanded (4:71) — but for clinging to the *dunyā* whose enjoyment is little. The plea is addressed to *rabbanā* — our Lord — showing that even in hesitation the speakers know who commands, which makes the hesitation more revealing: they ask the Commander why He commanded. The sūrah has said that messengers were sent to be obeyed by God's leave (4:64) and that faith is not complete until the Prophet ﷺ is accepted as judge without resistance and with whole submission (4:65); to ask why the order came, and to request a little delay, is the opposite of *yusallimū taslīmā* — submit wholeheartedly.

**The Enjoyment of This World Is Little**

The answer *qul matāʿu al-dunyā qalīl wa al-ākhiratu khayrun li man ittaqā* — say, the enjoyment of this world is little, whereas the Hereafter is far better for those mindful of God — reframes the delay request with proportion. *Matāʿ al-dunyā* — enjoyment, provision of this world — was read as the safety kept by lagging, the gain wished after bounty (4:73), and the heap of gold not reclaimed where the dowry was given (4:20): each is *qalīl* — little — when set beside the Hereafter, where Gardens with rivers and vast shade await believers who do good (4:57) and where martyrdom or victory in God's cause brings a great reward (4:74). *Li man ittaqā* — for those mindful of God — was stressed as the condition that links this verse to the sūrah's opening *be mindful of your Lord* (4:1) and to *be mindful of God and speak equitably* (4:9). Mindfulness makes the Hereafter appear greater because the mindful see with the sūrah's measure — not an atom wronged but multiplied (4:40) — rather than with the lagger's measure — safety now. The Qur'an elsewhere says *the Hereafter is better and more lasting*, and the sūrah's own division of shares — whether little or much (4:7) — is little beside the *ajr ʿaẓīm* promised for fighting.

**Not Wronged by a Thread**

The closing *wa lā tuẓlamūna fatīlā* — and none of you will be wronged even by the width of a thread of a date stone — seals the answer with exact justice. *Fatīl* was explained as the thin thread in the date stone's groove, the same family as *naqīr* — speck — that those with no share of kingdom would not give (4:53). The sūrah has said none will be wronged by a *fatīl* where self-elevation is claimed (4:49), and that God never wrongs by an atom but multiplies (4:40); here it tells the fearful that going forth as ordered will not diminish what is theirs by even a thread — the atom's weight kept in a just division and the great reward for obedience both remain. The fear that fighting will cost too much is answered: the One who orders fighting is the One who measures by *fatīl* and atom, who never wrongs, and whose Hereafter is better for the mindful. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the verse is not a harsh rebuke but a reminder of scale: the little of this world, even if kept by delay, remains little, while the better of the next, approached with precautions and with God as sufficient Helper (4:45), is not diminished by even a thread. To fear people as God should be feared is to mistake the scale; to fear God, to fight where He commands for the oppressed, and to trust that no thread is lost is to see it rightly.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:78

> Wherever you may be, death will overcome you—even if you were in fortified towers." When something good befalls them, they say, "This is from Allah," but when something evil befalls them, they say, "This is from you." Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ "Both have been destined by Allah." So what is the matter with these people? They can hardly comprehend anything

**Wherever You May Be, Death Will Overtake You**

The statement *aynamā takūnū yudrikkumu al-mawtu wa law kuntum fī burūjin mushayyadah* — wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you were in fortified towers — answers the plea *if only You had delayed the order for a little while* (4:77). The fear that made a group fear people as God should be feared was, at root, fear of death in fighting. The verse says death is not avoided by staying behind, as the lagger imagined his absence at disaster was a blessing (4:72). *Burūj mushayyadah* — fortified, high, plastered towers — were explained as the strongest shelters known, high forts that seemed to put death at a distance. *Yudrikkumu* — will overtake, will reach — was stressed as pursuing, not merely occurring. The One who created from a single soul and spread countless (4:1), who is Ever-Pardoning and All-Forgiving in purification (4:43), and who is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45) is also the One who brings death wherever the person is. The Qur'an elsewhere says *every soul will taste death*, and the term is fixed — appointed — as inheritance shares are fixed after debts (4:11–12). To take precautions and go forth as commanded (4:71) is not to hasten death; to lag is not to delay it. The towers that seem to delay it are still within the appointment, so the wish for a little delay (4:77) mistakes the nature of the term.

**When Something Good Befalls Them, This Is From Allah**

The portrait shifts to speech after events: *wa in tuṣibhum ḥasanatun yaqūlū hādhihi min ʿindi Allāhi* — when something good befalls them, they say, this is from Allah. *Ḥasanah* — good — was read as victory, bounty, safety — the *faḍl* the lagger envied as great gain (4:73). To say *from Allah* at good is not false; the sūrah itself will say *whatever good befalls you is from Allah* (4:79). The fault here is not the attribution at good but the inconsistency that follows, where attribution changes at harm. The sūrah has shown that bounty is *faḍl* to be asked from God rather than craved (4:32) and that donation from what was provided would have harmed no one (4:39); to acknowledge good from Him when it arrives is therefore the beginning of the gratitude the sūrah invites. The persons described acknowledge that beginning — which makes their next turn more revealing.

**But When Evil Befalls Them, This Is From You**

The counterpart *wa in tuṣibhum sayyiʾatun yaqūlū hādhihi min ʿindika* — but when something evil befalls them, they say, this is from you — was read as the hypocrites and weak blaming the Prophet ﷺ for setbacks in battle, as though the order to fight (4:77) he conveyed had caused the harm. *Sayyiʾah* — evil, hardship — was explained as defeat, injury, or drought — the *muṣībah* that hits because of what hands put forward (4:62). To say *from you* — *min ʿindika* — to the Messenger ﷺ is to place the cause in the command rather than in the deed, the desire, and the divine decree. The sūrah has already corrected the lagger who called absence at disaster a blessing (4:72) and the fearful who said *Our Lord, why have You ordered us to fight?* (4:77); this saying — *this is from you* — is the same deflection in another form: good is from God, evil is from the Messenger's order. The Qur'an will soon show that failure to refer news of security or fear to the Messenger and the authorities led them to publicise alarm (4:83), which spreads the same *from you* logic.

**Both Have Been Destined by Allah**

The correction *qul kullun min ʿindi Allāh* — say, both have been destined by Allah — was explained as both good and evil befalling within divine decree, not as the Messenger's authorship. *Min ʿindi Allāh* — from Allah — was read as from His decree, creation, and knowledge — the same knowledge that never wrongs by an atom but multiplies good (4:40) and that fully knows who deserves favour (4:70). That does not remove human responsibility: the sūrah will immediately add *whatever evil befalls you is from yourself* (4:79) to show the secondary cause. Here the corrective is for those who split the source — good from God, evil from you — to tell them the source of decree is one. The sūrah has said God wills to make things clear and guide to noble ways (4:26) and that He is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45); to say *both from God* is to return the fearful to that clarity: the Prophet ﷺ is the one sent to be obeyed by God's leave (4:64) and to be accepted as judge without resistance (4:65), not the author of the decree. To attribute evil to him is to confuse the messenger with the sender.

**They Can Hardly Comprehend Anything**

The reproach *fa mā li hāʾulāʾi al-qawmi lā yakādūna yafqahūna ḥadīthā* — so what is the matter with these people? They can hardly comprehend any statement — was read as amazement at the split attribution and at the fear that made them request delay. *Ḥadīth* — statement, discourse — was explained as any statement that would make them understand: that the enjoyment of this world is little and the next better for the mindful (4:77); that not a thread is wronged (4:77); that Satan's schemes are ever weak (4:76); that both good and evil are within God's decree. The phrase *lā yakādūna yafqahūna* — they hardly understand — was read as barely grasping, as though understanding is a surface they skim. The sūrah will soon ask *do they not reflect on the Qur'an? Had it been from other than God they would have found many inconsistencies* (4:82) and will criticise those who publicise news of security or fear instead of referring it (4:83); the same lack of comprehension operates. Good and evil are both within God's decree, yet the means — taking precautions, asking for bounty, referring disputes — are entrusted to people, so that evil that befalls through a person's hand is from that hand as secondary cause while remaining within God's decree. To fail to see that is to be among the people who can hardly comprehend any statement — even when told that death overtakes wherever you are, fortified towers included.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:79

> Whatever good befalls you is from Allah and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself. We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ as a messenger to ˹all˺ people. And Allah is sufficient as a Witness

**Good From Allah, Evil From Yourself**

The verse states *mā aṣābaka min ḥasanatin fa min Allāhi wa mā aṣābaka min sayyiʾatin fa min nafsika* — whatever good befalls you is from Allah and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself. This corrects the split attribution just described, where good was said to be from God but evil was said to be from the Messenger (4:78). Both good and evil befall within divine decree — *both from Allah* (4:78) — yet the secondary cause differs. Good as bounty, victory, safety, and guidance is from God as favour — *faḍl min Allāh* (4:70, 4:73) — and even an atom's weight of it is multiplied many times (4:40). Evil as *muṣībah* because of what hands put forward (4:62) — defeat where precaution was abandoned (4:71), withheld shares, or seeking false judges (4:60) — is from the self as deed and desire. The Qur'an elsewhere says *whatever affliction strikes you is because of what your hands have earned*, and the sūrah has tied disaster to *bi mā qaddamat aydīhim* repeatedly. To say evil is from yourself is therefore not to deny decree; it is to name the path by which decree arrives where the servant's choice was the vessel. The sūrah has said humankind was created weak and burdens lightened (4:28); where the weak follows desire — craving another's portion (4:32), believing in *jibt* (4:51) — the evil that befalls through that following is from that self, while the good that befalls when the weak does what was advised — better, more reassuring, great reward, straight path (4:66–68) — is from God's grace.

**We Have Sent You as Messenger to All People**

The clause *wa arsalnāka li al-nāsi rasūlan* — We have sent you as a messenger to all people — follows the correction to show the Messenger's role in both good and evil that befalls. He is *rasūl* — sent, messenger — not the source of decree, as those who said *this is from you* (4:78) implied. The sūrah has said messengers were sent to be obeyed by God's leave (4:64) and that whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God (4:80); to be sent to all people — *li al-nāsi* — matches the sūrah's opening *O humanity, be mindful of your Lord who created you from a single soul* (4:1) and its witness scene where a witness is brought from every community and the Prophet ﷺ as witness over his (4:41). The message he brings includes the limits about inheritance after debts (4:11–12), the bar on devouring by falsehood with trade by consent (4:29), and the purification through earth where water fails (4:43). Good that befalls when those limits are kept is from God through the messenger's clarification; evil that befalls when they are rejected is from the self that turned away stubbornly — *yaṣuddūna ṣudūdā* (4:61) — and sought *ṭāghūt*. To send him to all people is to make the means of good universally available, so that no soul can say the call to *come to what God revealed and to the Messenger* (4:61) was not addressed to it.

**And Allah Is Sufficient as Witness**

The closing *wa kafā bi Allāhi shahīdā* — and Allah is sufficient as a Witness — seals both attributions. *Shahīd* — witness, present testifier — was read as God witnessing that the Messenger is truly sent, as He is Witness over all things (4:33), hears and sees trusts and judgments (4:58), and knows best who enemies are though sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45). To say He suffices as witness is to say the Messenger's truth does not depend on the hypocrites' claim that good is from God but evil from you; God witnesses that both are within His decree and that good's favour and evil's responsibility are as stated. The phrase *kafā bi Allāhi* — sufficient is God — appears elsewhere where the community is told not to fear enemies' schemes, whose patron's schemes are weak (4:76), and where the Prophet ﷺ is told to put trust in Him as Trustee (4:81). Here sufficiency as Witness tells the community that the correction — good from God, evil from self — is not a slogan to be debated but a witnessed truth. The One who never wrongs even by an atom and who will bring a witness from every community (4:41) witnesses that where good befalls it is from His bounty, and where evil befalls through a hand's doing it is from that hand — while both remain within His decree.

**A Balance Between Decree and Responsibility**

Placed after *both from Allah* (4:78), this verse holds decree and responsibility together without merging them. The sūrah maintains that nothing befalls except by God's leave — towers do not prevent death (4:78) — and at the same time maintains that hands earn: the laggers' disaster talk, the distorters' *rāʿinā*, and the deviators' wish to misguide are from selves. Early authorities explained the balance as: evil as affliction is decreed, but evil as sin is from the self that chose the scheme Satan made to seem fair. The sūrah has shown that choice repeatedly — trading a portion for misguidance (4:44), fabricating lies as blatant sin (4:50), believing in *jibt* (4:51), seeking false judges (4:60). Each is a self's doing that decree allowed but did not compel. Good, by contrast, is from God even as secondary cause, because the sūrah's good — guidance to the straight path (4:68), honourable company (4:69), vast shade (4:57) — is given as *faḍl* and *ajr ʿaẓīm* from grace (4:67). To say good from God and evil from self is therefore to teach the community to thank Him for the first and to turn from the self in the second, rather than to blame the Messenger for either. The next verse will make that turning practical: whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God, and whoever turns away — the Prophet ﷺ is not a keeper over them (4:80).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:80

> Whoever obeys the Messenger has truly obeyed Allah. But whoever turns away, then ˹know that˺ We have not sent you ˹O Prophet˺ as a keeper over them

**Obedience to the Messenger Is Obedience to God**

The statement *man yuṭiʿi al-rasūla fa qad aṭāʿa Allāha* — whoever obeys the Messenger has truly obeyed Allah — gathers the sūrah's long argument about referral. The sūrah commanded *obey God and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you, and refer disputes to them* as best outcome (4:59); said messengers were sent to be obeyed by God's leave (4:64); and made acceptance of the Prophet ﷺ as judge without resistance the condition of true belief (4:65). Between those, it exposed those who claim belief yet seek false judges (4:60) and who turn away stubbornly when called to the revelations and the Messenger (4:61). This verse's *man yuṭiʿi* — whoever obeys — was read as obedience in the matters the sūrah has detailed: returning trusts to rightful owners and judging fairly (4:58), not devouring by falsehood but trading by mutual consent (4:29), guardianship with witnesses (4:6), and fighting for the oppressed where commanded (4:75). To obey the Messenger in those is not to obey a second source beside God: the sūrah has said the Messenger is sent to make clear (4:26) what God wills to make clear, and that good befalls from God and evil from the self (4:79), so obeying the clarifier is obeying the One who gave the limit. The *fa qad* — has truly — was stressed as already accomplished: the act of obeying the Messenger is counted as obedience to God without remainder.

**But Whoever Turns Away — You Are Not a Keeper Over Them**

The counterpart *wa man tawallā fa mā arsalnāka ʿalayhim ḥafīẓā* — but whoever turns away, We have not sent you as a keeper over them — was read as release of the Prophet ﷺ from compulsion. *Tawallā* — to turn away, to turn the back — matches the hypocrites' *yaṣuddūna ʿanka ṣudūdā* — turning away stubbornly, barring (4:61) — and the lagger's lagging (4:72). *Ḥafīẓ* — keeper, guardian over — was explained as one who keeps count and compels, as God is ever Watchful (4:1) and sufficient as Reckoner (4:6). The Prophet ﷺ is not that keeper; his mission is conveyance and clarification, not coercion of hearts that God knows (4:63). The sūrah's method for such people is *turn away from them, caution them, and give penetrating advice* (4:63), and *put your trust in God; He is sufficient as Trustee* (4:81). The community that was told *had they come after wronging themselves seeking forgiveness and the Messenger prayed for them, they would have found God ever Accepting* (4:64) is told that coming remains their choice. To obey the Messenger is to have obeyed God; to turn away is to bear the turning — because the sender has not made the Messenger a keeper who forces, but a witness who will be brought as witness over his community (4:41) where no statement can be hidden (4:42).

**Why the Identity Holds**

The identity — obeying him is obeying Him — was explained as following from *bi idhni Allāh* — by God's leave — that messengers are sent to be obeyed (4:64). The leave means the limits the Messenger judges by — half, quarter, eighth, sixth after debts and bequests (4:11–12), four witnesses required before sanction (4:15), earth that purifies where water fails (4:43) — are not his invention but the One who sent him. The sūrah has shown that God is sufficient as Witness (4:79) that he is sent to all people, and sufficient as Trustee (4:81) for those who put trust in Him while others spend the night contradicting what was said. To obey the Messenger in those limits is therefore not to follow a man for the man's sake but to follow the One whose command is always executed (4:47) through the man He chose to make the command audible. The Qur'an elsewhere says *say, if you love God, follow me, God will love you*; this verse is the sūrah's legal form of that love: follow the one sent to be obeyed, and you have followed the One who sent him.

**A Line Between Claim and Obedience**

Placed after the correction that good is from God and evil from self (4:79), this verse draws the line between claim and deed. Those who say *we obey* but spend the night contradicting what was said (4:81) claim obedience with the tongue while turning with the heart; the verse says true obedience is to the Messenger, and it is counted as obedience to God. Those who claim *we believe in what was revealed to you and before you* yet seek *ṭāghūt* (4:60) claim belief as *yazʿumūna* but do not obey; the verse excludes them. The line matters because the sūrah's public ethic — return trusts, judge fairly, take precautions and go forth (4:58, 4:71) — depends on a single authority to be obeyed. Without that, each dispute would be referred to the judge who favours him — the *ṭāghūt* whose schemes are weak (4:76) but whose flattery is strong. With it, the community has a head whose judgment, when accepted without *ḥaraj* and with whole submission (4:65), keeps the straight path that would have been granted had they done what was advised (4:68). The verse therefore does not add a new law; it names the hinge on which the sūrah's laws turn.

**Not a Keeper as Constraint and Mercy**

The final *We have not sent you as a keeper over them* was read as both constraint on the Prophet ﷺ and mercy for all. Constraint, because he is not to coerce the turning; the sūrah's method for hypocrites is turn away, caution, and penetrating advice (4:63), not forced compliance. Mercy, because the same God who is sufficient as Witness that the Messenger is sent (4:79) is also *tawwāb* — ever Accepting — for those who come after wronging themselves (4.64). To turn away remains possible, but the door to return remains open until death is present (4:18). The verse therefore steadies the believers who might despair at the hypocrites' lagging and at the fearful who ask *why have You ordered us to fight?* (4:77): the Prophet ﷺ is not a keeper who must bring them by force; his sufficient task is conveyance, and the believers' task is obedience and referral where they can, with trust that God suffices as Trustee. The one who obeys him has obeyed God; the one who turns bears the turning where witnesses will be brought and no statement hidden. Between those two, the sūrah leaves the path clear and the keeper's role in the right hands.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:81

> And they say, "We obey," but when they leave you, a group of them would spend the night contradicting what they said. Allah records all their schemes. So turn away from them, and put your trust in Allah. And Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs

**We Obey — but the Night Tells Otherwise**

The verse pictures a double speech: *wa yaqūlūna ṭāʿatun fa idhā barazū min ʿindika bayyata ṭāʾifatun minhum ghayra alladhī taqūl* — and they say, we obey, but when they leave you, a group of them would spend the night contradicting what they said. *Ṭāʿatun* — obedience — is the word they offer in presence, the same word the sūrah requires as *whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah* (4:80) and as true belief until they accept him as judge without resistance (4:65). *Barazū min ʿindika* — when they leave your presence — marks the test: in presence they claim obedience; in absence they *bayyata* — spend the night, plan by night — what contradicts. *Tabyīt* — night-plotting — was explained as deliberating after hours, reworking what was said in daylight, as those who take words out of context play with tongues (4:46) and those who are stingy promote stinginess (4:37). The sūrah has exposed hypocrisy that swears goodwill after disaster (4:62) and turns away stubbornly after revelation (4:61); here it is nightly contradiction. The group — *ṭāʾifatun minhum* — shows not all who said *we obey* do so, but a party, enough to mislead others, as the lagger among you who makes others lag (4:72).

**Allah Records All Their Schemes**

The clause *wa Allāhu yaktubu mā yubayyitūn* — and Allah records all their schemes, what they plot by night — was read as the counterpart to the sūrah's watch over market and home. The sūrah has said God is ever Watchful (4:1), sufficient as Reckoner (4:6), Witness over all things (4:33), and never wrongs by an atom but multiplies good (4:40). To record *mā yubayyitūn* — what they spend the night on — means the nightly contradiction, not only the daytime claim, is entered. The Qur'an elsewhere says that angels record, and that no small or great is left except counted; here the recorder is named as God Himself, because the sūrah wants the Prophet ﷺ to know that the nightly schemes are not a hidden variable that will surprise the community — they are already written. That record matters for the hypocrites who publicise news of security or fear without referral (4.83) and for those who contradict *we obey* after leaving. Their *tabyīt* may feel like secret counsel, but the One who knows what is in hearts (4:63) and has perfect knowledge of them (4:39) writes it.

**So Turn Away From Them**

The instruction *fa aʿriḍ ʿanhum* — so turn away from them — repeats the counsel given for those whose hearts are known and whose oaths are hollow — *turn away, caution, and give penetrating advice* (4:63). *Iʿrāḍ* — turning away — was explained as not taking their nightly counsel as guidance, not seeking their approval, and not exposing their schemes with harsh retaliation that would deepen hypocrisy. The same turning was told where hypocrites turned away stubbornly (4:61) — answer with a measured withdrawal rather than with mimicry. The sūrah's ethic is to return trusts and judge with fairness as noble exhortation from the All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:58); to turn away from the night-plotters is to keep that fairness without being drawn into night-plotting oneself. Early authorities noted that the Prophet ﷺ was not told to punish the group at this stage but to disregard their nightly contradiction, because the record is kept and the trust put in God suffices.

**Put Your Trust in Allah**

The positive *wa tawakkal ʿalā Allāhi* — and put your trust in Allah — follows the turning as its support. *Tawakkul* — to entrust affairs, to rely — was explained as placing the matter of the night-plotters, of the coming fight, and of news that is publicised (4:83) in the hands of the One who is sufficient. The sūrah has built that sufficiency as Guardian and Helper (4:45), as Witness that the Messenger is sent to all people (4:79), and as sufficient to curb the disbelievers' might (4:84). To trust is to fight in God's cause after taking precautions (4:71) while knowing that the night-plotters' schemes, like their patron's, are ever weak (4:76). The one who says *we obey* and then spends the night contradicting trusts in darkness; the one told to turn away and trust entrusts the darkness to Him who records it. That trust was lived by the Prophet ﷺ when he put trust in God as Trustee after their schemes were recorded, and it is the same trust the sūrah will commend to believers who refer security or fear to the Messenger and authorities (4:83) rather than publicising it.

**And Allah Is Sufficient as Trustee of Affairs**

The closing *wa kafā bi Allāhi wakīlā* — and Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs — seals both recording and reliance. *Wakīl* — trustee, disposer of affairs, one entrusted with the outcome — was explained as the One to whom trust is returned, as trusts are returned to rightful owners (4:58) and as judgment is referred upward as best outcome (4:59). To say He is sufficient as *Wakīl* is to say that the nightly contradiction, the lagging at disaster, and the wishing at bounty all end in a trust He will dispose. The sūrah has used *kafā bi Allāhi* — sufficient is God — for Guardian, Helper, Witness, and Knower, and here for Trustee, showing that each need has one sufficiency. For the community learning to go forth in groups or together, to distinguish blessing from gain (4:72–73), and to fight for the oppressed (4:75), sufficiency as Trustee means the night that others spend contradicting need not be spent fearing, because the recorder and the disposer are one — His record misses no *tabyīt* and His disposal misses no *faḍl*. That is why the verse pairs recording with trust: what He writes He also handles, and what He handles as Trustee is sufficient.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:82

> Do they not then reflect on the Quran? Had it been from anyone other than Allah, they would have certainly found in it many inconsistencies

**Do They Not Reflect on the Qur'an**

The question *a fa lā yatadabbarūna al-Qurʾān* — do they not then reflect on the Qur'an — follows the nightly contradiction of those who say *we obey* and then spend the night contradicting (4:81). *Tadabbur* — to reflect, to follow through to the end — was explained as reading not only the first word but the whole, following each limit to its place and seeing how it connects. The sūrah has shown much to reflect on: creation from one soul and guarding womb-ties (4:1); returning orphan wealth with witnesses (4:6); honouring shares after debts (4:11–12); guarding marriage with dowries and chastity (4:24); making things clear, guiding to noble ways, and turning in mercy (4:26–27); taking precautions and going forth (4:71); fighting for the oppressed (4:75). The night-plotters' *tabyīt* — spending the night contradicting — is the opposite of *tadabbur*: one spends the night to distort, the other spends the night to understand. The question *do they not then* implies that reflection would have prevented the contradiction, because the Qur'an's coherence would have answered the very dispute they took to false judges (4:60) and the excuse they swore after disaster (4:62).

**Had It Been From Other Than Allah**

The test *wa law kāna min ʿindi ghayri Allāhi la wajadū fīhi ikhtilāfan kathīrā* — had it been from anyone other than Allah, they would have found in it many inconsistencies — was read as proof of divine origin by internal coherence. *Ikhtilāf kathīr* — many inconsistencies — was explained as contradiction between its rulings: inheritance shares that divide little and much (4:7); dowry as free gift not reclaimed (4:4, 4:20–21); trade by mutual consent (4:29); guardianship with witnesses (4:6); fighting for the oppressed (4:75) — each could clash if man-made, yet they cohere. Had the Book been from a human — the Prophet ﷺ himself, a committee, or a school — variance would have appeared as forgetfulness, favour, or change of mind under pressure. The sūrah's detailed legislation — where a mother's share shifts from third to sixth when siblings exist (4:11), where a wife's share is quarter or eighth (4:12), where a bondwoman's penalty is half (4:25), where earth purifies where water fails (4:43) — is precisely detailed yet without contradiction, because the distributor is not the community that craves what others have (4:32) but the One who never wrongs by an atom (4:40). To reflect is to see that a Book that governs both the little enjoyment (4:77) and the great reward (4:40, 4:67) without tilting is not a patchwork.

**The Inconsistency They Would Have Found Elsewhere**

Early authorities noted that human works show inconsistencies of three kinds: factual, where a claim made early is forgotten later; moral, where a limit praised in one place is excused in another; and stylistic, where voice shifts betray many hands. The Qur'an, though revealed over years in Makkah and Madinah, in ease and hardship, shows none of that. Its ethic of *iḥsān* — kind doing to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, neighbours, companions, travellers, and those in possession (4:36) — appears with the same force where orphans are guarded and where fighting is commanded; its ethic of *ḥudūd* — limits — appears with the same word where inheritance is divided and where faces could be wiped (4:47). The hypocrites who spend the night contradicting contradict precisely because their plan is from other than God: it must vary, it must hide, and it is recorded (4:81). The Book they hear by day does not vary, which is why the Prophet ﷺ is told to put trust in the sufficient Trustee (4.81) — the Trustee's word does not change between day and night. The sūrah elsewhere says *do they not reflect, or are there locks on their hearts?* — and *had it been from other than God they would have found many inconsistencies* is the key that would open those locks, if they reflected.

**Reflection as the Opposite of Night-Plotting**

Placed after nightly contradiction, this verse offers the alternative night. The same night that a party spends plotting what contradicts *we obey* could be spent in *tadabbur* — following the Qur'an to its ends. The sūrah has taught that news of security or fear should be referred to the Messenger and the authorities, where those with sound judgment would validate it (4:83); reflection is that referral at the level of the individual. A community that reflects will not publicise fear for the weak schemer's profit, nor fear people as God should be feared when the order to fight comes (4:77). It will see that death overtakes wherever you are, even in towers (4:78), and that both good and evil fall within God's decree while good is from Him and evil from the self as means (4:78–79) — a coherence that only reflection holds together. The verse generalises the sūrah's method since *Allah wills to make things clear* (4:26): clarity is given, but it requires *tadabbur* to be entered. The night-plotters who do not reflect choose the weak scheme that is ever weak (4:76); the reflectors find the Book whose many detailed limits do not contradict, because they were not from a weak plotter but from the All-Knowing, All-Wise.

**A Verse That Holds the Book's Trust**

Between the record of nightly schemes and the publicising of security or fear (4:81, 4:83), this verse holds the Book's trust. The trust that the sūrah commanded to return — *return trusts to rightful owners and judge with fairness* (4:58) — includes the greatest trust: the Qur'an itself. To reflect on it is to return it to its purpose — to be the judge in tangles (4:65) and the referent for disputes as best outcome (4:59). To fail to reflect is to leave it as sound while contradicting it by night, which is the precise breach the previous verse named. The sūrah's question *do they not then reflect?* is therefore not a critique of intelligence but of will, as the next verse will say *had it not been for God's grace and mercy you would have followed Satan, except for a few* (4:83). Reflection is grace-enabled, and its fruit is seeing no inconsistency where inconsistency would have been many had the source been other than God. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, that seeing is itself lightening: the Book that commands a mother's sixth and a wife's eighth can be trusted to command fighting and purification without wavering, because its Source does not waver — and the one who reflects will find that the path from orphan to inheritance to marriage to battle is one straight path walked.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:83

> And when they hear news of security or fear, they publicize it. Had they referred it to the Messenger or their authorities, those with sound judgment among them would have validated it. Had it not been for Allah's grace and mercy, you would have followed Satan—except for a few

**When They Hear News of Security or Fear, They Publicise It**

The verse says *wa idhā jāʾahum amrun min al-amni aw al-khawfi adhāʿū bihi* — and when news comes to them of security or fear, they publicise it — broadcasting it, spreading it wide. *Amn* — security, safety — and *khawf* — fear, threat — were explained as reports from the front, rumours of victory or defeat, or news about expeditions like those the believers were told to go forth in, in groups or together, with precautions (4:71). *Adhāʿū bihi* — to publicise — was read as hurrying the news to others without verification, driven by love of being first, by anxiety, or by the laggers' wish to justify not being present (4:72). The sūrah has shown that news in Madinah was a trust: the community's safety depends on whether reports are true and on who hears them when. To spread security prematurely can breed complacency; to spread fear prematurely can breed the fear of people as God should be feared (4:77) that made a group ask *why have You ordered us to fight? Delay us*. The verse therefore diagnoses a habit that harms the same community that was taught to return trusts and judge with fairness (4:58) and to obey and refer disputes (4:59): news, too, is a trust to be returned to rightful handlers before it is passed on.

**Had They Referred It to the Messenger or Their Authorities**

The corrective *wa law raddūhu ilā al-rasūli wa ilā ulī al-amri minhum la ʿalimahu alladhīna yastanbiṭūnahu minhum* — had they referred it to the Messenger or their authorities, those with sound judgment among them would have validated it — was read as the sūrah's method for reports. *Radd* — to refer, to return — matches *ruddūhu ilā Allāhi wa al-rasūl* — refer disputes to God and Messenger as best outcome (4:59). *Ulī al-amr* — those in authority — here are the leaders and those with insight, whose obedience within obedience was commanded and whose referral is best (4:59). *Yastanbiṭūnahu* — to draw out, to validate, to extract by sound inference — was explained as the work of those with *istinbāṭ* — expertise, the ability to test a report, know its source, and judge its implication before publicising. The sūrah has shown that prayer requires knowing what is said (4:43), that fighting requires *ḥidhr* — precaution — and that judging requires hearing and seeing (4:58); referring news for *istinbāṭ* is that precaution applied to information. The hypocrites who spend the night contradicting what was said (4:81) and who do not reflect on the Qur'an (4:82) are the type who would spread without referring — because the nightly plot and the hasty broadcast share the same root: bypassing the lawful handlers.

**Those With Sound Judgment Would Have Validated It**

The phrase *alladhīna yastanbiṭūnahu minhum* was stressed as showing that not every listener can validate news; it is those among the authorities with sound inference who can. The community was therefore taught to distinguish between hearing and validating, as it distinguishes between craving another's portion and asking God for bounty (4:32). To validate — *istinbāṭ* — includes checking the transmitter, the context, and whether publicising serves the community or serves fear. Early reports linked the verse to the Prophet's handling of the expedition against the Confederates, where news of security and fear about the Banū Qurayẓah and the approaching parties needed to be managed rather than broadcast. The sūrah generalises: whether news is good — *ḥasanah* from God — or evil — from the self where hands put forward (4:79) — its handling belongs to those who can draw out its meaning. The believers who were told *do they not reflect on the Qur'an? Had it been from other than God they would have found many inconsistencies* (4:82) are here told to reflect on news as they reflect on the Book: refer it, extract, and then speak.

**Had It Not Been for Allah's Grace and Mercy**

The reminder *wa law lā faḍlu Allāhi ʿalaykum wa raḥmatuhu la ittabaʿtumu al-shayṭāna illā qalīlā* — had it not been for Allah's grace and mercy, you would have followed Satan, except for a few — was read as both history and warning. *Faḍl* and *raḥmah* — grace and mercy — were explained as the sending of the Messenger to be obeyed by God's leave (4:64), the witness brought and the Day where no statement can be hidden (4:41–42), the earth that purifies where water fails (4:43), and the lightening because humankind was created weak (4:28). Without that, the community that heard security or fear would have followed Satan's weak schemes (4:76) that the lagger and the fearful already followed when they feared people as God (4:77) and said *this is from you* at evil (4:78). The phrase *illā qalīlan* — except for a few — matches *few would have obeyed* the hard command to sacrifice or leave homes (4:66) and *few believed* among those given a portion (4:55). The few represent those who, by grace, did refer, did validate, and did not publicise. The verse therefore tells the broader community that the habit of broadcasting without referral is not a small slip; without grace and mercy, it is the path by which Satan is followed.

**A Verse That Guards Information as Trust**

Placed between the call to reflect on the Qur'an's coherence (4:82) and the command to fight where the Prophet ﷺ is accountable only for himself but must motivate believers (4:84), this verse guards information as trust. The sūrah has commanded *return trusts to rightful owners and judge with fairness* as a noble exhortation (4:58); news of security or fear is a trust to be returned to the Messenger and authorities before it is judged publicly.
