To publicise without referral is to handle a trust as devouring by falsehood handles wealth (4:29) — quickly and without consent — while to refer for *istinbāṭ* is to handle it as trade by consent. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the verse is lightening: you need not decide every report alone; refer it to those with sound judgment, and the validation will be drawn out. The sūrah's ethic of *iḥsān* — kind doing — to parents, relatives, neighbours, and travellers (4:36) becomes, at the level of news, not spreading fear that harms the weak and not spreading security that lulls the guard. Had the community not been graced, the broadcast of fear would have made it fear people as God; by grace, it can refer, validate, and then — if fighting is required — go forth with precautions, as commanded, rather than as rumour drives.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:84

> So fight in the cause of Allah ˹O Prophet˺. You are accountable for none but yourself. And motivate the believers ˹to fight˺, so perhaps Allah will curb the disbelievers' might. And Allah is far superior in might and in punishment

**So Fight in the Cause of Allah**

The command *fa qātil fī sabīli Allāhi* — so fight in the cause of Allah — is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ alone, after the diagnosis that many lag, that news of security or fear is publicised without referral (4:83), and that some were told *do not fight; establish prayer and give alms*, then feared people as God when fighting was prescribed (4:77). *Fa* — so — ties the command to that diagnosis: though many hesitate, the cause remains God's — the same *sabīl* that believers fight for while disbelievers fight for the Devil whose schemes are ever weak (4:76), and the same cause for which the oppressed cry for a guardian and helper (4:75). The sūrah has said to take precautions and go forth in groups or together (4:71) and to let those who sell this life for the next fight, with a great reward whether martyred or victorious (4:74); here the Prophet ﷺ is told to fight even if others do not. The cause does not depend on the laggers' measure — *blessed we were not there* at disaster (4:72) — nor on the fearful's plea for delay; it is God's path made clear (4:26) and the straight path to which doing what was advised would have guided (4:68).

**You Are Accountable for None but Yourself**

The clause *lā tukallafu illā nafsaka* — you are accountable for none but yourself — was read as both limit and liberation. The Prophet ﷺ is responsible for his own fighting, not for compelling the hypocrites who turn away stubbornly (4:61) and spend the night contradicting (4:81). The sūrah has said messengers are sent to be obeyed by God's leave (4:64), that obedience to him is obedience to God (4:80), and that he is not a keeper over those who turn (4:80) but a warner and witness (4:41). To be accountable only for himself frees him from measuring his mission by the laggers' absence; the mission remains to convey, to fight, and to motivate. The same clause was read as mercy for the community: each believer is accountable for his own referral to the Messenger and authorities (4:83) and for his own taking of precautions. The sūrah elsewhere says *no soul is charged beyond what it can bear*; here that charging is individualised at the point of fighting, where fear of people can make a person feel responsible for all.

**Motivate the Believers**

The addition *wa ḥarriḍ al-muʾminīna* — and motivate, urge, rouse the believers — was explained as the Prophet's second task beyond his own fighting: to stir the believers with reminders of what the sūrah has shown — the Gardens with vast shade for believing and doing good (4:57), the great reward for selling this life for the next whether martyred or victorious (4:74), and the cry of the oppressed who ask for a guardian and helper from grace (4:75). *Taḥrīḍ* — to urge, to sharpen — was read as encouragement that makes the reluctant firm — *ashadda tathbītā*, the firmness that doing what was advised would have given (4:66). The sūrah has shown why urging is needed: some fear people as God (4:77), some lag and call absence a blessing (4:72), some publicise fear (4:83). Urging counters each with the sūrah's measures — *Satan's schemes are weak* (4:76), *death overtakes wherever you are, even in towers* (4:78), *good from God, evil from self by what hands put forward* (4:79). To motivate is therefore not to push the weak beyond the lightening granted (4:28) but to remind them that fighting after precautions, in God's cause, is the form obedience takes where oppression exists.

**Perhaps Allah Will Curb the Disbelievers' Might**

The hope *ʿasā Allāhu an yakuffa baʾsa alladhīna kafarū* — so perhaps Allah will curb, restrain, the might of the disbelievers — was read as the divine outcome of the Prophet's fighting and urging. *Baʾs* — might, force, violence — was explained as the power by which the land of oppressors holds the weak — men, women, children — who cry for deliverance (4:75). To curb that *baʾs* is the sūrah's answer to that cry: the guardian and helper appointed from grace (4:45, 4:75) curbs the might that made the town of oppressors oppressive. The word *ʿasā* — perhaps — was explained as assurance from God, as elsewhere *perhaps your Lord will...* means He will, because the speaker is God. The sūrah has shown that curbing comes not by the believers' numbers alone but by God's might, as the next clause says He is superior in might and punishment. Early reports placed the verse when the Prophet ﷺ faced the Confederates with few, and God curbed them by wind and division; the type was read as every time believers fight with precautions after referral, God curbs.

**Allah Is Far Superior in Might and in Punishment**

The closing *wa Allāhu ashaddu baʾsan wa ashaddu tankīlā* — and Allah is far superior in might and in punishment — was read as the ground for *perhaps He will curb*. *Ashaddu baʾsan* — more intense in might — than any *baʾs* believers face; *ashaddu tankīlā* — more intense in punishment, in making an example — than any deterrent the disbelievers deploy. The pair matches the sūrah's earlier *Satan's schemes are ever weak* (4:76) and *that is easy for Allah* where deliberate devouring leads to Fire (4:30). The might that appoints heirs after debts (4:11), that renews skin for tasting (4:56), and that multiplies an atom's weight (4:40) is the might that curbs. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the verse is the final lightening for fighting: you are accountable only for yourself, urge the believers, and perhaps God will curb the might that made you fear people as God should be feared. The superior might and punishment are not threats to the believers who fight for the oppressed; they are guarantees that the cause they fight in — God's — is supported by a might no *baʾs* can match and a punishment no *kayd* can withstand.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:85

> Whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a share in the reward, and whoever intercedes for an evil cause will have a share in the burden. And Allah is Watchful over all things

**Intercession for Good and for Evil**

The verse states *man yashfaʿ shafāʿatan ḥasanatan yakun lahu naṣībun minhā wa man yashfaʿ shafāʿatan sayyiʾatan yakun lahu kiflun minhā* — whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a share in the reward, and whoever intercedes for an evil cause will have a share in the burden. *Shafāʿah* — intercession, mediation, joining — was explained as adding one's effort to another's so that a matter is accomplished: recommending, urging, or making a cause possible. *Ḥasanah* — good — was read as the causes the sūrah has commended: motivating believers to fight where fighting is in God's cause for the oppressed (4:74–75, 4:84); appointing mediators who desire harmony where God brings it (4:35); returning trusts and judging with fairness (4:58); referring news of security or fear to those with sound judgment (4:83). *Sayyiʾah* — evil — was read as the opposite: interceding with *ṭāghūt* (4:60), promoting stinginess (4:37), encouraging lagging (4:72), or publicising fear (4:83). *Naṣīb* — share in reward — and *kifl* — share in burden — were explained as the intercessor's recorded portion of the outcome, because intercession makes the outcome possible. The sūrah has said that the atom's weight is not wronged but multiplied (4:40) and that whoever obeys the Messenger is with the blessed (4:69); intercession for good is the social form of that obedience, where the urger shares the reward of the doer.

**A Share in Reward and a Share in Burden**

The pairing *naṣīb* and *kifl* was stressed as exact. *Naṣīb* — share — echoes *naṣīban mafrūḍan* — obligatory share — for heirs (4:7) and *naṣīb* of what men and women earn (4:32), showing that intercession earns as deeds earn. *Kifl* — portion, like the load on a camel's side — was explained as the burden of evil intercession, the weight the intercessor bears of the sin he helped make possible, as the sūrah warns that deliberate devouring leads to Fire easy for God (4:30) and that trading a portion of the Book for misguidance bears humiliating punishment (4:37). Early authorities gave examples: interceding to free an oppressed person, to reconcile spouses, or to motivate fighting in God's cause brings a share of reward; interceding to protect an oppressor, to treat a widow as inheritance (4:19), or to seek a false judge (4:60) brings a share of burden. The sūrah's ethic is therefore collective: no one acts alone, and no one's speech — *we hear and obey* or *we hear and disobey* (4:46) — is without share.

**Why Intercession Follows Motivating to Fight**

Placed after *motivate the believers to fight, perhaps God will curb the might* (4:84), this verse generalises that urging. *Taḥrīḍ* — to motivate — is a form of *shafāʿah* where the motivator joins the fighter's cause and shares its reward, the *ajr ʿaẓīm* promised whether martyred or victorious (4:74). The verse was linked to the Prophet ﷺ urging the believers while he himself fights though accountable only for himself (4:84); his urging is intercession for a good cause whose share is great. The opposite — interceding for evil — was linked to those who intercede with *ṭāghūt*, who reassure disbelievers they are better guided (4:51), and who lag and wish for gain (4:73). The sūrah has shown that Satan's schemes are weak (4:76); to intercede for the Devil's cause is to join weakness and bear its burden. The verse therefore tells the community that urging matters: the one who says *do not fight, delay us* (4:77) will have a share in the burden of those who stay from fighting for the oppressed, while the one who says *take precautions and go forth* (4:71) will have a share in the reward of those who go.

**And Allah Is Watchful Over All Things**

The closing *wa kāna Allāhu ʿalā kulli shayʾin raqībā* — and Allah is Watchful over all things — was read as the recorder of shares. *Raqīb* — watchful, observer — was explained as watching intercession as deeds are watched, not missing the atom's weight (4:40) and not wronging by a thread (4:49, 4:77). To say He is Watchful over all things is to say that intercession for good done quietly — a word that moves a hesitant fighter, a mediation that seeks harmony (4:35), a referral of news to sound judgment (4:83) — is known and weighted, and that intercession for evil done by night — *yubayyitūna* what contradicts *we obey* (4:81) — is also known and weighted. The sūrah has used *ḥasīb* for the orphan's handover — *sufficient is God as Reckoner* (4:6) — and *shahīd* for witnessing the Messenger's mission (4:79), and *wakīl* for trusting affairs (4:81); here *raqīb* gathers them as the watch over every joining. The one who intercedes for a good cause, even if the cause does not fully succeed — *perhaps God will curb* (4:84) — still has his *naṣīb*; the one who intercedes for evil, even if the evil is not fully realised, still bears *kifl*. Watchfulness ensures both, which is why the verse is both invitation and warning.

**A Community Where Urging Earns**

Between the command to fight and the greeting that answers with better (4:86), this verse holds the community's social economy together. The economy was stated as: do not crave what God gave some over others; ask Him for bounty (4:32) — because shares are from Him. Here it adds: whoever joins a good cause will have a share in it; whoever joins an evil, a burden. The community that was told *if you avoid major sins We will cover lesser ones* (4:31) and *good from God, evil from yourself* (4:79) is here told that joining amplifies both: joining good multiplies good; joining evil burdens. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the verse is the lightest encouragement to speak: a word of intercession for the oppressed who cry for a helper (4:75), for the couple seeking mediators, for the fighter needing urging, earns a *naṣīb* as though the speaker had done the deed. The sūrah therefore invites the tongue that once lagged or publicised fear to become a tongue that intercedes for good, whose share is reward and whose watcher is the One who is Watchful over all things.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:86

> And when you are greeted, respond with a better greeting or at least similarly. Surely Allah is a ˹vigilant˺ Reckoner of all things

**Respond With a Better Greeting or At Least Similarly**

The verse commands *wa idhā ḥuyyītum bi taḥiyyatin fa ḥayyū bi aḥsana minhā aw ruddūhā* — and when you are greeted, respond with a better greeting or at least similarly. *Taḥiyyah* — greeting — was explained as *al-salām* — peace — the word whose misuse the sūrah will soon warn against, where some say to one who offers peace *you are no believer* for fleeting gain (4:94). The command to answer with better — *aḥsana minhā* — or to return it equally — *aw ruddūhā* — was read as the ethic for all greetings among believers, and by extension for any kindness. The sūrah has commanded *iḥsān* to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, neighbours, companions, travellers, and those in possession (4:36), and has warned that interceding for good brings a share in reward (4:85). To answer a greeting with better is the smallest *iḥsān* that keeps the larger ones alive; it is intercession for good at the level of a word. The community that was told to take precautions and go forth (4:71), to reflect on the Qur'an that has no inconsistency (4:82), and to refer news of security or fear to those with sound judgment (4:83) is here told that the first sound of meeting is peace, and its reply should be more peace. Early authorities noted that the better greeting was exemplified as *wa ʿalaykum al-salām wa raḥmatu Allāh* in reply to *al-salām ʿalaykum*, and at least the same where equality is required.

**Greeting as Peace After Battle and Before**

The placement matters. The sūrah has moved through fighting — believers fight for God, disbelievers for the Devil whose schemes are weak (4:76); those who sell this life for the next fight, whether martyred or victorious (4:74); the oppressed cry for a guardian and helper (4:75). In that field, greetings can be mistaken for stratagem, as the coming verses warn against saying to one who offers peace *you are no believer* for fleeting gain (4:94). This verse establishes the rule before that warning: when a greeting of peace is offered, answer it with better or same. The rule applies on the battlefield where a combatant may offer *salām*, and in the town where neighbours meet. The sūrah has said *do not kill yourselves, surely Allah is ever Merciful to you* (4:29); greeting with peace is the opposite of killing — it is the invitation to keep the bond the lagger treated as if it were none (4:73). To answer peace with more peace is therefore the opposite of the night-plotters who spend the night contradicting *we obey* (4:81): one adds peace, the other plots harm — the verse chooses which night the tongue should keep.

**At Least Similarly — the Minimum That Protects**

The option *aw ruddūhā* — or at least similarly — was explained as the minimum that prevents greeting from becoming a hierarchy. To return the same — *wa ʿalaykum al-salām* for *al-salām ʿalaykum* — was read as obligatory where better is recommended, so that no one is left without an answer. The sūrah has used similar minima elsewhere: the atom's weight not wronged (4:40), the thread not wronged (4:49, 4:77), the intercessor's share for good (4:85) — each ensures that the small is counted; to answer at least similarly ensures the small greeting is counted. The ethic was extended to those in possession — bondspeople — and to neighbours near and distant (4:36): a greeting is due to each without regard to status, because *you are from one another* (4:25) and the sūrah opened with *from a single soul* (4:1). To withhold a greeting or to answer with less would be the stinginess that conceals bounty (4:37) at the scale of a word, while to answer with better is the donation from what was provided (4:39) at the same scale. The sūrah's measure of *naṣīb* — share — for intercession (4:85) thus includes the share of peace returned.

**Surely Allah Is a Vigilant Reckoner of All Things**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna ʿalā kulli shayʾin ḥasībā* — surely Allah is a vigilant Reckoner of all things — matches the smallness of the act with the greatness of the watcher. *Ḥasīb* — reckoner, guardian, sufficient — was explained as counting the greeting and the reply as deeds, not missing the better — *aḥsan* — nor the equal — *radd* — just as intercession's share is not missed (4:85). The sūrah has used *ḥasīb* for the orphan's handover — *sufficient is God as Reckoner* (4:6) — and for the watch over all things where intercession's share is weighed (4:85); here it is the watch over greetings. That continuity shows greetings are not courtesies outside law; they are entries in the ledger that also records trusts and judgments, and that ledger is kept with the same sufficiency that multiplies an atom's weight. The One who is All-Hearing, All-Seeing over trusts and judgments (4:58) is the Reckoner over peace offered and peace returned. To answer with better is therefore not only kindness to the greeter; it is reckoning before the Reckoner, where even a better peace is multiplied.

**A Verse That Holds the Community's Tongue**

Placed between the share for intercession (4:85) and the declaration of the gathering about which there is no doubt (4:87), this verse holds the community's tongue at its first word. The sūrah has diagnosed distorted words — *we hear and disobey* veiled as obedience (4:46), *rāʿinā* played with tongues (4:46), *we obey* contradicted by night (4:81) — and has prescribed straight speech — *qawlan sadīdā* (4:9) and *qawlan balīghā* that reaches souls (4:63). Greeting with peace and answering with better is the daily practice of that straightness where speech is most frequent. A community that learns to answer *al-salām* with *aḥsan* will be the community that does not say to the one who offers peace *you are no believer* for fleeting gain (4:94), that does not call absence at disaster a blessing (4:72), and that does not wish after gain as if no bond existed (4:73). For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the command is also light: when greeted, add a word. That added word, counted by the Reckoner and weighted as an atom, is the least burden that still joins the great reward — and it is the sound of the straight path walked.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:87

> Allah, there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. He will certainly gather ˹all of˺ you together on the Day of Judgment—about which there is no doubt. And whose word is more truthful than Allah's

**There Is No God Except Him**

The verse opens with *Allāhu lā ilāha illā huwa* — Allah, there is no god worthy of worship except Him — the same declaration that the sūrah placed at the root of worship: *worship God and associate none with Him* (4:36) and *association is not forgiven* (4:48). The sūrah has shown what association looks like in practice — belief in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* (4:51), seeking judgment of false judges though commanded to reject them (4:60). To say *lā ilāha illā huwa* is to deny those rivals at the level of worship, judgment, and truth. The phrase follows the command to answer greeting with better or same and the reckoning of all things by the Reckoner (4:86), to remind that the Reckoner is the only God to be worshipped. The sūrah elsewhere pairs *lā ilāha illā huwa* with the declaration that *whoever is condemned by Allah will have no helper* (4:52), showing that the One who alone is to be worshipped is the One who alone suffices as Guardian and Helper (4:45). Here the declaration stands as the premise for what follows: He who alone is God is the One who will gather.

**He Will Certainly Gather You on the Day of Judgment**

The promise *la yajmaʿannakum ilā yawmi al-qiyāmati lā rayba fīhi* — He will certainly gather all of you together on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt — was read as the gathering that the witness scene required. *Yajmaʿannakum* — will gather you — with emphatic letters was explained as the muster where a witness is brought from every community and the Prophet ﷺ as witness over his (4:41), where those who denied and disobeyed will wish to be dust and will not hide any statement (4:42), and where every soul that tasted death — even in towers (4:78) — is brought. The Day was called *yawm al-qiyāmah* — Day of Standing — because all stand before the Reckoner who counts even a better greeting (4:86) and an intercessor's share (4:85). *Lā rayba fīhi* — no doubt about it — was stressed as removing the doubt that made a group fear people as God and ask *why have You ordered us to fight? Delay us* (4:77), and that made laggers call absence a blessing (4:72). That doubt treats the *dunyā*'s little enjoyment as more certain than the Hereafter; the verse says the gathering is more certain. The One who is Reckoner over all things (4:86) is the One who will certainly gather all things.

**About Which There Is No Doubt**

The clause *lā rayba fīhi* was linked to the Qur'an's opening — *this is the Book, no doubt in it* — and to the sūrah's question *do they not reflect on the Qur'an? Had it been from other than God they would have found many inconsistencies* (4:82). To have no doubt about the Day is the fruit of reflecting on the Book that has no inconsistency: the Book that governs inheritance whether little or much (4:7), dowry not reclaimed (4:20–21), and trade by mutual consent (4:29) without contradiction is the same Book that promises the gathering without doubt. The sūrah has shown doubt's practical fruit: publicising news of security or fear without referral (4:83), seeking *ṭāghūt* though commanded to reject it (4:60), distorting *rāʿinā* (4:46) — each is a doubt about whether the Book and Messenger can handle the affair. To say *no doubt about it* is to answer that doubt at its root: the gathering where every atom is weighed and multiplied (4:40) is as sure as the Book's coherence, because both are from the same One.

**Whose Word Is More Truthful Than Allah's**

The question *wa man aṣdaqu min Allāhi ḥadīthā* — and whose word is more truthful than Allah's — seals the declaration and the promise. *Aṣdaqu* — more truthful, most truthful — was explained as a comparison that denies any competitor: no *ḥadīth* — statement, discourse — is truer. The sūrah has shown competing statements: *we hear and disobey* veiled as obedience (4:46); *rāʿinā* twisted (4:46); *we obey* contradicted by night-plotting (4:81); *we intended only goodwill* after disaster (4:62); *this is from you* at evil (4:78) — the speech of people who *can hardly comprehend any statement* (4:78). Against those, God's *ḥadīth* — that there is no god except Him, that He will certainly gather, that an atom is not wronged but multiplied — was presented as the only truthful measure. The Qur'an elsewhere says *Allah's promise is truth*, and that the hypocrites' oaths are a shield; this question asks the listener to choose which *ḥadīth* to trust. On the Day gathered without doubt, God's word will be the one by which every other word is judged, as no statement can be hidden from God (4:42) and the intercessor's share is known (4:85).

**A Verse That Holds Worship and Gathering Together**

Placed between greeting with peace and the division over hypocrites who regressed because of misdeeds (4:88), this verse holds worship and gathering together. To say *there is no god except Him* is to worship without association — the first command (4:36); to believe He will certainly gather on the Day about which there is no doubt is to live as one who will be gathered — and therefore to return trusts, judge fairly, and fight for the oppressed where commanded. The two are one, because the One to be worshipped is the Gatherer. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the gathering is not a threat that crushes; it is the assurance that the better greeting answered, the share interceded for good, and the atom donated are all gathered and counted by the Reckoner. Whose word is more truthful? The sūrah answers with the Book that would have shown many inconsistencies had it been from other than God, and shows none — and with the Day about which there is no doubt, which will show that the truthful *ḥadīth* was God's, and that to have worshipped Him alone was to have trusted the only word that never varies.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:88

> Why are you ˹believers˺ divided into two groups regarding the hypocrites while Allah allowed them to regress ˹to disbelief˺ because of their misdeeds? Do you wish to guide those left by Allah to stray? And whoever Allah leaves to stray, you will never find for them a way

**Why Are You Divided Into Two Groups Regarding the Hypocrites**

The question *fa mā lakum fī al-munāfiqīna fiʾatayni* — why are you believers divided into two groups regarding the hypocrites — addresses the community after the diagnosis that some among you lag (4:72) and some turn away stubbornly from the Book and Messenger (4:61) while claiming *we hear and obey* by day and plotting by night (4:81). *Fiʾatayni* — two groups, two factions — was explained as a split among Companions after the setback at Uḥud, where hypocrites lagged and believers differed over whether they were still counted as believers to be helped or as a group to be treated as having regressed. The sūrah has shown the hypocrites' many signs — seeking false judges though commanded to reject them (4:60), publicising security or fear without referral (4:83) — and the believers' instruction to refer disputes to God and Messenger as best outcome (4:59). To be *fiʾatayni* about them is to disagree about the very case the sūrah has been clarifying, as though the limits about trust, greeting, and fighting were not yet clear enough to judge.

**While Allah Allowed Them to Regress Because of Misdeeds**

The clause *wa Allāhu arkasahum bi mā kasabū* — while Allah allowed them to regress because of what they earned — was read as divine recompense that inverts progress. *Arkasa* — to turn over, to make regress, to return to the start — was explained as turning them back into disbelief after they had outwardly moved forward, because of *bi mā kasabū* — because of what they earned — the same phrase that ties disaster to hands (4:62) and evil to the self (4:79). The sūrah has tied their earning to many acts: seeking *ṭāghūt* (4:60), distorting *rāʿinā* (4:46), fabricating lies as blatant sin (4:50), believing in *jibt* (4:51), envying for bounty (4:54). To earn those is to earn regression, because the path God made clear (4:26), and to which He would have guided had they done what was advised (4:68), was left, and the far straying Satan desires (4:60) was followed. The sūrah has said that God guides to the straight path whom He wills; *arkasa* shows the opposite dispensation: those who earn deviation are allowed to regress, as the sūrah earlier said *Allah has condemned them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except for a few* (4:46).

**Do You Wish to Guide Those Left to Stray**

The question *a turīdūna an tahdū man aḍalla Allāhu* — do you wish to guide those God has left to stray — was read as correction of the faction that wanted to treat the regressed as still guided. *Man aḍalla Allāhu* — those God has left to stray — was explained as those whom He allowed to regress after they chose what earns regression; the sūrah warns that whoever He leaves to stray, you will never find a way for them. To wish to guide them as though the choice had not been made is to dispute the divine recompense itself. The sūrah has shown that guidance is favour from God known to Him (4:70) and that whoever obeys is with the blessed (4:69): favour and guidance follow obedience, not claim. To seek to count as believers those whose earning was to seek false judges and to lag at disaster as if no bond existed (4:73) is to confuse the community's *mawaddah* — bond — with approval. The Qur'an elsewhere says that God guides not those who do wrong after clear signs, and *arkasa* is the term for that wrong's end, where guidance is withdrawn.

**Whoever He Leaves to Stray, You Will Never Find a Way**

The closing *wa man yuḍlili Allāhu fa lan tajida lahu sabīlā* — and whoever Allah leaves to stray, you will never find for them a way — was read as sealing the case. *Sabīl* — way — was explained as the path God wills to make clear (4:26), the noble ways of those before, the straight path (4:68). To be left without *sabīl* is to be without the straight path that would have been granted had they done what was advised, and without the referral that is best outcome (4:59). The sūrah repeats this principle where hypocrites are concerned, showing that where God allows regression, human effort cannot force guidance. The phrase *lan tajida* — you will never find — was addressed to the Prophet ﷺ and to any believer, as though to say: look for a way for them and you will not find one, because the sūrah has already shown that the distributor of bounty and guidance is not the envious who would not give a speck (4:53) but the One who never wrongs by an atom. To seek a way for those He has left to stray is to seek *sabīl* where He has closed it — while the sūrah's open *sabīl* — trade by mutual consent (4:29), greeting with better (4:86), fighting for the oppressed (4:75) — remains for those who have not regressed.

**A Verse That Steadies the Community's Judgment**

Placed after the gathering on the Day about which there is no doubt, and the question whose word is more truthful than God's (4:87), this verse steadies judgment before the next verses describe who may be fought and who must be left because of a treaty or their withdrawal from fighting (4:89–90). The community divided into two groups about hypocrites is told that division itself is mistaken where God has already allowed regression because of what was earned; the hypocrites are not a middle group to be guided as though they were steadfast, because the sūrah has shown their many signs — night-plotting, publicising without referral, seeking *ṭāghūt* — and their recompense is regression. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the verse is also lightening: you need not guide those God has left to stray; you need only be clear about who has regressed because of misdeeds, so that the bond *you are from one another* (4:25) is not used to excuse the one who treats it as if it were none. The sūrah therefore teaches the community to judge as God judges — by what was earned — and to keep its two groups as one in that judgment, so that the straight path remains clear.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:89

> They wish you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so you may all be alike. So do not take them as allies unless they emigrate in the cause of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take any of them as allies or helpers

**They Wish You Would Disbelieve as They Have**

The verse states *waddū law takfurūna kamā kafarū fa takūnūna sawāʾ* — they wish you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so you may all be alike. *Waddū* — they wish, they desire — was explained as the desire of the regressed hypocrites and those who turned away (4:88) that the believers join their regression. The sūrah has shown that wish before: those who follow desires wish you to deviate greatly (4:27), those given a portion trade it for misguidance and wish you to deviate from the path (4:44), and the lagger wishes after gain to be alike in share (4:73). Here the wish is more radical: that you disbelieve as they have, so that sameness — *sawāʾ* — replaces distinction. To disbelieve as they have was read as leaving the limits about wealth and marriage, the referral to the Messenger (4:59), and the obedience that places with the blessed (4:69), and returning to a covering of the Fire (4:56) and belief in *jibt* (4:51). Their wish is not for your opinion but for your sameness: if all are alike in disbelief, their regression is no longer visible. The Qur'an elsewhere says that disbelievers would love you to be as they are, because likeness removes the witness that they were left to stray.

**So Do Not Take Them as Allies Unless They Emigrate**

The command *fa lā tattakhidhū minhum awliyāʾa ḥattā yuhājirū fī sabīli Allāhi* — so do not take them as allies unless they emigrate in the cause of Allah — was read as the sūrah's test of that wish. *Awliyāʾ* — allies, close protectors — was explained as the bond the sūrah opened as *mawaddah* — affection (4:73) — and as *you are from one another* (4:25). To take them as *awliyāʾ* while they remain regressed would be to accept sameness on their terms. Emigration — *hijrah* — *in the cause of Allah* was the sūrah's concrete sign of reversal, as the migrants endured the hard command to leave homes that few would have obeyed (4:66), and as fighting for the oppressed required going forth (4:71). Early reports placed the verse after Uḥud, where hypocrites lagged, and after groups in the desert sought safety with both sides; to emigrate in God's cause meant to join the community that returns trusts and refers disputes (4:58–59) and that fights where the oppressed cry (4:75). The condition *ḥattā yuhājirū* — until they emigrate — was read as the threshold where sameness could be on belief, not on disbelief. Until then, the believers' *mawaddah* is not extended as alliance, because the regressed wish the believers to be alike in the wrong direction.

**But If They Turn Away**

The clause *fa in tawallaw* — but if they turn away — was explained as turning away from that emigration, persisting in regression after the test. *Tawallā* — to turn the back — matches the hypocrites' turning away stubbornly — *yaṣuddūna ṣudūdā* (4:61) — and seeking *ṭāghūt* though commanded to reject it (4:60). To turn away here is to refuse the route that would have shown that doing what was advised is better and more reassuring (4:66). The verse does not command hostility for mere hesitation; it commands it after the wish to make you alike has been displayed and after the path to join has been offered and refused. The sūrah has said that whoever God leaves to stray, you will never find a way for them (4:88); *tawallaw* is the human side of that leaving — they turn, and He allows regression. The community divided into two groups about them (4:88) is here given a single rule: no alliance until emigration; and if they turn from that, then the next measure.

**Seize and Kill Wherever You Find Them**

The measure *fa qātilūhum* — then seize them and kill them wherever you find them — was read as the wartime ruling for the regressed who are combatants or who align with combatants against the believers, not as a rule for every individual who errs. Context shows the sūrah immediately adds exceptions: those allied to a treaty people, and those opposed to fighting either side (4:90), and those who keep away, offer peace, and refrain from attacking — for whom God does not permit harm. Early authorities noted that this measure addresses the hostile group that wishes you disbelieve and that, if it turns away from emigration, remains a threat to the oppressed who cry for a helper (4:75). The sūrah forbids killing a believer except by mistake, with expiation and blood-money (4:92), and threatens Hell for intentional killing (4:93), showing that the permission here is delimited by treaty, by peace offered, and by withdrawal from fighting. To seize the hostile turner is therefore not a lapse of the ethic *do not kill yourselves* (4:29) but its protection at community scale, where the Devil's schemes are weak (4:76) yet must still be curbed (4:84).

**No Allies or Helpers Among the Hostile Turners**

The closing *wa lā tattakhidhū minhum waliyyan wa lā naṣīrā* — and do not take any of them as allies or helpers — repeats the opening prohibition with the two sufficiencies the sūrah said God alone provides — *sufficient as Guardian and sufficient as Helper* (4:45). *Walī* and *naṣīr* — guardian and helper — were explained as the two roles the oppressed ask for from grace (4:75). To take the hostile turner as *walī* or *naṣīr* would be to seek guardianship from those God allowed to regress because of misdeeds, and who wish you alike in disbelief. The sūrah has said that whoever is condemned will have no helper (4:52) and that if those given no share of kingdom had it, they would not give a speck (4:53); the hostile turners are therefore not helpers in any case. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the rule is light: do not take as allies those who wish you to disbelieve as they have; wait for emigration in God's cause as the sign of reversal; and if they turn away as hostile, meet hostility with the measure the sūrah bounds — taking no ally among them, because the Guardian and Helper who suffices for the oppressed is sufficient for you.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:90

> except those who are allies of a people you are bound with in a treaty or those wholeheartedly opposed to fighting either you or their own people. If Allah had willed, He would have empowered them to fight you. So if they refrain from fighting you and offer you peace, then Allah does not permit you to harm them

**Except Those With a Treaty or Those Opposed to Fighting**

The verse adds *illā alladhīna yaṣilūna ilā qawmin baynakum wa baynahum mīthāqun aw jāʾūkum ḥaṣirat ṣudūruhum an yuqātilūkum aw yuqātilū qawmahum* — except those who are allies of a people you are bound with in a treaty, or those wholeheartedly opposed to fighting either you or their own people, whose chests are constricted at fighting you or their own. The exception follows the command to seize and kill the hostile turners who wish you to disbelieve as they have (4:89). *Yaṣilūna ilā qawmin* — to reach, to join a people — was read as seeking refuge with a tribe allied to the believers by covenant — *mīthāq* — the same word used for the firm commitment — *mīthāq ghalīẓ* — of marriage (4:21) and for trusts returned (4:58). To be joined to treaty people is to be covered by that treaty, as the sūrah respects the firm word given. The second group — those whose chests are constricted — *ḥaṣirat ṣudūruhum* — was explained as people whose hearts cannot bear to fight either side, neither the believers nor their own. The sūrah has described *ḥaraj* — constriction — as the inner resistance the believer must remove when accepting the Prophet ﷺ as judge (4:65); here constriction is the reason some cannot fight, and the sūrah spares them. Both groups are excepted from the hostile measure, showing that hostility, not identity, is the cause.

**If He Had Willed, He Would Have Empowered Them**

The clause *wa law shāʾa Allāhu la sallaṭahum ʿalaykum fa la qātalūkum* — if Allah had willed, He would have empowered them to fight you and they would have fought — was read as a reminder that the sparing of the constricted is not due to their power but to divine restraint. *Sallata* — to give power, to make prevail — was explained as God's leave, the same *idhn* by which messengers are to be obeyed (4:64). To say He would have empowered them and they would have fought is to say that the fact they do not fight is itself within His will, as the sūrah says both good and evil fall within His decree while evil comes from the self as means (4:78–79). The reminder humbles the believers who might credit their treaty or their deterrence alone; the restraint of the constricted is also God's doing. Early reports placed the verse among tribes who had treaties or who disliked fighting either side in the conflict between Madinah and the Quraysh; the exemption of such neutrals shows the sūrah's distinction between the land whose people are oppressors (4:75) and people whose chests are constricted at fighting.

**So If They Refrain and Offer Peace**

The condition *fa in iʿtazalūkum fa lam yuqātilūkum wa alqaw ilaykumu al-salām fa mā jaʿala Allāhu lakum ʿalayhim sabīlā* — so if they refrain from fighting you, do not fight you, and offer you peace, then God does not permit you to harm them; He has not given you a way over them — was read as the sūrah's rule of peace. *Iʿtazalūkum* — to withdraw, to keep aside — and *alqaw al-salām* — to offer peace, to cast peace — were explained as the two signs of neutrality: withdrawal from fighting and offering *salām*, the same peace the sūrah commanded to answer with better or same (4:86). *Fa mā jaʿala Allāhu lakum ʿalayhim sabīlā* — no way, no permission, no path — was read as removing the *sabīl* — way — over them that was given over the hostile turners (4:89). The sūrah has used *sabīl* for the path God wills to make clear (4:26), the noble ways, and the far straying Satan desires (4:60); to have no *sabīl* over those who withdraw and offer peace is to be kept on the straight path. The verse was linked to the later rule *if they refrain, you do not kill* — showing that the ethic of *do not kill yourselves, God is ever Merciful to you* (4:29) governs the field as well as the home.

**A Verse That Holds Treaty and Conscience Together**

Placed after the wish to make you alike in disbelief and the permission to seize the hostile turner (4:89), this exception holds treaty and conscience together. Treaty — *mīthāq* — is the sūrah's firm word; conscience — *ḥaṣirat ṣudūruhum* — is the heart's constriction that God sees. Both are respected: the first group is spared because a word was given; the second because a heart cannot bear to fight either side. The sūrah has said that God knows what is in hearts (4:63), knows best who enemies are (4:45), and is sufficient as Guardian and Helper; here that knowledge sees the constricted chest and spares it. The verse therefore draws a line that the community divided into two groups about hypocrites (4:88) needed: not all who are among the turners are the same as those who fight; some are allies of treaty people, and some are neutral by distress. The exception keeps the sūrah's larger ethic — return trusts, judge fairly as noble exhortation from the All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:58), and fight for the oppressed whose cry is for a guardian and helper from grace (4:75) — from becoming indiscriminate. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the verse is the lightest of burdens: where the other withdraws and offers peace, there is no way over him — and the peace offered is answered with better or same, as the greeting rule already commanded.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:91

> You will find others who wish to be safe from you and their own people. Yet they cannot resist the temptation ˹of disbelief or hostility˺. If they do not keep away, offer you peace, or refrain from attacking you, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them. We have given you full permission over such people

**Others Who Wish to Be Safe From Both Sides**

The verse opens *sa tajidūna ākharīna yurīdūna an yaʾmanūkum wa yaʾmanū qawmahum* — you will find others who wish to be safe from you and safe from their own people. The pattern is double desire: safety from the believers and safety from their own tribe, without joining either in commitment. The previous exception had spared two groups — those joined to treaty people and those whose chests are constricted at fighting either side (4:90) — for whom God did not give a way. This verse finds a third face that looks like the second but is not: a people who display peace to both sides while keeping a door open to hostility. *Yurīdūna an yaʾmanūkum* — they wish to be safe from you — was explained as showing faith before the believers and showing hostility before their own, so that neither side harms them. The sūrah has shown this oscillation before: the lagger who says *God blessed me for not being there* when you suffer, and *would that I had been there* when you gain (4:72–73) — the speaker whose *mawaddah* — affection — shifts with gain. The wish for double safety is another *mawaddah* that changes with advantage.

**Whenever Returned to Temptation They Are Plunged Back**

The description *kullamā ruddū ilā al-fitnati urkisū fīhā* — yet they cannot resist the temptation: whenever they are returned to temptation, they are plunged, thrown headlong into it — was read with *fitnah* as the trial of hostility and sedition, or of disbelief. *Fitnah* in the Book ranges from civil strife — *fight them until there is no strife* — to trial — *We made some of you a trial for others* — to the testing of belief — *We tried them as We tried the owners of the garden*. Commentators noted the ease of return: whenever they are called back to *fitnah* they fall in, as if their display of safety was only a surface. The sūrah has already described this slide: the hypocrites who turn away stubbornly when called to God and the Messenger (4:61), the people whose trade was for misguidance and who wish you to deviate (4:44), and the regressed whom God allowed to regress because of misdeeds (4:88). Ibn ʿAjībah compared this group to the wavering aspect of the soul, torn between obedience and disobedience, that must be restrained when it urges disobedience. The verb *urkisū* — they were cast, plunged — was explained as being turned upside down into it, as one thrown headlong: not a slip but a relapse. The phrase gives the criterion that separates this group from the constricted of 4:90 — the constricted are distressed at fighting either side and stay withdrawn; these, when returned to hostility, are plunged back without distress.

**If They Do Not Keep Away or Offer Peace**

The condition *fa in lam yaʿtazilūkum wa yulqū ilaykumu al-salām wa yakuffū aydiyahum* — if they do not keep away from you, offer you peace, or refrain from attacking you — repeats the three signs of genuine peace from 4:90 — withdrawal, casting peace, and restraining hands — but as a negative test. To keep away — *iʿtazala* — was explained as withdrawing from the conflict; to offer peace — as casting *salām* with sincerity, the same peace the sūrah commanded to answer with better or same (4:86); to restrain hands — as refraining from fighting. The triple condition was read as sparing any of the three: if they do any one sincerely, they are spared, as the previous verse gave no way over those who withdraw and offer peace. Early reports identified such people among tribes between Madinah and Makkah who tried to be at peace with both, and among persons who outwardly professed belief in Madinah then returned to idolatry in Makkah — showing that the category is not an ethnicity but a behaviour: the wish for double safety plus the ease of being returned to *fitnah*. The sūrah's standard — fight for the oppressed who cry for a guardian and helper (4:75) — does not extend to fighting those who genuinely withdraw; this verse says the same negatively: if they do not withdraw or offer peace or restrain their hands, then they are not the constricted, and the permission returns.

**Seize and Kill Where You Find Them — With Clear Warrant**

The measure *fa khudhūhum wa aqtulūhum ḥaythu thaqiftumūhum* — then seize them and kill them wherever you find them — was explained as the same wartime measure given for the hostile turners who wish you alike in disbelief (4:89), limited by the three signs of peace. To seize — *khudh* — and to kill — *uqtilū* — wherever you find them — *thaqiftumūhum*, to come upon, to gain mastery — was read as upon encounter in the field, not pursuit into the protected. The closing *wa ulāʾikum jaʿalnā lakum ʿalayhim sulṭānan mubīnā* — We have given you full permission, a clear warrant, over such people — was explained as *sulṭān* — proof, warrant, authority — openly shown: the law has made the cause clear. Those who do not withdraw, do not offer peace, and do not restrain their hands — and who whenever returned to *fitnah* are plunged back — may be seized. The sūrah has said that God is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45), that the oppressed cry for a helper from grace (4:75), and that good and evil fall within His decree while evil comes from the self as means (4:78–79); the warrant here is the community's instrument of that guardianship where double-faced hostility would otherwise expose the weak for whom burdens were lightened.

**A Verse That Separates Hesitation From Duplicity**

Placed after the exception for treaty and for the constricted, this verse completes the sūrah's threefold map: bound by treaty; constricted and withdrawn; double-seeking. The first two are not to be harmed; the third is to be, unless it meets the same three signs. The distinction matters for the community that was divided into two groups about the hypocrites (4:88) and that was commanded not to take as allies those who wish you alike in disbelief until they emigrate (4:89). To be safe from both sides while ready to be plunged back into hostility is not neutrality; it is duplicity that leaves the oppressed without a guardian. The sūrah's ethic — *do not kill yourselves, God is ever Merciful to you* (4:29); return trusts and judge fairly (4:58); fight so that God may curb the might of the disbelievers (4:84) — is therefore not indiscriminate: where a heart is constricted it is spared; where a treaty holds it is respected; and where double safety hides readiness to be plunged back into *fitnah*, the clear warrant is given unless peace is offered and hands restrained. The next verses turn from the field to the blood of the believer, with the rule that a believer does not kill a believer except by mistake (4:92).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:92

> It is not lawful for a believer to kill another except by mistake. And whoever kills a believer unintentionally must free a believing slave and pay blood-money to the victim's family—unless they waive it charitably. But if the victim is a believer from a hostile people, then a believing slave must be freed. And if the victim is from a people bound with you in a treaty, then blood-money must be paid to the family along with freeing a believing slave. Those who are unable, let them fast two consecutive months—as a means of repentance to Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**It Is Not Lawful for a Believer to Kill a Believer**

The verse opens *wa mā kāna li muʾminin an yaqtula muʾminan illā khaṭaʾan* — it is not lawful, it is not for a believer to kill another believer except by mistake. *Mā kāna* — it is not fitting — was explained as a negation of permissibility, not only of occurrence, the same construction as *it is not for a believer* to have a choice after God and Messenger decide. The exception *illā khaṭaʾan* — except by mistake, error — was explained as unintentional killing: a slip of aim, a misreading of identity, a cause where intent to kill a believer was absent — as when the sūrah earlier forbade killing yourselves and devouring wealth unjustly (4:29). The rule follows directly after the permission to seize and kill the double-faced who do not withdraw or offer peace (4:89–91); where that permission might be widened, the sūrah narrows it to its limit: the believer's blood is not lawful to the believer. The Book records the gravity elsewhere: *the shedding of blood* is paired with corruption on the earth, and *whoever kills a soul, it is as if he killed all mankind*. The verse anchors that sanctity in law: no believer kills a believer on purpose; if it happens, it is only by error — and error itself has a heavy remedy.

**Freeing a Believing Slave and Paying Blood-Money**

The remedy *fa taḥrīru raqabatin muʾminatin wa diyatun musallamatun ilā ahlihī illā an yaṣṣaddaqū* — then freeing a believing slave and blood-money delivered to the family, unless they waive it charitably as alms — was explained as two rights restored. *Taḥrīr raqabah* — freeing a neck — was read as liberating a believing bonds-person, a life returned for a life taken. *Diya musallamah* — blood-money delivered, handed over — was explained as wealth paid to the victim's people, delivered fully, as the return of trusts commanded earlier (4:58). The clause *illā an yaṣṣaddaqū* — unless they waive, give it as charity — was read as remission by the family, who may forgo it charitably; the sūrah has made gracious waiver a virtue where dowry is waived willingly (4:4) and where charity is given from what God provided (4:39). That a mistake still requires freeing and payment shows that the law does not treat error as nothing; it treats it as a harm whose maker must still repair, though without the curse of intention. Early reports noted that this freeing applies where the killer has means; where he does not, the alternative is named at the end of the verse.

**If the Victim Was From a Hostile People or From a Treaty People**

The two cases *fa in kāna min qawmin ʿaduwwin lakum wa huwa muʾminun fa taḥrīru raqabatin muʾminah; wa in kāna min qawmin baynakum wa baynahum mīthāqun fa diyatun musallamatun ilā ahlihī wa taḥrīru raqabatin muʾminah* — but if the victim is a believer from a hostile people, then only freeing a believing slave; and if from a people bound with you in a treaty, then blood-money to the family along with freeing — were explained as the sūrah's consistent respect for treaty — *mīthāq* — the firm word seen in marriage (4:21), in trusts (4:58), and in the exception of 4:90. If the mistakenly killed believer was from hostile people — living among those at war while himself a believer — there is no payment to his people, lest it strengthen the hostile; the right owed to God remains as freeing. If he was from treaty people — *baynakum wa baynahum mīthāq* — then the blood-money is delivered to his family, fulfilling the treaty, together with freeing for God. The former was understood to cover a believer who hid belief among the opponent or who joined without being known; the latter covers the covenanted person whose blood the treaty guarantees, as 4:90 had spared those joined to treaty people. The threefold pattern — full atonement where the family can receive; freeing alone where payment would aid hostility; payment plus freeing where treaty binds — shows the law weighing life, treaty, and the community's security together without contradiction.

**Those Unable — Fast Two Consecutive Months**

The alternative *fa man lam yajid fa ṣiyāmu shahrayni mutatābiʿayni tawbatan mina Allāhi* — those who are unable, let them fast two consecutive months as repentance, a turning from God — was explained as expiation for the one who cannot free a slave. *Man lam yajid* — whoever does not find, cannot afford — was read as lacking a bonds-person to free or the means to acquire one; for him, the bodily worship of consecutive fasting replaces the freeing, as fasting also replaces what is lacking in other atonements. *Mutatābiʿayni* — consecutive, successive — was stressed: two months without break, showing that the error's repair requires continuity, not fragments. *Tawbatan mina Allāhi* — repentance from God, a turning granted by Him — was explained as His acceptance of this replacement; the same root appears in the sūrah's promise that if wrongdoers came seeking forgiveness and the Messenger prayed for them, they would find Him ever Accepting of Repentance (4:64). The closing *wa kāna Allāhu ʿAlīman Ḥakīmā* — and God is All-Knowing, All-Wise — was read as the seal: He knows error from intent, and judges with wisdom where means fail. The verse also links to the wider law where killing a believer intentionally carries Hell and curse (4:93), while error carries freeing, payment, or fasting — a distinction the community kept when evaluating reports of accidental killings on campaigns.

**A Verse That Guards Blood After Giving Permission Over Hostility**

Placed after the clear warrant over the double-faced (4:91), this verse guards blood where permission might be misread. The sūrah that began by creating from a single soul and commanding mindfulness of ties (4:1), that forbade consuming orphans' wealth, that said *do not kill yourselves, God is ever Merciful to you* (4:29), and that threatens Hell for intentional killing (4:93), here converts the sanctity of the believer into procedure: freeing, payment, treaty fidelity, and fasting where there is no means. The order itself teaches that permission over hostility (4:89–91) is not permission over belief: the believer's life is unlawful to the believer except by mistake — and even mistake requires repair. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the closing *tawbah* is the lightest of burdens: where the hand slipped without intent, the law opens a path back through freeing or, where there is nothing to free, through consecutive fasting as repentance accepted by the All-Knowing, All-Wise. The next verse sets the opposite face — the intentional killing whose requital is Hell — so that mistake and purpose are never confused.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:93

> And whoever kills a believer intentionally, their reward will be Hell—where they will stay indefinitely. Allah will be displeased with them, condemn them, and will prepare for them a tremendous punishment

**Whoever Kills a Believer Intentionally**

The verse states *wa man yaqtul muʾminan mutaʿammidan fa jazāʾuhu Jahannam khālidan fīhā* — and whoever kills a believer intentionally, their requital will be Hell, where they will stay indefinitely. *Mutaʿammidan* — intentionally, deliberately, with determination — was explained as purposeful killing with knowledge that the victim is a believer and with a lethal means — the opposite of the mistake, *khaṭaʾ*, whose remedy was freeing, blood-money, or fasting (4:92). The sūrah has moved by deliberate steps: hostility is curbed by fighting for the oppressed (4:75); the believer fights for God and the schemes of the Devil are weak (4:76); permission is given over the hostile who do not withdraw or offer peace (4:89–91), with clear warrant; then that permission is bounded by the prohibition that a believer does not kill a believer except by mistake (4:92). This verse sets the far limit of that bound: intentional killing of a believer is not a mistake to be repaired but a crime whose requital is named in the same language as Paradise for the obedient — *jazāʾ*, requital. Where obedience brought Gardens forever (4:13), intentional killing brings Hell abiding. Early authorities stressed the verse's gravity by pairing it with associating others with God: *those who do not call upon another god with God, nor kill a soul God made unlawful except with right* (25:68).

**Four Threats Together — Hell, Anger, Curse, and Mighty Torment**

The verse joins four: *wa ghaḍiba Allāhu ʿalayhi wa laʿanahū wa aʿadda lahū ʿadhāban ʿaẓīmā* — Allah will be displeased with them, condemn them, and prepare for them a tremendous punishment. *Ghaḍab* — anger — was explained as divine displeasure at the violation of the sanctity established from a single soul (4:1) and from *do not kill yourselves, God is ever Merciful to you* (4:29). *Laʿnah* — curse — was read as expulsion from mercy, the same word used for those condemned who await no helper (4:52) and for Satan, cursed by God (4:118). *Aʿadda* — He has prepared — matches the preparation language elsewhere: as Paradise was prepared for those who believe and do good (4:57), so a tremendous torment is prepared here. Classical commentators noted that this is one of the few verses where four terrors are gathered for a single sin: abiding in Hell, anger, curse, and mighty torment. The sternness carries a report: Ibn ʿAbbās was asked whether repentance avails the intentional killer, and he held that this verse was among the last revealed on the subject and nothing abrogated it (al-Bukhārī 4477; Muslim 2797 in similar wording), while the majority understood that sincere repentance remains possible because God forgives what is less than association if He wills (4:48) and accepts the return soon after error (4:17) — yet the threat remains as stated, to block the hand. The sūrah's balance is therefore not softened: the warning is left as given.

**Abiding Indefinitely — Khālidan Fīhā**

The phrase *khālidan fīhā* — abiding therein indefinitely — was explained with attention to *khulūd* — remaining, abiding. Some read it as unending abiding for the one who deems the killing lawful, making it akin to disbelief in the sanctity itself; others read it as the recompense deserved, with an ultimate return to divine forgiveness still under *He forgives anything else of whoever He wills* (4:48) if repentance intervenes. The sūrah says elsewhere *those who reject Our signs, We will cast into the Fire; whenever their skins are burnt, We replace them* (4:56), joining abiding with renewal of torment; this verse joins abiding with anger and curse for killing a believer. The point for the community is not to settle the unseen calendar but to see that the threat has no light edge: the intentional stripping of a believer's life — of a soul God tied to the single soul (4:1) — is met with abiding, anger, curse, and mighty preparation. Where mistaken killing was met with freeing, blood-money, treaty fidelity, and consecutive fasting as accepted repentance (4:92), intentional killing is met with no such procedural remedy in this verse; the remedy lies elsewhere, in sincere repentance that must answer four terrors.

**A Verse That Closes the Permission Given Over Hostility**

Placed after the clear warrant over the double-faced (4:91) and the detailed law for mistake (4:92), this verse closes the permission precisely where overreach would be most dangerous: on the battlefield where a believer might be mistaken, or in the city where a believer might be envied. The sūrah has shown that envy moved those given a portion of the Book to wish you deviate (4:54) and to trade guidance for misguidance (4:44); if envy or anger were allowed to move a hand to kill a believer intentionally, the claim would be the highest misguidance. The sūrah's earlier promise — *whoever obeys God and the Messenger will be in the company of the blessed: the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous* (4:69) — is inverted here: whoever kills a believer intentionally will be under anger and curse, with a mighty torment prepared. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the verse lightens by removing ambiguity: permission to seize the hostile turner (4:89) and the double-seeking who refuse peace (4:91) is not permission over a believer; and the atonement that suffices for mistake (4:92) does not suffice for purpose. The next verse turns to the search for gain on that same field, warning against calling one who offers peace *you are no believer* for fleeting worldly gain (4:94).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:94

> O believers! When you struggle in the cause of Allah, be sure of who you fight. And do not say to those who offer you ˹greetings of˺ peace, "You are no believer!"—seeking a fleeting worldly gain. Instead, Allah has infinite bounties ˹in store˺. You were initially like them then Allah blessed you ˹with Islam˺. So be sure! Indeed, Allah is All-Aware of what you do

**When You Struggle — Be Sure of Who You Fight**

The verse opens *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū idhā ḍarabtum fī sabīli Allāhi fa tabayyanū* — O believers, when you strike out, travel, struggle in the cause of God, be sure, verify, make clear. *Ḍarabtum fī sabīli Allāhi* — striking out in the path — was explained as going forth to fight for the oppressed who cry for a helper (4:75), and where permission had just been given over the hostile who do not withdraw or offer peace (4:89–91). *Tabayyanū* — to clarify, to make sure — was read as verification before the sword, the opposite of the haste of spreading untested news of security or fear (4:83) and of the haste that kills a believer and calls it mistake (4:92–93). The command to be sure is placed here because the field blurs: a man may offer peace while his people remain hostile, and the believer must distinguish. The sūrah has said that God knows best who enemies are and is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45); to be sure is to act on what can be seen — the casting of peace — and leave the heart to the All-Aware. Early reports linked the verse to a detachment that met a lone man who greeted them with *al-salām* and was killed for his flock as spoil; the verse came down to forbid that haste.

**Do Not Say to the One Who Offers Peace — You Are No Believer**

The prohibition *wa lā taqūlū li man alqā ilaykumu al-salāma lasta muʾminā* — and do not say to those who offer you greetings of peace, You are no believer — was explained with *al-salām* as the greeting of peace, *al-salām ʿalaykum*, or more widely the casting of peace, submission — *salām*. *Lasta muʾminā* — you are no believer — was read as denying the faith of one who displays its sign. To say it where peace is offered was explained as claiming to see beyond the offered word into the heart, while God alone knows what is in hearts (4:63) and the Book forbids that unveiling. The sūrah has commanded that when greeted, the answer be better or similar, and that God is Reckoner of all things (4:86); to reply to a greeting with a denial of faith is the inverse of that ethic. A widely reported incident illustrates the rule: a man offered *al-salām* to a detachment led by Usāmah ibn Zayd, was killed, and his flock taken; the Prophet ﷺ reproved the killing and recited this verse (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4292; Muslim 96 in similar wording). The verse's wording covers both readings: do not deny belief to one who offers the Muslim greeting, and do not deny it to one who lays down arms and offers *salām* as peace.

**Seeking a Fleeting Worldly Gain**

The motive clause *tabtaghūna ʿaraḍa al-ḥayāti al-dunyā* — seeking a fleeting worldly gain, the passing display of the nearer life — was explained as the spoil taken — the flock, the goods — for which the hasty hand declares another's peace false. *ʿAraḍ* — display, transient gain — was read as gain that passes, as the enjoyment of this world is little and the Hereafter better for the mindful (4:77). The sūrah has warned against devouring wealth unjustly (4:29), against envying what God gave some over others (4:32), and against those given a portion who wish you deviate for such gain (4:44). To kill a bearer of peace for his goods is to exchange what is *with God* — *fa ʿinda Allāhi maghānim kathīrah* — infinite bounties in store — for a flock. That clause was explained as the true spoil: provision multiplied, forgiveness, mercy, and ranks (4:96), and the great reward promised to the striver and the excused (4:95). The contrast is not that gain is forbidden — lawful gain is lawful, as in marriage with dowry (4:24) and trade by mutual consent (4:29) — but that the fleeting gain may not be sought by denying peace.

**You Were Initially Like Them, Then God Blessed You**

The reminder *ka dhālika kuntum min qablu fa manna Allāhu ʿalaykum* — you were initially like them, then Allah blessed you — was read as the sūrah's moral recall. *Kuntum min qablu* — you were before — was explained as that the believers themselves were once without the guidance that now protects them, until God's grace directed them; some reports add that some had once concealed belief or gone unrecognized among the hostile. The favour — *manna* — recalls the grace without which the community would have followed Satan except for a few (4:83) and the mercy that lightened burdens because humanity was created weak (4:28). The sūrah has said that had they done what they were advised, it would have been better and more reassuring, bringing great reward and guidance (4:66–68), and that obedience places one with the blessed (4:69). To remember that you were as they were is to remove the pride that allows a hand to call another's peace a lie. The Qur'an elsewhere says *you were on the brink of the Fire and He saved you* (3:103); this is the same memory applied to the sword: you too were once a bearer of a tentative *salām* whose acceptance was your life.

**So Be Sure — God Is All-Aware of What You Do**

The double close *fa tabayyanū, inna Allāha kāna bi mā taʿmalūna khabīrā* — so be sure; indeed God is All-Aware of what you do — repeats the opening *tabayyanū* to frame the prohibition with practice. *Khabīr* — All-Aware — was explained as awareness of outward act and inward motive: whether the hand sought peace or spoil. The sūrah closed the mistake law with All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:92) and the intentional threat with Hell, anger, curse, and mighty torment (4:93); here the close is awareness of deeds where mistake and intent look alike. The verse generalises the sūrah's method: verify reports before spreading (4:83), verify belief before denying it (4:94), verify the fast as consecutive where atonement requires (4:92). For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the command to be sure is itself a lightening: it spares the bearer of peace from the haste for gain, and it spares the striver from a killing that would demand Hell, anger, curse, and mighty torment unless repented. The next verse sets the striver against the one who stays behind — both promised good, but not made equal (4:95).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:95

> Those who stay at home—except those with valid excuses—are not equal to those who strive in the cause of Allah with their wealth and their lives. Allah has elevated in rank those who strive with their wealth and their lives above those who stay behind ˹with valid excuses˺. Allah has promised each a fine reward, but those who strive will receive a far better reward than others—

**Not Equal — Those Who Stay and Those Who Strive**

The verse states *lā yastawī al-qāʿidūna mina al-muʾminīna ghayru ulī al-ḍarari wa al-mujāhidūna fī sabīli Allāhi bi amwālihim wa anfusihim* — those who stay at home among believers, except those with valid excuses, are not equal to those who strive in the cause of God with wealth and lives. *Qāʿidūn* — those who sit, stay — was explained as remaining behind from going forth in groups or together as commanded (4:71). *Ghayru ulī al-ḍarar* — except those with valid excuse — was read as blindness, illness, lameness, or need that prevents going forth; the phrase was reported to have been added after the first wording when Ibn Umm Maktūm, the blind Companion, asked about his excuse and the Prophet ﷺ received the addition (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2832). *Mujāhidūn* — strivers — with *amwālihim wa anfusihim* — wealth and lives — was explained as the two expenditures the sūrah has praised: spending from what God provided (4:39) and offering this life for the Hereafter in the fight for the oppressed (4:74–75). To say they are not equal — *lā yastawī* — is not to say the sitter is condemned; the verse immediately promises good to both. It is to rank the acts, as the sūrah has ranked obedience that places with the prophets and the truthful (4:69) above disobedience whose end is abiding (4:14).

**Elevated in Rank — a Degree Above Those Who Stay**

The rank *faḍḍala Allāhu al-mujāhidīna bi amwālihim wa anfusihim ʿalā al-qāʿidīna darajatan* — God has elevated in rank, preferred, those who strive with wealth and lives above those who stay, by a degree — was explained as a degree of closeness and reward. *Darajah* — rank, degree — was read as the standing given to the striver who verified before fighting (4:94) and who fought where trusts and justice are guarded (4:58–59). The sūrah has used degree language elsewhere where envy of God's bounties was condemned (4:54) and where God's favour upon the Prophet ﷺ is great (4:113); here the degree is not of envy but of effort. Early reports noted that the striver who goes forth, light or heavy, is not the same as the one whose excuse keeps him, though both believe; the former bears the cost that earlier only a few would have borne had God commanded to sacrifice selves or abandon homes (4:66). The degree is therefore proportioned to the cost that the lightened burden (4:28) still leaves: to give wealth where stinginess is a temptation (4:37), and to risk life where death will overtake even in fortified towers (4:78).

**Each Promised a Fine Reward — Ḥusnā for Both**

The assurance *wa kullan waʿada Allāhu al-ḥusnā* — Allah has promised each a fine reward, the beautiful — was explained as the promise to both the sitter with excuse and the striver: Paradise for faith held, as the sūrah promised Gardens under rivers for those who believe and do good (4:57). *Each* — *kullan* — was stressed: the excused sitter is not erased, because his sitting is not the lagging that rejoices at disaster and envies gain (4:72–73) nor the regression God allowed because of misdeeds (4:88). His harm — *ḍarar* — is real, and the sūrah that lightens burdens for the weak spares him. The promise of *ḥusnā* was also read as goodness in this world — where God gives earth spacious for emigration and many refuges (4:100) — and goodness in the next, where ranks, forgiveness, and mercy follow (4:96). The assurance prevents two errors: that the excused is despised, and that the striver's degree means the other has nothing. Both have — but not equally.

**A Far Better Reward — Ajran ʿAẓīmā**

The increase *wa faḍḍala Allāhu al-mujāhidīna ʿalā al-qāʿidīna ajran ʿaẓīmā* — but those who strive will receive a far better, mighty reward than the others — was explained as beyond the single *darajah*: a mighty wage. *Ajr ʿaẓīm* — mighty reward — appears where the atom is multiplied by grace (4:40), where doing what was advised brings great reward (4:67), and where fighting in God's cause is honoured whether martyred or victorious (4:74). The detail is given in the next verse: ranks, forgiveness, and mercy from Him (4:96). The pattern matches the sūrah's arithmetic — the base reward, *ḥusnā*, is promised to each, then multiplied for the striver. Early reports note that the Prophet ﷺ described different degrees between those who strive and those who sit, and commentators expounded *darajah* as many degrees; the text itself names the increase as mighty without numbered limit, and the next verse names its form.

**A Verse That Ranks Without Breaking Brotherhood**

Placed after verification before killing and the warning against seeking fleeting gain by denying peace (4:94), this ranking prevents the opposite error: that staying is the same as striving where striving is required. The sūrah has already distinguished the lagger who stays and then envies (4:72–73) from the one who offers life for the Hereafter (4:74); here it distinguishes the excused stayer from the striver, promising good to both, then preferring the striver by degree and mighty wage. The ethic is the sūrah's own: *those who believe and do good, We will admit into Gardens* (4:57) — yet within good there are ranks. For the community divided into two groups about hypocrites (4:88) and commanded to be sure before fighting (4:94), the verse steadies judgment: do not equalise what God made unequal, and do not condemn whom God excused. The sūrah's leniency for weakness — *He wills to lighten burdens, humankind was created weak* (4:28) — remains, even while wealth and lives are asked where the oppressed cry for a helper (4:75). The next verse describes that mighty wage as ranks, forgiveness, and mercy from Him — the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:96).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:96

> far superior ranks, forgiveness, and mercy from Him. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**Far Superior Ranks From Him**

The phrase *darajātin minhu* — far superior ranks, degrees from Him — completes *those who strive will receive a far better reward* (4:95). *Darajāt* — ranks — was explained as levels of reward, stations of nearness, each above the other. The plural was stressed: not one degree but degrees, as the mighty wage — *ajran ʿaẓīmā* — was said to be beyond a single step. The addition *minhu* — from Him — was read as source: these ranks are not market wages earned by measure alone but grace given, as every good is multiplied many times over by His grace (4:40) and as the great reward for doing what was advised is by grace (4:67). The sūrah has shown that those who obey God and the Messenger will be with the blessed — prophets, the truthful, martyrs, righteous — what honourable company (4:69), and that obedience to the sent one is obedience by God's leave (4:64). The ranks from Him place the striver with the martyrs among that company where striving costs life, and with the truthful where striving costs wealth against stinginess (4:37). Early reports illustrated the breadth: between two ranks is like the distance between heaven and earth — yet the text leaves the count unnamed, keeping the face toward the Giver rather than the number.

**And Forgiveness and Mercy**

The triad *darajātin… wa maghfiratan wa raḥmah* — ranks, forgiveness, and mercy — was explained as the content of the mighty wage. *Maghfirah* — forgiveness — and *raḥmah* — mercy — were read as the removal of fault and the bestowal of favour, the two that make Paradise admission possible. The sūrah has paired them where burdens are lightened because humanity is weak (4:28), where avoidance of major sins covers lesser ones (4:31), where wrongdoers who come seeking forgiveness find Him ever Accepting of Repentance (4:64), and where the return soon after error is pardoned (4:17–18). To place forgiveness among the striver's wages shows that striving is not sinless: the one who goes forth still needs covering for haste, for the claim of peace denied, for the gain sought. The sūrah has just warned not to say to a bearer of peace *you are no believer* for fleeting gain, and to remember you were as they were (4:94); forgiveness is the remainder that makes the rank secure. Mercy is the surplus beyond covering, as the sūrah said He multiplies a good deed and gives a great reward from grace (4:40). Forgiveness wipes; mercy lifts — together they make ranks more than wage.

**And God Is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu Ghafūran Raḥīmā* — and God is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — repeats the two names that sealed the removal of mistake by fasting as repentance (4:92). *Ghafūr* — All-Forgiving — was explained as forgiving the striver's faults where verification was imperfect yet sincere, and forgiving the sitter with excuse whose harm kept him home. *Raḥīm* — Most Merciful — was read as the mercy that gave ranks from Him and that made the earth spacious for the emigrant (4:100). The pairing after ranks shows that the whole elevation is inside mercy, not outside it.
