The sūrah has said *God does not wrong even an atom, and if it is good He multiplies* (4:40), and *if you avoid major sins We cover lesser ones* (4:31): forgiveness and mercy are the mechanism of that multiplication where the good is striving with wealth and life. Where the intentional killer was sealed with anger, curse, and mighty preparation (4:93), the striver — and by inclusion the excused sitter promised *ḥusnā* (4:95) — is sealed with forgiveness and mercy.

**Degrees Are Gift, Not Contract**

The wording *minhu* was read as partitive and honorific: ranks that are *from Him* — originating with Him, bestowed as gift, not bargained as wage. That matches the sūrah's language where the great reward for doing what was advised is *by Our grace* (4:67), where the multiplied good is *from His grace* (4:40), and where guidance to the straight path is a gift after reward (4:68). To strive with wealth and life where the oppressed cry (4:75) is costly, yet the verse says the cost does not purchase rank as trade purchases goods by mutual consent (4:29); it receives rank as gift from the One who created from a single soul (4:1) and who wills to lighten burdens because humanity is weak (4:28). The striver's wealth, given against stinginess (4:37), is therefore not a loan repaid with interest but an offering answered with degrees whose distance only the Giver measures. That is why the verse leaves the number unnamed: between two degrees is as between heaven and earth in reports, yet the text keeps the eye on source — *minhu* — rather than count, so that striving is not calculated as profit but trusted as bounty.

**A Short Verse That Holds the Sūrah's Weight Together**

Though brief — *ranks, forgiveness, and mercy from Him, and God is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful* — the verse carries the sūrah's weight. It follows the prohibition of unjust taking (4:29) with the call to spend wealth for God where the oppressed cry (4:75); it follows the command to verify before fighting (4:94) with the assurance that verification's owner gives ranks; it follows the distinction between sitting and striving (4:95) with the answer that the distinction is not enmity but mercy's distribution. The sūrah opened with creation from a single soul and mindfulness of ties (4:1), showed envy of God's bounties as the disease (4:54), and taught that good is from God and evil from the self as means (4:79); here the medicine is named as forgiveness and mercy from Him, which make degrees real yet keep brotherhood. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the triad is the lightest yet highest: where life and wealth are given, He gives degree; where fault remains, He forgives; where nothing more can be offered, mercy carries. The next passage turns from those who strive to those who stayed wrongly, whose excuse the angels will interrogate at soul-taking (4:97).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:97

> When the angels seize the souls of those who have wronged themselves—scolding them, "What do you think you were doing?" they will reply, "We were oppressed in the land." The angels will respond, "Was Allah's earth not spacious enough for you to emigrate?" It is they who will have Hell as their home—what an evil destination

**Those Who Wronged Themselves — at the Taking of Souls**

The verse opens *inna alladhīna tawaffāhumu al-malāʾikatu ẓālimī anfusihim* — when the angels seize, take fully, the souls of those who have wronged themselves. *Tawaffā* — to take in full — was explained as the angels' taking at death, the same taking that precedes the gathering on a Day about which there is no doubt (4:87). *Ẓālimī anfusihim* — wrongers of themselves — was read as those who abandoned what preserved them, not those wronged by another; as the sūrah says *whoever does evil or wrongs himself, then seeks forgiveness, will find God All-Forgiving* (4:110) — wronging the self is the description of sin that remains with the doer, not imposed from outside. The image is the sūrah's moral audit at the border: the angels — the same who witness communities and are brought as record (4:41) — seize the wronger while his claim is still *we were oppressed*. The taking is the moment where claims are tested, as the sūrah has shown that God knows what is in hearts (4:63) and that He is Reckoner of all things (4:86).

**What Were You Doing? — Fī Mā Kuntum**

The question *qālū fī mā kuntum* — scolding them, What were you doing? In what state were you? — was explained as a rebuke, not a request for information. *Fī mā* — in what — was read as asking about the religion they were upon, the land they remained in, the company they kept. The answer *qālū kunnā mustaḍʿafīna fī al-arḍ* — they will reply, We were oppressed, deemed weak in the land — was explained as the claim that remaining among the hostile was not choice but oppression: that they could not go forth or declare. The same word *mustaḍʿaf* — deemed weak, oppressed — was used where the oppressed men, women, and children cry for a saviour (4:75); there the cry is for a guardian and helper from grace and is answered by the command to fight for them, while here the claim is used to justify staying where the way to emigrate was open. The angels' question exposes the difference between being truly oppressed — the helpless for whom pardon is hoped (4:98) — and displaying oppression as excuse.

**Was God's Earth Not Spacious Enough to Emigrate**

The reply *a lam takun arḍu Allāhi wāsiʿatan fa tuhājirū fīhā* — Was God's earth not spacious enough for you to emigrate therein? — was read as the sūrah's definition of the remedy. *Arḍ Allāh wāsiʿah* — God's earth spacious — was explained as His earth made wide for movement: the emigrant finds many refuges and abundant provision (4:100), and the single soul's creation spread countless men and women across lands (4:1). *Fa tuhājirū fīhā* — so that you might emigrate therein — recalls the test *do not take them as allies unless they emigrate in God's cause* (4:89) and the hard command few would have obeyed, to leave homes (4:66) — yet here the same leaving is shown as the exit from wronging oneself. The sūrah has said that God wills to lighten burdens because humanity is weak (4:28); emigration is not presented as an unbearable weight but as the spaciousness that makes remaining in hostility unnecessary. Early reports placed the verse concerning people of Makkah who stayed among the idolaters, were marched to Badr under compulsion, and were killed among the hostile ranks while claiming compulsion; the angels' answer declares that the earth's spaciousness was itself the answer to compulsion where the heart could still choose.

**Their Home Is Hell — What an Evil Destination**

The verdict *fa ulāʾika maʾwāhum Jahannam wa sāʾat maṣīrā* — it is they who will have Hell as their home, refuge; what an evil destination — was read with *maʾwā* — refuge, shelter — inverted: the refuge they sought among the hostile becomes Hell as refuge. *Sāʾat maṣīrā* — evil as destination — was explained as the sūrah's closing formula for the abode of those who remain where belief cannot be lived, matching *the Fire suffices as blaze* (4:55) and the threat over intentional killing and siding with wrong (4:93, 4:109). The contrast with the previous tier is exact: those who strive with wealth and lives are given ranks, forgiveness, and mercy (4:96); those who stay claiming oppression while the earth is wide are given Hell as home. The distinction is not that every stayer is condemned — the next verse exempts the truly helpless who cannot find a way (4:98) — but that the claim of weakness is audited at soul-taking. Where the sūrah earlier absolved those with valid excuse who stay behind from striving (4:95), here it condemns those whose excuse was a wide earth left unused.

**A Verse That Turns Geography Into Moral Responsibility**

Placed after ranks and mercy for strivers (4:96), this verse turns geography into responsibility. The sūrah that began with a single soul spread across lands (4:1), that promises earth spacious for emigration (4:100), and that teaches that good and evil fall within decree while evil comes from the self as means (4:79) — here makes the earth's width the measure of the excuse. To wrong oneself by remaining where the weak are oppressed (4:75), when the earth is wide, is not weakness but choice hidden as weakness. The angels' question — *fī mā kuntum* — and the reply — was not God's earth spacious? — will be heard again where the community is asked why it does not fight for the oppressed (4:75); the answer in both is movement. For the weak for whom the sūrah lightens, the next verses lighten further: the helpless who truly cannot find a way are excepted, and for them pardon may rightly be hoped (4:98–99) — while the one who does emigrate finds refuge and abundance, and if death overtakes him on the way, his reward is secured with God, the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:100).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:98

> Except helpless men, women, and children who cannot afford a way out—

**Except the Helpless — al-Mustaḍʿafīn**

The exception *illā al-mustaḍʿafīna mina al-rijāli wa al-nisāʾi wa al-wildāni* — except helpless men, women, and children — qualifies the verdict that those who remained claiming oppression while the earth is wide will have Hell as home (4:97). *Mustaḍʿaf* — deemed weak, reckoned oppressed, held down — was explained not as moral weakness but as lack of means: those judged weak by circumstance, not those who chose weakness where a way existed. The sūrah has used the same root where the oppressed men, women, and children cry for a saviour (4:75); there the cry was a reason to fight for them; here the same class is a reason to excuse them. To name *men, women, and children* was read as comprehensive: not only fighting men are assessed, but women and children whose movement depends on others and whose legal capacity the sūrah has guarded throughout — in dowry (4:4), in inheritance (4:7–12), in marriage limits (4:3), and in the command to return trusts and judge fairly (4:58). Where 4:97 counted those who wronged themselves by staying when they could leave, this verse counts those who are truly *mustaḍʿaf* and therefore did not wrong themselves — because staying was not chosen.

**Who Cannot Afford a Way Out**

The definition *lā yastaṭīʿūna ḥīlatan wa lā yahtadūna sabīlā* — who cannot afford a way out, cannot manage a device, and cannot find a way — was explained as inability at both ends: no means to move and no knowledge to move. *Ḥīlah* — device, means, resource — was read as affordability: provision for the journey, mount, guide, refuge at the other end — the very provision the emigrant is promised to find on His spacious earth (4:100). *Wa lā yahtadūna sabīlā* — nor are they guided to a way — was explained as not knowing the road, the pass, the contact among believers, the treaty people to join (4:90). The double negation was stressed: neither resource to scheme a departure nor guidance to a road. The sūrah has said that God wills to lighten burdens because humanity was created weak (4:28), and eased matters for the one who cannot afford to marry a free woman (4:25); here the same lightening appears as exemption from the threat of Hell as refuge. Early reports illustrated it with persons in Makkah — the aged, the nursing, the blind — who could not walk or did not know the desert tracks to Madinah, even while they wished to be with the believers. Their inability was not claimed oppression but a real lack of *ḥīlah* and *sabīl*.

**A Verse That Holds Two Judgments Together**

The brevity of the verse was read as the sūrah's balance between two judgments that might otherwise collide. The first judgment is mobility as duty where the earth is wide: *Was Allah's earth not spacious enough for you to emigrate?* (4:97). The second is mercy that does not burden beyond capacity: *God wishes to lighten* (4:28), *do not kill yourselves, God is ever Merciful* (4:29), *if you avoid major sins We cover lesser ones* (4:31). To hold both, the sūrah inserts this exception between threat and hope: the threat remains for those who could find *ḥīlah* and *sabīl* and did not, while the hope remains for those who truly could not. The construction also mirrors the earlier distinction between those who stay with valid excuse — *ulī al-ḍarar* — who are promised *ḥusnā* though not equal to strivers (4:95), and those who stay claiming oppression when excuse is absent. Here the women and children are named explicitly because the sūrah has guarded their shares and claims throughout; their explicit exemption shows that the law that guards the weak also excuses them.

**The Trap That Holds the Sentence Open**

Grammatically the verse is a dependent clause — *except helpless… who cannot…* — whose main clause is the next: *it is right to hope God will pardon them* (4:99). The suspension was explained as deliberate: the exception is not left as praise but as the condition for a hoped pardon, keeping both divine threat and divine mercy in place. The sūrah sealed pardon for error by mistake with *tawbatan mina Allāhi* (4:92) and the strivers' wages with forgiveness and mercy (4:96); here the pardon for the helpless is left as hope — so that neither presumption nor despair settles. Classical commentators noted that the inclusion of children — whose accountability is not that of adults — shows that the exception describes a class of persons left behind whose journey depends on guardians; their inclusion underscores that emigration is a household obligation where the household can move, not only a warrior's. The verse therefore draws a line the divided community (4:88) needed: not every remaining person is a hypocrite who wishes you alike in disbelief, and not every claim of *we were oppressed* is accepted at soul-taking; only those who cannot afford a device and cannot find a way are excepted from the evil destination.

**A Light Verse That Makes the Next Mercy Intelligible**

Though a fragment — the categories and the double negation — the verse makes the next mercy intelligible. Without it, *it is right to hope God will pardon them* (4:99) would have no subject; with it, the hope has precisely these: men, women, children without *ḥīlah* or *sabīl*. The sūrah's ethic — return trusts, judge fairly, verify reports (4:58, 4:83), be sure before fighting (4:94), and not confuse permission over hostility with permission over believers (4:92–93) — is here extended to the judgment of those who remained: verify inability, then except. For the weak the sūrah lightens, this is the lightest of sentences: where you truly could not afford a device and could not find a way, the evil destination does not attach, and the next verse places the case under hoped pardon from the Ever-Pardoning. The verse after that shows the opposite face: the one who could find a device and a way and did emigrate finds many refuges — and if death meets him on the way, his reward is secured with the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:100).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:99

> it is right to hope that Allah will pardon them. For Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving

**It Is Right to Hope That God Will Pardon Them**

The verse states *fa ulāʾika ʿasā Allāhu an yaʿfuwa ʿanhum* — for those, it is right to hope that God will pardon them. *ʿAsā* — to be hoped, perhaps — was explained with attention because it follows an exception for the truly helpless (4:98) after the threat of Hell for those who wronged themselves while the earth was wide (4:97). When *ʿasā* is from God about Himself, commentators said it carries certainty — His hope is not doubt but a gracious promise phrased as hope, to keep both fear and longing alive. The sūrah has sealed other pardons with certainty — *if you avoid major sins We cover lesser ones* (4:31) and the strivers' forgiveness among their wages (4:96). Here the phrasing is softer, as befits the helpless whose case is known to God and who remain under His mercy. *Yaʿfuwa ʿanhum* — to pardon them — was read as *ʿafw* — effacement, removal of trace — distinct from *maghfirah*, covering: *ʿafw* removes the record as if it were not written, while *maghfirah* covers it from consequence. The pronoun *ulāʾika* — those — refers precisely to the men, women, and children who cannot manage a device nor find a way (4:98), not to those who could and did not emigrate.

**For God Is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu ʿafuwwan ghafūrā* — for God is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving — was explained as the suitability of the names to the case. *ʿAfuww* — Ever-Pardoning, much effacing — recurs where an error might be held: where approaching prayer in impurity is taught, sealed with *ʿafuwwan ghafūrā* (4:43), and here, where helplessness might still be judged as shortcoming. *Ghafūr* — All-Forgiving — adds covering beyond effacement. The sūrah has paired *Ghafūr Raḥīm* for strivers (4:96) and for the mistake law (4:92); here the pair is *ʿAfuww Ghafūr*, emphasising that pardon for the helpless is not merely not punishing but wiping the sin of staying. The addition *kāna* — is ever — was read as a timeless attribute: He was ever Pardoning before they were helpless, and remains so. The two names together show that the hope — *ʿasā* — rests not on the helplessness itself as merit, but on the Pardoner whose nature is to pardon. Classical notes added that the sequence — *mustaḍʿafīn* (4:98) → *ʿasā yaʿfuwa* (4:99) → spacious earth for the emigrant (4:100) — teaches conduct: the helpless hope, the able move, and the Pardoner covers both according to what was possible.

**A Verse That Keeps Fear and Hope Together**

Placed between the evil destination for those who wronged themselves while able (4:97) and the spacious earth promised to the emigrant (4:100), this verse keeps fear and hope together without confusing them. It does not declare the helpless forgiven as a flat verdict, lest staying become light; it does not leave them under threat, lest mercy be despaired of. The phrasing *ʿasā* was understood to move the heart to keep seeking means — *ḥīlah* and *sabīl* — even while hoping, and to keep the community fighting for the oppressed who cry for a helper (4:75) rather than abandoning the helpless to their excuse. The sūrah elsewhere says *God wills to lighten burdens, humankind was created weak* (4:28) and *God does not wrong even an atom* (4:40); hope for pardon here is that lightening applied to geography — where the earth is wide yet unreachable for these, pardon is hoped just as wide. The sūrah has also shown that doing what was advised would have been better and would have brought great reward (4:66–67): for the able, that advice was emigration; for the helpless, the advice is to remain under hope and to seek means where means appear.

**The Helpless Whose Pardon Is Hoped — Not Declared for the Able**

The verse was read to define its subject precisely so that no able person borrows it. The helpless are men, women, and children who cannot afford a device nor find a way (4:98) — the aged who cannot ride, the mother who cannot walk with infants, the blind who cannot see the pass, the one who does not know a contact among treaty people (4:90) to secure passage. Their helplessness is double — no *ḥīlah* to devise and no *sabīl* to follow — and it is real, not claimed. For them *ʿasā* is not uncertainty in God but the Book's pedagogy: the believer is taught to hope and keep purifying intention, while the verdict is left to the Ever-Pardoning. The sūrah has warned against taking disbelievers as allies for honour (4:139) and against envying God's bounties (4:54); the helpless who remain are neither those allies nor the envious — they are those left behind whom the community must still remember. The next verse sets the other face: whoever does find device and way and emigrates finds many refuges and abundance, and if death meets him on the way, his reward is secured — by the same God who is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful there (4:100).

**A Short Verse That Anchors the Sūrah's Mercy in Geography**

Though only *it is right to hope God will pardon them, for God is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving*, the verse anchors mercy in geography. The sūrah that began from a single soul spread across the earth (4:1), that asks *was not God's earth spacious enough?* (4:97), and that promises spaciousness to the emigrant (4:100), here says that where the earth's spaciousness could not be reached, pardon's spaciousness is hoped. The law that counts the excused sitter as promised *ḥusnā* though not equal to strivers (4:95), that counts the mistaken killer as expiating by freeing or fasting (4:92), here counts the truly helpless as under hoped effacement. For the weak this is the lightest sentence: not a burden added, but a hope placed — that the One whose earth was not yet reachable will, being Ever-Pardoning, efface the sin of not reaching it.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:100

> Whoever emigrates in the cause of Allah will find many safe havens and bountiful resources throughout the earth. Those who leave their homes and die while emigrating to Allah and His Messenger—their reward has already been secured with Allah. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**Whoever Emigrates Finds Many Refuges and Abundance**

The verse opens *wa man yuhājir fī sabīli Allāhi yajid fī al-arḍi murāghaman kathīran wa saʿah* — whoever emigrates in the cause of God will find in the earth many safe havens and bountiful resources, spaciousness. *Murāgham* — safe haven, place of turning — was explained as a refuge where the emigrant can live openly, as Madinah became for those leaving Makkah, as Abyssinia briefly was, and as any land where belief can be practised. *Saʿah* — spaciousness, abundance, ample provision — was read as breadth of earth and of provision: the same spaciousness the angels cited — *was not God's earth spacious enough?* (4:97) — now answered as found. The promise *yajid* — will find — was explained as certainty for the one who moves: the earth asked about as a question becomes answer as discovery. The sūrah has shown that the oppressed cry for a deliverer from the land of oppressors (4:75) and that the helpless who cannot find *ḥīlah* or *sabīl* are hoped to be pardoned (4:98–99); here the one who can find device and way and uses them finds not desert but refuge and abundance. The verse generalises emigration beyond the historical Hijrah: after the Conquest the Prophet ﷺ declared no further Hijrah from Makkah was required (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3080; Muslim 1353), yet the wider hijrah — *the emigrant is the one who abandons what Allah forbade* (al-Bukhārī 10) — remains, and for it the promise of many havens still holds wherever a land permits God's worship.

**Those Who Leave Homes and Die — Reward Secured**

The second clause *wa man yakhruj min baytihī muhājiran ilā Allāhi wa rasūlihī thumma yudrikhu al-mawtu fa qad waqaʿa ajruhu ʿalā Allāhi* — those who leave their homes emigrating to God and His Messenger, then death overtakes them, their reward has already been secured with God — was explained as the sūrah's assurance that intention and movement complete the wage even before arrival. *Yakhruj min baytihī* — leaving home — echoes the earlier hypothetical — *had We commanded them to abandon their homes, few would have done so* (4:66) — now shown as praised where done for God. *Muhājiran ilā Allāhi wa rasūlihī* — emigrating to God and Messenger — was read as the intention that distinguishes hijrah from mere travel; the same distinction the Prophet ﷺ drew: *actions are by intentions, and the emigrant's reward is according to what he emigrated for* (al-Bukhārī 1; Muslim 1907). *Thumma yudrikhu al-mawtu* — then death overtakes — was explained as dying on the way, before refuge is enjoyed; *fa qad waqaʿa ajruhu ʿalā Allāhi* — his reward has fallen upon God, is secured — was read as a completed right upon divine generosity. Early reports attached the verse to a man who left Makkah for Madinah while ill and died at Tanʿīm, and it was feared he had lost his reward — upon which this assurance came. The legal point drawn: the reward is secured at departure with right intention, not at arrival — which is why those who die after leaving are not counted among those who wronged themselves by staying (4:97).

**And God Is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu Ghafūran Raḥīmā* — and God is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — was explained as suitable to both clauses: forgiving the emigrant's past sins in the land left, faults in the manner of leaving, and the incompleteness of a journey cut by death; merciful in giving many havens where one was expected and in securing reward where death intervened. The same pair sealed the striver's ranks (4:96), and *ʿAfuww Ghafūr* sealed the pardon hoped for the helpless (4:99); here again *Ghafūr Raḥīm* covers both movement and mortality. The sūrah has said *God does not wrong even an atom, and if it is good He multiplies* (4:40) and *had they done what they were advised it would have been better and would have brought great reward* (4:66–67); emigration is that advice made spatial, and the multiplication is many havens and a secured wage even when death cuts short. The pairing also shows that emigration is not presented as heroic autonomy but as forgiveness and mercy received: the emigrant does not earn spaciousness by might; he finds it because the Ever-Forgiving opens it.

**A Verse That Answers the Angels' Question With Geography and Grace**

Placed after the angels' *was not God's earth spacious enough?* (4:97), the exception for the helpless (4:98), and the hope for pardon (4:99), this verse answers the question with geography and grace. To those able to devise and find a way, the answer is *yajid* — you will find — many havens and abundance; to those whose way was cut by death, the answer is *waqaʿa ajruhu* — reward secured. The sūrah that opened from a single soul spread across the earth (4:1) and that said God wills to make clear, guide to noble ways, and turn in mercy (4:26–27), now makes clear that the earth's width is not an abstraction but a set of actual refuges where prayer can be shortened without blame when fear comes (4:101) and where the burdens lightened for the weak (4:28) are lightened further by place. The ethic extends beyond place to intention: the emigrant to God and Messenger is secured even without arrival, as the fighter is honoured whether martyred or victorious (4:74). For the community commanded to go forth in groups or together (4:71) and to be sure before fighting (4:94), the verse lightens departure: you will find refuge and abundance, and if death finds you first, your wage has already fallen upon the One who never wrongs.

**The Hijrah That Remains**

Though revealed about the Hijrah from the land of oppressors, the verse was read as a remaining principle: wherever a land makes faith unlivable and another makes it livable, the instruction to find *murāgham* holds. The Prophet's declaration after the Conquest (8 AH) that no further Hijrah from Makkah was required did not close the wider meaning: the emigrant is one who abandons what God forbade, and such abandonment still finds many havens. The verse therefore holds geography and morality together: to leave a place where the self is wronged for a place where the self can obey is not flight from God's decree — both good and evil fall within decree (4:78) — but the means by which the evil that is from the self is refused. The next verse applies the same spaciousness to prayer itself, permitting its shortening when travel brings fear of attack from those who are your sworn enemies (4:101).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:101

> When you travel through the land, it is permissible for you to shorten the prayer—˹especially˺ if you fear an attack by the disbelievers. Indeed, the disbelievers are your sworn enemies

**When You Travel — Permission to Shorten the Prayer**

The verse opens *wa idhā ḍarabtum fī al-arḍi fa laysa ʿalaykum junāḥun an taqṣurū mina al-ṣalāti* — when you strike through the land, travel through the earth, there is no blame, no sin upon you, to shorten the prayer. *Ḍarabtum fī al-arḍi* — striking through land — was explained as journeying: the same phrase used for struggling in God's cause (4:94), now widened to any travel, as the sūrah has just promised many havens to the emigrant (4:100) and a wide earth to those asked at soul-taking (4:97). *Fa laysa ʿalaykum junāḥ* — no blame — was read as permission, not sin; the sūrah uses *junāḥ* for the law's ease elsewhere, where dowry is adjusted by mutual consent (4:24) and where a wife fears indifference and settlement is sought (4:128). *An taqṣurū mina al-ṣalāti* — to shorten from the prayer — was explained as the four-unit prayers — Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, ʿIshāʾ — shortened to two, while Maghrib and Fajr remain full. The practice was shown by the Prophet ﷺ on travel even when no fear was present, establishing that the permission is general: ʿUmar asked why shorten when now safe, and the Prophet ﷺ replied, *it is a charity God has given you, so accept His charity* (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 695). The sūrah that wills to lighten burdens because humanity is weak (4:28), that taught purification with earth where water lacks (4:43), now lightens prayer itself within the spacious earth.

**Especially If You Fear an Attack by the Disbelievers**

The condition *in khiftum an yaftinakumu alladhīna kafarū* — if you fear that those who disbelieve may put you to trial, attack you — was explained as fear of *fitnah* during travel, where the hostile who do not offer peace may assault the worshippers. *Yaftinakum* — to put to trial, to attack — matches *fitnah* as strife and hostility and as the temptation into which the double-faced are plunged whenever returned (4:91). The phrase *especially if you fear* in translation was read to mark the occasion that occasions the permission most clearly, not to limit it to danger alone: the Prophet's shortening even without an enemy present shows the condition is illustrative, as travel itself brings *fitnah* — hardship, exposure, the need for vigilance. The sūrah has described the oppressed who cry for a helper from the land of oppressors (4:75) and the permission to seize the hostile who refuse peace (4:89–91); shortened prayer is the worship that fits that terrain, where worshippers must remain armed and vigilant, as the next verse will detail with ranks of prayer while armed (4:102). The condition also teaches that fear does not cancel prayer but reshapes it — remembrance remains standing, sitting, lying down when prayers are finished (4:103).

**Indeed the Disbelievers Are Your Sworn Enemies**

The seal *inna al-kāfirīna kānū lakum ʿaduwwan mubīnā* — indeed the disbelievers are your clear, sworn enemies — was explained as the reason for the permission and for the caution that follows. *ʿAduww mubīn* — clear enemy — was read as open hostility, not hidden envy only; the sūrah has said God knows best who enemies are and is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45), and here the clarity of enmity is declared so that the traveller does not treat the hostile as neutral. *Kānū* — they were — was read as a standing trait of that hostility where disbelief hardens into fighting, as the Devil's schemes are weak yet still must be curbed (4:76), and as Satan is the accursed enemy who vowed to mislead (4:118–119). The manifest enmity does not contradict the exception for treaty and for the constricted who offer peace (4:90); it defines the default of the hostile collective where no treaty or peace holds. For the weak for whom burdens are lightened, the declaration is a protection: to shorten prayer when travelling is not laxity but realism about a clear foe; and to keep guard while praying (4:102) is not suspicion but obedience to the notice that enmity is manifest.

**A Verse That Lightens Worship for the Road**

Placed after many havens for the emigrant (4:100), this verse lightens worship for the road that leads to them. The sūrah that opened from a single soul, that will command prayer at appointed times (4:103), that allowed earth for purification when water lacked (4:43), here allows prayer curtailed when earth is struck through. The Prophet's regular shortening, and the Companions' agreement that even without fear the shortening stands, were read as the sūrah's principle that God's earth is spacious and His law is spacious within it. The permission was also linked to the wider ease where expiation can be fasting when freeing is unaffordable (4:92) and where settlement between spouses bears no sin (4:128): *lā junāḥ* is the sūrah's lightest law-terminology, removing blame where burden would crush. The traveller who shortens is therefore not cutting prayer but receiving charity — *ṣadaqah* — from God, whose charity the weak are told to accept.

**Prayer Shortened Without Prayer Lost**

The verse was read to keep two truths together: prayer is shortened, prayer is not abandoned. The sūrah will say when the prayers are over, remember God standing, sitting, lying down — and when secure, establish regular prayers, for prayer is a duty at appointed times (4:103). The shortening is within the duty, not instead of it, as the next verse's armed prayer will show: one group prays while armed and prostrates, then the other prays while the first guards (4:102). The declaration that disbelievers are your clear enemies explains why that choreography is needed — and why mercy in worship, to shorten and to guard, is itself worship. The verse generalises emigration's spaciousness into law: the earth is wide, the prayer travels with you, shorter where the road makes long standing a burden — and the enemy's clarity does not cancel the prayer but gives it its travel form.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:102

> When you ˹O Prophet˺ are ˹campaigning˺ with them and you lead them in prayer, let one group of them pray with you—while armed. When they prostrate themselves, let the other group stand guard behind them. Then the group that has not yet prayed will then join you in prayer—and let them be vigilant and armed. The disbelievers would wish to see you neglect your weapons and belongings, so they could launch a sweeping assault on you. But there is no blame if you lay aside your weapons when overcome by heavy rain or illness—but take precaution. Indeed, Allah has prepared a humiliating punishment for the disbelievers

**When You Are With Them and Lead Them in Prayer**

The verse opens *wa idhā kunta fīhim fa aqamta lahumu al-ṣalāta fa l-taqum ṭāʾifatun minhum maʿaka wa l-yākhudhū asliḥatahum* — when you, O Prophet, are among them and you establish prayer for them, let one group stand with you while armed and let them take their weapons. *Kunta fīhim* — you being among them, campaigning with them — was explained as the Prophet ﷺ present on expedition, leading the force earlier told to go forth in groups or together (4:71) and to be sure before fighting (4:94). *Fa aqamta lahumu al-ṣalāta* — you establish prayer for them — was read as the prayer whose shortening was just permitted for travel (4:101), now given its battle form: *ṣalāt al-khawf*, the fear prayer. *Ṭāʾifah* — group, party — was explained as a portion of the force, dividing into two: one prays with the imām while armed, the other faces the enemy. *Wa l-yākhudhū asliḥatahum* — let them take weapons — was stressed: even in prayer the sword is not laid aside, because the disbelievers are your clear enemies (4:101) and would wish to see weapons neglected. The sūrah that promised many havens to the emigrant (4:100) now shows prayer itself finding haven in ranks while still armed.

**When They Prostrate, Let the Other Stand Guard**

The instruction *fa idhā sajadū fa l-yakūnū min warāʾikum wa l-taʾti ṭāʾifatun ukhrā lam yuṣallū fa l-yuṣallū maʿaka wa l-yākhudhū ḥidhrahum wa asliḥatahum* — when they prostrate, let the other group be behind you; then the group that has not prayed comes and prays with you, taking vigilance and weapons — was explained as the alternating prayer in authentic forms (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 413; Muslim 842 for the fear prayer). The first group prays a portion with the imām, then moves to guard; the second completes with him. *Sajadū* — they prostrated — marks the portion of prayer most exposed, where the worshipper is lowest and least able to see. *Min warāʾikum* — behind you — was read as facing the enemy, guarding the praying rank's back. *Ḥidhrahum* — vigilance, precaution, guard — was read as alertness distinct from weapons: weapons without vigilance are still neglect. The choreography teaches that prayer is not abandoned before fear, nor fear ignored before prayer; both duties are kept by dividing the body so that worship and warfare each have eyes. The sūrah will say remembrance continues standing, sitting, lying down when the prayers are finished (4:103); this arrangement shows the prayer itself contains remembrance while armed.

**They Wish to See You Neglect Weapons and Belongings**

The motive *wadda alladhīna kafarū law taghfulūna ʿan asliḥatikum wa amtiʿatikum fa yamīlūna ʿalaykum maylatan wāḥidatan* — the disbelievers would wish you neglect weapons and belongings, so they could sweep upon you in one assault — was explained as the enemy's wish for a single heedless moment. *Waddū* — they wish — matches the regressed who wish you disbelieve as they have (4:89) and those who wish you deviate greatly (4:27); here the wish is tactical: that you be *ghāfil* — heedless. *Asliḥatikum wa amtiʿatikum* — weapons and belongings, goods — was read as the two vulnerabilities of a travelling force: arms and baggage. *Maylatan wāḥidah* — one sweeping assault — was explained as a single rush while heads are bowed. The warning makes the armed prayer intelligible: the Devil's schemes are weak (4:76), yet the human enemy remains a clear foe (4:101) who watches for neglect. The sūrah has shown that those given a portion wish to trade guidance and make you deviate (4:44); here the wish is more concrete — to find you without sword and without guard at the moment of prayer.

**No Blame to Lay Aside Weapons in Rain or Illness — but Take Precaution**

The ease *wa lā junāḥa ʿalaykum in kāna bikum adhan min maṭarin aw kuntum marḍā an taḍaʿū asliḥatakum wa khudhū ḥidhrakum* — no blame if you lay aside weapons when overcome by heavy rain or illness, but take precaution — was explained as the law's lightening where rain soaks and weight exhausts, or wounds prevent bearing arms. *Adhan min maṭar* — harm from rain — was read as heavy, cold rain that makes holding arms a hardship, as *ḥaraj* — constriction — was removed where ablution with earth replaces water (4:43). *Marḍā* — ill — matches the illness allowances that eased purification; here it eases carrying. Yet *khudhū ḥidhrakum* — take precaution — remains even when weapons are laid aside: vigilance is not laid aside. The pairing shows the sūrah's method: God wills to lighten burdens because humanity is weak (4:28), yet does not lighten into heedlessness. Where the sūrah says *lā junāḥ* for shortening prayer (4:101) and for spousal settlement (4:128), here *lā junāḥ* permits laying arms aside without permitting neglect. The close *inna Allāha aʿadda li al-kāfirīna ʿadhāban muhīnā* — God has prepared a humiliating punishment for the disbelievers — was read as assurance that the guarded prayer is not mere survival: the outcome is His preparation, where humiliation corresponds to the humiliation they would have inflicted on the weak.

**A Verse That Keeps Prayer and Guard as One Worship**

Placed after permission to shorten prayer for travel (4:101), this verse gives that shortened prayer its battlefield body. The sūrah that will command firmness in pursuit — if you suffer, they suffer, yet you hope from God what they do not (4:104), and warns not to be an advocate for the deceitful (4:105) — here shows the Prophet ﷺ leading prayer in ranks where one prays and one guards, weapons and vigilance together. The lesson for the weak for whom the sūrah lightens burdens is not laxity but measured precaution: prayer may be shortened, weapons may be laid aside in rain or illness, but precaution is not laid aside, because the clear enemy (4:101) wishes precisely neglect. The next verse extends prayer beyond its formal time: when the rank disperses, remembrance remains standing, sitting, lying down, and when secure, the regular prayers are established at their appointed times (4:103).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:103

> When the prayers are over, remember Allah—whether you are standing, sitting, or lying down. But when you are secure, establish regular prayers. Indeed, performing prayers is a duty on the believers at the appointed times

**When the Prayers Are Over — Remember Standing, Sitting, Lying**

The verse states *fa idhā qaḍaytumu al-ṣalāta fa adhkurū Allāha qiyāman wa quʿūdan wa ʿalā junūbikum* — when you have completed the prayer — the fear prayer just described (4:102) — then remember God standing, sitting, and lying on sides. *Qaḍaytum* — completed, fulfilled — was explained as ending the formal prayer with its bows and prostrations, the shortened travel form (4:101) and its guarded ranks. *Fa adhkurū* — then remember, mention, invoke — was read as keeping remembrance after the guarded rank disperses, so that prayer does not end as awareness ends. *Qiyāman wa quʿūdan wa ʿalā junūbikum* — standing, sitting, upon sides — was explained as all postures, the same triad used where those of understanding remember God in all states and reflect (3:191). The sūrah has shown that even in the fear prayer one group stands guard while the other prostrates (4:102), and that vigilance remains even when weapons are laid aside in rain or illness; remembrance in all postures is the inward counterpart to that outward vigilance. The verse was also linked to the emigrant's many havens (4:100): whether moving standing, resting sitting, or fallen on sides from wound, the remembrance accompanies.

**But When You Are Secure — Establish Regular Prayers**

The clause *fa idhā aṭmaʾnantum fa aqīmū al-ṣalāta* — but when you are secure, at rest, then establish the prayer — was explained as returning to full prayer when fear lifts and place is safe. *Aṭmaʾnantum* — you are secure, hearts at rest — matches the security opposite the fear that shortened prayer (4:101) and required the guarded rank (4:102). To *aqīmū al-ṣalāta* — establish prayer — after having shortened it on travel is to return to its complete, timed form: four units restored, boundaries kept, congregation reformed. The sūrah has used *iqāmah* throughout for prayer established at its time — after purification with earth where water lacked (4:43) — and will present it as witness before God (4.41). The shift from shortened to established was read as the law's responsiveness: prayer's form follows security, not the other way. Where the emigrant found many havens and abundance (4:100), security is the haven for prayer itself, allowing it to stand at its full height. The instruction shows that the traveller's shortened prayer is not lesser worship but worship fitted to insecurity; when insecurity leaves, the form returns without needing a new command beyond *aqīmū*.

**Prayer Is a Duty at Appointed Times**

The seal *inna al-ṣalāta kānat ʿalā al-muʾminīna kitāban mawqūtā* — indeed, prayer is a duty, a decree, a writ upon the believers at fixed, appointed times — was explained as the sūrah's anchoring of all else in time. *Kitāban* — writ, decree, obligation inscribed — was read as a firm obligation, as inheritance shares are *farīḍah mina Allāh*, an ordinance from God (4:11). *Mawqūtā* — timed, appointed — was explained as fixed moments that do not move with convenience. The phrase was linked to *guard the prayers* (2:238) and to the Prophet's teaching that each prayer has its appointed opening and closing. The sūrah has said that the good deed is multiplied (4:40) and that striving is given ranks, forgiveness, and mercy (4:96); here the daily multiplication — the five writs at their times — is the steady practice that makes striving and guarded prayer possible. The appointed time also explains why shortening is permission and remembrance is extension: the writ's time does not depart; its form adapts while its time holds.

**A Verse That Binds Guarded Prayer to Constant Remembrance**

Placed after the choreography of prayer under arms (4:102), this verse binds that choreography to constant remembrance and to regular establishment when secure. The sūrah that warned the enemy wishes you neglect weapons and belongings for one sweeping assault (4:102) counters that neglect with remembrance in every posture, so that no posture is without guard. The sūrah that declared God knows best who enemies are and is sufficient as Guardian (4:45) then said the disbelievers are your clear enemies (4:101); remembrance is the inward reliance upon that Guardian while the guard is the outward means. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the sequence is a lightening: prayer shortened on travel, guarded under fear, remembered standing, sitting, lying, and established in security — always at its appointed writ, so that no state — fear, rain, illness, security — leaves the believer without prayer. The next verse turns from prayer's guard to pursuit's steadiness: do not falter in seeking the enemy; if you suffer, they suffer, and you hope from God what they never can (4:104).

**The Writ That Holds the Sūrah's Discipline Together**

The final writ — *kitāban mawqūtā* — was read as the sūrah's discipline. The chapter has commanded returning trusts and judging fairly (4:58), referring disputes to God and Messenger (4:59), verifying reports (4:83), being sure before fighting (4:94), and not confusing permission over hostility with permission over believers (4:92–93). Prayer at fixed times is the training that makes those commands possible: it punctuates the day with reference, divides travel and fear into measured intervals, and returns the community from the rank to the standing, sitting, lying remembrance. The verse therefore closes the passage on prayer that began with purification where water lacked (4:43) and will meet the judgment passage where the Book was sent to judge by what He has shown (4:105): both begin with a writ — purity and time — that secures justice.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:104

> Do not falter in pursuit of the enemy—if you are suffering, they too are suffering. But you can hope to receive from Allah what they can never hope for. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**Do Not Falter in Pursuit of the Enemy**

The verse opens *wa lā tahinū fī ibtighāʾi al-qawmi* — do not falter, do not weaken, do not flag in seeking, pursuing the people — the enemy. *Tahinū* — to be weak, to waver, to lose heart — was explained as slackening after the strain of travel, fear prayer, and guarded worship just taught (4:101–103). *Ibtighāʾ* — seeking, pursuing — was read as following after: not merely defending where attacked, but seeking the hostile who refuse peace (4:89–91) and who wish you neglect for a sweep (4:102). The prohibition was understood as addressed to a community that had been told to go forth in groups or together (4:71), to fight for the oppressed who cry (4:75), and whose struggle had included Uḥud's wound and the questioning *why was fighting ordered now and not delayed a little?* (4:77). To *not falter* was read as the sūrah's steadiness: the same discipline that makes prayer a writ at fixed times (4:103) makes pursuit a writ where justice requires it. The Qur'an elsewhere says *do not be like those who left their homes boastfully, showing off, and hindering from God's way* (8:47); here the command is internal: let not wound become weakness.

**If You Are Suffering, They Too Are Suffering**

The measure *in takūnū taʾlamūna fa innahum yaʾlamūna kamā taʾlamūna* — if you are suffering, feeling pain, they too are suffering as you suffer — was explained as the sūrah's equalisation of pain. *Taʾlamūna* — you suffer — was read as wounds, fatigue, hunger, fear: the same suffering the sūrah counts as shared human weakness (4:28), and death overtakes even in fortified towers (4:78). To say they suffer as you do removes the illusion that the enemy's side is without cost; the hostile who wish you to be as they are (4:89) and who plunge back into *fitnah* (4:91) also bear loss. The comparison was linked to *if a wound touches you, a like wound has touched the other people* (3:140), revealed after Uḥud, where both sides were wounded yet the believers faltered. The sūrah that taught that good and evil fall within decree while evil comes from the self as means (4:78–79) here applies that symmetry to pain: pain is destined for both in conflict — but its meaning differs, as the next clause shows.

**But You Hope From God What They Never Can**

The distinction *wa tarjūna mina Allāhi mā lā yarjūn* — but you can hope to receive from God what they can never hope for — was explained as the sūrah's asymmetry of hope. *Tarjūn* — you hope, expect — was read as hope for ranks, forgiveness, and mercy from Him (4:96); for many havens and a secured reward even if death overtakes on hijrah (4:100); and for the Gardens where the prayer writ is kept (4:103). That hope was explained as the believers' exclusive because the disbeliever, by turning away from trust and referral to the Messenger (4:58–61), has no standing to expect it. The clause therefore does not deny the enemy's pain but denies his hope, as the Qur'an elsewhere says *do not think their prolonged time is good for those who disbelieve; it only increases them in sin* (3:178). The hope is not a claim of victory only: it is forgiveness for the mistaken, mercy for the helpless, and reward for the striver — all sealed *Ghafūr Raḥīm* (4:96, 4:100) or *ʿAfuww Ghafūr* (4:99). The sufferers on one side have a door that sufferers on the other do not: the same suffering, divergent destination.

**And God Is All-Knowing, All-Wise**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu ʿAlīman Ḥakīmā* — and God is All-Knowing, All-Wise — was read as the knowledge that weighs faltering and the wisdom that times pursuit. *ʿAlīm* — All-Knowing — was explained as knowing who falters from wound and who from desire to deviate (4:27); who verifies before fighting (4:94) and who seeks fleeting gain by denying peace (4:94); whose earth is wide yet unreachable (4:98) and whose heart can still seek pardon. *Ḥakīm* — All-Wise — was read as the wisdom that commands pursuit where the oppressed cry (4:75), permits shortening where travel and fear constrict (4:101–102), establishes prayer at fixed time (4:103), and sent the Book to judge by what He shows (4:105). The pair *ʿAlīm Ḥakīm* has sealed the mistake law (4:92); here it seals the ethic of pursuit: He knows pain, and knows who bears it for hope and who bears it without hope — and He judges with the wisdom that does not command beyond weakness yet does not excuse faltering where hope is offered.

**A Verse That Turns Shared Pain Into Divergent Hope**

Placed after the law that guards prayer under arms (4:102) and the writ that prayer is at appointed times (4:103), this verse turns the shared fact of suffering into divergent hope. The sūrah that began from a single soul and commanded mindfulness of ties (4:1), that promised lightening because humanity is weak (4:28), here acknowledges weakness — you suffer — then refuses to let suffering become faltering while the enemy still refuses peace (4:89–91). The suffering is equal as wound, unequal as meaning, because one side's suffering can be met with hope for ranks and mercy, and the other's cannot. For the weak this is steadying: to pursue the hostile who would sweep upon neglect (4:102) is not to deny pain but to place pain inside hope — as the sūrah's later command to stand firm for justice though against yourselves (4:135) will place justice inside pain. The next passage turns from pursuit to judgment, where the Book was sent to judge between people by what He has shown — and not to be an advocate for the deceitful (4:105).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:105

> Indeed, We have sent down the Book to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth to judge between people by means of what Allah has shown you. So do not be an advocate for the deceitful

**We Have Sent Down the Book in Truth to Judge Between People**

The verse opens *innā anzalnā ilayka al-kitāba bi al-ḥaqqi li taḥkuma bayna al-nāsi bi mā arāka Allāhu* — Indeed We have sent down the Book to you in truth to judge between people by what God has shown you. *Anzalnā* — We sent down — was read as the Book given as the noble command from the All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:58) and as the referral point where disputes are taken (4:59). *Bi al-ḥaqq* — in truth — was explained as that the Book's content is true, its descent is true, and its judgment is true — against the false judges, *ṭāghūt*, sought by those who claim belief (4:60). *Li taḥkuma bayna al-nās* — to judge between people — was read as judging among humanity without faction, the same phrase as *when you judge between people, judge with fairness* (4:58). *Bi mā arāka Allāhu* — by what God has shown you — was explained as by what He taught, inspired, and made clear, not by outward claim alone; the sūrah has shown that God teaches what you did not know (4:113) and that He guides to noble ways (4:26). Early reports attached the verse to a theft dispute: a Muslim's armour was hidden with a Jew, and pressure came to shield the Muslim — the verse forbade it, commanding judgment by what God shows, which settled on evidence, not tribal tie.

**So Do Not Be an Advocate for the Deceitful**

The prohibition *wa lā takun li al-khāʾinīna khaṣīmā* — so do not be an advocate, a disputant, a defender for the deceitful, the treacherous — was explained with *khāʾin* as one who betrays trust: the same treachery the sūrah commands to be returned rather than defended (4:58), and the same self-betrayal the next verses name (4:107). *Khaṣīm* — disputant, advocate, pleader — was read as standing in argument for them, contesting on their side; the sūrah will repeat *do not advocate for those who wrong themselves* (4:107) and ask *you advocate for them in this life — who will advocate for them before God on Resurrection Day?* (4:109). The command was addressed to the Prophet ﷺ directly, showing that even his advocacy is not for deceit, and through him to every judge and every believer: to be sure before fighting (4:94) is matched here by being sure before judging. The verse generalises the spaciousness of the earth (4:100): just as the earth is wide for the wronged to find haven, the law is wide for the truth to find voice — and it is narrowed when an advocate lends his tongue to deceit.

**A Verse That Makes Revelation the Criterion of Judgment**

The opening *bi al-ḥaqq* and the condition *bi mā arāka Allāhu* were read together as the sūrah's theory of judgment: the Book in truth, applied by what God shows. That showing was explained as knowledge given — scripture, prophetic practice, evidence, insight — not personal desire; the sūrah has warned against following desires that wish you to deviate greatly (4:27) and against seeking judgment of false judges (4:60). To judge by what God shows was linked to the Prophet's reported clarification: *I am but a human, and you bring your disputes to me, and perhaps one of you is more eloquent than the other, so if I give one the right of his brother by his eloquence, it is a piece of fire* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2680; Muslim 1713). The verse therefore makes procedure — evidence, oaths, witnesses as in orphan property (4:6), and referral to God and Messenger (4:59) — the means by which *arāka* is actualised. The sūrah's promise that a dispute referred to God and Messenger is best and fairest (4:59) is here instantiated as the Book judging between people, not clan judging between its own.

**Deceit Is Not a Minor Fault**

The term *khāʾinīn* — deceitful, treacherous — was read as weighty: those who hide deception from people but cannot hide from God, in whose presence they plot by night what displeases Him (4:108). The sūrah has shown deceit's kin: lagging with two faces (4:72–73), double safety while plunging into *fitnah* (4:91), denying peace for fleeting gain (4:94), and spending to show off without belief (4:38). To be an advocate for the deceitful was explained as joining that partnership — taking deceit as associate, and whoever takes Satan as associate, what an evil associate (4:38). The sūrah will say God does not like the deceitful sinner (4:107) and that there is no good in most secret talks except charity, kindness, reconciliation (4:114); advocacy for deceit falls outside that good. The Prophet ﷺ was therefore told not to be *khaṣīm* for them, just as earlier he was told to turn away from hypocrites who turn away stubbornly (4:63) and to put trust in God as Trustee (4:81).

**A Judging Verse Placed After Prayer and Pursuit**

Placed after pursuit without faltering, where both sides suffer yet only the believer hopes (4:104), this verse assigns the judge the discipline of that hope: the same hope that steadies pursuit steadies judgment — judging by what God shows rather than by clan. The sūrah that began from a single soul (4:1), that promised many havens to the emigrant (4:100), that shortened and guarded prayer (4:101–102) and fixed it at its appointed writ (4:103), now places the Book as the haven for disputes — where a person bound by treaty is honoured even when mistakenly killed (4:90, 4:92), because the *mīthāq* is part of what God shows. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28), the verse is a shield: where power tempts to be advocate for the deceitful, the Book in truth is the advocate for the deceitful's victim, showing the judge what to see. The next verses unfold the response: seek forgiveness (4:106), do not advocate for those who wrong themselves (4:107), for they hide from people what they cannot hide from God (4:108).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:106

> And seek Allah's forgiveness—indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**And Seek God's Forgiveness**

The verse states *wa astaghfiri Allāha* — and seek God's forgiveness, ask Him to cover and efface. *Istaghfara* — to seek *maghfirah* — was explained as requesting the covering of fault and the wiping of trace, as the sūrah has shown that even religious error is covered by purification with earth where water lacks (4:43) and that mistaken killing is covered by freeing or consecutive fasting as repentance (4:92). The command was addressed to the Prophet ﷺ directly after *do not be an advocate for the deceitful* (4:105), showing that even the thought of inclining to defend the deceitful — or the distress of having nearly done so — calls for seeking forgiveness. Through him the command reaches every judge and every believer: where judgment is to be by what God shows (4:105) and not by clan, the fear of having favoured tie over truth requires seeking cover. The sūrah has taught that if wrongdoers came after wronging themselves, seeking forgiveness with the Messenger's prayer, they would find Him ever Accepting of Repentance (4:64), and that whoever does evil or wrongs himself, then seeks forgiveness, will find Him All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:110). To *seek forgiveness* is therefore not an admission of having betrayed trust, but the sūrah's discipline of staying under cover while judging.

**Indeed God Is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful**

The seal *inna Allāha kāna Ghafūran Raḥīmā* — indeed God is ever All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — was explained as reason for the command, not merely its afterthought. *Ghafūr* — All-Forgiving, much covering — and *Raḥīm* — Most Merciful — have sealed the strivers' wages (4:96), the emigrant's secured reward (4:100), and the mistake law (4:92); *ʿAfuww Ghafūr* sealed the hope for the helpless (4:99); here they seal the judge's recourse. *Kāna* — is ever — was read as a timeless attribute: He was forgiving before the deception occurred, before advocacy was even considered. To name these two names right after prohibiting advocacy for the deceitful was explained as opening the door that advocacy would close: the deceitful themselves, if they abandon plotting by night what displeases Him (4:108) and seek forgiveness, will also find Him forgiving — as the next verses make clear: *whoever commits evil… then seeks God's forgiveness will find Him* (4:110). The *inna* — indeed — was read as assurance where shame might keep one from seeking: the judge who almost defended deceit and the deceitful who were defended both have the same recourse — to seek.

**A Short Verse Between Two Prohibitions**

The verse's brevity — placed between *do not be an advocate for the deceitful* (4:105) and *do not advocate for those who wrong themselves* (4:107) — was explained as deliberate interruption. The sūrah inserts seeking forgiveness between the two advocacy warnings so that judgment is not left as mere negation — do not defend — but as positive turn — seek cover. The pattern matches the sūrah's earlier insertion: between asking *was not God's earth spacious?* (4:97) and promising many havens (4:100), the sūrah inserted the exception and hope for the helpless (4:98–99). Here, between two warnings to advocates, the sūrah inserts the remedy that corrects both advocate and wrongdoer. Classical notes added that the sequence shows the advocate's fault, if he inclined, is not equal to the deceitful's treachery (4:107) in degree — but both need the same names: the judge's seeking is for inclination, the wrongdoer's for act. The verse therefore holds the community that was divided into two groups about hypocrites (4:88) together under one covering: whichever group erred by advocating, the path back is seeking.

**Forgiveness as the Guarantor of Fair Judgment**

To command seeking forgiveness where the Book was sent to judge by what God shows (4:105) was read as guaranteeing fair judgment, not undermining it. A judge who must not be an advocate for the deceitful carries pressure from kin, from secret talks that are mostly not good (4:114), and from the temptations that come even where law excuses laying aside arms (4:102). Seeking forgiveness — *istighfār* — was explained as the inward counterpart to the outward precaution — *khudhū ḥidhrakum* — still taken even when weapons are laid aside. Where vigilance guards prayer, seeking forgiveness guards judgment. The sūrah has said that the good deed is multiplied many times over by grace (4:40) and that God does not like the stingy who promote stinginess (4:37); the most withheld bounty in disputes is fairness, and seeking forgiveness restores it by recalling that the Judge over judges is All-Forgiving — whose forgiveness the advocate will himself need on the Day when advocacy is before God (4:109). For the weak this is the lightest discipline: where terrain required guarding prayer (4:102), judging requires guarding intention by seeking cover — and the Coverer is ever Forgiving, ever Merciful.

**A Two-Phrase Command That Opens the Next Three Verses**

Though only two phrases, the command opens the next three verses: do not advocate for those who wrong themselves (4:107); they hide from people but cannot hide from God, where they plot by night (4:108); and the advocates pleading for them in this world will not plead for them on Resurrection Day (4:109). To seek forgiveness before that exposure is to move from hiding to disclosure. The sūrah that warns *do not kill yourselves, God is ever Merciful* (4:29) and that promises *He wills to lighten burdens; you were created weak* (4:28) here lightens the judge's burden: where you feared to judge between kin and Jew, between host and emigrant, between treaty people and hostile — seek, and you will find cover. The Book was sent in truth not to burden beyond seeing, but to show what to see — and the One who shows is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful. The next verse applies the seeking to the advocates themselves: do not advocate for the self-wrongers, for He does not like the deceitful sinner — and seeking remains open (4:110).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:107

> Do not advocate for those who wrong themselves. Surely Allah does not like those who are deceitful, sinful

**Do Not Advocate for Those Who Wrong Themselves**

The verse states *wa lā tujādil ʿani alladhīna yakhtānūna anfusahum* — and do not plead, advocate, or dispute for those who betray, deceive, themselves. *Tujādil* — to argue, to plead, to dispute — was explained as standing as *khaṣīm* — a disputant, an advocate — the same prohibition just given to the Prophet ﷺ not to be an advocate for the deceitful (4:105). Here the address widens to the community that was advocating for them: tribal kin who pleaded for the accused before evidence was shown. *Alladhīna yakhtānūna anfusahum* — those who betray themselves — was read as that betrayal of another is betrayal of the self, as the sūrah has shown that those who consume orphans' wealth consume fire into their bellies (4:10), and will say that whoever earns sin earns it only against himself (4:111). To betray the community's trust by theft and then conceal it is to wrong the self before wronging the other — because the Book was sent to judge by what God shows (4:105), and hiding from Him by night displeases Him (4:108). The prohibition therefore forbids advocacy for self-wrongers even where kinship pulls, as the sūrah forbade taking the hostile who wish you alike as allies (4:89) and warned against denying a bearer of peace for gain (4:94): ties do not convert wrong into right.

**Surely God Does Not Like the Deceitful, Sinful**

The reason *inna Allāha lā yuḥibbu man kāna khawwānan athīmā* — surely God does not like anyone who is deceitful, treacherous, and sinful — was explained with two intensives: *khawwān* — much betraying, repeatedly treacherous — and *athīm* — much sinning, laden with sin. Both were read as persistent traits, not a single slip; the sūrah pardons the return soon after error (4:17) and accepts repentance for mistake by freeing or fasting (4:92), but *khawwān athīm* names the one who plots by night what displeases Him (4:108) and hides it from people. *Lā yuḥibbu* — does not like, does not love — was explained as removal of divine love and support, as the sūrah says He does not like the arrogant boaster who withholds (4:36–37). To be not loved while being *khawwān athīm* means no advocacy can bring love where treachery remains. The phrase was also linked to *God does not wrong even an atom* (4:40): His not loving the treacherous is not wrong — it is the accurate measure of a treachery that chose to betray itself before betraying others.

**A Verse That Generalises the Advocate Warning**

Placed after *do not be an advocate for the deceitful* to the Prophet ﷺ (4:105) and the insertion *seek forgiveness* (4:106), this verse generalises to every advocate: do not plead for those who wrong themselves. The sūrah has shown that advocates were pleading before evidence was seen, as the community was divided into two groups about hypocrites (4:88) and as reports are to be referred to the Messenger and those in authority for validation (4:83). The generalisation shows that the law is not personal: no one — not the Prophet as judge, not the tribe as pleader — may make treachery lovable by advocacy. The sūrah's ethic of returning trusts and judging fairly as noble exhortation from the All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:58), and of verifying before fighting (4:94), here becomes an ethic of arguing: do not dispute for the self-betrayer, for the One who does not love treachery will not be made to love it by dispute. The verse was read as closing clan advocacy where theft was at stake: the armour hidden with a Jew was not made clean by the Muslim's clan pleading, because the self had already been betrayed by hiding.

**Advocacy Does Not Change the Act's Owner**

The phrase *yakhtānūna anfusahum* was stressed: they wrong themselves. The sūrah will say that whoever commits sin does so only to his own loss (4:111), and whoever earns evil and then throws it upon the innocent bears slander and blatant sin (4:112). To advocate for them is therefore to carry what is not yours: the sin remains on the self-wronger, and the advocate earns only argument without merit. The sūrah has said that lawful gain by mutual consent is permitted (4:29) and that consuming orphans' property is fire (4:10); here the usurpation is argued away, but the owner — the self — remains. Where the sūrah elsewhere commands standing firm for justice though against yourselves or parents (4:135), this verse applies that standing to speech: do not lend your tongue to the one who wronged himself, for your tongue will not transfer the wrong. The next verse shows why hiding will not help: they hide from people but cannot hide from God, in whose presence they plot by night (4:108) — and advocacy in that presence is not possible.

**A Short Verse That Anchors Love in Act, Not Lineage**

Though brief — *do not advocate for self-wrongers; God does not like the deceitful sinner* — the verse anchors divine love in act, not in lineage. The sūrah that opened from a single soul (4:1) and that promised ranks, forgiveness, and mercy for strivers (4:96) here says love is not tribal where deceit is present. The emigrant who finds many havens (4:100) does so not by clan advocacy but by hijrah to God; the helpless hoped to be pardoned (4:99) are not *khawwān athīm* but helpless; the advocate who pleads for the treacherous in this life will be asked who will plead for them before God on Resurrection Day (4:109). For the weak this is protective: where you are pressed to advocate for kin, the verse relieves you — do not; and where you are the self-wronger, the door is not closed, for whoever commits evil then seeks forgiveness finds Him All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:110).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:108

> They try to hide ˹their deception˺ from people, but they can never hide it from Allah—in Whose presence they plot by night what is displeasing to Him. And Allah is Fully Aware of what they do

**They Hide From People but Cannot Hide From God**

The verse states *yastakhfūna mina al-nāsi wa lā yastakhfūna mina Allāhi* — they try to hide from people, but they can never hide from God. *Yastakhfūn* — to seek concealment — was explained as the deceitful's attempt after theft: to move the armour, to place it with a Jew, to argue by night a story that would read clean by day. *Mina al-nās* — from people — was read as from the eyes of the community, from the Prophet ﷺ as judge before evidence was shown (4:105), from the kin whose advocacy they sought (4:107). *Wa lā yastakhfūna mina Allāhi* — but from God they cannot be hidden — was explained with the sūrah's repeated knowledge: God knows what is in hearts (4:63), knows best who enemies are (4:45), is All-Hearing, All-Seeing who commands the return of trusts (4:58), and is All-Aware of what you do (4:94). The contrast was read as the sūrah's exposure of night plotting: what can be hidden from people for a night cannot be hidden from the One in whose presence — *maʿahum* — they plot.

**In Whose Presence They Plot by Night What Displeases Him**

The circumstance *wa huwa maʿahum idh yubayyitūna mā lā yarḍā mina al-qawli* — and He is with them when they plot by night speech that displeases Him — was explained as divine presence not as indwelling but as knowledge and witnessing. *Yubayyitūn* — to harbour by night, to contrive in darkness — was read as the same root seen where a group spends the night contradicting what they said, and God records their schemes (4:81): night speech that does not match day speech. *Mā lā yarḍā mina al-qawl* — what He does not approve of speech — was explained as the false defence, the projection onto the innocent (4:112), the counsel to shift guilt. The sūrah has said that God records schemes (4:81) and that most secret talks have no good except charity, kindness, reconciliation (4:114); night plotting that shifts theft onto a Jew is the evil secret talk. That He is *maʿahum* — with them — at that hour was read as terrifying gentleness: the plotting is not done in absence but in presence, as the Qur'an elsewhere says *He is with you wherever you are* (57:4) by knowledge — and here adds displeasure — *lā yarḍā* — at the speech. Early reports noted that the plotters met by night to agree to accuse the Jew and to coach the defence, assuming darkness would cover counsel; the verse declares darkness itself is presence.

**And God Is Fully Aware of What They Do**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu bi mā yaʿmalūna muḥīṭā* — and God is Fully Aware, Encompassing, of what they do — was explained with *muḥīṭ* — encompassing, surrounding — not merely aware but encircling. *Muḥīṭ* appears where the sūrah says God encompasses all things in knowledge (4:126). To be *muḥīṭ* of what they do means no night speech escapes the perimeter: the theft, the moving of goods, the coaching, the advocacy sought (4:107), the advocacy given (4:109), and the advocacy withheld when the Book judges (4:105). The sūrah has sealed knowledge-names variously — All-Knowing, All-Wise where mistake law and pursuit meet (4:92, 4:104), All-Hearing, All-Seeing where trusts are judged (4:58) — here *Muḥīṭ* fits the night, whose darkness seems to create enclosure: the verse says the night is itself enclosed. The attribute was also linked to *God does not wrong even an atom* (4:40): His encompassing does not add weight; it measures the atom exactly — including the atom of night speech.

**A Verse That Turns Night Into Presence**

Placed after the two prohibitions to advocates (4:105, 4:107) and the insertion to seek forgiveness (4:106), this verse turns night into presence. The sūrah has shown that those who spend the night contradicting what they said are recorded (4:81) and that reflecting on the Qur'an would reveal no inconsistency because it is from God (4:82); inconsistency between day claim and night plot is the deceitful's equivalent. The sūrah that warns against taking disbelievers as allies for honour (4:139) and that declares hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire (4:145) here shows the advocate's risk: to plead by day for what was plotted by night in His presence is to plead for speech He displeases — while He encompasses. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the verse is not a burden but a clearing: where you are asked to hide a kinsman's theft plotted by night, you need not hide, because hiding from people is not hiding from the Encompassing — and the honest word that *whoever wrongs himself then seeks forgiveness finds Him* (4:110) remains open to the plotter if he leaves night plotting.

**From People's Eyes to God's Encompassing**

The triad — hide from people, not from God, God encompasses — was read as the sūrah's inversion of the human instinct to seek cover. The believer's cover is forgiveness sought (4:106) and found (4:110); the deceitful's cover is night. The sūrah has taught that those given a portion trade guidance for misguidance and wish you to deviate (4:44), and that Satan promises with delusion and commands what alters creation (4:119–120); night plotting that displeases is Satan's side of speech. The Book sent in truth to judge by what He shows (4:105) is the daylight that night cannot extinguish — because the night itself is with Him and encompassed by Him. The next verse draws the advocate into that daylight: you advocate for them in this life — but who will advocate for them before God on Resurrection Day, or who will be their defender? (4:109).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:109

> Here you are! You ˹believers˺ are advocating for them in this life, but who will ˹dare to˺ advocate for them before Allah on the Day of Judgment? Or who will come to their defence

**Here You Are — Advocating for Them in This Life**

The verse opens *hā antum hāʾulāʾi jādaltum ʿanhum fī al-ḥayāti al-dunyā* — here you are, you who have disputed for them, advocated for them, in the life of this world. *Hā antum* — behold you, here you are — was explained as a summons with gentle rebuke, as the sūrah elsewhere summons witnesses for justice though against yourselves (4:135). *Jādaltum ʿanhum* — you disputed for them — repeats the same root as *do not advocate for those who wrong themselves* (4:107) and *do not be an advocate for the deceitful* (4:105), showing that the community indeed did dispute after the theft. *Fī al-ḥayāti al-dunyā* — in this nearer life — was read as the place where advocacy can seem to work, because judges must weigh oaths and eloquence — *some of you may be more eloquent* (al-Bukhārī 2680) — and where kinship pulls. The sūrah has shown that the enjoyment of this world is little and the Hereafter better for the mindful (4:77), that fleeting gain is sought by denying peace (4:94), and that most secret talks have no good except charity, kindness, reconciliation (4:114); disputing for the deceitful in this life is another fleeting gain — a kinsman saved from shame — sought where speaking truth would have cost shame but gained the Book's favour. The phrase also reminds that this life is the only court where human advocacy can affect a verdict before the divine one.

**But Who Will Advocate for Them Before God**

The question *fa man yujādilu Allāha ʿanhum yawma al-qiyāmati am man yakūnu ʿalayhim wakīlā* — but who will dispute for them before God on Resurrection Day, or who will be their defender, trustee, agent? — was explained as two challenges. *Man yujādilu Allāha ʿanhum* — who will dispute God on their behalf — was read as impossible: there is no disputant against God's knowledge, for He is Fully Aware and Encompassing of what they do (4:108), and He records night plotting done in His presence. *Yawma al-qiyāmah* — the Day of Standing — was explained as the Day about which there is no doubt, where He will gather all (4:87) and where each will be judged by the Book sent in truth (4:105). *Man yakūnu ʿalayhim wakīlā* — who will be their *wakīl* — was read against the same name the sūrah commands to trust: *God is sufficient as Trustee of Affairs* (4:81, 4:132). To ask who will be their *wakīl* on that Day is to answer: no disputant can argue against the Encompassing, and no trustee can protect against the Sufficient Trustee who already knows. The verse was linked to *those who denied and disobeyed the Messenger will wish they were dust* (4:42) — for advocacy has no ground where every hidden night saying is present.

**A Verse That Measures This Life's Advocacy by the Next**

The comparison — *in this life* versus *the Day of Standing* — was read as the sūrah's measurement of advocacy. In this life, disputing for the self-wrongers may succeed where a story is coached, where armour is said to be with a Jew, where oaths are divided; on the Day, the Judge is the One who was with them while they plotted by night (4:108) and who cannot be disputed because He was never absent. The sūrah has said that God will gather all together — about which there is no doubt (4:87) — and that the self-wrongers will be asked *what were you doing?* at soul-taking (4:97); advocacy that might deflect a human question will not deflect that. The sūrah has also shown that seeking forgiveness remains open — *whoever wrongs himself then seeks forgiveness finds Him* (4:110) — which is the only advocacy that works on the Day: not a pleader for deceit, but a sinner's own seeking that meets the All-Forgiving.
