The question therefore reframes advocacy: the advocate's eloquence in this life is real, but the forum is small; the forum that matters has no disputant for deceit and no trustee besides Him who does not love the deceitful sinner (4:107).

**Why the Question Is Double — Disputant and Defender**

The two questions — who will dispute, who will be defender — cover both roles advocates play: the voice that argues and the guardian who manages affairs after argument. *Yujādil* covers speech — to dispute, to contend, to answer charges; *wakīl* covers standing — to be trustee, to take responsibility. The sūrah has distinguished speech — night speech displeasing to Him (4:108) — from act — theft, moving goods, throwing guilt on the innocent (4:112). Both need a defender on the Day; neither will have one where deceit persists. The double question also mirrors the sūrah's double prohibition — *do not be an advocate for the deceitful* (4:105) and *do not advocate for self-wrongers* (4:107) — showing that neither prohibition is light, because the Day's lack of advocate is heavier. Where the sūrah elsewhere promises honourable company for the obedient (4:69) and a humiliating punishment prepared where prayer was guarded (4:102), here the company on the Day for the deceitful's advocate is solitude: no pleader, no trustee.

**A Short Verse That Anchors Justice Beyond Eloquence**

Though brief — *you advocate for them in this life; who will advocate before God, or be their defender, on Resurrection Day?* — the verse anchors justice beyond eloquence. The sūrah that warns against taking disbelievers as allies for honour (4:139), that says the hypocrites try to deceive God but He deceives them when they stand for prayer to be seen (4:142), and that commands *do not let your desires cause you to deviate from justice* (4:135), here pulls the advocate's desire — loyalty to kin — into daylight: your dispute works here; it will not there. So let your dispute here be for what would still work there — charity, kindness, reconciliation (4:114) — or for seeking forgiveness that will find Him All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:110). For the weak for whom the sūrah lightens burdens, the verse relieves a burden: you need not be your kinsman's advocate in this life, because you cannot be his trustee in the next — and the only burden removed from him now is the one he removes himself by seeking.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:110

> Whoever commits evil or wrongs themselves then seeks Allah's forgiveness will certainly find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**Whoever Commits Evil or Wrongs Themselves**

The verse opens *wa man yaʿmal sūʾan aw yaẓlim nafsahu* — whoever commits evil, a bad deed, or wrongs themselves. *Sūʾ* — evil, bad deed — was explained as harm to another: theft, false accusation, consuming wealth unjustly — the armour theft and its projection onto the innocent that the preceding passage exposed (4:105–112). *Yaẓlim nafsah* — wrongs himself — was explained as that the same act is self-wrong: the sūrah has said *do not advocate for those who wrong themselves* (4:107) and will say *whoever earns sin earns it only against himself* (4:111). The pairing *evil or wrongs himself* was read as comprehensive: evil outward toward people and wrong inward toward the soul are not two categories but two faces of one act, because to betray trust (4:58) is to betray the self that will stand before God, who is with the plotters by night (4:108). The sūrah has shown that human weakness makes evil possible — *humankind was created weak* (4:28), desires wish you to deviate greatly (4:27), the regressed wish you alike in disbelief (4:89) — yet the same weakness, acknowledged, opens the next clause. Classical notes stressed *man* — whoever — as unrestricted: believer, Companion who erred, deceitful who plotted, even the falsely accused — the door is for whoever acted.

**Then Seeks God's Forgiveness**

The clause *thumma yastaghfiri Allāha* — then seeks God's forgiveness — was explained with *thumma* — then, afterwards — as indicating sequence after the act, not delay only. *Yastaghfir* — to seek *maghfirah*, covering — was read as the act commanded to the Prophet ﷺ directly — *seek forgiveness; God is All-Forgiving* (4:106) — now universalised to every wrongdoer. The sūrah has taught that wrongdoers who came after wronging themselves, with the Messenger's prayer, would find Him ever Accepting of Repentance (4:64); that seeking after mistake is sealed *tawbatan mina Allāh*, repentance from God (4:92); and that the helpless have *ʿAfuww Ghafūr* hoped for them (4:99). To seek was explained as confession, remorse, abandoning the act, and resolve — not merely speech — as the sūrah refuses repentance that waits until death says *now I repent* (4:18) and accepts the return soon after error (4:17). The *thumma* also separates the advocacy that fails on the Day (4:109) from the seeking that succeeds: no one will be his trustee there, but he himself seeking here will find. Early reports noted that the thief, once exposed, could still — by seeking — find the same names the advocate was told to seek.

**Will Certainly Find God All-Forgiving, Most Merciful**

The promise *yajid Allāha Ghafūran Raḥīmā* — will certainly find God All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — was explained as certainty of finding: *yajid* — will find — not *perhaps will find*. The same *yajid* was used where the wrongdoers coming to the Prophet ﷺ would *certainly find God ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful* (4:64); here every evil-doer who seeks will find the same. *Ghafūr* — All-Forgiving, much covering — and *Raḥīm* — Most Merciful — were explained as the two that make finding more than acquittal: covering the evil, removing the trace of self-wrong, and bestowing mercy beyond covering — ranks, havens, secured reward as with the emigrant (4:100). The sūrah has sealed forgiveness variously — *Ghafūr Raḥīm* for strivers (4:96), *ʿAfuww Ghafūr* for the helpless (4:99), *Ghafūr Raḥīm* for the judge told to seek (4:106); here the pair is the universal seal for every evil and self-wrong that turns. The promise was linked to *God does not wrong even an atom* (4:40): to seek and not find would be a wrong measured in less than an atom; *yajid* declares He does not wrong. The verse was also placed against the threat for intentional killing, where anger, curse, and mighty preparation remain (4:93): seeking is the opening even there, where it is most needed.

**A Verse That Opens the Door Advocacy Could Not**

Placed after *you advocate for them in this life — who will advocate on the Day?* (4:109) and *they hide from people but not from God, with whom they plotted by night* (4:108), this verse opens the door advocacy could not: seeking forgiveness finds. The sūrah that pronounced *God does not like the deceitful sinner* (4:107) and that said there is no good in most secret talks except charity, kindness, reconciliation (4:114), here says the good that remains open after the evil secret talk is to seek. The sūrah that warned the enemy wishes you neglect for a sweep (4:102) and commanded not to falter in pursuit (4:104), yet to judge only by what God shows (4:105), here steadies the heart that fears judgment has been corrupted by advocacy: whoever — advocate or wrongdoer — commits evil and then seeks will find. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, this is the lightest of all: after teaching prayer shortened and guarded (4:101–102) and remembered standing, sitting, lying (4:103), the sūrah lightens the heaviest burden — guilt — by making finding certain upon seeking.

**The Finding That Makes the Next Two Verses Intelligible**

The *yajid* — will find — makes the next two verses intelligible: *whoever commits sin does so only to his own loss; God is All-Knowing, All-Wise* (4:111), and *whoever earns evil or sin then throws it upon the innocent bears slander and blatant sin* (4:112). Both assume that sin's owner is the self, not the advocate, and that the self's recourse is seeking, not throwing. The verse was read as the pivot of the judgment passage that began with the Book sent in truth (4:105): the Book judges between people; night plotting cannot hide from the Encompassing; advocacy perishes on the Day — yet seeking succeeds here, because the Judge who is All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:111) is also All-Forgiving, Most Merciful, and is found by whoever seeks before death closes the seeking.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:111

> And whoever commits a sin—it is only to their own loss. Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**Whoever Commits a Sin — Only to His Own Loss**

The verse states *wa man yaksib ithman fa innamā yaksibuhu ʿalā nafsihi* — and whoever commits, earns, a sin, it is only upon, against, his own self. *Yaksib* — to earn, to acquire — was explained as the Book's commerce language: sin is earning, as a good deed is multiplied many times over by grace (4:40) and as striving earns degree (4:96). *Ithm* — sin, offence — was read broadly: theft, false accusation, advocacy for deceit, hiding from people by night. *ʿAlā nafsihi* — only upon himself — was explained as that the weight does not transfer to the advocate who disputed for him in this life (4:109), nor to the innocent upon whom it is later thrown (4:112). The sūrah has shown the same principle where *those who wrong themselves* are not to be advocated for (4:107) and where *whoever wrongs himself then seeks forgiveness finds Him* (4:110). Here the principle is the ledger: to *earn* sin is to deposit loss into the self's account, because God does not wrong even an atom — He measures the atom exactly (4:40) and knows what is in hearts (4:63). Early commentators stressed *innamā* — only — as restriction: the sin's burden is not on the clan, not on the Jew falsely accused, not on the community divided into two groups (4:88); it is on the earner.

**Allah Is All-Knowing, All-Wise**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu ʿAlīman Ḥakīmā* — and God is All-Knowing, All-Wise — was explained as the attribution that makes the ledger certain. *ʿAlīm* — All-Knowing — was read as knowing the earning while it is hidden from people but not from Him in whose presence they plot by night (4:108), encompassing what they do. *Ḥakīm* — All-Wise — was read as the wisdom that places each earning on its earner with exactness, that judges between people by what He shows (4:105) and not by eloquence, and that distinguishes mistake requiring freeing or fasting (4:92) from intent requiring Hell unless turned from (4:93). The pair *ʿAlīm Ḥakīm* has sealed the mistake law (4:92) and pursuit without faltering (4:104); here it seals earning. The sūrah has said that God is sufficient as Witness (4:79) and Reckoner (4:86); to be All-Knowing is to be the Witness who never misses, and to be All-Wise is to be the Reckoner who never wrongs. The burden on the self is therefore not a metaphor but a measured account with the One who knows and judges with wisdom.

**A Verse That Ends Clan Transfer of Guilt**

Placed after *whoever commits evil then seeks forgiveness finds Him* (4:110), this verse ends clan transfer of guilt. The preceding passage concerned a theft where advocates sought to transfer guilt from a Muslim thief to a Jewish neighbour by hiding the armour with him and coaching the story by night (4:105–108). The verse declares that transfer fails at the divine ledger: whoever earns sin earns it only against himself, even if people are persuaded. The sūrah has warned that most secret talks have no good except charity, kindness, reconciliation (4:114), and will warn that throwing sin on the innocent bears slander and blatant sin (4:112); this verse is the premise for both — sin stays where earned, so throwing adds a second sin upon the first. The sūrah has also shown that burdens are lightened because humanity is weak (4:28), yet lightening is not transfer; the helpless hoped to be pardoned (4:99) are not told their sin is on another, but that pardon is hoped from the All-Pardoning. The restriction *ʿalā nafsihi* therefore lightens the community: no need to carry another's sin — and no ability to.

**Earning Sin as Commerce That Only Loses**

The verb *yaksib* was read to keep commerce in view: the sinner thinks to *earn* — gain, profit — by theft, by shifting blame, by seeking fleeting gain while denying peace (4:94); yet the verse says the earning is *ʿalā* — upon, against — the self, as a debt, not *lahu* — for him as profit. The sūrah has contrasted true earning — *God has promised each a fine reward* (4:95) and *many havens and abundance* for the emigrant (4:100) — with false earning — devouring orphans' wealth as fire (4:10) and reclaiming the dowry unjustly (4:20). To *earn* sin is therefore to be the merchant who puts loss into his own pouch while thinking he put gain. Classical notes added that *ithm* here is the general term that includes *khaṭīʾah* — error — and *buhtān* — slander — made explicit next (4:112); all are earned only as loss. The only reversal of that loss is not another's advocacy (4:109) but seeking forgiveness, which finds Him All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:110) — and even then the original earning remains recorded until covered.

**A Short Verse That Anchors the Next Two**

Though brief — *whoever commits sin does so only to his own loss; God is All-Knowing, All-Wise* — the verse anchors the next two: *whoever earns evil or sin then throws it upon the innocent bears slander and blatant sin* (4:112), and *had God's grace and mercy not been upon you, a group of them would have sought to deceive you — yet they deceive only themselves* (4:113). Both assume retained ownership: throwing does not move ownership but adds slander to it; deceiving the Prophet ﷺ would have deceived only the deceiver's self. The sūrah that judges between people by what God shows (4:105) and that warns secret plotters they plot in His presence (4:108) here inscribes the ledger: knowledge and wisdom guarantee that what is earned stays where earned — so that justice — returning trusts, judging fairly (4:58), verifying reports (4:83), being sure before fighting (4:94) — can proceed without fear that clan eloquence will move burden from where God placed it.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:112

> And whoever commits an evil or sinful deed then blames it on an innocent person, they will definitely bear the guilt of slander and blatant sin

**Whoever Earns an Error or Sin, Then Throws It Upon the Innocent**

The verse states *wa man yaksib khaṭīʾatan aw ithman thumma yarmi bihi barīʾan* — and whoever earns an error — a mistake — or a sin, then throws it, casts it, upon the innocent, the clear, the free. *Khaṭīʾah* was read as unintentional or lesser fault, *ithm* as sin. *Yaksib* — to earn — continues the ledger language: sin is earned only upon the self (4:111), not transferable by advocacy (4:109). *Thumma yarmi bihi* — then throws it — was explained as adding projection to earning: having earned the fault, he casts the blame, as the deceitful threw the stolen armour's guilt onto the Jewish neighbour and plotted by night speech displeasing to Him (4:105–108). *Barīʾ* — innocent, free, clear — was read as one free of the act, as the Jew was — as any person is until shown otherwise by what God shows the judge (4:105). The sūrah has warned against devouring wealth unjustly (4:29) and against denying a bearer of peace for gain (4:94); to throw sin on the innocent is the judicial equivalent — to devour honour as wealth. The disjunction *error or sin* was read as covering both degrees: whether the original fault was smaller error or grave sin, throwing makes it heavier, as the verse closes.

**They Bear Slander and Blatant Sin**

The recompense *fa qad iḥtamala buhtānan wa ithman mubīnā* — they will definitely bear slander and blatant, manifest sin — was explained with two loads: *buhtān* — slander, false accusation, calumny — and *ithm mubīn* — clear, manifest sin. *Iḥtamala* — to bear, to carry — was read as carrying as a burden, the opposite of the ranks borne as honour (4:69). *Buhtān* was explained as the lie that confounds — from a root meaning to bewilder with false charge; the sūrah has shown that the deceitful hide from people but cannot hide from the Encompassing (4:108), so the slander confounds people for a night but not Him. *Ithm mubīn* — blatant sin — was read as that throwing does not make sin less manifest; it makes the sinner's sin manifest as slander plus the original — doubly clear to the All-Knowing. The doubling was stressed: before throwing he bore *khaṭīʾah* or *ithm* upon himself (4:111); after throwing he bears that plus *buhtān* plus another manifest sin — a multiplication of burden unlike God's multiplication of good many times over (4:40). Early reports noted this verse completed the theft case: the Muslim thief's clan sought to make the Jew bear the theft; the verse says the thrower bears slander and manifest sin, not the innocent.

**A Verse That Protects the Innocent Whom Advocacy Would Harm**

Placed after *whoever earns sin earns only upon himself* (4:111) and before *had God's grace and mercy not been upon you, they would have deceived you — yet they deceive only themselves* (4:113), this verse protects the innocent whom advocacy would harm. The sūrah has shown that advocacy for the deceitful in this life would have succeeded for a moment had God's grace not been upon the Prophet ﷺ to show him the evidence, yet advocates advocated (4:109); the innocent — the Jew on whom the armour was hidden — would have borne punishment for another's earning. The verse generalises beyond that case: any innocent upon whom an error or sin is thrown is not made bearer — the thrower is. The sūrah elsewhere commands standing firm for justice even against yourselves or kin (4:135) and declares no good in most secret talks except charity, kindness, reconciliation (4:114); throwing sin in secret night speech is the evil secret talk that the Book in truth (4:105) exposes. For the weak this is protection: where you are innocent and power seeks to make you bearer, the One who is All-Knowing, All-Wise has already declared you not bearer.

**From Night Plotting to Double Burden**

The sequence was read as moral causality: night plotting displeasing to Him while He is with them (4:108) → human advocacy in this life attempting to sustain it (4:109) → earning that stays on the self (4:111) → throwing that adds slander and blatant sin. The *thumma* — then — marks not time only but increase: the second burden is added to the first, so that hiding from people (4:108) and disputing before a human judge (4:109) does not reduce but increases the load where the innocent is targeted. The sūrah has paired *Ghafūr Raḥīm* for the seeker of forgiveness (4:110) — covering and mercy — and pairs here *buhtān* and *ithm mubīn* — exposure and manifest sin — for the thrower who does not seek. The contrast links to *whoever wrongs himself then seeks, finds* (4:110): the thrower could still seek and find, but throwing while persisting keeps the slander as carried. The verse was also linked to *those who conceal testimony wrong their hearts* (2:283) and to *do not let hatred of a people cause you to deviate from justice* (5:8), showing that throwing sin inherits both false speech and injustice.

**A Short Verse That Anchors the Judge's Caution**

Though brief — *whoever earns error or sin then blames the innocent bears slander and blatant sin* — the verse anchors the judge's caution after the Book-sent-to-judge verse (4:105). The judge is told to judge by what God shows, not by eloquence, because throwing is eloquent and seems clear for a night; the verse says the thrower's burden becomes more manifest thereby, not less. The sūrah that shortened and guarded prayer (4:101–102) and fixed it at its appointed writ (4:103) here guards the court as it guards prayer: take vigilance even when rain excuses arms, seek forgiveness between the prohibitions of advocacy, verify reports (4:83), be sure before fighting (4:94), and know that the innocent remains innocent under the Encompassing (4:108). The next verse shows how near the Prophet ﷺ came to being deceived — and how grace and teaching prevented it, for great is God's favour upon him (4:113).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:113

> Had it not been for Allah's grace and mercy, a group of them would have sought to deceive you ˹O Prophet˺. Yet they would deceive none but themselves, nor can they harm you in the least. Allah has revealed to you the Book and wisdom and taught you what you never knew. Great ˹indeed˺ is Allah's favour upon you

**Had Not God's Grace and Mercy Been Upon You**

The verse opens *wa law lā faḍlu Allāhi ʿalayka wa raḥmatuhu la hammat ṭāʾifatun minhum an yuḍillūka* — had it not been for God's grace, bounty, upon you and His mercy, a group of them would have resolved to deceive, to lead astray. *Faḍl* — grace, bounty — and *raḥmah* — mercy — were explained as the two that preserve the Prophet ﷺ where human eloquence and kin pleading pull (4:105–112). *Law lā* — were it not for — was read as the sūrah's counterfactual that declares actual protection, as earlier *had it not been for God's grace and mercy, you would have followed Satan, except for a few* (4:83). *Hammat* — resolved, intended — was explained as firm intent: the group intended to make the judge misjudge, to make the Book-sent-to-judge (4:105) seem to support the deceitful. *An yuḍillūka* — to lead you astray — was read as seeking to make the Prophet ﷺ an advocate for the deceitful despite the prohibition not to be an advocate for the treacherous (4:105) and not to plead for self-wrongers (4:107). The group — *ṭāʾifatun minhum* — was explained as the clan of the thief and its advocates, who hid the armour with a Jew, coached night speech displeasing to Him (4:108), and argued in this life expecting advocacy to succeed (4:109). That they only *hammat* — intended — and did not succeed was read as grace and mercy intervening by showing the evidence.

**Yet They Deceive None but Themselves and Cannot Harm You**

The counter *wa mā yuḍillūna illā anfusahum wa mā yaḍurrūnaka min shayʾ* — yet they would deceive none but themselves, nor can they harm you in the least — was explained with two restrictions: deception returns to the deceiver, and harm does not reach the protected. *Yuḍillūna illā anfusahum* — they deceive only themselves — matches the prior principle *whoever earns sin earns only upon himself* (4:111) and *bears slander and blatant sin where he throws it on the innocent* (4:112). To seek to deceive the Prophet ﷺ, where God is with the plotters by night encompassing what they do (4:108), is to deceive the self that thinks night hides. *Wa mā yaḍurrūnaka min shayʾ* — they cannot harm you with anything — was read as divine protection of the messenger's judgment, as the sūrah said He is sufficient as Trustee (4:81) and told the Prophet ﷺ to put trust in Him and turn aside from those who contradict by night. Early reports noted the Prophet ﷺ was distressed at nearly defending the wrong party; the verse comforts that the distress was not harm, as *God will protect you from the people* (5:67) protects the message even while the pressure is felt. The clause also generalises: whoever throws sin on the innocent (4:112) harms only himself, with slander.

**He Has Sent Down to You the Book and Wisdom, and Taught You What You Did Not Know**

The reason for non-deception *wa anzala Allāhu ʿalayka al-kitāba wa al-ḥikmata wa ʿallamaka mā lam takun taʿlam* — and God has sent down upon you the Book and wisdom, and taught you what you did not know — was explained as the three that make deception impossible where grace and mercy hold. *Al-Kitāb* — the Book — is the Book sent in truth to judge between people by what He shows (4:105), the criterion against the false judges (4:60). *Al-ḥikmah* — wisdom — was explained as the Sunna, the judicious application, the prophetic practice that shows how the Book judges: evidence, oaths, witnesses — and the Prophet's own clarification that eloquence does not convert false to true (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2680). *Wa ʿallamaka mā lam takun taʿlam* — and taught you what you never knew — was read as the knowledge given before this incident and within it: the hidden moving of the armour, the night counsel, the Jew's innocence, the law of throwing sin (4:112). The sūrah has said God wills to make clear, to guide to noble ways, to turn in mercy (4:26–28); teaching what you did not know is that will made personal. The sequence was also linked to the beginning, where God taught humanity from a single soul (4:1), and to *He has sent down to you the Book with truth, confirming what came before* (4:47): teaching is the continuity from creation to judgment.

**Great Is God's Favour Upon You**

The seal *wa kāna faḍlu Allāhi ʿalayka ʿaẓīmā* — great, mighty indeed is God's favour upon you — was explained as the sūrah's acknowledgment that the Prophet's firmness is not his own firmness alone but favour. *Faḍl ʿaẓīm* — mighty grace — appears where Gardens, shade, and purity are promised, yet here it is for being preserved from misjudgment. The same favour underlay the promise that had they done what they were advised, it would have been better and brought great reward and guidance (4:66–68); favour here is that he was shown what to do before doing the opposite. The verse was read to comfort every judge after him: the grace that taught what you did not know remains available through the Book and wisdom, so that where most secret talks are not good (4:114), the good — charity, kindness, reconciliation — can be seen. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the favour is that the Prophet's preservation is the community's preservation, because the Book and wisdom continue to show the judge what to see.

**A Verse That Closes the Judgment Passage With Grace**

Placed after the double burden of throwing sin on the innocent (4:112) and before the rule that no good is in most secret talks except three (4:114), this verse closes the judgment passage with grace. The passage that began *do not be an advocate for the deceitful* (4:105) traverses seeking forgiveness (4:106), not advocating for self-wrongers (4:107), hiding from people but not from the Encompassing (4:108), advocating in this life versus no advocate on the Day (4:109), seeking then finding (4:110), earning only upon the self (4:111), throwing that adds slander (4:112) — and ends where it began: had not grace and mercy been upon you, they would have deceived you. The passage is therefore not a lesson in distrust of people but in trust in the Book and wisdom taught. The sūrah that declared the disbelievers your clear enemies (4:101) here declares the Prophet's protection as the community's protection, so that judgment between people — including those bound by treaty whose blood-money is paid even when the killing was mistaken (4:92) — remains by what God shows. And great is His favour upon the one shown.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:114

> There is no good in most of their secret talks—except those encouraging charity, kindness, or reconciliation between people. And whoever does this seeking Allah's pleasure, We will grant them a great reward

**No Good in Most Secret Talks**

The verse states *lā khayra fī kathīrin min najwāhum* — there is no good in most of their secret talks, private counsels. *Najwā* — secret talk, whispering, private counsel — was explained as the night plotting just exposed: harbouring by night speech that displeases Him (4:108), advocating for self-wrongers (4:107), and throwing sin on the innocent (4:112). *Lā khayra* — no good — was read as no benefit, no virtue, no reward, matching the sūrah's exposure of advocates who dispute in this life but will find no disputant on the Day (4:109). *Kathīr* — much, most — was stressed: most secret talks are not good, though some are — so that secrecy itself is not condemned, only its content. The sūrah has shown that reports are to be referred to the Messenger and those in authority for validation (4:83) and that verification is required before fighting (4:94); secret talk that bypasses referral and verification is the opposite. Classical notes added that *their* refers to the deceitful group and, by extension, any private counsel not turned to good — widening the rule beyond the theft case to every confidentiality that hides deceit.

**Except Three — Charity, Kindness, Reconciliation**

The exception *illā man amara bi ṣadaqatin aw maʿrūfin aw iṣlāḥin bayna al-nāsi* — except one who commands charity, kindness, or reconciliation between people — was explained as the three goods that make secrecy good. *Ṣadaqah* — charity, alms — was read as giving from what God provided, the opposite of devouring orphans' wealth and of withholding bounty (4:37–40), and as the blood-money waived charitably (4:92) and the dowry graciously adjusted (4:4). *Maʿrūf* — kindness, what is known and recognised as good — was explained as every act the sound heart knows as decent: fair speech, trusts returned (4:58), verification, judging by what God shows. *Iṣlāḥ bayna al-nās* — reconciliation between people — was read as the sūrah's own procedure where a split is feared — appoint a mediator from his family and hers (4:35) — and as settlement where a wife fears indifference (4:128). To *amara* — to command, to enjoin, to encourage — was stressed: the good is not merely doing charity or kindness privately, but making the secret talk itself a counsel toward it. Where night plotting commanded throwing sin on the innocent, this exception commands the inverse.

**Whoever Does This Seeking God's Pleasure — a Great Reward**

The promise *wa man yafʿal dhālika ibtighāʾa marḍāti Allāhi fa sawfa nuʾtīhi ajran ʿaẓīmā* — and whoever does this seeking God's pleasure, approval, We will grant them a great reward — was explained with two conditions: doing the commanded good — *yafʿal* — and seeking thereby God's pleasure — *ibtighāʾa marḍāti Allāhi* — not reputation. *Marḍāt* — pleasure, approval — was read as the same seeking that distinguishes true striving with wealth and lives (4:95) from seeking fleeting gain by denying peace (4:94) and from spending to show off without belief (4:38). *Fa sawfa nuʾtīhi ajran ʿaẓīmā* — We will grant a great reward — was explained as the same *ajr ʿaẓīm* promised for doing what was advised (4:67), for the striver above the sitter (4:95–96), and for holding fast after repentance (4:146); the reward for counselling charity, kindness, and reconciliation in secret is therefore ranked with striving. *Sawfa* — will, soon — was read as certainty, as the emigrant's reward is already secured even where death overtakes (4:100). Early reports illustrated *iṣlāḥ* with the one who reconciles two disputants by private counsel, where public speech would have shamed — achieving a peace that is itself worship.

**A Verse That Generalises the Theft Case Into an Ethic of Speech**

Placed after the Prophet's preservation by grace and teaching (4:113), this verse generalises the theft case into an ethic of speech. The Book and wisdom taught him what he did not know — the hidden moving of the armour, the night counsel — and by that teaching the community learns that most private counsels are not good unless they encourage the three. The sūrah has shown that *God wishes to lighten burdens* (4:28), that purification is eased with earth (4:43), that prayer is shortened on travel (4:101), and that precaution remains even when arms are laid aside (4:102); here speech is eased: private talk is not burdened with prohibition, only guided — make it about charity, kindness, or reconciliation, and it is great reward. The sūrah has also warned that following desires is to deviate greatly (4:27) and that Satan commands alteration and deludes with hopes (4:119–120); secret talk that deludes is Satan's whispering, while secret talk that reconciles is God's. For the weak the sūrah lightens, this is a practical lightening: you need not be present at every dispute, but if you whisper, whisper toward giving, kindness, mending.

**The Great Reward That Makes Secrecy Worship**

The closing *ajran ʿaẓīmā* — a great reward — was explained as making secrecy itself worship where it would otherwise be suspicion. The sūrah that opened from a single soul and commanded mindfulness of ties (4:1), that multiplies a good deed many times over (4:40), here multiplies a private word that mends people into a mighty wage. The contrast with the double burden — slander and manifest sin — for throwing on the innocent (4:112) is exact: there private talk earned two burdens; here it earns great reward — according as the intention was God's pleasure or concealment from people. The next verse sets the boundary of that intention: whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance is clear and follows a path other than the believers' will be left to what he chose and burned — what an evil end (4:115) — for he chose the counsel that had no good.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:115

> And whoever defies the Messenger after guidance has become clear to them and follows a path other than that of the believers, We will let them pursue what they have chosen, then burn them in Hell—what an evil end

**Whoever Defies the Messenger After Guidance Is Clear**

The verse opens *wa man yushāqiqi al-rasūla min baʿdi mā tabayyana lahu al-hudā* — and whoever defies, opposes, splits from the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him. *Yushāqiq* — to defy, to take the opposite side — was explained as going to the other side from the Messenger ﷺ after the Book in truth sent to judge by what He shows (4:105) and the wisdom taught (4:113) made guidance clear. *Min baʿdi mā tabayyana lahu al-hudā* — after guidance became clear to him — was read as after the evidence of truth had reached him: the Qur'anic commands about trusts, judgment, verification, and the theft case just judged — so that defiance is not error but choice after clarity. The sūrah has shown guidance become clear where the Book judges between people in place of *ṭāghūt* (4:60), where reflection would show no inconsistency had it been from other than God (4:82), and where the Prophet ﷺ was taught what he never knew (4:113); to defy after that clarity is to choose the other path with eyes open — as the sūrah said *whoever God leaves to stray, you will never find a way for him* (4:88) after regression by misdeeds. The same root appears where *whoever defies God and His Messenger — God is severe in punishment* (8:13), marking defiance as more than disagreement: it is adoption of enmity.

**And Follows a Path Other Than That of the Believers**

The second condition *wa yattabiʿ ghayra sabīli al-muʾminīna* — and follows a path other than the way of the believers — was explained as taking a way distinct from the community's way. *Sabīl* — path, way — is the sūrah's standing word: God wills to make the path clear and guide to noble ways (4:26); Satan wishes the deviant path far away (4:60); verification is the path before fighting (4:94); the earth's spaciousness is the path for emigration (4:97–100). *Sabīl al-muʾminīn* — the path of the believers — was explained as the believers' collective way in creed, law, and conduct: the same congregation commanded to go forth together (4:71) and to stand for justice even against selves (4:135). Early authorities, including al-Shāfiʿī, inferred from this phrase the authority of the community's consensus — *ijmāʿ* — where the believers' path in understanding the Book is protected, though the core meaning remains moral: to follow other than their path after guidance is clear is to follow desires that deviate greatly (4:27) and to join Satan's party. The sūrah has warned that most secret talks have no good except the three that seek God's pleasure (4:114); following other than the believers' path was read as the secret talk made public as doctrine — private deceit become alternative way.

**We Will Let Him Pursue What He Has Chosen**

The recompense *nuwallīhi mā tawallā* — We will let him pursue, turn him to, what he has turned to, chosen — was explained as handing the defier over to his choice, as the sūrah said God allowed the hypocrites to regress because of their misdeeds (4:88) and as *whoever He leaves to stray, you will never find a way for him* (4:88). *Nuwallīhi* — We entrust him to his direction — was read as divine leave: he chose the other side after clarity, so God leaves him there — as the emigrant who chose God's side finds many havens (4:100), and the helpless who could not choose are hoped to be pardoned (4:99). The phrase was linked to *We will turn their hearts and eyes, as they did not believe at first* (6:110); the *tawallā* — turning — that began as a human act becomes divine *nuwallīhi* — We turn him. Classical notes added that this shows freedom's weight: the Book in truth does not coerce; it shows — and where one defies after being shown, God does not drag back, but lets the path chosen become the path walked. The sūrah has said that God does not wrong even an atom (4:40); to let the defier pursue his chosen side is not wrong — it is the atom measured exactly.

**Then Burn Him in Hell — What an Evil End**

The outcome *wa nuṣlihi Jahannam wa sāʾat maṣīrā* — then We will burn him in Hell, and evil is that destination — was explained with *nuṣlihi* — to cause to burn, to roast — the same verb for those who consume orphans' wealth unjustly, who will be burned in a blazing Fire (4:10), and those who reject signs, cast into Fire where skins are replaced (4:56). *Jahannam* was read as the abode already assigned to the intentional killer with anger and curse (4:93) and to those who wronged themselves while the earth was wide (4:97); here it is for defiance after clarity and following other than the believers' way. *Wa sāʾat maṣīrā* — evil as destination — is the sūrah's closing formula for the abodes of those who choose other than God's cause. The phrase links back to the opening limits: keeping God's limits admits to Gardens forever (4:13), exceeding them casts into Fire forever (4:14); defying the Messenger after guidance is exceeding that limit at its root — the referral to God and Messenger where disputes are taken (4:59).

**A Verse That Follows the Theft Case With the Broad Principle**

Placed after *no good in most secret talks except charity, kindness, reconciliation, seeking God's pleasure* (4:114), this verse follows a particular case — theft, night plotting, advocacy, throwing sin — with the broad principle: after guidance is clear, defying the Messenger and following other than the believers' path is a chosen turning that God lets continue to its end — burning. The sūrah has moved from individual excuses — sitters with harm promised good though not equal (4:95), the helpless hoped to be pardoned (4:99) — to collective guard — prayer with vigilance (4:102), pursuit without faltering for hope (4:104), judgment by the Book (4:105). This verse anchors collective guard in loyalty to the Messenger's way: the path of the believers is not a tribal way but the way the Book shows and wisdom teaches (4:113). For the weak the sūrah lightens, this is a guard: where private talk tempted toward other than the believers' way, the warning that He will let you pursue what you chose — and burn — steadies the step back onto the spacious path where He wills to make clear and to turn in mercy (4:26–27).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:116

> Surely Allah does not forgive associating ˹others˺ with Him ˹in worship˺, but forgives anything else of whoever He wills. Indeed, whoever associates ˹others˺ with Allah has clearly gone far astray

**God Does Not Forgive Association — but Forgives What Is Less**

The verse states *inna Allāha lā yaghfiru an yushraka bihi wa yaghfiru mā dūna dhālika li man yashāʾ* — God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but forgives anything less than that for whomever He wills. The same sentence was given at 4:48, and its return here was explained as deliberate closure after defiance following guidance and following other than the believers' path, whose end is burning (4:115). *An yushraka bihi* — that association be made with Him — was read as setting a partner beside God in worship, the *shirk* the sūrah repeatedly measures against its limits, and the anchor of its whole monotheism. *Mā dūna dhālika* — anything below that — was explained as every sin besides association: error, sin, throwing sin on the innocent (4:111–112), deceit, advocacy for deceit, even intentional killing where repentance might yet be sought. The sūrah has shown that whoever earns sin earns only upon himself (4:111) and whoever commits evil then seeks finds Him All-Forgiving (4:110); the limit is that association, persisted in without repentance, is not covered. The seal *li man yashāʾ* — for whom He wills — was read as divine will in forgiveness, not human claim: *it will not be in accordance with your wishes, nor the wishes of the People of the Book* (4:123) — but by His will after justice to His measure.

**Indeed Whoever Associates Has Gone Far Astray**

The reason *wa man yushrik bi Allāhi fa qad ḍalla ḍalālan baʿīdā* — whoever associates with God has clearly gone far astray — was explained as distance in path. *Ḍalla ḍalālan baʿīdā* — strayed a far straying — was read as the opposite of the straight path the Book guides to (4:68) and of the noble ways He wills to make clear (4:26). The sūrah has said that those who follow desires wish you to deviate greatly (4:27), that seeking false judges leads to far straying (4:60), and that defying the Messenger and following other than the believers' path ends in being left to stray (4:115); association is the furthest of those distances, because it sets an equal beside the Single Source who created from a single soul (4:1) and to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth (4:126). Early notes linked *baʿīd* — far — to remoteness of return: the one who thinks forgiveness is bound by human wish (4:123) and yet associates has gone so far that return requires abandoning the partner — not merely seeking pardon while holding it.

**A Verse That Follows the Threat of Burning With the Unforgivable Root**

Placed after *We will let him pursue what he chose and burn him — an evil destination* (4:115), this verse names the root that makes the burning not arbitrary: association is the one sin not forgiven without repentance, because it denies the very One to whom forgiveness is sought. The sūrah has traced association's allies — devouring wealth unjustly (4:29), envy of God's bounties (4:54), believing in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* (4:51) — and here gathers them: to associate is to have gone far, while the helpless hoped to be pardoned (4:99) and the emigrant who finds many havens (4:100) remain within forgiveness' range. The repetition from 4:48 to 4:116 was explained as bracketing the judgment passage: the first came among the limits of inheritance; the second after the law of deceit and advocacy — both saying: the framework — trusts returned, disputes referred, prayer guarded, judgment by Book — assumes the One to whom referral is made. To associate while referring to Him is the contradiction the Book in truth came to remove (4:105).

**Forgives What Is Less — but Only for Whom He Wills**

The clause *wa yaghfiru mā dūna dhālika li man yashāʾ* was explained as opening hope without opening presumption. The sūrah has shown that intentional killing earns Hell with anger and curse, yet the door of seeking remains (4:93, 4:110); that throwing sin on the innocent earns a double burden, yet seeking remains; that defying the Messenger earns burning, yet seeking before that end remains. *Li man yashāʾ* — for whom He wills — was read to prevent the wishful from counting forgiveness as debt. The sūrah pairs this will with knowledge and wisdom: *All-Knowing, All-Wise* where earning stays on the self (4:111), *All-Hearing, All-Seeing* where trusts are judged (4:58). Forgiveness below association is therefore neither automatic nor random, but a will governed by knowledge — of repentance, of night plotting, of advocacy, of throwing. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the verse is steadying: what is below association remains within the spaciousness the earth's havens image (4:100) — many exits — while association removes the earth itself, because the earth's spaciousness is *His* earth (4:97).

**The Far Straying After Clear Guidance**

The description *ḍalālan baʿīdā* — far astray — was linked to *after guidance has become clear* (4:115): going far after being shown nearness is the furthest. The sūrah has said that reflecting on the Qur'an reveals no inconsistency because it is from God (4:82); to associate after that reflection is to impose the inconsistency upon the Source. The verse generalises the particular defiance of the theft case into theology: to follow other than the believers' path after clarity is often a step before setting a partner beside God — for Satan's next claim is to be taken as guardian instead of God and to command altering creation (4:119). Association is therefore not only an altar act but a path act — choosing the other side after guidance was clear — and its distance is measured as *far*. The next verses anatomise that far straying: invoking female gods, and none but a rebellious Satan (4:117), the cursed who claims a share of servants (4:118).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:117

> Instead of Allah, they only invoke female gods, and they ˹actually˺ invoke none but a rebellious Satan—

**They Invoke Nothing Besides Him Except Females**

The verse states *in yadʿūna min dūnihi illā ināthan* — they call, invoke, nothing besides Him — instead of God — except females, female beings. *Yadʿūna* — to call, invoke, pray to — was explained as worship by invocation, the same calling condemned where people call upon another god with God (25:68) and where association is not forgiven (4:116). *Min dūnihi* — besides Him, instead of Him, short of Him — was read as departure from the Single Source to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth (4:126). *Illā ināthan* — except females, female gods — was explained as the Meccan invocation of female-named deities — al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā, Manāt — called daughters of God, and more broadly as weak, powerless beings chosen as partners: in that culture's idolatry the female was taken as a symbol of weakness, though in reality both male and female besides God are powerless. The sūrah has shown that those given a portion believe in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* (4:51) and wish you to deviate; invoking females besides God was read as the religious form of that deviation: to give what belongs to the Creator of the single soul (4:1) to imagined females. The phrase was read as a sign of the far straying — *ḍalālan baʿīdā* (4:116) — where association takes the form of venerating the weakest claimants.

**They Actually Invoke None but a Rebellious Satan**

The correction *wa in yadʿūna illā shayṭānan marīdā* — and they actually invoke none but a rebellious, obstinate, defiant Satan — was explained as the reality behind the image. *Shayṭān* — Satan, the adversary — was read as Iblīs, granted respite until the appointed Day, who vowed to lie in ambush for God's servants (7:16–17), whose schemes are weak (4:76) yet whose whisper deludes. *Marīd* — rebellious, defiant, obstinate — was explained as one who has broken away and become excessively disobedient, as the sūrah will say: the one cursed by God who said, *I will take an appointed share of Your servants* (4:118). To invoke females besides God was explained as invocation of Satan in effect, because Satan commands the veneration of the idols and the altering of creation (4:119). The sūrah has said that God does not like the deceitful sinner (4:107) and that night plotting displeases Him (4:108); here the displeasing invocation is shown to have a commander — the rebellious Satan — who orders it. Early reports noted that idol worshippers thought they called Lāt and ʿUzzā; the Qur'an says they call Satan, because obedience to Satan is worship of him even where his name is not spoken.

**A Verse That Unmasks Idolatry**

Placed after *whoever associates has gone far astray* (4:116), this verse unmasks idolatry. The arc from defying the Messenger and following other than the believers' path (4:115), to association's far straying (4:116), to invoking females besides Him is the path of deviation: guidance was clear, yet *ṭāghūt* was sought (4:60), trust betrayed (4:107), night plots hidden from people (4:108); the religious expression is to call upon what cannot hear. The sūrah elsewhere says those given a portion believe in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* (4:51); here the female idols and the rebellious Satan are that *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* named in Meccan form. The identification — females but really Satan — was read as the Book's demystification: the many gods dissolve into one enemy, the rebellious Satan, whose promise is only delusion (4:120) and whose portion is Hell without escape (4:121). Where the sūrah promised a great reward for counselling charity, kindness, and reconciliation, seeking God's pleasure (4:114), this verse shows the opposite counsel — Satan ordering the slitting of cattle's ears and the altering of creation (4:119) — and promising nothing but loss.

**Female Naming as Weakness Chosen**

The phrase *illā ināthan* — except females — was explained linguistically as showing that the worshippers chose the weakest form of partner: the female idols were not chosen for strength but as offspring, as daughters — implying God has children, a claim the sūrah later refutes with *the Messiah Jesus, son of Mary, was only a messenger of God, His Word directed to Mary, a spirit from Him — so believe in God and His messengers, and do not say "Three"* (4:171). To call females besides the Single who created from a single soul and spread men and women (4:1) was read as inversion: from Him who creates both, they make the female a separate deity. The Qur'an elsewhere notes that when a daughter is announced to a man, his face darkens (16:58–59); yet they assign daughters to God — showing the desire was not truth but a partner that cannot challenge. The sūrah pairs this with *shayṭānan marīdā* to show that weakness worshipped is not harmless: the rebellious Satan uses that weakness as a doorway, ordering the slitting of cattle's ears and the altering of creation — imposing human will upon what God formed intact.

**A Short Verse That Bridges Association and Satan's Vow**

Though brief — *they invoke beside Him only females, and they invoke only a rebellious Satan* — the verse bridges association's doctrine (4:116) and Satan's vow (4:118–119). The sūrah has shown that the Devil's cause is fought for by disbelievers (4:76), that his followers wish you to deviate greatly (4:27), and that whoever takes Satan as guardian instead of God suffers tremendous loss (4:119). To invoke females besides Him is the act; to invoke rebellious Satan is the agency. The verse was read as the sūrah's answer to those who claim *we only worship them to bring us near to God* (39:3): you claim nearness by females, but you arrive at Satan, for his command is behind the rite. The next verses let Satan speak: cursed, he says *I will take a share, mislead, delude with hopes, order slitting and altering* (4:118–119); *he promises them only delusion* (4:120); his end is Hell without escape (4:121) — versus the Gardens promised truly to those who believe and do good (4:122).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:118

> cursed by Allah—who said, "I will surely take hold of a certain number of Your servants"

**Cursed by God**

The verse opens *laʿanahu Allāhu* — cursed by God: expelled from mercy, removed from favour, condemned. *Laʿanahu* — He cursed him — was explained as God's removal of the rebellious Satan — *shayṭānan marīdā* — invoked besides Him in the form of female gods (4:117) — from mercy, as the sūrah said God is angered by, curses, and prepares mighty punishment for the intentional killer (4:93), and as it says the deceitful are not loved (4:107). The curse here was read as the original curse upon Iblīs after refusing to prostrate to Adam and after requesting respite until the appointed Day (7:13–17; 15:34–35; 38:77–78), where *cursed* — *malʿūn*, *rajīm* — is named. The sūrah has said that the Devil's schemes are weak (4:76) yet must be curbed, and that whoever takes Satan as guardian instead of God suffers tremendous loss (4:119); the curse is the foundation of that loss: the guardian taken is already expelled. Early reports linked the curse to the declaration *upon you is curse until the Day of Recompense* (38:78) after his rebellion. The sūrah's seal *God does not wrong even an atom* (4:40) frames the curse: it is not arbitrary; it is the measure for rebellion — *marīd* — after guidance was clear and prostration refused.

**Who Said — I Will Surely Take an Appointed Share of Your Servants**

The vow *wa qāla la-attakhidhanna min ʿibādika naṣīban mafrūḍā* — and he said, I will surely take hold, seize for myself, from Your servants an appointed share, a fixed portion — was explained as Satan's declared program after being cursed. *La-attakhidhanna* — surely I will take — is emphatic, with oath and the letter of certainty, as the hostile who wish you to disbelieve as they have (4:89) also speak with emphasis — but Satan's oath here is before God Himself. *Min ʿibādika* — from Your servants — was read as from humanity created from a single soul (4:1) and for whom the earth was made spacious (4:97, 4:100). *Naṣīban mafrūḍan* — an appointed share — was explained as a portion he will claim as if due: a fixed share of those who follow him besides God — to call on females (4:117), to believe in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* (4:51), to desire deviation greatly (4:27). The word *mafrūḍ* — appointed — was linked to the inheritance shares appointed as *farīḍah* (4:11–12), where God's apportioning is just; Satan's *mafrūḍ* is the counterfeit apportioning, where he claims servants as if inheritance. The sūrah has shown that those given a portion trade it for misguidance (4:44); here Satan claims a portion for misguidance.

**A Verse That Places Curse Before Program**

Placed between *they invoke only a rebellious Satan* (4:117) and *I will mislead, delude, order slitting ears and altering creation* (4:119), this verse places curse before program. He is not cursed because he takes a share; he takes a share because he is cursed — expelled first, then vowing. The order was read as the sūrah's causal chain after association's far straying (4:116): association is the human side of accepting the share Satan claimed, and Hell without escape (4:121) is the share's end. The sūrah has shown that whoever defies the Messenger after guidance and follows other than the believers' path is left to what he chose (4:115); to accept Satan's share is that defiance made worship. Where the emigrant's reward is said to have fallen upon God, secure (4:100), and the striver's wages are ranks from Him (4:96), the Satanic share is the inverse inheritance — a portion that fell upon the cursed, not upon God. The verse also inverts the theft case's throwing sin on the innocent (4:112): Satan throws his curse-burden onto his claimed share, but the burden stays with the thrower — borne here as slander upon creation.

**A Share Claimed With Oath — Not With Right**

The oath *la-attakhidhanna* was explained to show that Satan claims not by right but by vow, by force of declaration. The sūrah has said God suffices as Guardian and Helper (4:45) and that whoever takes Satan as guardian instead of God suffers tremendous loss (4:119); the guardian taken by oath cannot protect, because the oath was made from curse, not from authority. The phrase *naṣīban mafrūḍan* was linked to the fixed shares that belong to God alone — those who envied would not give a speck even if they controlled a kingdom (4:53) — while Satan claims a share of humanity as if controlling a kingdom; the claim is shown as false apportioning. The sūrah elsewhere says the Devil promises only delusion (4:120) and has no warrant; his *mafrūḍ* is therefore not a writ like the prayer's appointed times (4:103) but a boast whose writ is Hell without escape. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the verse is a warning that the share Satan claims is not only of the strong: his program targets every servant — but his share is only those who accept invocation besides God, female or otherwise, as worship.

**From Female Idols to Appointed Share**

Though brief — *cursed by God, who said, I will surely take an appointed share of Your servants* — the verse moves from the single act, calling females besides Him (4:117), to the system, taking a share. The sūrah that began from a single soul spread into countless men and women (4:1) now sees that spread claimed portionwise by the cursed. The sūrah has shown that those who remained, claiming oppression while the earth was wide, wronged themselves (4:97), while the helpless hoped for pardon (4:99); Satan's appointed share is those who remain in invocation besides Him where the earth's havens were available. The next verse details his program upon that share: to mislead, to delude with empty hopes, to order the slitting of cattle's ears and the altering of God's creation — where whoever takes him as guardian instead of God suffers tremendous loss (4:119).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:119

> I will certainly mislead them and delude them with empty hopes. Also, I will order them and they will slit the ears of cattle and alter Allah's creation." And whoever takes Satan as a guardian instead of Allah has certainly suffered a tremendous loss

**I Will Certainly Mislead and Delude With Empty Hopes**

The vow continues *wa la-uḍillannahum wa la-umanniyannahum* — I will certainly mislead them and certainly delude them with hopes, with empty promising. *Uḍillannahum* — to lead astray — was explained as Satan's first work upon his appointed share (4:118), after curse: the far straying of association (4:116). *Ummaniyannahum* — to delude with hopes, to cast wishes — was read as the mechanism of misguidance: not force but hopes, as the sūrah shows that Satan promises only delusion (4:120) and that his hopes are empty — *ghurūr* — while God's promise is true (4:122). The sūrah has shown desires that wish you to deviate greatly (4:27), and that the deceitful hide from people while God is with them where they plot by night (4:108); empty hopes delude because they hide consequence. The one misled thinks delay is generosity — the gradual destruction the Qur'an names elsewhere — while the Book says *I will grant them respite, but My plan is firm* (7:183). The hopes delude where the believer's true hope is for ranks, forgiveness, and mercy (4:96) and many havens (4:100); Satan's hope is the counterfeit that spending to show off (4:38) or withholding bounty (4:37) is honour preserved.

**I Will Order Them and They Will Slit the Ears of Cattle**

The program *wa la-āmurannahum fa la-yubattikunna ādhāna al-anʿāmi* — and I will surely order them, and they will surely slit the ears of cattle — was explained as Satan ordering rites upon livestock. *Āmurannahum* — I will command — was read as Satan issuing command as if a lord, in rivalry to God who commands the return of trusts (4:58) and to whose Book disputes are referred (4:59). *Yubattikunna* — to slit, to notch — the *ears of cattle* — was explained as the Meccan custom of dedicating livestock to idols — *baḥīrah, sāʾibah, waṣīlah, ḥām* (5:103) — slitting the ear as a mark, forbidding its use, devoting it to the female gods (4:117). The act was read not as pastoral technique but as a worship-mark: to alter the ear is to claim ownership of the animal beyond the Creator's intact creation. The sūrah has shown that those given a portion believe in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* (4:51); slitting ears is the ritual of that belief. The double emphasis in *la-yubattikunna* — they will surely slit — shows obedience: his order is executed.

**And Alter God's Creation**

The wider command *wa la-āmurannahum fa la-yughayyirunna khalqa Allāhi* — and I will order them, and they will alter, change, God's creation — was explained as the generalisation of slitting ears: changing what God created intact, wholesome, upon the innate disposition. *Khalq Allāh* — God's creation — was read as the form, the wholeness, the natural disposition, the law inscribed in creation: the sūrah began from a single soul created and from it its mate (4:1). Commentators explained altering as physical mutilations dedicated to idols, as tattooing, as claiming the lawful as forbidden and vice versa, and morally as altering the religion — changing the limits God set (4:13–14) — and altering the self that wrongs itself (4:110). The common element was explained as Satan commanding a claim of lordship over creation: to cut what God made whole and to call the cut devotion. Where the sūrah says there is no good in most secret talks except commanding charity, kindness, and reconciliation (4:114), this is the evil command — to slit and to alter — whose compliance proves which guardian was taken.

**Whoever Takes Satan as Guardian Instead of God Suffers Tremendous Loss**

The verdict *wa man yattakhidh al-shayṭāna waliyyan min dūni Allāhi fa qad khasira khusāran mubīnā* — whoever takes Satan as a guardian, patron, ally instead of God has certainly suffered a tremendous, manifest loss — was explained with *walī* — the same guardian and helper the oppressed cry for from grace (4:75) and that God alone suffices as (4:45). To take Satan as *walī* instead — *min dūni Allāh* — was read as choosing the cursed (4:118) as guardian whose promise is delusion (4:120). *Khasira khusāran mubīnā* — suffered manifest loss — was explained as loss clear in both worlds: in this world, by slitting what was wholesome and altering what was created balanced; in the next, by Hell without escape (4:121) versus Gardens forever under a true promise (4:122). The sūrah has shown that whoever takes Satan as associate — what an evil associate (4:38) — and that the share Satan takes is the share of those who invoke besides Him (4:117–118); to take him as *walī* is to become that share. The loss is *mubīn* — clear — because the alternative was clear: the Book and wisdom taught (4:113), the great reward for charity and reconciliation (4:114), the forgiveness found upon seeking (4:110) — and the choice of the cutter over the Creator is clear deviation.

**A Verse That Makes Satan's Program Concrete**

Placed after the curse and the appointed share (4:118), this verse makes Satan's program concrete: mislead, delude with hopes, order the slitting of ears and the altering of creation. The sūrah that warned not to deviate by following desires (4:27) and not to follow other than the believers' path (4:115) here shows what the other path orders and what its followers execute: cutting creation to mark it for another. The sūrah that began with unity from a single soul (4:1) and that says to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth, encompassing all (4:126), sees the altering of creation as assault on that unity. For the weak this is protective: to alter creation is not light craft but tremendous and clear loss, because the Creator who made humanity weak yet wills to lighten (4:28), and who gives many havens (4:100), is replaced by a commander who orders cutting. The next verse summarises the commander's economy: he promises and deludes — promising nothing but delusion (4:120) — whose end is Hell without escape (4:121).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:120

> Satan only makes them ˹false˺ promises and deludes them with ˹empty˺ hopes. Truly Satan promises them nothing but delusion

**Satan Promises and Deludes With Empty Hopes**

The verse states *yaʿiduhum wa yumannīhim* — he promises them and deludes them with hopes, with *umnīyah*, wishing. *Yaʿiduhum* — to promise, to hold out — was explained as Satan's currency after being cursed and claiming an appointed share (4:118), and ordering misleading, slitting ears, and altering creation (4:119). The promises were explained as the hopes already named: that association is nearness; that invoking females brings intercession (4:117); that cutting cattle is devotion; that altering creation is honour; that throwing sin on the innocent cleans the thrower (4:112); that advocacy in this life will have advocacy on the Day (4:109). The sūrah has shown that those who wish you to deviate wish it greatly (4:27), that the lagger wishes to share gain without sharing faith (4:73), that the regressed wish you alike in disbelief (4:89); Satan's promising is the source-wish that generates all those. *Wa yumannīhim* — and he deludes with hopes — was read as keeping them in wishing, so that the wish never becomes turning — as the sūrah warns that repentance delayed until death says *now I repent* is not accepted (4:18).

**Truly He Promises Nothing but Delusion**

The qualification *wa mā yaʿiduhumu al-shayṭānu illā ghurūrā* — Satan promises them nothing but delusion, deception, vanity — was explained with *ghurūr* — delusion, deceptive vanity, a gloss that vanishes. *Ghurūr* was read as promise that looks like benefit but is harm, as the moment weapons are left unguarded looks safe for an instant before the sweeping assault (4:102). The Qur'an elsewhere says *do not let the deceiver deceive you about God* (31:33; 35:5), with *gharūr* as Satan's very trait — delusion is his title. To say he promises *only* delusion — *illā ghurūrā* — was explained as exclusivity: there is no true promise in his portfolio, as the next verses contrast his delusion with Hell without escape (4:121) and with Gardens where God's promise is always true (4:122). Early notes linked *ghurūr* to the world's fleeting enjoyment — the little enjoyment the sūrah says is little versus the Hereafter better for the mindful (4:77) — and to the fleeting gain sought by denying peace (4:94): Satan promises that little as if it were great. The sūrah has shown that good and evil fall within decree while evil comes from the self as means (4:79); Satan's delusion is to make the means — altering creation, slitting ears — seem to change destiny toward good.

**A Verse That Follows the Order With Its True Price**

Placed after *he will order slitting ears and altering creation, and whoever takes him as guardian suffers tremendous loss* (4:119), this verse follows the order with its true price: the order is paid in delusion. The sūrah that warns there is no good in most secret talks except charity, kindness, and reconciliation (4:114) here unmasks the secret counsels that command altering: their payment is *ghurūr*. The sūrah that commands verifying reports (4:83) and being sure before fighting (4:94) shows verification failing where hope is empty: the deluded do not verify Satan's promise, because it is a hope, not a proof. The sūrah has shown that God's promise — admission into Gardens where rivers flow forever, *God's promise is always true; whose word is more truthful than God's?* (4:122) — is tied to *God does not wrong even an atom* (4:40); Satan's promise is tied to loss manifest. The verse was read as the sūrah's ledger for transactions with Satan: he promises and deludes; you alter; you take him as guardian; you bear clear loss — and his promise, when examined, is nothing but vanity.

**The Economy of Empty Hope**

The concept *umnīyah* — empty hope, wish — was explained linguistically as wishing for what cannot be attained by wishing, as when people wish grace by belonging alone — *neither by your wishes nor those of the People of the Book* (4:123). Satan's economy was described as selling hope without means: he commands slitting ears and altering, which cost the cutter, and pays with hope, which costs him nothing. The sūrah has shown that the believer's hope is *you hope from God what they never hope for* (4:104) — a hope tied to ranks and mercy (4:96) and many havens (4:100) — while Satan's hope is tied to nothing. The contrast was linked to the beginning where God created from a single soul and spread humanity (4:1) intact: to alter that creation on a hope is to damage the known for the imagined. The verse was also linked to the prior deception where advocates hoped to deceive the Prophet ﷺ yet deceived only themselves (4:113): self-deception is the product sold.

**A Short Verse That Anchors the Two Destinations**

Though brief — *he promises and deludes; he promises nothing but delusion* — the verse anchors the two destinations that follow. Immediately after: *they will have Hell as home, and they will find no escape* (4:121) — the delusion's end; and then: *those who believe and do good, We will admit into Gardens forever — God's promise is always true* (4:122) — the true promise's end. The sūrah that let the defier be turned to what he turned to (4:115) and declared association far straying (4:116) here names the engine of that turning: a promise that is nothing but gloss. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the verse is a lightening: you need not be deluded, because the promise that would delude you has been labelled — *nothing but delusion* — so that verification (4:94) can dismiss it and choose the promise that is ever true.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:121

> It is they who will have Hell as their home, and they will find no escape from it

**They Will Have Hell as Home**

The verse states *ulāʾika maʾwāhum Jahannam* — it is they whose refuge, shelter, home is Hell, *Jahannam*. *Maʾwā* — refuge, shelter, place of return — was explained as the home that receives: as the emigrant finds many havens — *murāgham* — and abundance where God's earth is spacious (4:100), so these find *maʾwā* as Hell, the inverse haven. The sūrah has used *maʾwā* for the self-wronger who remained where the earth was wide — Hell as home, evil destination (4:97) — and for the defier left to what he chose — burning, evil destination (4:115); here the pronoun *ulāʾika* — it is they — restricts to Satan's share: the appointed portion he claimed (4:118). *Jahannam* was read as the Fire where skins are replaced to taste the punishment (4:56), where the intentional killer abides under anger and curse (4:93), where the humiliating punishment is prepared for disbelievers who would sweep upon neglect (4:102). To have Hell as *maʾwā* means it is not a passing visit but the place of stay — as Gardens are *maʾwā* for those who believe and do good, staying forever (4:122).

**And They Will Find No Escape From It**

The clause *wa lā yajidūna ʿanhā maḥīṣā* — and they will find no escape, no flight, no diversion from it — was explained with *maḥīṣ* — an escape-place, a refuge from. *Lā yajidūna* — they will not find — contrasts with the emigrant's *yajid* — will find — many havens (4:100), and with the helpless who could not find a way yet are hoped pardon (4:98–99). *ʿAnhā* — from it — was read as Hell's encompassing: there is no haven from Hell, no spaciousness away from it, because the one taken as guardian was cursed (4:118) and promises only delusion (4:120) — the only Guardian who could provide escape was rejected. The sūrah has said that the wronged who sought havens found them (4:100) and that prayer at fixed times is the writ that secures hours (4:103); Hell without escape is the writ that secures consequence where the promise was delusion. *Lā yajidūna maḥīṣā* was also compared to *they will find no protector or helper besides God* (4:123): no guardian, no helper, no escape, no diversion.

**A Verse That Seals Satan's Economy With Its Destination**

Placed after *Satan promises only delusion* (4:120), this verse seals Satan's economy with its destination. The program — *I will mislead, delude, order slitting ears and altering creation* (4:119) — paid in delusion, ends in Hell as home. The sūrah has shown that the deceiver would deceive none but themselves (4:113) and that throwing sin on the innocent bears slander (4:112); here self-deception's wage is Hell without diversion. The sūrah has also shown that the believer's hope is what the disbeliever never hopes for (4:104) — ranks, forgiveness, mercy (4:96) — and that those who believe and do good are promised Gardens where God's promise is ever true (4:122); the deluded hope that was nothing but gloss ends where no escape is found, because no true promise was behind it. Where the sūrah earlier said *God has prepared a humiliating punishment for the disbelievers* (4:102), here the preparation is shelter itself — Hell as *maʾwā* — the humiliation of having no exit from the delusion's own house.

**No Escape Because the Guardian Was the Cursed**

The phrase *wa lā yajidūna ʿanhā maḥīṣā* was explained as the consequence of taking Satan as guardian (4:119). The sūrah has repeated that God is sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45), that the oppressed cry for a guardian and helper from grace (4:75), and that the Messenger ﷺ is told to put trust in Him as Trustee (4:81). To take Satan as *walī* instead of Him is to choose a guardian who was cursed (4:118) and whose promise is delusion (4:120); on the Day where this life's advocates find no advocate before God (4:109), there will be no escape-place, because the only Guardian and Helper who could provide it was rejected. Classical notes added that *maḥīṣ* matches *murāgham* — both are places of turning: the emigrant who turned to God finds many turnings; the follower of Satan who turned to him finds none. The sūrah that promised the emigrant his reward secured even if death overtakes (4:100) here secures the follower of Satan his loss, where death overtakes into Hell.

**A Short Verse That Holds the Two Promises Apart**

Though brief — *Hell as home and no escape* — the verse holds the two promises apart. Immediately before: Satan's promise, nothing but delusion (4:120). Immediately after: *those who believe and do good, We will admit into Gardens under which rivers flow forever; God's promise is always true; whose word is more truthful than God's?* (4:122). The sūrah that judges by the Book in truth (4:105) and that shows there is no good in most secret talks except charity, kindness, and reconciliation (4:114) here shows that the speaker behind the evil secret talk leads to a home with no secret exit. For the weak for whom the sūrah lightens burdens, the verse is a clarification: delusion's home has no exit, while God's earth has many havens and His forgiveness many entries (4:100, 4:110) — so that choosing the Guardian who is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving over the guardian whose promise is gloss is the lightest and most spacious choice.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:122

> And those who believe and do good, We will soon admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there for ever and ever. Allah's promise is ˹always˺ true. And whose word is more truthful than Allah's

**Those Who Believe and Do Good — Into Gardens Forever**

The verse states *wa alladhīna āmanū wa ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāti sa-nudkhiluhum jannātin tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhāru khālidīna fīhā abadan* — and those who believe and do good — righteous deeds — We will soon admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there forever and ever. *Āmanū wa ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt* — faith and righteous deeds — was explained as the sūrah's shorthand for the faithful, opposed to those who take Satan as guardian (4:119), who invoke others besides Him (4:117), who follow other than the believers' path (4:115), and who will have Hell without escape (4:121). *Sa-nudkhiluhum* — We will soon admit — was read as divine assurance that admission is from Him, as the emigrant's reward falls upon God secure (4:100) and as forgiveness is found upon seeking (4:110). *Jannātin tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhār* — Gardens under which rivers flow — is the sūrah's repeated promise: the same phrase as for those who believe and do good earlier (4:57) and for those who keep God's limits (4:13). *Khālidīna fīhā abadan* — staying therein forever and ever — was read with double emphasis — *khālidīn* and *abadan* — unlike *khālidan* alone for the intentional killer (4.93): for belief and good, abiding is forever and ever; the symmetry keeps each *maʾwā* — refuge — lasting in its direction (4:121).

**God's Promise Is Always True**

The affirmation *waʿda Allāhi ḥaqqan* — God's promise is truth, truly, as right — was explained as the contrast to Satan's promise that is nothing but delusion (4:120). *Waʿd Allāh* — God's promise — was read as His word that Gardens are for the faithful; that good is multiplied; that ranks, forgiveness, and mercy are from Him (4:96); that many havens are found (4:100); that prayer at fixed times is writ (4:103); that whoever seeks finds forgiveness (4:110). *Ḥaqqan* — truly, as due — was explained as that the promise corresponds to reality, not wish, unlike empty wishes that claim grace by belonging (4:123). The sūrah has said the Book was sent with truth — *bi al-ḥaqq* (4:105) — to judge by what He shows; to say His promise is *ḥaqq* is to say judgment by it will be true, as *God does not wrong even an atom* (4:40). Where Satan orders cutting and altering (4:119) promising honour, God's promise keeps creation intact and ends in Gardens whose rivers flow beneath — nothing cut away.

**And Whose Word Is More Truthful Than God's?**

The question *wa man aṣdaqu mina Allāhi qīlā* — and whose word, speech, saying, is more truthful than God's? — was explained as rhetorical negation: none is more truthful, as earlier *whose word is more truthful than Allah's?* (4:87), where the gathering on a Day about which there is no doubt was affirmed. *Qīl* — word, saying — was read as speech that judges. The question was linked to night speech displeasing to Him (4:108) and to advocacy that disputes in this life but not before Him (4:109): all speech besides His — Satan's promising, the plotters' whispering — is delusion or displeasing; His *qīl* is truth. Classical notes added that *qīl* matches *waʿd* — promise — as both are speech acts: to ask whose word is more truthful after calling His promise *ḥaqq* is to say, if the promise is truth, the Promiser's every saying is truth, and there is no *ghurūr* in it. The verse also answers the particular case of slander thrown on the innocent (4:112): human speech can bear falsehood — God's cannot.

**A Verse That Completes the Contrast of Two Refuges**

Placed after Hell as home without escape (4:121), this verse completes the contrast of two *maʾwās* — refuges — that the sūrah has built since the angels' question about the spacious earth (4:97). One branch — the helpless hoped to be pardoned (4:99); the emigrant finds many havens (4:100); the traveller shortens and guards prayer (4:101–102), remembers in all postures (4:103), pursues without faltering for hope (4:104), judges by the Book (4:105) — ends in Gardens forever whose promise is truth. The other — invoking others, following Satan, accepting his appointed share, cutting creation, hoping his empty hope (4:117–120) — ends in Hell without escape. The sūrah that warns not to deviate by following desires (4:27) and not to follow other than the believers' path (4:115) here shows that the two paths end in two homes whose endurance is described with the same word — *khulūd*, abiding — yet opposite in quality: one as mercy — *Ghafūr Raḥīm* — one as humiliation prepared (4:102).
