For the weak the verse is the lightest of weights: belief and good — which the sūrah elsewhere defines as faith in God, the Messenger, the Book, without distinction among messengers (4:136, 4:152), together with doing what is *maʿrūf* — charity, kindness, reconciliation (4:114) — is tied to an always-true promise, while Satan's promise is nothing but delusion.

**The Always-True Promise Against the Always-Delusive One**

The pairing *waʿda Allāhi ḥaqqan* versus *nothing but delusion* (4:120) was read as the sūrah's ledger of speech: one promise true, one delusion. The question *whose word is more truthful than God's?* answers the implicit question of the weak — whom to trust where advocacy is loud, private talk is many, the enemy is clear (4:101), and judgment must be by what God shows (4:105): trust the Speaker whose promise is *ḥaqq* and whose saying none exceeds in truth. The verse was also linked to *God is sufficient as Witness* (4:79) and *God is sufficient as Trustee* (4:132): His saying suffices as witness; His promise suffices as trustee. The next verse removes wishful trust in any group's claim, so that the forever-abode is tied not to wish but to belief, good, and the ever-true word (4:123).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:123

> ˹Divine grace is˺ neither by your wishes nor those of the People of the Book! Whoever commits evil will be rewarded accordingly, and they will find no protector or helper besides Allah

**Neither by Your Wishes Nor Those of the People of the Book**

The verse opens *laysa bi-amāniyyikum wa lā amāniyyi ahli al-kitāb* — it is not by your wishes, nor the wishes of the People of the Book. *Amāniy* — wishes, fancies, empty hopes — was explained as the wishing already unmasked as Satan's delusion (4:119–120), and as the human wish that grace be by claim. The sūrah has shown wishes that mislead — those who wish you to deviate greatly (4:27), who wish you alike in disbelief (4:89), who wish you neglect weapons for a sweep (4:102) — here it says neither set of wishes governs divine grace. *Not by your wishes* — addressing the believers who might count on belonging alone while committing evil; *nor the People of the Book's* — addressing Jews and Christians who claimed *we are God's children* and *none will enter Paradise except one who was a Jew or Christian* (2:111). The sūrah has shown that the People of the Book demanded a written revelation from heaven (4:153) and that some distort words (4:46); both groups' wishes are set aside. Early reports linked the verse to mutual boasting between Muslims and People of the Book, where each claimed Paradise by belonging; the verse removed belonging as claim and installed deed and promise as measure.

**Whoever Commits Evil Will Be Rewarded Accordingly**

The rule *man yaʿmal sūʾan yujza bihi* — whoever commits evil will be recompensed with it — was explained as the ledger law already given — *whoever earns sin earns only upon himself* (4:111) and *whoever throws it on the innocent bears slander and blatant sin* (4:112) — now stated as recompense law for all. *Sūʾ* — evil — was read broadly: association, falling to Satan's promises, night plotting, devouring wealth, killing a believer, throwing sin. *Yujza bihi* — will be recompensed with it — was explained as exact recompense — *jazāʾ* — the same root by which the intentional killer's requital is Hell (4:93) and the believer's is Gardens (4:122). The sūrah has said *God does not wrong even an atom; if it is good He multiplies many times over* (4:40) — punishment is according to the deed; reward is multiplied. The pronoun *bihi* — with it — was read as equivalence: the evil's own weight as recompense, not another's, not less than an atom. The Most Truthful's word about consequence — whose word is more truthful than God's (4:122) — is what *yujza bihi* states, not a wish.

**And They Will Find No Protector or Helper Besides God**

The closure *wa lā yajid lahu min dūni Allāhi waliyyan wa lā naṣīrā* — and they will find no protector, guardian, nor helper besides God — was explained with *walī* and *naṣīr* — the same pair the oppressed cry for from grace (4:75) and that God alone suffices as (4:45), and the same pair the self-wronger's advocate cannot provide on the Day (4:109). *Min dūni Allāh* — besides God — was read as the failure of every alternative guardian: clan, People of the Book status, the female gods invoked (4:117), Satan the rebellious guardian (4:119) whose promise is delusion and whose abode is Hell without escape (4:121). To find no guardian and no helper where evil is committed and not turned from (4:110) is the law's complement to *whoever seeks forgiveness finds Him All-Forgiving, Most Merciful*: the only guardian besides Him who could rescue is none. The sūrah has warned *do not take disbelievers as allies instead of believers* (4:139, 4:144) and *do not take them as allies unless they emigrate* (4:89); here every ally beside God is declared absent where evil is chosen.

**A Verse That Follows the Gardens With the Rule of Wishes**

Placed after Gardens forever with rivers beneath and God's promise ever true (4:122), this verse follows true promise with the rule that neither side's wishes govern grace. The sūrah has shown Satan promising and deluding with empty hopes (4:120) and contrasted it with God's true promise; this verse names *amāniy* again as the false measure the community might substitute — our wishes, their wishes. The sūrah that promised great reward for counselling charity, kindness, and reconciliation, seeking God's pleasure (4:114), framed *ibtighāʾ marḍāt Allāh* — seeking His approval — as the valid seeking, not wishful claim. *Not by your wishes* was therefore read as the hinge where the theology of 4:116 — He forgives what is less than association for whom He wills — meets practice: will is not wish. For the weak the verse is clarifying: to hope for pardon as the helpless (4:99) and to seek it after evil (4:110) is not wish alone but an act of seeking; to commit evil expecting belonging to protect is wish — and it will be recompensed with itself.

**Not by Claim but by Recompense — With No Guardian Besides Him**

The construction — not by wishes, then *whoever commits evil will be recompensed with it* — was read as the substitution of claim by recompense. The sūrah has said that to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth, and He is Fully Aware of everything (4:126), and that He is sufficient as Trustee (4:132); recompense is therefore not by your computation but by His awareness — yet measured exactly, never wronging an atom. The closing *no protector nor helper besides Him* generalises the particular question *who will be their defender on the Day?* (4:109): the answer is none besides Him. The verse generalises the theft case's lesson, where advocates for self-wrongers found no advocate on the Day: every evil, by whomever — Muslim or Person of the Book — finds no protector besides Him, only the recompense of the act, unless forgiveness is sought and found. The next verse sets the opposite face: those who do good, male or female, with faith will enter Paradise, not wronged even the speck on a date stone (4:124).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:124

> But those who do good—whether male or female—and have faith will enter Paradise and will never be wronged ˹even as much as˺ the speck on a date stone

**Those Who Do Good — Male or Female — With Faith**

The verse states *wa man yaʿmal mina al-ṣāliḥāti min dhakarin aw unthā wa huwa muʾminun fa ulāʾika yadkhulūna al-jannah* — whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer, will enter Paradise. *Man yaʿmal mina al-ṣāliḥāt* — whoever does righteous deeds — was explained as the Book's shorthand for faithful act: charity, kindness, reconciliation seeking God's pleasure (4:114); standing firm for justice though against selves (4:135); spending from what God provided, not to show off (4:38–39); striving with wealth and lives (4:95); the good whose reward is multiplied many times over (4:40). *Min dhakarin aw unthā* — whether male or female — was read as the sūrah's consistent equalisation: the single soul spread into countless men and women (4:1); obligatory shares for men and women (4:7, 4:11–12); the believing bondwoman marriable where harm is feared (4:25); helpless men, women, and children each named for pardon and haven (4:75, 4:98). To name both was to remove the wish that grace is by belonging — *neither by your wishes nor those of the People of the Book* (4:123) — and to place it on act plus faith. *Wa huwa muʾmin* — while being a believer — was stressed: good alone without faith is not the entry described, as the sūrah commands *O believers, have faith in God, His Messenger, and the Book He sent down* (4:136); association is not forgiven (4:116) because it breaks the faith itself.

**And Will Never Be Wronged Even the Speck on a Date Stone**

The assurance *wa lā yuẓlamūna naqīrā* — and they will never be wronged even the speck, the groove, on a date stone — was explained with *naqīr*, the sūrah's smallest measure: the tiny speck in the stone's groove. The same measure appeared where the envious who lacked a share of kingdom would not give even a speck (4:53) and where none will be wronged even by a speck though the world's enjoyment is little (4:77). *Lā yuẓlamūna* — never be wronged — was read with the sūrah's principle *God does not wrong even an atom; if it is good He multiplies* (4:40): not wronging is the baseline; multiplying is grace. The sūrah has also said that whoever earns sin earns only upon himself (4:111), and whoever commits evil is recompensed accordingly with no protector besides Him (4:123); here the complement: whoever does good with faith will not be wronged even a speck's weight. The *naqīr* measure was therefore read as the smallest thing the eye sees on the stone — the least deserving deed is not cut from the account.

**A Verse That Follows Recompense With Reward Without Wrong**

Placed after *whoever commits evil will be recompensed accordingly and will find no protector besides God* (4:123), this verse follows recompense with reward without wrong. The sūrah has moved from two homes — Hell without escape (4:121) and Gardens forever where the promise is true (4:122) — through the rule of wishes (4:123) — to the entry: they will enter Paradise and not be wronged a speck (4:124). The symmetry was noted: evil is recompensed *with it* — exactly — and no guardian besides Him rescues; good is rewarded into Paradise and not wronged even a speck, with His promise true and His word unmatched (4:122). Where the sūrah says *do not consume wealth unjustly; trade by mutual consent* (4:29), doing good with faith is trade by consent with Him, where no wronging occurs. The verse was also placed against the sūrah's warning not to crave what God gave some over others but to ask of His bounty (4:32): the speck not wronged is the bounty asked and given without envy.

**Male or Female — the Sūrah's Equality of Entry**

The phrase *male or female* was explained as the sūrah's equality of entry. The single soul created and its mate and the spread of men and women (4:1), the command to be mindful of ties (4:1), inheritance for both (4:7), the dowry protected (4:4), standing for justice even against yourselves (4:135) — all are instances where male and female stand on one account before the All-Knowing. The verse generalises that sharing to Paradise entry: whether male or female, the condition is one — *and he is a believer* — the act one — *does good* — and the result one — *will enter Paradise*. Classical notes added that *min* — from among righteous deeds — as partitive shows that not all good must be done by each: whoever does among them, with faith, enters; and the measure *naqīr* shows that even the smallest among them is not wronged. The People of the Book claimed by wish; here female and male alike enter not by wish but by belief and good.

**A Short Verse That Anchors Grace in Act Plus Faith**

Though brief — *those who do good, male or female, and have faith will enter Paradise, not wronged a speck* — the verse anchors grace exactly where wishes were removed. Immediately after: *who is better in religion than one who submits, does good, and follows Abraham upright? God took Abraham as a close friend* (4:125) — the model of submission. Immediately before: *whoever commits evil will be recompensed accordingly* (4:123) — the threat; now the promise with equal precision, secured by *God does not wrong even an atom* (4:40). For the weak for whom burdens were lightened — the one who cannot afford a free woman may marry a believing bondwoman, her faith's value known best to God (4:25) — this is the lightest of entries: belief, and a good among goods, from whatever speck you can — and you will not be wronged a speck, because the One whose word none exceeds has promised entry, and He is the One who created you from a single soul and knows the ties.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:125

> And who is better in faith than those who ˹fully˺ submit themselves to Allah, do good, and follow the Way of Abraham, the upright? Allah chose Abraham as a close friend

**Who Is Better in Faith Than One Who Submits and Does Good**

The verse opens *wa man aḥsanu dīnan mimman aslama wajhahu li Allāhi wa huwa muḥsinun wa ittabaʿa millata Ibrāhīma ḥanīfā* — and who is better in religion than one who submits his face to God, does good, and follows the creed of Abraham, upright? *Man aḥsanu dīnan* — who is better in religion — was explained as rhetorical negation: none is better, as earlier *whose word is more truthful than God's?* (4:87, 4:122). *Aslama wajhahu li Allāh* — submitted his face to God — was read as full submission: the face as the noblest part and the direction of prayer, standing for the whole self — the sūrah elsewhere says *whoever submits his whole self to God while doing good has grasped the firm handhold* (31:22). *Wa huwa muḥsin* — while being a doer of good — was explained as *iḥsān* — doing good, making beautiful — the same *iḥsān* that encompasses parents, relatives, orphans, neighbours (4:36), that commands charity, kindness, reconciliation seeking God's pleasure (4:114), and that does good male or female with faith (4:124). *Wa ittabaʿa millata Ibrāhīma ḥanīfā* — and follows the creed of Abraham, inclining to truth and away from crookedness — was read as the *ḥanīf*, the pure monotheist who turns away from associators, as Abraham turned from his people's idols and obeyed command without altering creation (4:119). The three — submission, goodness, following Abraham upright — are the sūrah's definition of the best religion, against wishes that claimed grace by belonging (4:123) and against taking Satan as guardian instead of God (4:119).

**The Way of Abraham the Upright**

The phrase *millata Ibrāhīma ḥanīfā* was explained with history. *Millah* — creed, way — was read as the path God made clear as the noble ways of those before you (4:26), which Abraham exemplifies. *Ḥanīf* — upright, inclining — was explained as one who inclines from association (4:116) to the Single: Abraham was not of the associators (6:161) and was tested with commands and fulfilled them (2:124). The sūrah has said the People of the Book claim by wish, yet some distort words (4:46, 4:153), and that the Qur'an came confirming what came before it (4:47); following Abraham *ḥanīf* was read as return to the common monotheism before distortion, where invocation is of God alone — not female gods, nor Satan (4:117). The Way of Abraham was also linked to *We gave the descendants of Abraham the Book and wisdom and great authority* (4:54) and to *God chose Abraham as a close friend* here: Abraham's way is not tribal claim but submitted face and beautiful deed — the same *islām* that began with creation from a single soul (4:1) and that remains as spacious as the earth's havens (4:100).

**And God Chose Abraham as Close Friend**

The seal *wa ittakhadha Allāhu Ibrāhīma khalīlā* — and God chose, took, Abraham as a close friend — was explained with *khalīl* — intimate friend, the one whose love has penetrated the core (*khullah*). *Ittakhadha* — took — was read as divine choosing, not human claiming; the sūrah has said God elevates whomever He wills and knows who deserves favour (4:49, 4:70), and that to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth (4:126) — so friendship is by His taking, not by wish. The title *khalīl* was explained with reports of Abraham's hospitality, his steadfastness when thrown into the fire, and his plea for his father even after enmity was shown — a face fully submitted; God's taking him as *khalīl* is therefore not inherited status but the response to *submitted and did good*. Classical notes mentioned that the Prophet ﷺ said, *were I to take a close friend among you, I would have taken Abū Bakr — but your companion is the close friend of God* (al-Bukhārī 466; Muslim 2383 in similar wording), showing the station's uniqueness — yet the verse invites emulation: whoever submits and does good and follows that upright way is best in religion.

**A Verse That Answers Wishes With Abraham's Submission**

Placed after *those who do good, male or female, with faith will enter Paradise, not wronged a speck* (4:124) and before *to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth, and He is Fully Aware of everything* (4:126), this verse answers wishes with Abraham's submission. The sūrah removed claim by wish — *neither by your wishes nor those of the People of the Book* (4:123) — and gave Paradise by belief and good without wrong (4:124); now it asks who is better than the submitter, the doer of good, the follower of Abraham upright — and the answer is none. The sūrah has traced Satan's path — defying the Messenger after guidance (4:115), association's far straying (4:116), invoking females and Satan (4:117), the cursed share-taker (4:118), ordering cutting and altering (4:119), promising only delusion (4:120) — against God's path: the Book in truth (4:105), wisdom taught (4:113), no good except charity, kindness, reconciliation (4:114). Abraham is the human embodiment of God's path: he left his people's idols, submitted his face, and was taken as close friend. For the weak this is an accessible model: the best religion is not speculation about wishes but submission of face, beautification of deed, and following the upright way — whose Friend is the Owner of the heavens and earth.

**The Close Friend Whose Way Is the Believers' Path**

The phrase *the path of the believers* (4:115) was linked here to *millata Ibrāhīma*: the believers' path is Abraham's upright way, where defiance after clarity is refused. The sūrah that warns against taking disbelievers as allies for honour (4:139, 4:144), and that declares hypocrites in the lowest depth (4:145), makes Abraham the criterion: his alliance was with the Single; his honour was friendship taken by Him. The verse also echoes the judgment passage where grace preserved the Prophet ﷺ from being deceived (4:113): preservation came via Book and wisdom teaching what he did not know; Abraham's preservation came via upright submission. Both say: the best faith is submitted face, goodness, and the upright way — taken as friend by the One to whom all belongs. The next verse seals that ownership: to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth, and He is Fully Aware of everything (4:126).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:126

> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And Allah is Fully Aware of everything

**To God Alone Belongs Whatever Is in the Heavens and Earth**

The verse states *wa li Allāhi mā fī al-samāwāti wa mā fī al-arḍ* — and to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. *Mā fī al-samāwāti wa mā fī al-arḍ* — whatever is in heavens and on earth — was explained as absolute ownership: the angels nearest to Him who never disdain to serve (4:172); the single soul spread into humanity (4:1); the orphans' wealth held as trust (4:2, 4:10); the women whose dowries are given graciously (4:4); the inheritance shares appointed (4:11–12); the earth made spacious for emigration (4:100); the prayer shortened on travel (4:101); and the true promise whose two abodes are Gardens or Hell (4:121–122). *Li Allāh* — to God — was read as exclusive belonging, as the sūrah repeats *to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth* (4:131, 4:132) to frame this passage. The phrase was explained as the reply to invoking female gods besides Him (4:117) — they belong to Him, not beside Him — and to taking Satan as guardian instead of Him (4:119) — the guardian taken belongs to Him, and is cursed (4:118). The sūrah has said grace is not by wishes (4:123), that Abraham was taken as close friend (4:125) — friendship with the Owner of all is the highest honour — and that whoever desires the reward of this world, with God is the reward of both worlds (4:134); ownership here is the ground of those promises.

**And God Is Fully Aware of Everything**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu bi kulli shayʾin muḥīṭā* — and God is Fully Aware, Encompassing, of everything — was explained with *muḥīṭ* — encompassing, encircling — the same name that sealed night plotting in His presence — *He is Fully Aware of what they do* (4:108) — now universalised to everything. *Bi kulli shayʾin* — of every thing — was read as covering the heavens and earth just said to belong to Him; the charity, kindness, and reconciliation commanded (4:114); the dispute judged by what He shows (4:105); the good of male and female with faith (4:124); and the measures of the speck (*naqīr*, 4:124) and the atom (4:40), which He never wrongs. The sūrah has sealed knowledge variously — All-Knowing, All-Wise where sin is earned (4:111); All-Hearing, All-Seeing where trusts are judged (4:58); All-Aware of what you do where verification was commanded (4:94); *Muḥīṭ* where night hides (4:108) — here *Muḥīṭ* of everything gathers them: nothing escapes the perimeter, because everything belongs. Early notes linked *muḥīṭ* to spaciousness: the earth was said to be spacious (4:97, 4:100), yet His awareness is more spacious — encompassing the spacious.

**A Verse That Follows Best Faith With Ownership**

Placed after *who is better in religion than the submitter, doer of good, follower of Abraham — whom God took as friend* (4:125), this verse follows best faith with the ownership that makes such friendship intelligible. Abraham was taken as *khalīl* by the One to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth; his upright creed was submission to the Owner — not to the female gods who themselves belong to Him and are invoked only as Satan's share (4:117–118). The sūrah has said *God suffices as Guardian and Helper* (4:45), *God is sufficient as Trustee* (4:81, 4:132), *God is sufficient as Witness* (4:79); to say *to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth* is to say that guardianship, help, trusteeship, and witnessing are His by right of ownership. Where the sūrah taught that the Book was sent with truth to judge by what He shows (4:105), ownership as *Muḥīṭ* explains why judging by what He shows succeeds: the One who shows is the One who owns and encompasses.

**The Belonging That Makes Oaths and Treaties Possible**

The sūrah repeats *to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth* as the oath-ground for the contracts this chapter has detailed: the firm commitment of marriage — *mīthāq ghalīẓ* — taken from women (4:21); the treaty with covenanted peoples, whose blood-money is delivered even when the killing was mistaken (4:92), whose allies are excepted from hostility (4:90); and the single soul's tie that makes family honour a due (4:1). To say all belongs to Him is to say oaths sworn by Him have the Owner as witness — *God is sufficient as Witness* (4:79) — and trustee — *God is sufficient as Trustee* (4:132). The sūrah has shown that those who trade a portion of the Book for misguidance and believe in *jibt* (4:51) act as if oaths belonged to other lords; this verse returns every *mā* — every thing — to the One whose earth is spacious and whose promise is ever true, so that settlement between spouses (4:128) and reconciliation between people (4:114) hold, because the Holder holds all.

**Ownership That Makes Wishes Void and Promises True**

The pairing — *to God belongs* and *He encompasses everything* — was explained as making *neither by your wishes* (4:123) void and *God's promise is ever true; whose word is more truthful?* (4:122) true: wishes do not move ownership; promise from the Owner does. The sūrah has moved from two abodes — Hell without escape (4:121) and Gardens forever, true (4:122) — through the law of wishes, the entry of doers of good with faith not wronged a speck (4:124), and best faith as submission to the Owner following Abraham, whom the Owner took as friend (4:125) — to the Owner's declaration that all belongs and all is encompassed. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the declaration is lightening: the One to whom your lack of device and way was known when unknown to others (4:98) is the One who owns the heavens and earth and encompasses — so your hoped pardon (4:99), your emigration to many havens (4:100), and your shortened prayer (4:101) are all under the same Ownership. The next passage uses that ownership to teach about women: they ask you for a ruling regarding women — say, God instructs you about them, and what is recited to you in the Book concerns orphan women deprived of their due yet wished in marriage, and helpless children, and standing for orphans with justice — and whatever good you do is well known to Him (4:127).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:127

> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ regarding women. Say, "It is Allah Who instructs you regarding them. Instruction has ˹already˺ been revealed in the Book concerning the orphan women you deprive of their due rights but still wish to marry, also helpless children, as well as standing up for orphans' rights. And whatever good you do is certainly well known to Allah."

**They Ask You Regarding Women — God Instructs**

The verse states *wa yastaftūnaka fī al-nisāʾi qul Allāhu yuftīkum fīhinna* — they ask you, seek your ruling, regarding women — say: God instructs you, gives you ruling, regarding them. *Yastaftūnaka* — to seek a ruling — was explained as the community asking the Prophet ﷺ about women's rights, as earlier the chapter taught them to marry orphan women with justice or marry others — two, three, or four — where justice is feared (4:3), to give dowries graciously (4:4), and to return orphans' property with witnesses (4:6). *Qul Allāhu yuftīkum fīhinna* — say, God gives you ruling about them — was read as referral to the Owner to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth and who is Fully Aware of everything (4:126); instruction is not by wishes (4:123) nor by Satan's ordering to alter creation (4:119), but by the One who created from a single soul and spread men and women (4:1). The sūrah has shown that the Book was sent in truth to judge between people by what He shows (4:105); here the Book judges between men and women as between peoples. Early reports linked the asking to questions about orphan girls under guardianship, where the guardian desired to marry them without full dowry; the verse ties past instruction to present asking — a single instruction, extended.

**Instruction Already Revealed — Orphan Women Deprived Yet Wished in Marriage**

The reference *wa mā yutlā ʿalaykum fī al-kitābi fī yatāmā al-nisāʾi allātī lā tuʾtūnahunna mā kutiba lahunna wa targhabūna an tankiḥūhunna* — and what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women you deprive of what is prescribed for them, yet desire to marry — was explained as the earlier ruling in 4:3 — *if you fear you will not be just to the orphan women, marry other women* — and in 4:19–21 — not to inherit women against their will, and the firm commitment of marriage. *Mā kutiba lahunna* — what is prescribed, written for them — was read as dowry, inheritance, kind maintenance: the obligatory shares for women, whether little or much (4:7). *Targhabūna an tankiḥūhunna* — you desire to marry them — was explained with two inclinations the guardian might have: to marry the beautiful or wealthy orphan while withholding her due for her property — or to leave her unmarried, refusing her marriage to protect her wealth — both counted as injustice. The instruction already recited — *mā yutlā* — was read as showing the Qur'an as ongoing recital: what was revealed at the start is re-cited as the answer to new asking, so that the instruction about women is not new but the same justice extended.

**Also Helpless Children, and Standing for Orphans With Justice**

The continuation *wa al-mustaḍʿafīna mina al-wildāni wa an taqūmū li al-yatāmā bi al-qiṣṭ* — and for the helpless children, and that you stand up for orphans with justice — was explained as the same inclusive justice seen where men, women, and children were named for pardon and haven (4:75, 4:98). *Mustaḍʿafīna mina al-wildān* — helpless among children — were those without guardian, whose shares the covetous might diminish. *Wa an taqūmū li al-yatāmā bi al-qiṣṭ* — and that you stand for orphans with equity — was read as the command *return trusts and judge with fairness* (4:58) applied to orphans as the prime trust: the sūrah warns against devouring orphans' wealth as fire into bellies (4:10) and commands testing them until marriageable, then returning property with witnesses (4:6); here it generalises: stand up — as you stand for prayer at its appointed time (4:103) and for justice though against yourselves (4:135). The sūrah has said that God is sufficient as Witness (4:79) and Trustee (4:132); to stand for orphans *with justice* is to stand with Him as witness.

**And Whatever Good You Do Is Well Known to God**

The seal *wa mā tafʿalū min khayrin fa inna Allāha kāna bihi ʿalīmā* — and whatever good you do, indeed God is ever All-Knowing of it — was explained as the encouragement matching the warning. *Whatever good you do* was read as the good commanded in secret talks — charity, kindness, reconciliation, seeking His pleasure (4:114) — and the good of submitting the face while doing good, following Abraham (4:125), and the good of male or female with faith, entering Paradise without wrong of a speck (4:124). *God is ever All-Knowing of it* was explained as that He who owns the heavens and earth (4:126) and is Fully Aware of everything knows the speck of good as He knows the speck not wronged (4:124) and multiplies rather than wrongs an atom (4:40). The sūrah has said *you do not know* which of the heirs is nearer in benefit (4:11); here He knows the good done for the orphan girl deprived yet desired, for the helpless child, for the orphan stood for. For the weak this is the promise: good for the weakest is the most known.

**A Verse That Follows Ownership With Instruction for the Weakest**

Placed after *to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth, and He is Fully Aware of everything* (4:126), this verse follows ownership with instruction for the weakest owned: women, asked about. The sūrah that opened with creation from a single soul and honouring ties (4:1) — and will say humans are ever inclined to selfishness, yet gracious mindfulness is All-Aware (4:128) — here says: the One to whom all belongs instructs you regarding them, and the instruction already recited about orphan women and helpless children is this: give what is prescribed or marry others with justice — and stand for orphans with equity. The circle closes where the sūrah began with orphans' wealth and marriage justice (4:2–4): the question reopens it, and the answer cites the earlier verses as still recited, still ruling — so that the chapter's ethic — return trusts, judge fairly, verify reports, be sure before fighting, do not advocate for deceit — is again applied to the household. The next verses apply that ethic within marriage: if a woman fears indifference or neglect, no blame to seek settlement, which is best — though humans incline to selfishness, yet gracious mindfulness is All-Aware (4:128).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:128

> If a woman fears indifference or neglect from her husband, there is no blame on either of them if they seek ˹fair˺ settlement, which is best. Humans are ever inclined to selfishness. But if you are gracious and mindful ˹of Allah˺, surely Allah is All-Aware of what you do

**If a Woman Fears Indifference or Neglect — No Blame to Seek Settlement**

The verse opens *wa in imraʾatun khāfat min baʿlihā nushūzan aw iʿrāḍan fa lā junāḥa ʿalayhimā an yuṣliḥā baynahumā ṣulḥā* — if a woman fears from her husband ill-conduct — *nushūz*, rising against — or desertion — *iʿrāḍ*, turning away — there is no blame upon them both if they reconcile, effect a settlement between them. *Khāfat* — feared — was explained as sensed and apprehended with signs, as earlier *if you fear ill-conduct* from women, advice and measures were given (4:34), and *if you anticipate a split, appoint mediators* (4:35): fear here is the moral perception that precedes action, not mere anxiety. *Nushūz* — rising — was read as the husband's rising above his duty, refusing what is right; *iʿrāḍ* — turning away — as withdrawal, neglect, leaving the marriage hanging (4:129). *Fa lā junāḥa ʿalayhimā* — no blame upon them both — was explained as the law's lightening alongside *no blame* to shorten prayer on travel (4:101) and *no blame* to set aside weapons in rain or illness while precaution remains (4:102): here settlement carries no sin. *An yuṣliḥā baynahumā ṣulḥā* — to reconcile with a settlement — was read as any fair adjustment: she waives part of her maintenance in exchange for keeping the marriage; he returns kindness. Early reports illustrated it with Sawdah bint Zamʿah offering her day to ʿĀʾishah to remain among the Prophet's ﷺ wives — accepted without blame. The sūrah has said most secret talks have no good except charity, kindness, and reconciliation, seeking God's pleasure (4.114); settlement is that reconciliation.

**Settlement — Which Is Best**

The affirmation *wa al-ṣulḥu khayr* — and settlement is best — was explained as the sūrah's maxim for dispute. *Al-ṣulḥ* — settlement — was read as the peace that mends: the *iṣlāḥ bayna al-nās* commanded as the good secret talk (4:114) and as the mediators' goal (4:35). *Khayr* — best — was explained as better than splitting, where the woman fears *nushūz* or *iʿrāḍ*, yet a fair settlement keeps ties honoured (4:1), as the single soul's creation spread into families whose ties are due. The phrase was linked to *appoint a mediator from his family and hers; if they desire reconciliation, God will bring harmony* (4:35): settlement is not the enemy of justice but its embodiment where justice is equity plus mercy. The sūrah has said humans crave what God gave some over others (4:32) and that burdens are lightened because humans are weak (4:28); to prefer settlement where the alternative is a marriage left hanging is to prefer the light, kind path — while the writ of prayer still holds at its fixed times (4:103). Classical notes added that *al-ṣulḥu khayr* is general: wherever reconciliation is possible, it is best — provided the rights prescribed for orphan women (4:127) are not voided.

**Humans Are Ever Inclined to Selfishness**

The diagnostic *wa uḥḍirat al-anfusu al-shuḥḥ* — and selves were made ever-present with selfishness, stinginess, avarice — was explained as human inclination. *Uḥḍirat* — made present, kept at hand — was read as that greed attends the soul, is ever near, as *humankind was created weak* (4:28) and *God does not like the stingy who promote stinginess* (4:37). *Shuḥḥ* — selfishness, grasping — was explained as the soul's holding onto its share, its comfort, its wealth, its right — unwilling to concede where settlement requires waiving. The sūrah has shown stinginess promoted among people (4:37); here *shuḥḥ* is the barrier to settlement: each side fears losing. To name *shuḥḥ* was read as the Book's realism before its ideal: settlement is best, yet greed is present with souls — so settlement needs graciousness and mindfulness to overcome what is near. The same selfishness was seen where the dowry is sought back unjustly (4:20) and where the lagger wishes gain without risk (4:73).

**But If You Are Gracious and Mindful — God Is All-Aware**

The encouragement *wa in tuḥsinū wa tattaqū fa inna Allāha kāna bi-mā taʿmalūna khabīrā* — but if you do good, act graciously, and are mindful of God, then indeed God is ever All-Aware of what you do — was explained with *tuḥsinū* — to do *iḥsān*, to be gracious — the same graciousness as the one who submits his face and does good following Abraham (4:125), and who does good, male or female, with faith (4:124). *Wa tattaqū* — and are mindful — was read as the sūrah's *taqwā* that began *be mindful of your Lord who created you from a single soul* (4:1) and that seals the next verse — if you do what is right and are mindful, He is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:129). *God is ever All-Aware of what you do* was explained as that He who owns the heavens and earth (4.126) and knows whatever good you do (4:127) is aware of the settlement sought, of the selfishness present, of the graciousness where offered. The sūrah has sealed knowledge variously — *ʿAlīm Ḥakīm* where sin is earned (4:111), *Muḥīṭ* where night plots (4:108) — here *Khabīr* fits the act: He is aware of what you do in settlement, where your doing is waiving and being gracious.

**A Verse That Follows Instruction for Orphans With Instruction for Wives**

Placed after the instruction for orphan women deprived of their due and helpless children (4:127), this verse follows that instruction with settlement where a wife fears rising or turning away. The sūrah that began with marriage limits — two, three, or four where justice is feared, else one (4:3) — returns to marriage limits at its other end: *you will never be able to do perfect justice between wives, however keen* (4:129). Between those limits is this middle path — settlement is best — where the soul's greed is named as ever-present, yet graciousness and mindfulness are the act that God, All-Aware, sees. For the weak this is protective: the woman who fears *nushūz* or *iʿrāḍ* is not told the only path is divorce; no blame attaches to seeking a settlement that keeps the marriage with adjusted rights — and for either to be gracious and mindful is best. The next verse states the limit of justice between wives and the ethic of not inclining wholly away — do not leave the other hanging — and if you do right and are mindful, He is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:129).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:129

> You will never be able to maintain ˹emotional˺ justice between your wives—no matter how keen you are. So do not totally incline towards one leaving the other in suspense. And if you do what is right and are mindful ˹of Allah˺, surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**You Will Never Be Able to Be Just Between Wives, However Keen**

The verse states *wa lan tastaṭīʿū an taʿdilū bayna al-nisāʾi wa law ḥaraṣtum* — and you will never be able to be just, equitable, between wives, even if you are keen, eager. *Lan tastaṭīʿū* — never be able — was explained as incapacity in emotional justice — love and inclination of the heart, which cannot be weighed — even where legal justice — maintenance, nights, kindness — remains possible. *An taʿdilū* — to equalise — was read as making equal in love, in the heart's turning; the sūrah elsewhere shows even the Prophet's ﷺ heart inclined, where he was taught to say *O God, this is my division in what I have control of; do not blame me for what You control and I do not* (Abū Dāwūd 2134, graded ḥasan). *Wa law ḥaraṣtum* — however keen — was explained as that keenness does not create capacity, because God created inclination unequal, as humanity was created weak (4:28) and greed is ever present with souls (4:128). The sūrah's marriage limits — two, three, or four where justice is feared, else one (4:3) — assume justice as condition; here the condition is refined: legal justice remains commanded; emotional equality is declared impossible — so the one who cannot equalise love is not told the faith is divorce, but is taught how to incline.

**So Do Not Incline Entirely, Leaving the Other Suspended**

The command *fa lā tamīlū kulla al-mayli fa tadharūhā ka al-muʿallaqah* — so do not incline entirely toward one, so that you leave the other hanging, suspended — was explained with *mayl* — inclination, leaning — the same word as the great deviation the desire-followers wish (4:27) and the one sweeping assault wished upon the heedless (4:102). *Kulla al-mayl* — all inclination — was read as total turning to one and away from another: not sharing nights, not providing, not speaking, so that the wife remains *muʿallaqah* — suspended, hanging — neither fully married nor divorced, like one tied up with no way. *Fa tadharūhā ka al-muʿallaqah* — leaving her as the hanging one — was explained as the sūrah's protection for the wife who earlier feared *nushūz* or turning away (4:128): there the remedy was settlement, which is best, where both sought it; here the remedy is the prohibition of total inclining that creates the hanging. Not to incline entirely is to practise mindfulness — *taqwā* — where love cannot be equalled.

**And If You Do What Is Right and Are Mindful — He Is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful**

The encouragement *wa in tuṣliḥū wa tattaqū fa inna Allāha kāna Ghafūran Raḥīmā* — and if you set right, reconcile, do what is right, and are mindful, then indeed God is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — was explained with *tuṣliḥū* — the same *iṣlāḥ* as reconciliation between people (4:114), as the mediators' desired reconciliation (4:35), and as the settlement that is best (4:128). *Wa tattaqū* — and are mindful — was read as the sūrah's *taqwā* that began with mindfulness of the Lord who created from a single soul (4:1) and that seals every marriage rule: where emotional justice is impossible yet legal justice is commanded, setting right and mindfulness cover the shortfall. *Ghafūran Raḥīmā* — All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — was explained as the seal that excuses what you cannot equalise while holding you to what you can — not inclining entirely. Where the intentional killer was sealed with anger and curse (4:93) and the deceitful with not loved (4:107), the husband who cannot equalise love, yet does not incline totally and sets right and is mindful, is sealed with forgiveness and mercy — matching the earlier counsel to ask God for bounty rather than crave what He gave others (4:32): what you cannot equalise, seek from His forgiveness.

**A Verse That Places Limit Beside Permission**

Placed after settlement is best where she fears ill-conduct or turning away, and selves were made ever-present with greed (4:128), this verse places limit beside permission. The sūrah permitted settlement, waiving part of a right to keep the marriage; here it acknowledges that perfect equalising of hearts after settlement remains impossible. The two verses together teach the household ethic after the public ethic of judging by the Book (4:105) and the rule of secret talks (4:114): private settlement is best, yet private hearts remain unequal — so do not make the inequality total. The sūrah has shown that the Owner of the heavens and earth is Fully Aware of everything (4:126) and that whatever good you do is well known to Him (4:127); He knows the inclination you cannot weigh — and He is All-Forgiving for it, where you do not incline entirely and you set right and are mindful. For the weak this is protective: the wife left suspended is named as a wrong to be avoided, as the orphan girls were protected from being married for profit (4:3, 4:127); here the protection is the prohibition of total inclining.

**The Two Kinds of Inclination the Sūrah Has Named**

The word *mayl* was traced through the chapter: the great inclination away from God's way that the desire-followers wish (4:27) is one *mayl*; the husband's total inclining to one wife, leaving the other suspended, is the other *mayl* — within what God permitted, between wives. The first is prohibited absolutely; the second is limited — do not incline entirely. The sūrah that warns not to follow desires (4:27, 4:115) here warns that even lawful love can become unlawful neglect where it is total. The medicine is the sūrah's general medicine after exposing night plotting and thrown sin — *whoever wrongs himself then seeks, finds Him All-Forgiving* (4:110) — here expressed as *if you set right and are mindful, He is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful*. The next verse sets the other face: if they separate, He will enrich both from His bounty, and He is Ever-Bountiful, All-Wise (4:130) — so that staying with settlement and leaving with enrichment are both under mercy.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:130

> But if they choose to separate, Allah will enrich both of them from His bounties. And Allah is Ever-Bountiful, All-Wise

**But If They Separate — He Will Enrich Both**

The verse states *wa in yatafarraqā yughni Allāhu kullan min saʿatihi* — but if the two separate, God will enrich, make free of need, each of them from His bounty, His spaciousness, His abundance. *Yatafarraqā* — to separate, to part — was explained as divorce or separation after settlement was named best (4:128) yet total inclining was prohibited (4:129): where remaining together in a hanging marriage was not chosen, and settlement could not hold. *Yughni* — to enrich, to suffice, to make independent — was read as God making each free of need where the other was expected to suffice, as the emigrant finds many havens and abundance where the earth is spacious (4:100). *Kullan* — each, both — was explained as each — the man and the woman — not only the husband upon whom maintenance lay, nor only the wife who feared ill-conduct (4:128); both are enriched. *Min saʿatihi* — from His spaciousness — was explained as from His wide provision, the same *saʿah* as *many havens and spaciousness* promised the emigrant (4:100), and as *to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth* (4:126), whose spaciousness is the source. Early reports linked the verse to households where settlement with waiver was offered yet separation was chosen: no shame in separation where enrichment is promised to both from Him.

**From His Bounty — Min Saʿatihi**

The phrase *min saʿatihi* was explained as from His amplitude, which does not narrow when given, as the sūrah says *ask God for His bounty; God has perfect knowledge of all things* (4:32) where craving what others have is forbidden — here bounty is given to both from His bounty, not by taking between them. *Saʿah* — spaciousness — was read as breadth of provision, dwelling, tranquillity, and replacement — spouse, household, sustenance — as the sūrah says the single soul spread into countless men and women (4:1), showing that the earth's spaciousness holds replacements. The contrast with *shuḥḥ* — the greed ever present with souls (4:128) — was noted: where settlement failed because each kept grasping, separation enriched from spaciousness removes grasping by giving each from Him, not by stripping one. Where the sūrah warns there is no good in most secret talks except charity, kindness, and reconciliation (4:114), separation where graciousness and mindfulness remain is itself counted as good where it removes a hanging — *muʿallaqah* (4:129) — and enrichment from spaciousness is the broad good that follows.

**And God Is Ever-Bountiful, All-Wise**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu Wāsiʿan Ḥakīmā* — and God is Ever-Bountiful, All-Wise — was explained as suitability. *Wāsiʿ* — Wide, Bountiful, Encompassing — was read as whose bounty is wide enough to enrich both without diminishing, as He is Fully Aware, encompassing everything (4:126), and as the earth is spacious for emigration (4:97). *Ḥakīm* — All-Wise — was explained as the wisdom that legislates both staying — settlement best (4:128) with the prohibition of total inclining (4:129) — and leaving — enrichment from bounty where they separate — each in its place, as He is All-Knowing, All-Wise where sin is earned (4.111) and where pursuit must not falter (4:104). The sūrah has shown that God wills to make clear, to guide to noble ways, to turn in mercy (4:26–28); to be *Wāsiʿ Ḥakīm* here is to be the One whose spaciousness is guided by wisdom: not enrichment that encourages frivolous divorce, but enrichment where settlement was tried and a hanging remained. The two names together show that separation is not a failure of the law but a provision within the law, made by the Wide in wisdom.

**A Verse That Follows Limit With Provision**

Placed after *you will never be able to be just between wives however keen; do not incline entirely leaving the other suspended; yet if you set right and are mindful, He is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful* (4:129), this verse follows limit with provision. The sūrah's ethic for the household mirrors its ethic for the battlefield: many havens where emigration is chosen (4:100); shortening where travel and fear constrict (4:101); guarding where the enemy wishes neglect for a sweep (4:102); remembrance in all postures (4:103) — here, many enrichments where separation is chosen after settlement was tried. The sūrah that warns not to deviate by following desires (4:27) and not to follow other than the believers' path (4:115) does not bind spouses to a hanging marriage as piety; it says separation enriched from His bounty is better than a hanging, as settlement is better than ill-conduct. For the weak this is the lightest of provisions: where you feared rising or turning away and settlement with waiver was offered, if the tie still cannot be lived without total inclining — He will suffice both from His wide bounty.

**The Wide Who Can Replace Without Diminishing**

The verb *yughni* — to enrich, to suffice — was linked to *ask God for His bounty* (4:32) and to *with God are the rewards of this world and the Hereafter* (4:134): the enrichment promised here is not a vague hope but a writ from the Wide. Classical notes added that *kullan min saʿatihi* — each from His bounty — proves that provision is not zero-sum between the two who part: His spaciousness gives to each separately, as *to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth* (4:126) — so that the woman enriched is not enriched at the man's expense before God, though inter-human rights remain judged fairly as the Book judges (4:105, 4:135). The next passage anchors that bounty in universal ownership: to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth; We have commanded those given the Scripture before you, and you, to be mindful; if you disobey — to Him still belongs all — and He is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy (4:131).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:131

> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Indeed, We have commanded those given the Scripture before you, as well as you, to be mindful of Allah. But if you disobey, then ˹know that˺ to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. And Allah is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy

**To God Belongs Whatever Is in Heavens and Earth — and Commanded to Be Mindful**

The verse opens *wa li Allāhi mā fī al-samāwāti wa mā fī al-arḍ* — and to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth — repeated from 4:126 and to be repeated at 4:132, bracketing the passage on settlement and enrichment. *Whatever is in the heavens and on the earth* was explained as absolute ownership encompassing the single soul spread into humanity (4:1), the orphans' trusts (4:2), the dowries (4:4), the inheritance shares (4:11–12), the earth made spacious (4:100), the wives between whom justice cannot be perfected (4:129) yet whose separation is enriched from His bounty (4:130). *Wa laqad waṣṣaynā alladhīna ūtū al-kitāba min qablikum wa iyyākum ani ittaqū Allāh* — and indeed We have commanded, charged, those given the Scripture before you, as well as you, to be mindful of God — was explained as universal counsel: the same mindfulness that began the sūrah — *be mindful of your Lord who created you from a single soul* (4:1) — that seals settlement — *if you are gracious and mindful, God is All-Aware* (4:128) — and seals not inclining entirely — *if you set right and are mindful, He is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful* (4:129). To command those given the Scripture before you and you was read as continuity: the earlier Scriptures and the Qur'an enjoin the same *taqwā*, as *We gave the descendants of Abraham the Book and wisdom and great authority* (4:54) and *He taught you what you did not know; great is His favour* (4:113) — the teaching is one.

**But If You Disobey — to Him Still Belongs All**

The condition *wa in takfurū fa inna li Allāhi mā fī al-samāwāti wa mā fī al-arḍ* — but if you disbelieve, are ungrateful, then indeed to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth — was explained as the sūrah's reminder that mindfulness is not out of need for the Owner. *In takfurū* — if you disbelieve, are ungrateful — was read as covering both creedal disbelief and practical ingratitude: withholding trust; inclining totally, leaving the other suspended (4:129); devouring wealth unjustly (4:29); claiming wishes as grace (4:123). *Then to Him still belongs all* was explained as that disobedience does not reduce His ownership: the spaciousness that enriched both after separation (4:130) remains; the Gardens promised true (4:122) remain; even Hell without escape (4:121) remains under His dominion. The sūrah has said *whoever desires the reward of this world — with God are the rewards of this world and the Hereafter* (4:134): to disobey is to refuse the mindfulness that would have obtained both. The clause was linked to *whoever defies the Messenger after guidance and follows other than the believers' path — We let him pursue what he chose, then burn* (4:115): letting pursue does not transfer ownership; the Hell to which he is burned still belongs to Him, as the Gardens do.

**And God Is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu Ghaniyyan Ḥamīdā* — and God is Self-Sufficient, free of need, and Praiseworthy — was explained with *Ghanī* — Rich, Independent — and *Ḥamīd* — Praised, Praiseworthy — the same pairing where hypocrites are warned for seeking honour through allies — *surely all honour belongs to God* (4:139). To be *Ghanī* was read as that His command to be mindful is not for His need but for the servants' good: He does not need their *taqwā*, as the earth's spacious havens (4:100) were given not because He needed emigrants but because they needed refuge. *Ḥamīd* — Praiseworthy — was explained as that He is praised whether they obey or disobey, as the sūrah says *to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth, and He is Fully Aware of everything* (4:126) — praise belongs to the Fully Aware who measures even the speck not wronged (4:124). The two names together show that mindfulness enriches the mindful, not the Self-Sufficient; and ungratefulness impoverishes the ungrateful, not the Rich.

**A Verse That Brackets Settlement With Ownership and Command**

Placed after enrichment from His bounty where they separate, and He is Ever-Bountiful, All-Wise (4:130), this verse brackets settlement with ownership and universal command. The sūrah has moved from orphan women deprived yet desired, helpless children, and orphans stood for with justice, well known to Him (4:127) → the wife fearing ill-conduct or turning away, settlement best though greed is ever-present, yet graciousness and mindfulness are known to Him (4:128) → the impossibility of perfect emotional justice, the prohibition of total inclining, forgiveness upon setting right and mindfulness (4:129) → separation enriched from His spaciousness (4:130) — and here all is grounded: *to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth; We have commanded those before you and you to be mindful; if you disobey, to Him still belongs all; He is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy*. The sūrah that began *be mindful of your Lord who created you from a single soul* (4:1) returns to *be mindful* as its abiding charge for every Scripture people. For the weak this is the lightest of commands: where total justice between wives was declared impossible, mindfulness remains possible — and where separation was given, mindfulness remains the charge, whose Keeper needs nothing, and whose praise remains though you disobey.

**The Charge That Survives Disobedience**

The phrase *wa laqad waṣṣaynā* — and We have surely charged — was explained as a covenantal charge that survives disobedience, because ownership survives disobedience. Where the deceitful hide from people while He is with them where they plot displeasing speech (4:108), and where night plotting seems to succeed in this life but not before Him on the Day (4:109), the charge to be mindful is the daylight that night cannot void — because the night's owner is the One who commands mindfulness. The verse generalises the household law into cosmology: the same heavens and earth that belong to Him contain both the single soul spread (4:1) and the many havens for emigration (4:100), the prayer at fixed writ (4:103) and the two true abodes (4:121–122); to be mindful within them is to live inside an ownership that is Self-Sufficient yet Praiseworthy — so that obedience adds no need, and disobedience subtracts nothing except from the disobedient.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:132

> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs

**To God Belongs Whatever Is in Heavens and Earth — Again**

The verse restates *wa li Allāhi mā fī al-samāwāti wa mā fī al-arḍ* — and to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth — the third repetition after 4:126 and 4:131, sealing the passage on women, settlement, enrichment, and the universal charge to be mindful. *Whatever is in the heavens and on the earth* was explained to include all as before: the single soul and its mate (4:1); the orphans' wealth, the dowries, the shares; the earth spacious for haven (4:100); the wives between whom inclination is limited (4:129) yet each enriched from His bounty upon separation (4:130); and the heavens under which the fear prayer kept its vigilance (4:102). To repeat ownership three times was read as emphasis after law: where the chapter legislates for the weakest — the orphan girl deprived yet desired (4:127), the wife fearing ill-conduct where settlement is best (4:128), the suspended wife not left hanging (4:129) — the legislation is grounded in Ownership, so that no wish (4:123) and no Satanic order to slit and alter (4:119) can claim title. The sūrah has said the Book was sent with truth to judge between people by what He shows (4:105); to judge by that showing is to judge within His ownership — as witnesses for justice even against yourselves (4:135). The Meccan assignment of daughters as female gods besides Him (4:117) and the claim of Satan's appointed share (4:118) are both answered here: they belong to Him.

**And God Is Sufficient as Trustee of Affairs**

The seal *wa kafā bi Allāhi wakīlā* — and God is sufficient as Trustee, Disposer of affairs — was explained with *wakīl* — trustee, agent, defender — the same *wakīl* asked about on the Day — *who will be their trustee?* (4:109) — and the One the Prophet ﷺ was told to trust — *put your trust in God; God is sufficient as Trustee* (4:81) after turning away from the night contradictors. *Kafā bi Allāhi wakīlā* was read as that His trusteeship suffices for every affair where spouses fear, orphans are stood for, emigrants seek haven, prayers are guarded. The sūrah has sealed sufficiency variously: sufficient as Guardian and Helper (4:45), sufficient as Trustee after recording the night schemes (4:81); here *sufficient as Trustee* fits ownership — because to Him belongs all, He suffices to dispose of all. To take Him as *wakīl* was explained as entrusting affairs after doing what is incumbent: settlement sought (4:128), total inclining avoided (4:129), separation where needed, enriched from His bounty (4:130), mindfulness kept where commanded (4:131). Where the deceitful advocates seek to plead for self-wrongers in this life (4:107–109) and find no trustee on the Day for deceit, the believer who seeks settlement graciously finds the Trustee who suffices.

**A Verse That Moves From Owner to Trustee**

Placed after *We have commanded those before you and you to be mindful; if you disobey, to Him still belongs all; He is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy* (4:131), this verse moves from Owner to Trustee. The sūrah bracketed settlement and enrichment between ownership and *taqwā*; now it adds sufficiency: ownership without trusteeship would be awed but not approached; trusteeship says entrust. The sūrah has shown that those who put trust in Him and turn away from the night contradictors are covered (4:81), that the emigrant who leaves home toward God and His Messenger has his reward secured upon Him (4:100), and that the helpless hoped to be pardoned have *ʿAfuww Ghafūr* (4:99). To say *God is sufficient as Trustee* is to say the same for every hanging not left and every settlement made: entrust, and He suffices. The sūrah has warned *do not be an advocate for the deceitful* (4:105) and *no good in most secret talks except charity, kindness, reconciliation* (4:114); the Trustee who suffices is a better audience for secret counsel than the people from whom deceit hides (4:108).

**Sufficiency That Makes Wishes Unnecessary and Promises True**

The pairing — *to Him belongs* and *He suffices as Trustee* — was explained as making *neither by your wishes… whoever commits evil will be recompensed accordingly* (4:123) unnecessary to wish, and *God's promise is ever true; whose word is more truthful?* (4:122) sufficient to trust. The sūrah has contrasted Satan's promise — only delusion (4:120), ending in Hell without escape (4:121) — with God's true promise, ending in Gardens forever (4:122); to take the True Promiser as trustee is to take the only promise that is not delusion. Where the sūrah says *with God are the rewards of this world and the Hereafter* (4:134), sufficiency as Trustee explains why both are with Him: He disposes both. For the weak this is direct: the orphan for whom you stand with justice (4:127), the wife not left hanging (4:129), the two enriched after separation (4:130) — all are affairs whose Trustee suffices, so that you need not be left hanging nor leave another hanging, but can settle or part entrusted to the Sufficient.

**A Short Verse That Anchors Entrusting After Legislating**

Though only *to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth; He suffices as Trustee* — the verse anchors entrusting after legislating. The chapter has legislated from the single soul through orphans, marriage, inheritance, trusts, prayer, judgment, charity, and Abraham's way, and here returns to its pillar: ownership grounds the law; trusteeship carries it. The sūrah that began *be mindful of your Lord who created you from a single soul and its mate* (4:1) and that will say *if He wills, He can remove you, O humanity, and bring others — He is Most Capable* (4:133) — places between them this Trustee: sufficient — so that the creature who can be removed (4:133), and who may desire this world's reward (4:134), knows to whom affairs are entrusted when wishes fail and He remains.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:133

> If it is His Will, He can remove you altogether, O humanity, and replace you with others. And Allah is Most Capable to do so

**If He Will — He Can Remove You and Bring Others**

The verse states *in yashāʾ yudhhibkum ayyuhā al-nāsu wa yaʾti bi-ākharīn* — if He wills, He can remove you altogether, O humanity, and bring others in your place. *In yashāʾ* — if He wills — was explained with the will that governs the ownership just declared — *to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth* (4:126, 4:131, 4:132) — where *Wāsiʿ*, *Ghanī*, and *Ḥamīd* show He does not need you. *Yudhhibkum* — to remove, take away — was read as removal of a whole generation, as He removes one people and brings another where mindfulness is not kept. *Ayyuhā al-nās* — O humanity — was explained as address beyond the believers to all, as the sūrah opened *O humanity, be mindful of your Lord who created you from a single soul* (4:1) — and here warns humanity that the single soul's spread is not irreplaceable. *Wa yaʾti bi-ākharīn* — and bring others — was explained as replacement with those who are mindful where you disobeyed, as the Qur'an says elsewhere *if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, and they will not be like you* (47:38). Early reports illustrated *O humanity* here as the Meccans who invoked female gods besides Him (4:117) and took Satan as guardian (4:119); to tell them He can remove them is to tell them their claimed shares are not needed. The sūrah has shown that the emigrant finds many havens where the earth is spacious (4:100) — a spaciousness that can receive others if you remain, and do without you if you refuse.

**And God Is Most Capable to Do So**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu ʿalā dhālika qadīrā* — and God is Most Capable over that — was explained with *qadīr* — capable, powerful, determining — the One who created from a single soul spread into countless (4:1) is capable to return that spread to another. *ʿAlā dhālika* — over that — removal and bringing — was read as capability, not empty threat, as *God does not wrong even an atom* (4:40) is measure, so capability over removal is the measure of power. The sūrah has said He is Ever-Bountiful, All-Wise where He enriches both after separation (4:130), and Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy where mindfulness is commanded (4:131); capability to remove is the power behind bounty and self-sufficiency: He enriches from His bounty because He can remove and bring without loss. Where the sūrah says *with God are the rewards of this world and the Hereafter* (4:134), capability to replace explains why both rewards are with Him — the Guardian and Helper who suffices (4:45) can give or withhold either.

**A Verse That Follows Trust With Warning**

Placed after *to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth; He suffices as Trustee* (4:132) and before *whoever desires this world's reward — with God are both rewards* (4:134), this verse follows trust with the warning that the One who suffices can do without the one who fails to entrust. The sūrah bracketed the women's law — settlement best (4:128), no total inclining (4:129), enrichment from bounty (4:130) — with the universal charge to be mindful (4:131) and ownership-trusteeship (4:132); now it warns *O humanity* that mindfulness is not for His need. The sūrah has warned against advocating for deceit (4:105), against most secret talks without good (4:114), and that whoever defies after clarity is left to what he chose (4:115) — those are the traces of a humanity that could be removed if it persists, as prior communities were. For the weak this is protective: the One who can remove humanity and bring others is the One who was hoped to pardon the helpless (4:99) and who gives many havens to the emigrant (4:100) — His capability to replace is the same capability to rescue; and to trust Him as Trustee (4:132) where *He can* is to entrust to the Capable.

**Removal Not for His Need, but for Justice**

The address *O humanity*, after the charge to those before you and you (4:131), was explained as broadening to all descendants of the single soul — reminding that the single soul's lesson, that ties are to be honoured, is the same mindfulness commanded. To say *He can remove you* after *He is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy* shows removal is not for need: the Self-Sufficient does not remove for lack; He removes for justice, as He let the defier pursue what he chose, then burn (4:115), and made association far straying (4:116). The sūrah that will command *stand firm for justice as witnesses for God though against yourselves* (4:135) makes humanity itself the witness here: if you do not stand, others will be brought who will. The verse generalises the sūrah's replacement logic where *with Him are the rewards of both worlds* (4:134): desire for this world alone is answered not by giving the world alone, but by reminding that the World's Owner can replace the desirer.

**A Short Verse That Makes Ownership Dynamic**

Though brief — *if He wills, He can remove you altogether and bring others; God is Most Capable* — the verse makes ownership dynamic. The thrice-repeated *to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth* was static — all is His; *He can remove and bring* is dynamic — He does with His what wisdom wills. The sūrah that began with creation from a single soul and its spread, and taught law for orphans, women, inheritance, trusts, prayer, judgment, charity, and Abraham, will now say *stand for justice* (4:135) to the humanity that can be removed: to stand for justice is to be among the *others* brought, not the removed. The next verse sets the choice of reward: whoever desires this world's reward — with Him are both — so ask the Capable for both, not for little (4:134).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:134

> Whoever desires the reward of this world, then ˹let them know that˺ with Allah are the rewards of this world and the Hereafter. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing

**Whoever Desires the Reward of This World — With Him Are Both**

The verse states *man kāna yurīdu thawāba al-dunyā fa ʿinda Allāhi thawābu al-dunyā wa al-ākhirah* — whoever desires the reward of this nearer world, then with God — at His disposal — are the rewards of this world and the Hereafter, together. *Thawāb* — reward, wage — was explained as return for deed, as the sūrah promised a fine reward to both sitter with excuse and striver, greater for the striver (4:95–96); a great reward for seeking His pleasure through charity and reconciliation (4:114); tremendous loss for taking Satan as guardian (4:119); and recompense *with it* for evil (4:123). *Desires the world's reward* was read as the shortcut: to act for this world alone — as the lagger desired gain without sharing faith (4:73), as the denier of peace sought fleeting gain (4:94), as the wishers claimed grace by wish (4:123). *With God are both rewards* was explained as exclusive possession: both are *ʿinda Allāh* — with Him, from His bounty — as *to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth* (4:126, 4:131) — so to desire this world alone from other than Him is to seek little from the One who has much. The *and* joins the two: He has not divided them except where you divided desire; to ask Him is to obtain both — as the emigrant found many havens and abundance on earth (4:100), the separated were enriched from His spaciousness (4:130) — this world — while the believer hoping from Him finds forgiveness and mercy (4:96) — the Hereafter.

**And God Is All-Hearing, All-Seeing**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu Samīʿan Baṣīrā* — and God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing — was explained with *Samīʿ* — hearing every wish, every secret talk, every advocacy in this life (4:109), every dispute judged by what He shows (4:105) — and *Baṣīr* — seeing every act: every inclination not made equal between wives (4:129), every throwing of sin on the innocent (4:112), every charity meant for His pleasure (4:114). *Samīʿ Baṣīr* sealed the command to return trusts and judge fairly — a command from the All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:58) — and now seals the desire for reward: He hears the desire for this world, sees the act performed for it, and measures accordingly without wronging even an atom, multiplying the good many times over (4:40). To say *with Him are both rewards* and *He is All-Hearing, All-Seeing* is to say seeking from Him is neither unheard nor unseen: the One who hears the wife fearing ill-conduct (4:128) and sees the greed present with souls hears the desirer's wish and sees whether it was for Him or for little.

**A Verse That Follows Capability to Replace With Choice of Reward**

Placed after *if He wills, He can remove you, O humanity, and bring others — He is Most Capable* (4:133), this verse follows capability to replace with the choice of reward that determines whether you are removed or remain. The sūrah addressed *O humanity, be mindful of your Lord who created you from a single soul* (4:1) and later *O humanity, He can remove you* (4:133) — between the two addresses lies law for orphans, women, inheritance, trust, prayer, judgment, charity, Abraham, settlement, and now desire: to desire this world's reward alone, from other than Him, is to choose little where the great is with Him. The sūrah has shown that those who took Satan as guardian suffered tremendous loss, seeking what he promised as delusion (4:119–121), while those who believed and did good found Gardens ever true (4:122); to desire this world alone is to take the deluder's little. The sūrah will say *all honour belongs to God* (4:139) where hypocrites seek honour from disbeliever allies; here *both rewards are with Him* is the same ownership: honour, like reward, is with Him alone. For the weak this is an opening: you need not envy what God gave some over others (4:32) — ask Him: with Him are both, and He hears and sees the asking.

**Both Rewards With Him Makes Single Desire Small**

The phrase *with God are the rewards of this world and the Hereafter* was explained as making single desire small. If you desire this world alone, you ask the Capable who can remove and bring (4:133) for what perishes; had you asked Him, you would have both — this world as haven and spaciousness (4:100), and the Hereafter as Gardens forever true (4:122). The sūrah has shown that the Hereafter is better for the mindful than the little enjoyment (4:77); that prayer at its fixed writ (4:103) secures both; that standing firm for justice though against yourselves (4:135) secures both, though self-interest seems to favour this world alone. *Samīʿ Baṣīr* as the seal was linked to *do not let desires cause you to deviate from justice* (4:135): desire for this world's reward deviates where hearing and seeing are not recalled. To remember He hears and sees is to recall that *whoever commits evil will be recompensed accordingly, with no protector besides Him* (4:123), yet *whoever does good, male or female, with faith will enter Paradise, not wronged a speck* (4:124) — both measured by the All-Hearing, All-Seeing.

**A Short Verse That Anchors Asking**

Though brief — *whoever desires this world's reward, with God are the rewards of this world and the Hereafter; He is All-Hearing, All-Seeing* — the verse anchors asking. The chapter has commanded referral of disputes to God and Messenger (4:59), verification of reports (4:83), being sure before fighting (4:94), judgment by what He shows (4:105), counselling charity, kindness, reconciliation (4:114) — all acts whose reward the desirer might limit to this world. The verse says: ask the Owner who hears and sees for both, and you will find — as the emigrant found havens, the separated found enrichment, the seeker found forgiveness. The next verse applies that hearing and seeing to justice: stand firm for justice as witnesses for God even against yourselves, parents, and kin; rich or poor, God ensures their interests; do not let desires deviate; if you distort or refuse, He is All-Aware of what you do (4:135).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:135

> O believers! Stand firm for justice as witnesses for Allah even if it is against yourselves, your parents, or close relatives. Be they rich or poor, Allah is best to ensure their interests. So do not let your desires cause you to deviate ˹from justice˺. If you distort the testimony or refuse to give it, then ˹know that˺ Allah is certainly All-Aware of what you do

**Stand Firm for Justice as Witnesses for God, Even Against Yourselves**

The verse opens *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū kūnū qawwāmīna bi-al-qiṣṭi shuhadāʾa li Allāhi wa law ʿalā anfusikum awi al-wālidayni wa al-aqrabīn* — O believers, be steadfast upholders of justice, witnesses for God, even if against yourselves, or parents, or close kin. *Qawwāmīn bi-al-qiṣṭ* — upholders of justice, ever standing for equity — was explained with *qawwām* — much standing, firm — the same root as *stand up for orphans with justice* (4:127) and *establish prayer* at its fixed writ (4:103). *Shuhadāʾ li Allāh* — witnesses for God — was read as testimony offered for Him, not for clan, as the sūrah commands returning trusts and judging fairly as a command from the All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:58), judging between people by what He shows (4:105), and verifying before fighting (4:94). *Wa law ʿalā anfusikum awi al-wālidayni wa al-aqrabīn* — even against yourselves, parents, or close relatives — was explained as the Book's severest test of the single soul's ties (4:1): to honour ties is not to hide a kinsman's theft through night plotting (4:108) nor to advocate for self-wrongers (4:107); to be just even against those ties is to honour the Creator of the single soul above the soul's branch. Early reports noted this verse came where a dispute between parties of unequal rank pressed witnesses to favour the rich; the verse says witness for Him, though the testimony be against the self.

**Be They Rich or Poor — God Is Best to Ensure Their Interests**

The guidance *in yakun ghaniyyan aw faqīran fa Allāhu awlā bihimā* — be they rich or poor, God is nearer, more worthy, to the interests of both — was explained as the prohibition of partiality by wealth. The rich might be favoured for honour or repayment; the poor might be favoured by pity tilting justice; both tilts are condemned — as the sūrah warns *all honour belongs to God* (4:139) sought through ally company, and warns that most secret talks have no good except charity, kindness, reconciliation (4:114): pity without truth is not among those goods. *Fa Allāhu awlā bihimā* — God is more worthy of both — was explained as that He owns the heavens and earth (4:126), suffices as Trustee (4:132), and is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy (4:131): guardianship of rich and poor alike belongs to Him, so the witness need not be guardian to either by tilting. The sūrah has said the helpless men, women, and children are hoped to be pardoned (4:99) and the emigrant finds many havens (4:100) — protection is His; to stand for justice does not require protecting the poor by false testimony, nor the rich by distortion, because He ensures their interests better.

**So Do Not Let Desires Cause You to Deviate From Justice**

The warning *fa lā tattabiʿū al-hawā an taʿdilū* — so do not follow desires, lest you swerve from justice — was explained with *hawā* — desire, caprice — the same desire that makes you deviate greatly if followed (4:27), that would lead to other than the believers' path (4:115), and that makes counsels of charity insincere if for show. *Lest you swerve* was read against the sūrah's own justice in households — advise first, then avoid, then gentle discipline (4:34) — and in marriage — do not incline entirely, leaving the other suspended (4:129). Following desire was linked to the judge's caution that eloquence can persuade him to give one the right of his brother — a piece of fire (al-Bukhārī 2680); there, desire takes the form of eloquence, kin preference, pity, or greed for fleeting gain through denying peace (4:94).
