The sūrah elsewhere commands standing for justice though against yourselves (4:135) and permits settlement as best (4:128); public evil speech is the broad prohibition, with this exception for the wronged — as the helpless were excepted for pardon (4:98): not every loud complaint is evil; the wronged's is allowed.

**Allah Is All-Hearing, All-Knowing**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu Samīʿan ʿAlīmā* — and God is ever All-Hearing, All-Knowing — was explained with *Samīʿ* — hearing every open voicing, every secret counsel (4:114), every night plot displeasing (4:108) — and *ʿAlīm* — knowing whether the loud voicing is evil speech or a complaint of the wronged; whether settlement was sought graciously (4:128) or inclining was total (4:129). *Samīʿ Baṣīr* sealed the command to return trusts and judge fairly (4:58) and the promise that both rewards are with Him (4:134); here *Samīʿ ʿAlīm* fits speech: He hears the open evil and knows its motive, just as He hears the oppressed cry (4:75) and knows when a way was absent (4:98). Early reports illustrated *the wronged* with one whose property was usurped, or who was wronged by a spouse's ill-conduct, and who voices it for redress, not for slander — He hears and knows the difference between reporting wrong for justice and throwing sin on the innocent as slander (4:112). The pairing says: public evil speech is disliked — yet He hears the wronged's permitted voicing and knows its equity.

**A Verse That Follows Grateful Faith With the Discipline of Speech**

Placed after *why should He punish you if you are grateful and faithful? He is ever Appreciative, All-Knowing* (4:147), this verse follows grateful faith with the discipline of loud speech. Whoever is grateful and faithful is appreciated and known (4:147); to voice evil openly is ingratitude in speech — as the deceitful's night speech displeases Him (4:108) and the advocates' disputing for self-wrongers in this life is loud evil. The exception *except the wronged* was read as the sūrah's justice: the oppressed whose deliverance the believers were commanded to fight for (4:75), whose earth was made spacious (4:100), whose prayer is shortened and guarded (4:101–102) — their voicing is not evil but truth — a demand for right. The sūrah that warns most secret talks have no good except three (4:114), now warns open evil has no love except one — the wronged's. The sūrah that says He wills to make clear (4:26) and taught you what you did not know (4:113) makes open evil undesirable because His knowledge will judge it and His hearing will not miss it.

**Open Evil Versus Permitted Complaint**

The distinction — loud evil disliked, the wronged permitted — was explained as the same distinction as the secret talks rule (4:114): many complaints carry no good, except the complaint of the wronged seeking the goods of justice, kindness, and reconciliation. The sūrah has shown settlement is best where she fears ill-conduct (4:128); settlement may require voicing grievance — that voicing is the wronged's permission, not evil speech. The wronged were linked to *do not incline entirely, leaving the other suspended* (4:129) — the suspended wife's voicing of suspension is permitted as one wronged. Classical notes added that the wronged may invoke God against the oppressor, or report the oppressor to those in authority (4:59) — but not transgress beyond measure; the loud voicing remains measured before the All-Hearing.

**A Short Verse That Anchors Speech Between Love and Hearing**

Though brief — *God does not like the open voicing of evil speech, except by the wronged; He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing* — the verse anchors speech between love and hearing. The chapter has commanded referral of disputes to God and Messenger (4:59), verification of reports (4:83), being sure before fighting (4:94), judgment by what He shows (4:105), counselling charity, kindness, reconciliation (4:114), standing for justice even against yourselves (4:135) — all require voicing; the verse adds the qualifier: voicing evil for its own sake is not loved; voicing wrong for justice is allowed and heard. For the weak this is the lightest of speeches: where you are wronged — the orphan deprived (4:127), the wife left hanging (4:129), the party whose testimony is twisted (4:135) — you may voice it, and the One who can remove humanity (4:133) hears and knows: He appreciates gratitude (4:147) yet dislikes open evil where no wrong was done. The next verse sets the higher ethic: whether you reveal a good or conceal it, or pardon an evil — surely God is Ever-Pardoning, Most Capable (4:149) — so that even the permitted voicing may be surpassed by pardoning.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:149

> Whether you reveal or conceal a good or pardon an evil—surely Allah is Ever-Pardoning, Most Capable

**Whether You Reveal a Good, Conceal It, or Pardon an Evil**

The verse states *in tubdū khayran aw tukhfūhu aw taʿfū ʿan sūʾin* — whether you reveal, display, a good, or conceal it, hide it, or pardon, overlook, an evil done. *Tubdū khayran* — to reveal a good — was explained as doing good openly: charity, kindness, reconciliation seeking His pleasure (4:114) — the only good counsel — and standing for justice as witnesses for Him even against yourselves (4:135), where testimony is a good made public. *Aw tukhfūhu* — or conceal it — was explained as doing good secretly: the charity waived as blood-money (4:92), the dowry given or graciously waived (4:4), the good hidden lest showing it become showing off (4:38, 4:142). Both were read as equal where the intention is His pleasure — whether the good is displayed or hidden, it is known to Him. *Aw taʿfū ʿan sūʾin* — or pardon an evil — was explained as pardoning a forgivable wrong done to you, immediately after the wronged were permitted to voice their grievance (4:148): voicing is permission; pardoning is the higher way. *ʿAfā* — to pardon, efface — is the same root as *ʿAfuww* — Ever-Pardoning — the Name that seals the verse. The sūrah has shown settlement is best where she fears ill-conduct (4.128), and settlement involves mutual graciousness; pardoning an evil is that graciousness practised where grievance could have been voiced.

**Surely God Is Ever-Pardoning, Most Capable**

The seal *fa-inna Allāha kāna ʿAfuwwan Qadīrā* — surely God is ever Ever-Pardoning, Most Capable — was explained with *ʿAfuww* — much effacing, wiping away — the Name that sealed the helpless hoped to be pardoned (4:99). *Qadīr* — Most Capable — was explained as that He pardons though fully capable of punishing: He can remove humanity and bring others (4:133), yet appreciates gratitude (4:147); He owns the heavens and earth (4:126), yet forgives what is less than association (4:116). To be *ʿAfuww Qadīr* was read as pardoning after being wronged is divine imitation: you pardon though capable of voicing and retaliating, as He pardons though Most Capable to punish. The pairing was linked to *He does not like loud evil speech except by the wronged; He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing* (4:148) — the wronged may voice; the higher is to pardon — because the All-Hearing has heard, and *ʿAfuww Qadīr* shows the pardon that surpasses it. The sūrah has shown the emigrant's reward secured though He could withhold (4:100), and both rewards with Him though He could give none; *ʿAfuww Qadīr* is that generosity given to the believer as character.

**A Verse That Follows Permission to Voice With an Invitation to Pardon**

Placed after *He does not like loud evil speech except by the wronged; He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing* (4:148), this verse follows permission to voice with an invitation higher than permission. The structure mirrors the household law: *settlement is best* (4:128) is the invitation beyond mere permission; *do not incline entirely* (4:129) is permission bounded; here *reveal or conceal a good, or pardon an evil* is invitation beyond the wronged's permitted voicing. The sūrah has shown that most secret talks have no good except charity, kindness, reconciliation (4:114) — revealing or concealing good is that charity; and standing for justice though against yourselves (4:135) is the good voiced where needed — pardoning an evil is the good that forgives where justice's voice could have condemned. Where the deceitful hide from people while He is with them, displeased (4:108), and advocates dispute for self-wrongers (4:107), pardoning an evil is the believer's opposite: he effaces despite being wronged.

**Revealing or Concealing — Both Known, Both Rewarded**

The equalisation — *whether you reveal… or conceal it* — was explained as removing the show: whether good is displayed or hidden, it is good before Him who owns the heavens and earth and is Fully Aware (4:126), All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:134). To reveal is not automatically showing off; to conceal is not automatically sincerity — both are good where sought for His pleasure (4:114). The verse was linked to *God does not wrong even an atom* (4:40): the revealed atom and the concealed atom are both present before the All-Knowing. The addition *or pardon an evil* was read as the highest good: pardoning the evil done to you is forbearance, and its effacement is most like His *ʿafw*. The sūrah has said *why should He punish you if you are grateful and faithful? He is ever Appreciative, All-Knowing* (4:147) — gratitude for good is shown by doing good, whether revealed or hidden, and pardoning evil is gratitude that He is *ʿAfuww*.

**A Short Verse That Anchors Forbearance in Capability**

Though brief — *whether you reveal or conceal a good, or pardon an evil — surely God is Ever-Pardoning, Most Capable* — the verse anchors forbearance in capability. The chapter has commanded referral of disputes (4:59), verification of reports, being sure before fighting, judging by what He shows, commanding charity, standing for justice — all involve the power to reveal good or voice evil; the verse says the higher use of that power is to pardon, as the Higher is Pardoning though Capable. For the weak this is the lightest of strengths: where you were wronged — the orphan whose wealth was devoured, the wife left hanging, the party whose testimony was twisted — you may voice it as the wronged may; yet if you pardon while capable, you meet the Name *ʿAfuww Qadīr* where He meets you. The next passage turns from speech and pardon to creed: those who deny God and His messengers, seeking to make a distinction between them — desiring a compromise — they are the true disbelievers, for whom a humiliating punishment is prepared (4:150–151).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:150

> Surely those who deny Allah and His messengers and wish to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers, saying, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others," desiring to forge a compromise

**Those Who Deny God and His Messengers and Wish to Distinguish**

The verse opens *inna alladhīna yakfurūna bi Allāhi wa rusulihī wa yurīdūna an yufarriqū bayna Allāhi wa rusulihī* — surely those who deny God and His messengers, and wish to make a distinction, to separate, between God and His messengers. *Yakfurūna bi Allāhi wa rusulihī* — to deny God and messengers — was explained as the denial that makes association far straying (4:116) and defiance of the Messenger after clear guidance, following other than the believers' path (4:115). *Yurīdūna an yufarriqū bayna Allāhi wa rusulihī* — to wish to make distinction between God and His messengers — was read as claiming belief in God without His messengers, or in some messengers without others — as the sūrah shows the People of the Book demanding a written revelation from heaven (4:153) while earlier they demanded the greater from Moses — *show us God openly* — and were struck (2:55). To separate God from messengers was explained as theological division, where the Book was sent with truth to judge between people by what He shows through the Messenger (4:105), and obedience to the Messenger is obedience to God (4:80): to claim God without His Messenger is to claim a judgment without the showing. Early reports linked the verse to those who believed in Moses but disbelieved in Jesus and Muhammad ﷺ, and to those who believed in Jesus but disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ — both making distinction.

**Saying — We Believe in Some and Disbelieve in Others**

The speech *wa yaqūlūna nuʾminu bi-baʿḍin wa nakfuru bi-baʿḍ* — and they say, we believe in some messengers and disbelieve in others — was explained as the distinction's formula, the compromise already closed where *O you who believe, have faith in God, His Messenger, the Book He revealed to His Messenger, and the Scriptures He revealed before* (4:136) commanded comprehensive faith without selecting. *We believe in some* was read as the partial faith that wishes grace by belonging — *neither by your wishes nor those of the People of the Book* (4:123) — here the wish is *our group's messengers*. *We disbelieve in some* was read as denial of those sent before or after — as the sūrah will say *they are the true disbelievers* (4:151), and *those who believe in God and His messengers, making no distinction among any of them — He will give them their rewards* (4:152). The sūrah has shown that those who believed then disbelieved, then believed again and increased (4:137), make similar speech; the formula *we believe in some and disbelieve in others* was explained as hypocrisy's doctrinal side: to sway between neither these nor those (4:143) in creed. The phrase was linked to *they say, we hear and disobey* (4:46), where words were distorted; here the distortion is the selection of messengers.

**Desiring to Forge a Compromise**

The intention *wa yurīdūna an yattakhidhū bayna dhālika sabīlā* — and they wish to take, forge, between that — between believing in some and disbelieving in some — a way, a path, a compromise — was explained with *sabīl* — the way the sūrah wills to make clear as noble ways (4:26), the believers' path not to be left (4:115), and the way never granted to disbelievers over believers (4:141). *A way between that* was read as seeking a middle doctrine that is neither belief nor disbelief — God accepted, some messengers rejected. The sūrah has shown that settlement is best (4:128) where an equitable compromise between spouses is good — but compromise between God and His messengers is not settlement; it is division. The sūrah has also shown that most secret talks have no good except charity, kindness, reconciliation (4:114) — to take a way between believing and denying is the counsel that has no good. The verse generalises the particular hypocrisy of waiting between winners (4:141) into theology: waiting between messengers, believing some and disbelieving some, is desiring a way-between that is not a way — but the straying for which none will be found (4:143).

**A Verse That Follows Pardon With Distinction**

Placed after *whether you reveal or conceal a good or pardon an evil — surely God is Ever-Pardoning, Most Capable* (4:149), this verse follows pardon with the distinction that refuses the pardon's path where distinction persists unrepented. The sūrah has taught that the grateful and faithful will not be punished, because He is Appreciative, All-Knowing (4:147), and that repentance with mending, holding fast, and sincerity returns the hypocrite to being with the believers (4:146); those who make distinction between God and messengers do none of the four — they desire a way between. The sūrah that began the command *have faith in God, His Messenger, the Book, and the Scriptures before* (4:136) now defines its opposite: *surely those who deny God and His messengers, wishing to make distinction*. For the weak this is clarifying: where settlement between spouses is best, distinction between God and His messengers is never settlement; to believe in some and disbelieve in others is not waiving a right to keep a marriage — it is claiming the right to select the Sender.

**The Distinction the Sūrah Has Named and Closed**

The phrase *make a distinction between God and His messengers* was set against the distinctions the sūrah has already refused: the distinction of wishes — *neither your wishes nor those of the People of the Book* (4:123) — and now the distinction of messengers — *we believe in some and disbelieve in others*. Both are division seeking a way-between where none is, and both are answered with comprehensive faith: *believe in God, His Messenger, the Book, the Scriptures, the angels, the Last Day* (4:136) and *believe in God and His messengers, making no distinction among any of them* (4:152). The verse was read as the sūrah's answer to compromise theology: the only way that is, is the believers' path (4:115) — full submission to Him, doing good, following the upright Abraham (4:125) — not a path of selective belief. The next verse declares the verdict: *they are indeed the true disbelievers, and We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment* (4:151).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:151

> they are indeed the true disbelievers. And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment

**They Are Indeed the True Disbelievers**

The verse completes *ulāʾika humu al-kāfirūna ḥaqqan* — they — those who deny God and His messengers, wishing to make distinction between Him and them, saying *we believe in some and disbelieve in some, desiring a way between* (4:150) — they are indeed, truly, the disbelievers in truth. *Ḥaqqan* — truly, in truth — was explained as the Book's verdict after judgment by what He shows (4:105): distinguishing God from His messengers is not a middle position but disbelief in full — as *whoever denies God, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day has gone far astray* (4:136). *Humu al-kāfirūna* — they are the disbelievers — was read with emphasis: not merely among disbelievers, but they are them. The sūrah has shown that taking disbelievers as allies instead of believers hands God clear warrant against yourselves (4:144), and sitting where revelations are denied makes you like them (4:140); to make distinction between God and messengers is that likeness made into creed. The verdict is *ḥaqq* — true — as God's promise is ever true (4:122) and the Book was sent with truth (4:105). Early reports added that the swaying between neither these nor those (4:143) is not neutral: to desire a way between by distinguishing is, in truth, disbelief.

**And We Have Prepared for the Disbelievers a Humiliating Punishment**

The preparation *wa aʿtadnā li-al-kāfirīna ʿadhāban muhīnā* — and We have prepared, made ready, for the disbelievers a humiliating, degrading punishment — was explained with *aʿtadnā* — prepared — the same phrase as the humiliating punishment prepared for the disbelievers behind the guarded fear-prayer (4:102), and for those who hide God's bounty while promoting disbelief (4:37). *ʿAdhāban muhīnā* — humiliating punishment — was read as humiliation answering the honour — *ʿizzah* — they sought among disbeliever allies (4:139), where *all honour belongs to God entirely*: the honour sought in the wrong company ends as prepared humiliation. The sūrah has shown that the intent to deceive God while He outwits them (4:142) — and to deceive the Prophet ﷺ while grace preserved (4:113) — ends in inverted honour. Where the sūrah asks *would you give God clear warrant against yourselves?* (4:144), the preparation of humiliating punishment is that warrant made sanction: the proof was made clear by their own distinguishing.

**A Verse That Completes Distinction With Verdict**

Placed after the distinction was described — denying God and His messengers, wishing a way between (4:150) — this verse completes it with the verdict: true disbelievers, and a humiliating punishment prepared. The sūrah has shown that belief was commanded as comprehensive — God, His Messenger, the Book, the Scriptures before (4:136) — steadfast, not selective, as the upright Way of Abraham (4:125) was not selective among prophets. To be selective among messengers is to undo that comprehensive faith. The sūrah has shown that those who believe and do good are in Gardens where the promise is true (4:122), while those who disbelieve face Hell without escape (4:121); the humiliating punishment is the disbeliever's answer to the honour they sought. The phrase *prepared* was linked to the guarded prayer's context (4.102): as prayer under arms guards against the enemy who wishes your neglect for a sweep (4:102), comprehensive faith guards against the theology that accepts half the messengers and rejects half as compromise — and the tie steadies the choice: Gardens where they abide forever (4:122) versus preparation of humiliation.

**Truly Disbelievers After a Truly True Promise**

The word *ḥaqqan* — truly — for the disbelievers was contrasted with *ḥaqqan* for the promise: *God's promise is ever true* (4:122). The sūrah has used *ḥaqq* for the Book — sent with truth (4:105) — for the promise, and now for the verdict; truth is one. To call them *true disbelievers* is to say the judgment is not by wish — *neither by your wishes nor those of the People of the Book* (4:123) — but by truth, as *whoever commits evil will be recompensed accordingly* (4:123): distinction is the evil recompensed with itself. Where the sūrah asks *whose word is more truthful than God's?* (4:122) — none — this *ḥaqqan* is His word. For the weak this is clarifying: where settlement between spouses is best (4:128) and compromise may be gracious, compromise between God and His messengers is never best — it is true disbelief, whose preparation is humiliating.

**A Short Verse That Anchors Creed Before Its Opposite**

Though brief — *they are indeed the true disbelievers, and We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment* — the verse anchors the creed before its opposite: the next verse describes the believers who accept all the messengers, rejecting none, and are given their rewards with forgiveness and mercy (4.152). The two verses frame the choice after distinction was described: desire a way between and be counted a true disbeliever with humiliating preparation — or accept all without rejecting any, and be given rewards, forgiveness, and mercy. The passage after turns to the People of the Book demanding a book from heaven (4:153).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:152

> As for those who believe in Allah and His messengers—accepting all; rejecting none—He will surely give them their rewards. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**Those Who Believe in God and His Messengers — Accepting All, Rejecting None**

The verse states *wa alladhīna āmanū bi Allāhi wa rusulihī wa lam yufarriqū bayna aḥadin minhum* — and those who believe in God and His messengers, and make no distinction between any of them. *Believe in God and His messengers* was explained as the comprehensive faith just commanded — *have faith in God, His Messenger, the Book He revealed to His Messenger, and the Scriptures He revealed before* (4:136) — now described as its people. *And made no distinction between any of them* was read as the direct opposite of wishing to make distinction between God and His messengers, saying *we believe in some and disbelieve in some, desiring a way between* (4:150) — whose verdict was true disbelief with humiliating preparation (4:151). To make no distinction between any messenger was explained as accepting all — *We have sent revelation to you as We sent it to Noah and the prophets after him… Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon, and to David We gave the Psalms* (4:163) — all are God's; none is rejected. The sūrah has shown that the People of the Book demanded a book from heaven, having earlier demanded the greater from Moses — *show us God visibly* (4:153); distinguishing among messengers is that demand's theology — to accept Moses but not Jesus or Muhammad ﷺ is the calf made creed after clear signs. To make no distinction was also linked to *Gardens for those who believe and do good* (4:122): comprehensive belief is part of that good, as the upright Way of Abraham (4:125) includes all prophets.

**He Will Surely Give Them Their Rewards**

The promise *ulāʾika sawfa yuʾtīhim ujūrahum* — then to those He will surely give their rewards — was explained with *sawfa* — will, soon — certainty, as the emigrant's reward is secured upon God (4:100), and as the great reward was promised for good counsel (4:114) and for being with the believers after repentance (4:146). *Ujūrahum* — their rewards, wages — was read as *ajr* — wage — the wage hypocrites sought as honour among disbelievers (4:139), though all honour belongs to Him (4:139) and both rewards are with Him (4:134): the believers' wage is from Him, not from company. The verse generalises the promise that *whoever does good, male or female, with faith will enter Paradise, not wronged a speck* (4:124) — the comprehensive believer is such a doer; and *who is better in religion than one who submits his face, does good, and follows Abraham?* (4:125) — submission includes accepting all messengers, so the reward is friendship, as Abraham was taken as close friend (4:125). Early notes linked the wages to God's will to make clear, guide to noble ways, and turn in mercy (4:26): the wage is the mercy guided to.

**And God Is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu Ghafūran Raḥīmā* — and God is ever All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — was explained with *Ghafūr* — much forgiving, covering — and *Raḥīm* — ever merciful — the pair that sealed the grateful faithful (4:147), the seeker of forgiveness (4:110), and the pardon of what is less than association (4:116). To seal comprehensive belief with *Ghafūr Raḥīm* was read as that those who believe in all messengers still carry faults needing cover: strivers need forgiveness among the ranks (4:96), and emigrants find havens though weakness remains (4:100). *Ghafūr Raḥīm* here contrasts with *ʿadhāban muhīnā* — the humiliating punishment prepared for the true disbelievers (4:151): distinction's wage is humiliation; comprehensiveness's wage is reward plus forgiveness and mercy. Where the sūrah says *God does not wrong even an atom* (4:40) and *never wronged even a speck on a date stone* (4:124), the comprehensive believer's reward is the atom not wronged yet multiplied many times — and the Seal says the Multiplier is Forgiving, Merciful.

**A Verse That Follows True Disbelief With True Belief**

Placed after *they are indeed the true disbelievers, and We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment* (4:151), this verse follows true disbelief with true belief and its opposite preparation: not humiliating punishment prepared, but rewards given, with forgiveness and mercy. The sūrah has moved from the household law (4:127–130) through the universal charge to be mindful (4:131), trusteeship, capability, and both rewards (4:131–134), standing for justice (4:135) with the five articles (4:136), oscillation without forgiveness or way (4:137), the announcement to hypocrites (4:138), alliance for honour (4:139), sitting where mocked (4:140), waiting between winners (4:141), deceiving and lazy prayer (4:142), swaying between (4:143), alliance giving clear proof (4:144), the lowest depth without helper (4:145) except the four who repent, mend, hold fast, and are sincere (4:146), the principle that He punishes not the grateful faithful (4:147), the discipline of speech except by the wronged (4:148), pardoning though capable (4:149), and the distinction desiring a way between (4:150) — here the opposite: no distinction between any messenger, rewarded. The sūrah that warns not to deviate by following desires (4:27) nor let desires deviate from justice (4:135) names comprehensive acceptance as the just faith.

**Comprehensive Faith Mirrors the Comprehensiveness of Revelation**

The phrase *no distinction between any of them* was explained as mirroring the comprehensiveness of revelation itself — *We have sent revelation to you as We sent it to Noah and the prophets after him* (4:163): revelation came whole; faith receives it whole. To accept all and reject none is to say the single soul spread into humanity (4:1) received guidance through prophets one after another, all from the Owner of the heavens and earth (4:126). The sūrah has shown that the People of the Book demanded a book from heaven as sign, having demanded the visible God of Moses (4:153); to accept all prophets is to accept that the Book's descent is witnessed by His knowledge and the angels (4:166), and that God suffices as Witness — so no demand for visible proof suspends belief in any messenger. For the weak this is the lightest completeness: where settlement between spouses is best (4:128) and enrichment after separation comes from His spaciousness (4:130), the comprehensive believer's settlement with revelation is to take all — not to slit and alter (4:119) — and his enrichment is rewards, forgiveness, and mercy.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:153

> The People of the Book demand that you ˹O Prophet˺ bring down for them a revelation in writing from heaven. They demanded what is even greater than this from Moses, saying, "Make Allah visible to us!" So a thunderbolt struck them for their wrongdoing. Then they took the calf for worship after receiving clear signs. Still We forgave them for that ˹after their repentance˺ and gave Moses compelling proof

**The People of the Book Demand a Book From Heaven**

The verse opens *yasʾaluka ahlu al-kitābi an tunazzila ʿalayhim kitāban mina al-samāʾ* — the People of the Book ask you, demand of you, to bring down upon them a book from the sky, a written revelation from heaven. *People of the Book* was explained as the Jews and Christians given Scripture before — the same "those before you" commanded to be mindful (4:131) — whose wishes are not the measure (4:123), and some of whom traded a portion of the Book for misguidance (4:44). *Yasʾaluka* — they ask, demand — was read as a challenging demand, and the verse immediately deflates it: they demanded what is greater than this from Moses. *To bring down a book from heaven* was explained as requesting a written revelation descending as sheets — belief conditioned on spectacle. The sūrah has shown that the Book was sent with truth to judge between people by what He shows (4:105), and that God bears witness to what He sent down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness too (4:166); to demand a book from heaven as a condition is to condition belief on another spectacle while refusing the witness already given. Early reports noted this demand followed the recitation of comprehensive faith (4:152): they said, if you are truly a messenger, bring a book as Moses brought tablets — otherwise we maintain our distinction (4:150); the sūrah exposes the demand as the old distinguishing continued.

**They Demanded Greater Than That From Moses — Show Us God Plainly**

The reminder *faqad saʾalū Mūsā akbara min dhālika faqālū arinā Allāha jahratan* — yet they demanded of Moses greater than that, saying, show us God plainly, openly. *Greater than that* — greater than the book from heaven. *Show us God openly* was explained as a demand for theophany — to see the Lord with their eyes — as the sūrah recounts elsewhere: *they said, O Moses, we will never believe you until we see God plainly; so the thunderbolt seized them* (2:55). *Jahratan* — openly, visibly — was read as demanding sight of the Owner who declared *to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth, and He is Fully Aware* (4:126) — to see the Fully Aware before believing the Book He revealed. Elsewhere the Book says God suffices as Witness (4:166), and souls will be asked at taking *what were you doing?* (4:97); to demand the visible God is to refuse the witness of Book and angels. Classical notes added that Moses' people demanded this after the deliverance through the sea and after the manna — showing that spectacle produces no faith where the heart's distinction remains.

**So the Thunderbolt Struck Them — Then They Took the Calf After Clear Signs**

The consequence *fa-akhadhat-humu aṣ-ṣāʿiqatu bi-ẓulmihim* — so the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing — was explained with *ṣāʿiqah* — thunderbolt, the striking seizure. *For their wrongdoing* was read as that the demand itself was injustice — as association is far straying (4:116) and defiance after clarity is left to what was chosen (4:115). *Thumma ittakhadhū al-ʿijla min baʿdi mā jāʾat-humu al-bayyināt* — then they took the calf for worship after the clear proofs had come to them — was explained with *ʿijl* — the golden calf — worshipped while Moses was on the Mount, after *bayyināt* — clear proofs — the staff, the divided sea, the manna, the tablets. To take a calf after clear proofs was read as the chapter's illustration of distinguishing made image: they demanded the Most High visible and, not receiving it, took the lowest visible thing as god — the worst substitution. Elsewhere the chapter notes the female gods invoked besides Him (4:117) and the ordering to slit ears and alter creation (4:119); the calf is the same economy — creation altered into an object of worship.

**Still We Forgave Them and Gave Moses Compelling Proof**

The mercy *fa-ʿafawnā ʿan dhālika wa ātaynā Mūsā sulṭānan mubīnā* — still We pardoned them for that, after their repentance, and We gave Moses clear, compelling authority — was explained with *ʿafawnā* — We pardoned — the same root as *ʿAfuww* — Ever-Pardoning (4:99, 4:149), who pardons though Most Capable (4:149). The chapter has noted that whoever wrongs himself then seeks forgiveness finds Him All-Forgiving (4:110), and the helpless are hoped to be pardoned (4:99); here even the calf-takers were forgiven after their repentance — where the command to repentance after the calf is recounted (2:54). *Sulṭānan mubīnā* — clear warrant, compelling proof — was explained as the manifest authority Moses was given: the tablets, the signs, and the covenant sealed by the Mount raised (4:154). The phrase appeared as warrant against the double-faced who neither withdraw nor offer peace (4:91), and as the warrant warned against giving against yourselves (4:144); here Moses' compelling proof is the warrant against those who demanded greater than a book.

**A Verse That Frames Demand With Forgiveness**

Placed after comprehensive belief rewarded with forgiveness and mercy (4:152) versus distinction as true disbelief (4:151), this verse frames the demand for a book from heaven with history: the greater demand — visible God — the thunderbolt, the calf after clear signs, yet pardon and compelling proof. The sūrah has shown the Book sent with truth to judge between people, and God bearing witness with His knowledge (4:166); to demand a book from heaven as a condition is to condition acceptance of that witness on yet another. The sūrah will warn *do not go to extremes in your religion; say nothing about God except the truth: the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was only a messenger of God, His Word through Mary, and a spirit from Him* (4:171) — extremes begin as demands for spectacle and end as calf worship: the visible made god when the Invisible is demanded visible. For the weak this is opening: where the calf after clear signs was forgiven upon repentance, the sincere repentant with the believers (4:146) is within that forgiveness — and Moses' compelling proof is the evidence that separates demand from faith.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:154

> We raised the Mount over them ˹as a warning˺ for ˹breaking˺ their covenant and said, "Enter the gate ˹of Jerusalem˺ with humility." We also warned them, "Do not break the Sabbath," and took from them a firm covenant

**We Raised the Mount Over Them for Their Covenant**

The verse states *wa rafaʿnā fawqa-humu aṭ-ṭūra bi-mīthāqihim* — and We raised the Mount — *al-Ṭūr*, Sinai — over them, because of their covenant. *We raised over them* was explained as God lifting Sinai over the Children of Israel like a canopy until they accepted the covenant — after the calf had been forgiven and Moses given compelling proof (4:153). *Bi-mīthāqihim* — for their covenant — was read as that the covenant's terms were accepted under the raised Mount — a warning made physical. The sūrah has traced *mīthāq* — covenant — from the firm commitment of marriage (4:21) to the treaties with covenanted peoples (4:90, 4:92), and now to the firm covenant with the Children of Israel; raising a mountain over them was explained as the visible compelling proof (4:153) made substance — the covenant not kept remains above until kept. Where the sūrah says *to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth, and He is Fully Aware* (4:126), the Mount raised is that ownership displayed: the Owner may make earth's solid reach heaven's power.

**Enter the Gate With Humility, and Do Not Transgress the Sabbath**

The commands *wa qulnā la-humu udkhulū al-bāba sujjadan wa qulnā la-hum lā taʿdū fī as-sabt* — and We said to them, enter the gate — the gate of the town, Jerusalem — bowing, humbled; and We said, do not transgress in the Sabbath. *Enter the gate bowing* was read as the entry into the town after the wandering, where elsewhere *enter it with humility, seeking pardon — *ḥiṭṭah* — We will forgive you your sins and increase the doers of good* (2:58). To enter humbled was explained as the opposite of the demand for visible God (4:153): humility receives; demand demands. *Do not transgress in the Sabbath* — do not exceed the limit on the seventh day — was read against the sūrah's recounting elsewhere of the Sabbath-breakers made apes (7:166) and of the fish testing on the Sabbath (7:163): the Sabbath was made a test for them, as the sūrah says limits were set (4:13–14). Both commands were linked to *Gardens for those who believe and do good* (4:122): humility at the gate and restraint on the Sabbath are the submitted face following the upright Abraham (4:125) — restraint is keeping creation within God's measure, not altering it (4:119).

**And We Took From Them a Firm Covenant**

The closure *wa akhadhnā min-hum mīthāqan ghalīẓā* — and We took from them a firm, weighty covenant — was explained with *ghalīẓ* — firm, strong — the same word as the firm commitment of marriage (4:21), where the dowry may not be taken back unjustly; here the covenant with a community at Sinai. *We took* was read as divine taking witnessed — as God bears witness to what He sent down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness (4:166). The sūrah has shown the Book sent with truth to judge by what He shows (4:105); the firm covenant is that Book's predecessor, with the Mount as its witness. Early reports noted that the firmer the covenant, the more grievous the breach — and the thunderbolt had struck for the demand greater than a book (4:153) — yet the pardoning after the calf (4:153) shows the covenant also carried forgiveness for those who returned (4:110). The firm covenant was also linked to the charge to be mindful commanded to those before you and you (4:131): the covenant is the form that mindfulness took.

**A Verse That Follows the Calf Forgiven With the Mount Raised**

Placed after the People of the Book demanded a book from heaven, demanded the greater — visible God — were struck by the thunderbolt, took the calf after clear signs, yet were pardoned and Moses given compelling proof (4:153), this verse follows the pardon with the covenant's display: the Mount raised, the gate entered humbled, the Sabbath kept, the firm covenant taken. The sequence — demand, thunderbolt, calf, pardon, proof, Mount, gate, Sabbath — shows that pardon is not cancellation of law but renewal of law with visible witness. The sūrah has shown the Book sent with truth and God bearing witness with His knowledge (4:166); the Mount raised is that witness made physical, as the emigrant's many havens are the earth made spacious (4:100). For the weak this is steadying: where you feared the firm covenant is too heavy, the Mount shows it is heavier than mountain — yet the gate is entered bowed, not proudly; the Sabbath is kept by not doing, not only by doing; and the Pardoning after the calf shows that where it was broken, the return through repentance remained open.

**The Firm Covenant Above as Guardian**

The image — Mount above them for the covenant — was explained as the sūrah's ownership made canopy: as the fear prayer was guarded under arms (4:102) and trusteeship suffices (4:132), the covenant was guarded by a mountain. The firm covenant parallels the firm commitment taken from wives where trust and wealth are entrusted (4:21): both teach that God's earth is spacious (4:100), but the covenant is not spacious to break. The verse generalises the warning *do not consume wealth unjustly* (4:29) into *do not transgress the Sabbath* — both are limits; both have Keepers. The next verse names the breaking: for breaking their covenant, rejecting God's signs, killing the prophets unjustly, and saying *our hearts are unreceptive* — God sealed their hearts for their disbelief, so they believe only a few (4:155).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:155

> ˹They were condemned˺ for breaking their covenant, rejecting Allah's signs, killing the prophets unjustly, and for saying, "Our hearts are unreceptive!"—it is Allah Who has sealed their hearts for their disbelief, so they do not believe except for a few—

**For Breaking the Covenant, Rejecting the Signs, Killing the Prophets**

The verse opens *fa-bi-mā naqḍihim mīthāqahum wa kufrihim bi-āyāti Allāhi wa qatlihimu al-anbiyāʾa bi-ghayri ḥaqq* — for their breaking their covenant, and their disbelief in God's signs, and their killing the prophets without right. *For their breaking their covenant* corresponds to the firm covenant taken under the raised Mount, with the gate entered humbled and the Sabbath kept (4:154): where the Mount was raised for the covenant, they broke it. *Their disbelief in God's signs* was explained as rejecting the clear proofs after which the calf was taken (4:153) and the Mount raised (4:154): the staff, the divided sea, the manna, the tablets — the compelling proof Moses was given. *Their killing the prophets without right* was explained as the pattern recounted elsewhere: *whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you grew arrogant — some you denied and some you killed* (2:87) — culminating in the boast against Jesus, son of Mary (4:157). The sūrah has weighed killing throughout: devouring orphans' wealth is fire in bellies (4:10); killing a believer intentionally earns Hell with anger and curse (4:93); throwing sin on the innocent bears slander (4:112) — killing prophets without right is the furthest throw: to throw God's word back by killing its carrier. The phrase was read as the sūrah's ledger, where *whoever commits evil will be recompensed accordingly* (4:123).

**And for Their Saying — Our Hearts Are Unreceptive**

The addition *wa qawlihim qulūbunā ghulfun* — and for their saying, our hearts are wrapped, uncircumcised, unreceptive — was explained as their excuse for rejecting the signs: *ghulf* — wrapped, covered — claiming the heart cannot hear the Book sent with truth (4:105). The sūrah has shown that God bears witness to what He sent down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness (4:166), and that He suffices as Trustee (4:132); to say *our hearts are wrapped* is to claim the heart cannot receive witness — as if the Owner of the heavens and earth (4:126) cannot open them. The sūrah elsewhere says *they hardly comprehend anything* (4:78) — not because the heart is wrapped, but because they hardly reflect. *Ghulf* was read as the claim of incapacity; sealing was read as the consequence of the claim.

**It Is God Who Sealed Their Hearts for Their Disbelief**

The correction *bal ṭabaʿa Allāhu ʿalayhā bi-kufrihim* — rather, God has sealed them — the hearts — for their disbelief, because of their disbelief — was explained as divine sealing after human rejection. *Ṭabaʿa* — to seal, stamp — was read with the sūrah's causality: disbelief precedes sealing; sealing confirms disbelief — as He lets them pursue what they chose (4:115) after defying the Messenger, and *whoever God leaves to stray, you will never find a way for him* (4:88, 4:143). The phrase was linked to *God has condemned them for their disbelief* (4:46), where words were distorted out of context — sealing there also followed distortion. The sūrah has asked *why should He punish you if you are grateful and faithful? He is ever Appreciative* (4:147): sealing is not where gratitude and faith are — but where disbelief repeats after clarity.

**So They Believe Except for a Few**

The outcome *fa-lā yuʾminūna illā qalīlā* — so they do not believe except a few — was explained with *qalīl* — little, few — belief surviving only in a few after the sealing. The sūrah has shown that the calf-takers were forgiven (4:153) — some repented — and that *those of them well-grounded in knowledge believe in what was revealed to you and what was revealed before you* (4:162) — the few who stand firm. The few who believe are those who accepted all the messengers without distinction (4:150–152). The exception preserves hope — as the lowest depth for hypocrites carried its *except those who repent* (4:146): the sealing is not absolute where a few believe.

**A Verse That Binds the Broken Covenant to Sealed Hearts**

Placed after the Mount raised for the covenant, the gate with humility, the Sabbath, and the firm covenant (4:154), this verse binds the broken covenant to the sealed hearts — after rejecting signs, killing prophets unjustly, and claiming hearts are wrapped. The sūrah has shown that to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth and He is Fully Aware (4:126), that He suffices as Trustee (4:132), and that both rewards are with Him (4:134); to claim *our hearts are unreceptive* before such an Owner is to refuse the Trust — so the sealing is the Trusteeship withdrawn where trust was broken. The verse generalises the particular hypocrisy of waiting between (4:141) into covenantal history: the People of the Book who demanded a book from heaven (4:153) are the same who broke the covenant, rejected signs, killed prophets, and claimed closed hearts — the sealing follows the claimed closure. The next verses continue the condemnation: the denial and mighty slander against Mary, and the boast *we killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the messenger of God* — but they neither killed nor crucified him; it was made to appear so — they have no knowledge, only assumption — they certainly did not kill him (4:156–157).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:156

> and for their denial and outrageous accusation against Mary

**And for Their Denial and Their Mighty Slander Against Mary**

The verse continues *wa bi-kufrihim wa qawlihim ʿalā Maryama buhtānan ʿaẓīmā* — and for their disbelief, and their saying against Mary a tremendous, mighty slander. *Bi-kufrihim* — for their disbelief — continues the accumulated causes of condemnation: breaking covenant, rejecting signs, killing prophets unjustly, claiming hearts are wrapped and sealed for disbelief (4:155) — and now denial as such, joined with slander against Maryam. *Wa qawlihim ʿalā Maryama buhtānan ʿaẓīmā* — and their saying against Mary as a mighty slander — was explained with *buhtān* — slander, calumny, a false accusation that bewilders — the same *buhtān* and manifest sin borne by whoever throws sin on the innocent (4:112) — here thrown upon the innocent Maryam, mother of the Messiah. *ʿAẓīm* — mighty, tremendous — was explained as that the slander is not a private insult but defamation of the chosen devout woman and of the Word through her — *the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was only a messenger of God, His Word through Mary, and a spirit from Him* (4:171). Those who consume orphans' wealth consume fire (4:10), and throwing sin on the innocent bears slander (4:112); to slander Maryam with unchastity — accusing the pure who was given a spirit (66:12) — is the throw upon the purest, therefore *ʿaẓīm*. Early reports noted that those who rejected Jesus accused Maryam of fornication to deny his miraculous birth and messengership — the slander combining denial of a prophet with defamation of his mother.

**A Verse That Continues the Broken Covenant With Mary's Slander**

Placed after breaking the covenant, rejecting signs, killing prophets, and claiming hearts are wrapped and sealed (4:155), this verse continues the same condemnation with its next instance: denial and mighty slander against Mary. The sequence so far — the demand for a book from heaven, the greater demand for visible God, the thunderbolt, the calf after clear signs, yet forgiven (4:153), the Mount raised for the firm covenant (4:154), the breaking, rejecting, killing, the claim of wrapped hearts (4:155) — now adds slander against Mary: after rejecting the signs, they reject the sign of her purity and of the son born without father. The reminder that revelation was sent as to Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, Solomon, and David (4:163) — all accepted without distinction by believers (4:152) — shows that to slander Mary is to reject the chain that includes Jesus. The verse was linked to *Gardens for those who believe and do good* (4:122): Mary believed and did good; to accuse her is to refuse that good. For the weak this is protective: where orphan women deprived yet desired are protected from exploitation (4:127), Mary — the most alone — is protected by God Himself naming the slander against her *mighty*.

**The Slander That Mirrors Throwing Sin on the Innocent**

The word *buhtān* — mighty slander — was explained to mirror *he bears slander and manifest sin* — the one who throws sin on the innocent (4:112). There the innocent was falsely accused of theft; here the innocent is Maryam, accused to deny messengership. The sūrah has said there is no good in most secret talks except charity, kindness, and reconciliation (4:114): slander of Mary is the counsel that has no good. And *God does not like the open voicing of evil speech, except by the wronged* (4:148): the accusation against Mary was voiced not by the wronged but by the wrongdoers — therefore not permitted, not liked, and *mighty*. That teaching was linked to *He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing* (4:148): the accusers of Mary voiced their slander where they were not wronged but wronging.

**The Denial That Precedes the Slander**

The pairing *for their disbelief and their saying* was explained as showing that slander follows denial: denying Jesus as messenger required slandering his mother as pretext — as those who wish to make distinction between God and messengers say *we believe in some and disbelieve in some* (4:150); to disbelieve in Jesus, they defamed his mother. Association is far straying (4:116), and defiance after clarity is left to what was chosen (4:115); denial and slander here are that defiance applied to the Messiah. Early notes added that Maryam's chastity was attested by *We breathed into her of Our spirit* (66:12) and by the son speaking in the cradle; to deny the son was to need to deny the mother — the slander became necessary to the disbelief. The brevity — *and for their denial and outrageous accusation against Mary* — was read as the sūrah's compression before the next verse expands the denial into the boast *we killed the Messiah* (4:157): denial moves from slandering the mother to boasting the murder of the son — both false.

**A Short Phrase That Anchors Accusation as Cause of Condemnation**

Though brief — *and for their denial and outrageous accusation against Mary* — the phrase anchors accusation as a cause of condemnation beside breaking the covenant and killing the prophets. Its brevity compresses a history — demand, thunderbolt, calf, Mount, gate, Sabbath, breaking, rejecting, killing, wrapped hearts, denial, slander — into one litany of repeated breaking; yet the sūrah will still note *those of them well-grounded in knowledge believe* (4:162) — a few — so the mighty slander is not extended to all. The next verse completes the denial: the boast *we killed the Messiah, son of Mary, the messenger of God* — but they neither killed nor crucified him; it was made to appear so; they have no knowledge, only assumption; they certainly did not kill him (4:157).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:157

> and for boasting, "We killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the messenger of Allah." But they neither killed nor crucified him—it was only made to appear so. Even those who argue for this ˹crucifixion˺ are in doubt. They have no knowledge whatsoever—only making assumptions. They certainly did not kill him

**Their Boast — We Killed the Messiah, Son of Mary, Messenger of God**

The verse continues *wa qawlihim innā qatalnā al-masīḥa ʿĪsā ibna Maryama rasūla Allāh* — and for their saying, their boast, *we killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the messenger of God*. *Their saying* continues the accusation against Mary (4:156) — now the boast. *Al-masīḥ* — the Messiah, the anointed — Jesus, son of Mary, whose mother they had slandered mightily (4:156) and whose death they now claim. *The messenger of God* was explained as their own designation used in irony: they name him *messenger of God* while boasting of killing him — as they said *our hearts are wrapped* (4:155) while their hearts were sealed for disbelief. The sūrah has counted killing prophets without right among the causes of condemnation (4:155); to boast of killing the Messiah is its apex — the claim of murder against a messenger they never accepted, and against the Word through Mary and a spirit from Him (4:171). Early reports noted that those who instigated the attempt did not themselves kill Jesus; the Qur'anic *we killed* records their claim and pride — as plotting is attributed to them though He was with them (4:108).

**But They Killed Him Not, Nor Crucified Him — It Was Made to Appear So**

The correction *wa mā qatalūhu wa mā ṣalabūhu wa lākin shubbiha lahum* — but they killed him not, nor crucified him, but it was made to appear so to them — was explained as divine negation. The double negation — *killed not, crucified not* — was read as absolute: the act they claim did not befall him. *Wa lākin shubbiha lahum* — but it was made to appear so to them, made to resemble — was explained as a likeness cast so that the boasters believed they had killed him, while God raised him. Classical reports differed on the detail: some said a man was made to resemble Jesus and was seized in his place; others said the event itself was made ambiguous so that those present differed — all agree that *it was made to appear so* means resemblance, not the deed. The verse was linked to *God does not wrong even an atom* (4:40): to boast of killing the messenger is the gravest claimed wrong; the correction says the wrong did not reach him.

**Those Who Differ About Him Are in Doubt — No Knowledge, Only Assumption**

The addition *wa inna alladhīna ikhtalafū fīhi la-fī shakkin minhu mā lahum bihī min ʿilmin illā ittibāʿa aẓ-ẓann* — and surely those who differ concerning him are in doubt about him: they have no knowledge of it, only following assumption — was explained with *ikhtalafū* — differed, disputed. *In doubt about him* was read as that those who maintain the killing are not agreed even among themselves — some say killed, some crucified, some something else — all in conjecture, as the sūrah elsewhere says those given a portion distort words (4:46). *They have no knowledge of it, only following assumption* was explained as that the claim lacks *ʿilm* — knowledge — and stands on *ẓann* — conjecture — the sūrah having contrasted conjecture with the promise that is ever true (4:122) and the delusion that is only delusion (4:120). Where God bears witness to what He sent down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness (4:166), the crucifixion boast is *following assumption* — not witness.

**They Certainly Did Not Kill Him**

The seal *wa mā qatalūhu yaqīnā* — and they certainly did not kill him — was explained with *yaqīn* — certainty — as double: they did not kill him with certainty, and it is certain they did not kill him. The adverb re-negates the boast *we killed* — not only did they not kill; they possess no certainty of having done so. The sūrah has shown that He wills to make clear (4:26), taught you what you did not know (4:113), and allows no good counsel except charity, kindness, and reconciliation (4:114) — a boast of murder is neither clear nor kind; the decisive word is that they did not kill him in truth — as the next verse says: *rather, God raised him to Himself; He is Almighty, All-Wise* (4:158). For the weak this is an anchor: where loud evil speech is permitted only to the wronged (4:148) and pardoning is higher (4:149), a loud boast of killing a messenger is the loudest evil — voiced where no wrong had been done to the boaster.

**A Verse That Completes Denial With Correction and Doubt**

Placed after the broken covenant, rejected signs, killed prophets, the claim of wrapped hearts sealed (4:155), and the denial and mighty slander against Mary (4:156), this verse completes the denial with the boast corrected and the doubt exposed. The litany — the demand greater than a book, the thunderbolt, the calf after clear signs yet forgiven, the Mount raised, the gate with humility, the Sabbath kept, the firm covenant, then breaking, rejecting, killing, wrapped hearts, denial, slander, boast — is the history of a people given Scripture before you, commanded to be mindful (4:131), whose mindfulness was broken. The correction — not killed, not crucified, made to appear, disputants in doubt, no knowledge but assumption, certainly not killed — was read as the Book's truth against assumption: the Book was sent with truth (4:105) and its promise is ever true (4:122). The next verse sets the truth: rather, God raised him to Himself (4:158), and those given the Book will believe in him before his death, and on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them (4:159).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:158

> Rather, Allah raised him up to Himself. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise

**Rather, God Raised Him to Himself**

The verse states *bal rafaʿahu Allāhu ilayhi* — rather, God raised him up to Himself. *Bal* — rather, nay — was explained as the correction to *they killed him not, nor crucified him, but it was made to appear so* (4:157): the boast of killing is false; the truth is the raising. *God raised him to Himself* was explained as God lifting Jesus alive, as He raised the Mount over the covenant-breakers (4:154) — the sūrah's two raisings: one raised over breakers as warning, the other raised of a messenger as honour. *To Himself* — to His presence, to the heavens — as elsewhere *O Jesus, I will take you and raise you to Myself* (3:55). Early reports noted that the raising explains *it was made to appear so*: while his likeness was cast on another, he himself was raised. The sūrah has shown that God suffices as Trustee (4:132) and bears witness with His knowledge (4:166); raising the messenger is that Trusteeship executed: He can remove humanity and bring others (4:133) — here He removes the messenger from the killers and brings him to Himself, preserving the line of revelation. The phrase was linked to *Gardens for those who believe and do good* (4:122): the raising is the prototype of honour — nearness to Him.

**And God Is Almighty, All-Wise**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu ʿAzīzan Ḥakīmā* — and God is ever Almighty, All-Wise — was explained with *ʿAzīz* — Almighty, Mighty, invincible — the One able to raise against the killers, as He is Most Capable to remove humanity (4:133) and Most Capable to pardon though able to punish (4:149): here the might is the capability to protect the messenger whose killing was claimed. *Ḥakīm* — All-Wise — was read as the wisdom that made the likeness appear to the boasters while raising him, that left the disputants in their doubt following assumption (4:157), and that will make his future testimony decisive (4:159). *Almighty, All-Wise* also sealed the messengers who delivered good news and warnings so that humanity has no argument against God after the messengers (4:165): raising Jesus preserves the messenger line until the final messenger — revelation sent as to Noah and the prophets after him (4:163) — all by the Almighty, All-Wise. Where the sūrah says *all honour belongs to God entirely* (4:139), the raising of Jesus to Him is the honour given to the messenger whose honour the boasters thought to end.

**A Verse That Follows Not-Killed With Raised**

Placed after the whole history — thunderbolt, calf, pardon, Mount, gate, Sabbath, firm covenant, then breaking, rejecting, killing prophets, wrapped hearts, denial, slander of Mary, the boast of killing one neither killed nor crucified, disputants in doubt, no knowledge but assumption, certainly not killed (4:153–157) — this verse follows *not killed* with *raised*. The sūrah has shown *to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth* (4:126, 4:131): raising to Him is raising within His ownership — His heavens are the encompassing (4:126) that can receive. The sūrah has shown *God does not wrong even an atom* (4:40): to raise the messenger they wrongly boasted of killing is not wronging an atom but preserving him. The sūrah that allows no good counsel except charity, kindness, and reconciliation (4:114) sees the boast of murder as the worst counsel made loud; the raising is its public rebuttal as honour.

**The Raising as the Sūrah's Reply to the Demand for the Visible**

The raising was linked back to the initial demand — *bring down a book from heaven* (4:153) — and its predecessor — *show us God plainly*: those who demanded the visible God and then took the visible calf are shown that the messenger they boasted killing was taken beyond their sight by raising — spectacle's opposite. Where Moses' people saw the Mount raised over them as warning for the covenant, the Messiah's boastful enemies are shown that God raises whom He wills. The verse was read with *We have sent revelation to you as We sent it to Noah…* (4:163) — revelation continues, messengers are many; raising one does not end the mission — and *there are messengers We have told you of, and others We have not; and to Moses God spoke directly* (4:164): His speech reaches directly and His raising reaches powerfully. For the weak this is an anchor: where the Messiah was wronged by boasters — though being God's Word through Mary and a spirit from Him (4:171), not too proud to be a servant (4:172) — his raising shows the servant honoured though the boasters claimed his killing.

**A Short Verse That Anchors the Witness to Come**

Though brief — *rather, God raised him to Himself; He is Almighty, All-Wise* — the verse anchors the witness to come: the raised Messiah will be believed in by those given the Book before his death, and on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them (4:159). The sūrah that says God bears witness to what He sent down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness (4:166), makes that future testimony part of its proof. The next passages turn from the Book's people to the Book's law: forbidden foods, the Book completing its favour, and the great reward kept for those well-grounded in knowledge who believe in what was revealed to you and before you (4:160–162).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:159

> Every one of the People of the Book will definitely believe in him before his death. And on the Day of Judgment Jesus will be a witness against them

**Every One of the People of the Book Will Believe in Him Before His Death**

The verse states *wa in min ahli al-kitābi illā la-yuʾminanna bihi qabla mawtihi* — and there is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him before his death. *There is none… except* was explained as a universal: every one of the People of the Book will believe in Jesus — *ʿĪsā ibn Maryam* — the Messiah they boasted killing but did not, whom God raised to Himself (4:157–158), the Word through Mary and a spirit from Him (4:171). *La-yuʾminanna bihi* — will surely believe in him — was read with emphatic force: the same emphasis as Satan's vow (4:119), now God's own certainty. *Before his death* was read two ways: before each Person of the Book's own death — when death nears, truth becomes clear, though too late, as *repentance is not accepted when death comes and one cries now I repent* (4:18) — and before the death of Jesus himself, upon his return before the Hour, when he will descend, break the cross, and the People of the Book will believe while still alive — as the reports relate (al-Bukhārī 3448; Muslim 155). Both readings were kept: at death's threshold each will see, and before Jesus' second coming the community will believe. The sūrah has shown that those who distinguished between God and messengers — *we believe in some and disbelieve in some, desiring a way between* (4:150) — were true disbelievers (4:151); belief in Jesus before death undoes that distinguishing: they finally accept him as messenger, not god.

**And on the Day of Resurrection He Will Be a Witness Against Them**

The second clause *wa yawma al-qiyāmati yakūnu ʿalayhim shahīdā* — and on the Day of Standing he will be a witness against them — was explained with *shahīd* — witness — the same witness as *We will bring a witness from every community, and We will bring you as a witness against these* (4:41), and *God bears witness, and the angels bear witness* (4:166): here Jesus is the witness for his own community — against those who made distinction. *Against them* was read as that he will testify: they boasted *we killed the Messiah* (4:157); they slandered Mary with mighty slander (4:156); they said *our hearts are wrapped* (4:155) — he will witness that they knew and denied, as souls are asked at taking *what were you doing?* (4:97). The Day was explained as the Day about which there is no doubt, when He will gather you (4:87) and gather the hypocrites and disbelievers in Hell (4:140) — the witness decides the gathering. Classical notes added that his being a witness against them fits his raising: he who was raised above the boast of murder will testify that the murder did not occur — and *it was made to appear so* (4:157) will be clarified by the one raised.

**A Verse That Follows the Raising With Belief Before Death and Witness on the Day**

Placed after *rather, God raised him to Himself; He is Almighty, All-Wise* (4:158), this verse follows the raising with belief before death and witness on the Day. The sequence — demand, thunderbolt, calf, pardon, Mount raised, firm covenant, breaking, rejecting, killing, sealed hearts, denial, slander of Mary, the boast of a killing never done, the raising — now ends with belief and witness: the People of the Book's history does not end with the calf or the boast, but with belief in him and his testimony. The sūrah has shown *revelation sent as to Noah and the prophets after him* (4:163), all accepted without distinction by believers (4:152); the People of the Book's belief in Jesus is the correction of distinction, where Jesus is among those prophets. For the weak this is an opening: where evil speech about Mary was not permitted (4:148), belief in the son of Mary is the speech that repairs — and the raised witness, who was not too proud to be a servant (4:172), will witness that repair.

**Before His Death — Two Times for Witness**

The phrase *before his death* was explained to keep two times: before the death of each of the People of the Book — at the threshold where souls are taken and *what were you doing?* is asked (4:97) — truth becomes clear, but seeing after veils are removed is too late for those who increased in disbelief (4:137); and before the death of Jesus upon his return — the communal time when those given the Book believe while alive, before the Hour — for knowledge of that hour rests with Him (4:164). The verse was therefore read not as a promise that all die believers — since humiliating punishment was prepared for true disbelievers (4:151) — but as the certainty of seeing, either at death or at his return. The witness on the Day completes the sūrah's chain of witnesses: the witness from every community and the Prophet ﷺ against his (4:41) — here Jesus for his.

**A Short Verse That Anchors Future Belief to the Past Boast**

Though brief — *there is none of the People of the Book but will believe in him before his death; and on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them* — the verse anchors the future belief to the past boast of *we killed* (4:157): the boast said they killed the messenger; the witness will say they did not, and only followed assumption. The sūrah that says God bears witness to what He sent down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness (4:166), makes the raised messenger's belief and testimony part of that knowledge — so that the demand *bring down a book from heaven* (4:153) is answered not with a book dropped from the sky, but with a witness raised to heaven and returned. The next verses turn from history to law: good foods forbidden to Jews for wrongdoing and hindering, interest taken despite prohibition, wealth consumed unjustly — painful punishment for the disbelievers among them; but for those well-grounded in knowledge who believe in what was revealed to you and before — a great reward (4:160–162).
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:160

> We forbade the Jews certain foods that had been lawful to them for their wrongdoing, and for hindering many from the Way of Allah

**We Forbade the Jews Good Things for Their Wrongdoing**

The verse states *fa-bi-ẓulmin mina alladhīna hādū ḥarramnā ʿalayhim ṭayyibātin uḥillat lahum* — so for the wrongdoing of those who are Jews, We forbade them good, pure things that had been lawful to them. *For the wrongdoing of those who are Jews* was explained as the same *ẓulm* of the litany: the wrongdoing for which the thunderbolt struck (4:153), the Mount was raised (4:154), the covenant broken, signs rejected, prophets killed without right, hearts claimed wrapped and sealed (4:155), Mary slandered mightily (4:156), the killing of the Messiah boasted though it never occurred (4:157). *We forbade them pure things that had been permitted* was explained as foods once *ḥalāl* made *ḥarām* as discipline: certain fats and meats whose prohibition remains in the earlier law — the sūrah elsewhere says *all food was lawful to the Children of Israel except what Israel forbade himself before the Torah was sent down* (3:93) — this forbidding is additional, for wrongdoing. *Ṭayyibāt* — good, pure, wholesome — was read to show that what was forbidden is not evil in itself: the foods are pure; their prohibition is recompense, as *whoever commits evil will be recompensed with it* (4:123). The sūrah has shown that the calf was forgiven and Moses given clear proof (4:153); forgiveness did not cancel consequence for the wrongdoing that continued.

**And for Hindering Many From the Way of God**

The addition *wa bi-ṣaddihim ʿan sabīli Allāhi kathīrā* — and for their hindering many from the way of God — was explained with *ṣadd* — to block, bar, turn away — the same turning away as the hypocrites who turn away stubbornly when called to God and His Messenger (4:61). *God's way* was read as the noble ways He wills to make clear (4:26), the believers' path not to be left (4:115), the upright way of Abraham (4:125), the straight path to which He guides by His grace (4:175). *Many* was explained as the magnitude of the hindering: they hindered by rejecting signs, killing prophets, claiming closed hearts, demanding visible God, taking the calf — and by the legal prohibitions that remained. Early reports linked the hindering to rabbis who concealed the Prophet's ﷺ description in the Torah from their followers, and to the usury that consumes wealth unjustly (4:161) — hindering by economic oppression as well as doctrinal concealment. Since revelation came as to Noah and the prophets after him (4:163), all to be accepted without distinction (4:152) — hindering is the opposite: blocking that acceptance. The sūrah next says *those who disbelieve and hinder from God's way have certainly gone far astray* (4:167): far straying is hindering's fruit.

**A Verse That Follows the Corrected Boast With Law for Hindering**

Placed after the history — demand, thunderbolt, calf, pardon, Mount, covenant, breaking, rejecting, killing, sealed hearts, slander of Mary, boast corrected, raising, belief before death, witness on the Day (4:153–159) — this verse follows the corrected boast with law: for wrongdoing and hindering many from God's way, We forbade them pure things once lawful. The sūrah has shown that association is far straying (4:116) and defiance after clarity is left to what was chosen (4:115); hindering many is that straying made social — not only straying oneself, but blocking others — as Satan orders cutting and altering (4:119), hindering blocks God's creation. The forbidding of pure things was read as the sūrah's measure: as the emigrant finds many havens and abundance (4:100), the hinderer finds abundance removed — narrowed where he narrowed others' way. Where *He wills to lighten your burdens, for humanity was created weak* (4:28), lightening is giving pure things; hindering many removes the lightening.

**Good Things Forbidden as Measure, Not Origin**

The phrase *good things that had been lawful to them* was explained to show that the foods are pure, not foul — the forbidding is measure, not their nature. The sūrah elsewhere says what is beyond the marriage limits is lawful so long as sought with wealth in lawful marriage (4:24); so too *ṭayyibāt* are lawful in principle yet forbidden as recompense for wrongdoing. Classical notes added that this forbidding is distinct from Israel's self-forbidding before the Torah (3:93), and that the final Book makes the pure things lawful again except what remains as discipline — showing that the Qur'an restores what the earlier law had narrowed, as the Prophet ﷺ was sent *to release them from their heavy burdens and the shackles upon them* (7:157). The sūrah has said God wishes to lighten burdens (4:28) — the final lightening is not for those who persist in wrongdoing and much hindering, but for those who believe in what was revealed to you and before you (4:162).

**A Short Verse That Anchors Discipline in Hindering**

Though brief — *for wrongdoing of those who are Jews, and for hindering many from God's way, We forbade them good things once lawful* — the verse anchors discipline in hindering. The next verses add two more wrongs — taking interest despite prohibition, and consuming people's wealth unjustly — with painful punishment for the disbelievers among them, and a great reward for the well-grounded who believe in what was revealed to you and before you, establishing prayer and paying alms (4:161–162). The pattern shows that economic hindering — interest, unjust consumption — is the material counterpart of doctrinal hindering — concealing description, demanding visible God. For the weak this is an opening: where the hinderer's pure things were removed, the well-grounded are promised a great reward — the pure things restored in Gardens where the promise is true, as the emigrant's havens were restored after hindering.
## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:161

> taking interest despite its prohibition, and consuming people's wealth unjustly. We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment

**Taking Interest Despite Prohibition, and Consuming Wealth Unjustly**

The verse continues *wa akhdhihimu ar-ribā wa qad nuhū ʿanhu wa aklihim amwāla an-nāsi bi-al-bāṭil* — and their taking interest — *ribā* — though they were forbidden it, and their consuming people's wealth unjustly, by false means. *Their taking ribā* was explained as taking interest despite the Torah's prohibition — as the earlier warnings against devouring wealth by false means (2:188), against consuming orphans' wealth as fire (4:10), and against consuming wealth unjustly among yourselves (4:29) all make clear. *Though they were forbidden* was read as that ribā is not ignorance but disobedience after the compelling proof Moses was given (4:153) and the Mount raised for the firm covenant (4:154): where interest is forbidden yet taken, the covenant is broken again. *Consuming people's wealth unjustly* was explained as taking wealth by false claim, bribery, selling religion, concealing the Prophet's ﷺ description for gain — the trade where those given a portion trade it for misguidance (4:44) — and the economic half of hindering many from God's way (4:160). The two — ribā and consuming unjustly — were read as the pairing after the forbidding of pure foods: as some traded guidance, here they trade wealth — increase taken from hardship on the debtor.

**We Have Prepared for the Disbelievers Among Them a Painful Punishment**

The seal *wa aʿtadnā li-al-kāfirīna minhum ʿadhāban alīmā* — and We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment — was explained with *aʿtadnā* — prepared — the same preparation as the humiliating punishment for the true disbelievers who distinguish (4:151), the Fire for those who consume orphans' wealth (4:10), and Hell, anger, and curse for the intentional killer (4:93). *The disbelievers among them* was explained as not all of them: as the great reward comes next for *those of them well-grounded in knowledge* who believe (4:162), so punishment is for the disbelievers among them — not for every Jew — as the calf-takers were forgiven (4:153), showing some among them returned. *A painful punishment* — *alīm* — was read as pain matching the pains the sūrah has listed: fire in bellies (4:10), humiliating punishment (4:102, 4:151), the lowest depth without helper (4:145). The sūrah has said *whoever commits evil will be recompensed with it and find no protector besides God* (4:123): ribā and unjust consumption are evils recompensed with themselves — pain for the pain extracted. Where *God does not wrong even an atom* (4:40), every atom taken unjustly is measured in the punishment.

**A Verse That Follows Forbidden Foods With Forbidden Wealth**

Placed after *We forbade the Jews good things that had been lawful for their wrongdoing and for hindering many from God's way* (4:160), this verse follows forbidden foods with forbidden wealth — ribā and unjust consumption — for which painful punishment is prepared. That *to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth* (4:126) shows that wealth taken by ribā is taken from His ownership unjustly, as the female gods invoked besides Him (4:117) are taken from His worship unjustly. The law lightens because humanity is weak (4:28), yet lightening does not license consuming wealth unjustly (4:29) — ribā is the lightening inverted: increase manufactured from another's hardship. Earlier the sūrah praised charity, kindness, and reconciliation seeking His pleasure (4:114) as the good counsel; interest is the devouring economy behind the counsel that has no good. For the weak this is protective: where interest is taken from the debtor and wealth consumed unjustly, the sūrah that promised many havens to the emigrant (4:100) and enrichment to both who part (4:130) declares the taking painful for the disbelievers among them — while help stands with the well-grounded who give alms (4:162).

**Taking Despite Prohibition as Breaking After Knowledge**
